list.summary: Ambrosia, food of the gods, and nectar, their drink. The very name means “not dying.”
list.imageAlt: A Cypriot footed cup (kylix) of about 750–600 BCE, with scrolls and geometric designs in red and black on a pale ground.

list.title: Necklace of Harmonia
list.owner: Harmonia and the royal house of Thebes
list.power: Keeps its wearer young and beautiful forever but brings misfortune for generations.
list.summary: A wedding gift forged with a curse by Hephaestus, enraged at his wife's infidelity.
list.imageAlt: A Greek gold necklace of the fourth century BCE, with small spearhead-shaped gold ornaments packed closely along its length.

list.title: Arrows of Eros
list.power: A gold arrow makes one fall in love, a lead arrow makes one flee from it.
list.summary: The golden arrow that kindles love and the lead arrow that drives it away.
list.imageAlt: A Roman bronze statuette of the first to second century CE. A winged boy, Eros, strides forward holding what appears to be a long bow in his left hand with his right arm raised high.

list.title: Pegasus
list.power: Flies on its wings, and raises springs by striking the ground with its hooves.
list.summary: The winged horse that sprang up when Perseus beheaded Medusa.
list.imageAlt: A bronze statuette of Pegasus from the late sixteenth century. A horse with spread wings rears on its hind legs on a marble base.

list.title: The Argo
list.maker: The shipwright Argus, helped by Athena
list.power: Its prow, made of the sacred oak of Dodona, speaks like a person and tells the future.
list.summary: The ship that carried fifty heroes in search of the Golden Fleece, called “the Argo known to all.”
list.imageAlt: A wooden boat model from Middle Kingdom Egypt, about 1981–1975 BCE. Figures of rowers are packed on a green boat, their oars lowered into the water.

list.title: Girdle of Aphrodite
list.power: Embroidered with love, longing and beguiling words, it makes anyone fall in love.
list.summary: The embroidered band of Aphrodite that Hera borrowed to lull Zeus to sleep.
list.imageAlt: A Roman marble statue of Aphrodite of the first to second century CE. The nude goddess, with hair tied up, stands with both arms broken away.

list.title: Ring of Gyges
list.power: Turning the bezel inward makes its wearer invisible.
list.summary: A ring of invisibility. Plato used it to ask whether one would be just if no one were watching.
list.imageAlt: An Etruscan gold ring of the late fourth or early third century BCE. Letters are punched in dots across the front of the wide gold band.

list.title: Ascalon
list.maker: A one-eyed smith (in Richard Johnson's tale)
list.power: The dragon-slaying sword that cuts through any armor.
list.firstRecord: Richard Johnson, The Seven Champions of Christendom
list.summary: The sword of Saint George, who overcame the dragon. It is named after the Holy Land city of Ascalon.
list.imageAlt: A French walnut carving of Saint George and the Dragon from the early sixteenth century. A mounted knight drives down a lance while a dragon writhes beneath the horse's hooves.

list.title: Noah's Ark
list.maker: Built by Noah at God's command
list.power: Kept people and animals safe from the flood that covered the world.
list.summary: The great vessel that saved Noah's family and the animals from the flood.
list.imageAlt: A sixteenth-century engraving, Noah Leaving the Ark. In front of the huge ark, Noah's family and many animals step down to the ground.

list.title: Sword of Saint Peter
list.power: Swung to defend his master, and rebuked with “Put your sword into its sheath.”
list.summary: The sword with which Peter cut off the ear of the high priest's servant Malchus on the night Jesus was arrested.
list.imageAlt: A falchion from Venice, about 1490. A hooked hand guard and round pommel sit above a broad single-edged blade.

list.title: Dhu al-Fiqar
list.power: A blade forked at the tip. “No youth like Ali, no sword like Dhu al-Fiqar.”
list.firstRecord: Ibn Ishaq, Life of the Prophet
list.summary: The sword of Ali, fourth caliph of Islam, depicted with a forked tip.
list.imageAlt: A Turkish kilij. A nineteenth-century gold guard and curved grip of nephrite are mounted on a blade inlaid with gold designs and letters.

list.title: Flying Carpet
list.power: Sit on it, think of a place, and it takes you there in an instant.
list.firstRecord: Galland, French Thousand and One Nights
list.summary: The magic carpet in the Thousand and One Nights tale of Prince Ahmed and the Fairy Peri Banu.
list.imageAlt: The Seley Carpet from late sixteenth-century Iran, a long carpet with a round medallion at the center of a red ground, surrounded by flowers and vines.

list.title: Ring of the Jinn
list.power: Rub it and the jinni of the ring appears to grant your wishes.
list.firstRecord: Galland, French Thousand and One Nights
list.summary: The genie of the ring, who rescued Aladdin before the magic lamp did.
list.imageAlt: A gold ring from Iraq of the twelfth to thirteenth century. The hexagonal bezel is pierced with vines and script-like patterns, and animal-shaped ornaments sit on its shoulders.

list.title: Book of the Dead
list.titleOriginal: Book of the Dead (rw nw prt m hrw)
list.power: Reciting its spells carries one past the dangers of the underworld to the paradise of Osiris.
list.firstRecord: Funerary texts of the New Kingdom
list.summary: A guide to the afterlife buried with the dead. Its true title is “Spells for Going Forth by Day.”
list.imageAlt: An Egyptian Book of the Dead papyrus of 664–30 BCE. Columns of hieroglyphs run across the yellowed sheet, with drawings of boats carrying gods.

list.title: Emerald Tablet
list.power: Holds the secret of all things and the foundation of alchemy in fourteen lines: “As above, so below.”
list.firstRecord: Arabic Book of the Secret of Creation
list.summary: The scripture of alchemy, said to be inscribed by “thrice-great Hermes” on a tablet of emerald.
list.imageAlt: An Egyptian steatite magical stela (cippus of Horus) of about 300 BCE from the Ptolemaic period. The young Horus standing on crocodiles is carved in relief in the upper part of the dark slab, and spells are densely inscribed below.

list.title: Solar Barque of Ra
list.power: Crossing the sky by day and the underworld by night, it makes the sun rise again.
list.summary: The two ships in which the sun god Ra travels by day and by night.
list.imageAlt: A wooden boat model from Middle Kingdom Egypt. On a green boat with a raised sail stand figures of a rower, a seated person and a steersman.

list.title: Rakhsh
list.power: Fights lions to protect its master, strong as an elephant and swift as the wind.
list.summary: The horse of Rustam, greatest hero of Persia, spotted red as if strewn with rose petals.
list.imageAlt: A page from a Shahnameh manuscript painted in India around 1450, Rustam Lassos Rakhsh. Between Persian text above and below, a herd of horses runs on a meadow among people holding lassos.

list.title: Bucephalus
list.power: A wild horse no one could tame, afraid of its own shadow.
list.summary: The horse tamed by the boy Alexander, who rode it from Persia to India.
list.imageAlt: A silver tetradrachm of Alexander the Great from the Seleucid dynasty, about 325–319 BCE, bearing a profile wearing a lion skin in the guise of Heracles.

list.title: Sword of Light
list.owner: Nuada, king of the Tuatha Dé Danann
list.power: Once out of its sheath, no one can escape it.
list.summary: One of the four treasures of the Irish gods, a sword no one could evade once it was drawn.
list.imageAlt: A Celtic sword and scabbard of about 60 BCE. The copper-alloy scabbard is covered in blue-green patina, and the end of the hilt splits into two curls.

list.title: Spear of Lugh
list.owner: Lugh, god of light and skill
list.power: No battle can be won against the one who holds it.
list.summary: One of the four treasures of the Tuatha Dé Danann, the spear of victory from Gorias.
list.imageAlt: An Etruscan bronze spearhead. Two barb-like wings extend behind a long triangular blade with a central ridge.

list.title: Gáe Bulg
list.maker: Taught by the warrior woman Scáthach
list.power: Thrown with the foot, its barbs open inside the body so that it cannot be pulled out.
list.summary: The spear of Ireland's greatest hero, Cú Chulainn, given to him alone by his teacher Scáthach.
list.imageAlt: An Indonesian spear of the eighteenth to nineteenth century. Three pairs of crescent-shaped barbs rise in tiers along both sides of a broad steel blade.

list.title: Fragarach
list.owner: The sea god Manannán, later Lugh
list.power: Held to the throat, it prevents its victim from moving or lying. Wounds from it never heal.
list.firstRecord: The Fate of the Children of Tuireann
list.summary: The sword called “the Answerer,” given to Lugh by the sea god Manannán.
list.imageAlt: A Cypriot iron sword of the sixth century BCE. A hilt end survives above a straight blade thick with rust, with one silver rivet gleaming.

list.title: Caladbolg
list.owner: The Ulster hero Fergus mac Róich
list.power: When swung it lengthens like a rainbow and shears off the tops of hills.
list.summary: The sword of Fergus. Its name shares a root with the Welsh Caledfwlch, that is, Excalibur.
list.imageAlt: An iron sword from Roman Gaul of the second century BCE to first century CE. The blade, with its bronze hilt, is heavily rusted and uneven.

list.title: Cauldron of the Dagda
list.owner: The Dagda, god of the Tuatha Dé Danann
list.power: It never runs dry, however many eat. None left it unsatisfied.
list.summary: One of the four treasures of the Tuatha Dé Danann, the cauldron of plenty from Murias.
list.imageAlt: An Etruscan bronze cauldron of about 550 BCE. The round body has a lid and hanging rings, with blotches of blue-green patina on its surface.

list.title: Vajra
list.power: Unbreakable as diamond and striking like lightning. It slew Vritra, the serpent of drought.
list.summary: The thunderbolt of Indra, which became in Buddhism the ritual implement that shatters delusion.
list.imageAlt: A twelfth-century Vietnamese bronze vajra. Hook-like prongs gather at both ends of a central grip.

list.title: Trishula
list.owner: Shiva, god of destruction and renewal
list.power: Its three prongs govern creation, preservation and destruction, or past, present and future.
list.summary: Shiva's trident. Its three blades stand for three worlds and three powers.
list.imageAlt: A hand-colored lithograph from Calcutta, India, 1878–1883, Shiva Mahadev. Shiva, wearing a tiger skin, walks a mountain path with a trident on his shoulder.

list.title: Sudarshana Chakra
list.power: A disc with 108 teeth. Thrown, it cuts down enemies and returns to the hand.
list.summary: Vishnu's spinning disc, with which Krishna beheaded Shishupala.
list.imageAlt: A gilt-copper Vishnu from the Kathmandu Valley in Nepal, dated 1105. The four-armed Vishnu stands on a pedestal holding a wheel-shaped disc and a mace in his upper hands.

list.title: Gandiva
list.power: Paired with a quiver that never empties, its bowstring sounds like thunder.
list.summary: The bow of Arjuna, master archer of the Mahabharata, delivered to him by the fire god Agni.
list.imageAlt: A page from the Razmnama, the Persian translation of the Mahabharata, painted in Mughal India about 1616–17, Arjuna Battles Raja Tamradhvaja. Warriors on chariots, horses and elephants fight between blocks of text.

list.title: Amrita
list.maker: Obtained by churning the ocean of milk
list.power: Whoever drinks it does not die.
list.summary: The drink of immortality, won when gods and demons together churned the ocean of milk.
list.imageAlt: A painting from Mandi in the Punjab Hills of India, about 1780–90, The Churning of the Ocean of Milk. A serpent winds around a pillar set on a tortoise, with gods and demons pulling on either side; a many-armed Vishnu sits on a lotus above, among a white horse, an elephant, the sun and the moon.

list.title: Kavacha and Kundala
list.power: Golden armor and earrings one with his body. While he wears them, Karna cannot die.
list.summary: The armor and earrings Karna, son of the sun god, was born with, and gave away.
list.imageAlt: A gold earring from the Kathmandu Valley in Nepal, seventeenth or eighteenth century. Red and blue gems set in a gold wire framework show Vishnu riding the bird Garuda, with pearls and gold disks hanging below.

list.title: Cintamani
list.owner: Bodhisattvas such as Kshitigarbha and Cintamanicakra
list.power: A jewel that grants whatever one wishes.
list.summary: The wish-fulfilling jewel, revered in both Buddhism and Hinduism.
list.imageAlt: A tile from Ottoman Turkey of about 1560–70. On a deep blue ground it bears the cintamani pattern: three white orbs with red dots and rippling white stripes.

list.title: Gan Jiang and Mo Ye
list.maker: The sword-making couple Gan Jiang and Mo Ye
list.power: A male and female pair of swords that cut iron like mud.
list.firstRecord: Spring and Autumn Annals of Wu and Yue
list.summary: A pair of swords named for the couple who forged them, the beginning of China's famous-sword legends.
list.imageAlt: A Chinese bronze sword of the fifth to fourth century BCE, with a ridge along the center of its straight double-edged blade and rings around the grip.

list.title: Ruyi Jingu Bang
list.maker: An iron pillar once used by King Yu to measure the sea
list.power: Weighs 13,500 catties. Grows and shrinks at will, down to a needle for tucking in the ear.
list.firstRecord: Wu Cheng'en, Journey to the West
list.summary: The staff Sun Wukong took from the palace of the Dragon King of the East Sea, capped with gold at each end.
list.imageAlt: A Japanese woodblock print of about 1824 by Yashima Gakutei, Sun Wukong. The monkey king in red robes stands on ground spread with clouds, a long staff on his back, blowing out a swarm of tiny monkeys.

list.title: Green Dragon Crescent Blade
list.power: A great blade weighing 82 catties, also called “Cold Beauty.”
list.firstRecord: Luo Guanzhong, Romance of the Three Kingdoms
list.summary: The great crescent-shaped blade wielded by Guan Yu in the Romance of the Three Kingdoms.
list.imageAlt: A nineteenth-century Jingdezhen porcelain figure of Guan Yu. Dressed in green armor and robes, Guan Yu sits stroking his long beard with one hand.

list.title: Sky Piercer
list.power: A halberd with a crescent blade beside the spear point. Lü Bu hit its small branch with an arrow at 150 paces.
list.firstRecord: Luo Guanzhong, Romance of the Three Kingdoms
list.summary: The halberd of Lü Bu, greatest warrior of the Romance of the Three Kingdoms.
list.imageAlt: A Chinese bronze halberd head (ge) of the Zhou dynasty, 1122–255 BCE. A horizontal blade and the part inserted into the shaft form a T.

list.title: Red Hare
list.power: Runs a thousand li a day and crosses rivers and mountains as if on level ground.
list.firstRecord: Chen Shou, Records of the Three Kingdoms, Biography of Lü Bu
list.summary: A famous horse red as burning charcoal. “Among men Lü Bu, among horses Red Hare,” went the saying.
list.imageAlt: A bronze horse of the late seventeenth century. Mane flying, it leaps with forelegs raised high on a black base.

list.title: Nine Tripod Cauldrons
list.owner: The royal houses of Xia, Shang and Zhou
list.power: The legitimacy to rule all under heaven. They rest with dynasties of virtue.
list.summary: Nine cauldrons King Yu cast from metal sent by the nine provinces, signifying dynastic legitimacy.
list.imageAlt: A thirteenth-century BCE Chinese bronze tripod cauldron (ding) of the Shang dynasty. A band of animal-face design rings the round vessel with two upright handles, under blue-green patina.

list.title: Heirloom Seal of the Realm
list.owner: The First Emperor of Qin and later emperors
list.maker: Calligraphy by the Qin chancellor Li Si
list.power: “Having received the mandate of heaven, may it flourish forever.” Whoever holds this seal is emperor.
list.summary: The jade seal of the First Emperor, said to be made from the Jade of Bian He, the symbol of imperial legitimacy.
list.imageAlt: An early twentieth-century Chinese jade seal. A rounded knob sits on a square body and is pierced for a cord.

list.title: Banana-Leaf Fan
list.power: One wave puts out fire, two bring wind, three bring rain.
list.firstRecord: Wu Cheng'en, Journey to the West
list.summary: The fan of Princess Iron Fan that extinguishes the Flaming Mountains. Sun Wukong fought three times to get it.
list.imageAlt: A late nineteenth-century round fan painting by the Chinese painter Shu Hao, Zhou Dunyi Admiring Lotus Flowers. A scholar seated in a pavilion by a pond and lotus leaves are painted within a circular composition on silk.

list.title: Peaches of Immortality
list.owner: Xiwangmu, Queen Mother of the West
list.power: Fruiting once in three thousand years, they make those who eat them immortal and ageless.
list.summary: The peaches of the Queen Mother of the West, which Sun Wukong secretly ate while guarding them.
list.imageAlt: A mid-eighteenth-century porcelain vase from Jingdezhen, China, painted in overglaze enamels. Branches with nine pink peaches are painted on a white ground.

list.title: Golden Headband
list.power: When a spell is recited it tightens around the head and subdues Sun Wukong.
list.firstRecord: Wu Cheng'en, Journey to the West
list.summary: The gold band Tripitaka placed on the unruly Sun Wukong.
list.imageAlt: A Japanese iron sword guard (tsuba) of the Edo period. Pierced monkeys link around the central sword opening, holding hands in a ring.

list.title: Somersault Cloud
list.power: One somersault carries him 108,000 li.
list.firstRecord: Wu Cheng'en, Journey to the West
list.summary: The cloud ridden by Sun Wukong. A single somersault flies 108,000 li.
list.imageAlt: A Chinese hanging scroll of the sixteenth to seventeenth century, Cloud Rock. A strange rock billowing up like a cloud is painted in ink on silk.

list.title: Yasakani no Magatama
list.power: One of the three sacred treasures, holding the spirit of the gods and the legitimacy of the imperial line.
list.summary: The curved jewel used with the mirror to call Amaterasu out of the cave, one of Japan's three imperial treasures.
list.imageAlt: A Japanese necklace of about the seventh century. Curved chalcedony beads (magatama) are strung among green jasper tube beads and laid in a circle.

list.title: Ame-no-Nuboko
list.owner: The creator deities Izanagi and Izanami
list.maker: Bestowed by the gods of heaven
list.power: Churned the sea and made the first land.
list.summary: The jeweled spear that first made land in Japanese myth.
list.imageAlt: A seventeenth-century Japanese hand spear (nage-yari) with its sheath. A black sheath lies beside the slender blade, and the shaft is wrapped with cord.

list.title: Kurikara Sword
list.power: A sword wound by a dragon wreathed in flame. It severs delusion and evil.
list.firstRecord: Esoteric Buddhist scriptures and images of Fudō Myōō
list.summary: The sword in the right hand of Fudō Myōō, with the dragon Kurikara winding around it and swallowing its blade.
list.imageAlt: A seated Japanese cypress statue of Fudō Myōō from the early thirteenth century. The angry-faced deity with inlaid crystal eyes sits cross-legged holding a golden sword in his right hand and a rope in his left.

list.title: Totsuka no Tsurugi
list.power: A great sword ten fists long, which cut the eight-headed serpent to pieces.
list.summary: The sword Susanoo used on Yamata-no-Orochi. Striking Kusanagi inside the serpent's tail, it chipped.
list.imageAlt: A straight single-edged Japanese sword blade (chokutō) of the seventh century or earlier. Only the long, straight steel blade survives, with patches of rust.

list.title: Futsu-no-Mitama
list.power: A single stroke revived soldiers felled by poisonous vapors.
list.summary: The sword with which the thunder god Takemikazuchi pacified the land, sent down to the first emperor, Jimmu.
list.imageAlt: A fifth-century Japanese double-edged sword blade (ken) of the Kofun period. The rusted iron blade stands vertically, and the tang for the hilt survives at the bottom.

list.title: Jamyeonggo
list.power: Sounds by itself when enemies invade.
list.summary: The drum and horn of Nangnang that sounded by themselves when enemies came. A princess in love tore the drum open.
list.imageAlt: A nineteenth-century Korean janggu drum. Hide is fitted to both ends of a red-lacquered wooden body with a narrow waist and tightened with cords. It is photographed against a blue background.

list.title: Heavenly Jade Belt
list.owner: King Jinpyeong of Silla, later Taejo of Goryeo
list.maker: Delivered by a messenger from heaven
list.power: One of the three treasures of Silla. While it remained, no one dared attack the kingdom.
list.summary: The jade belt heaven gave King Jinpyeong, one of the three treasures of Silla.
list.imageAlt: A twelfth-century gilt-bronze belt ornament from Goryeo Korea. A seated deer is embossed on a square plaque against a background of scrolls, with blue-green patina.

list.title: Pandora's Box
list.maker: Zeus (all the gods shaped Pandora together)
list.power: Opened, it scatters every evil into the world, leaving only hope within.
list.summary: The vessel opened by Pandora. It was originally a large jar, and became a “box” in the sixteenth century.
list.imageAlt: A lidded pottery container (pyxis) from Apulia in southern Italy, about 300 BCE. The round body has red spirals on a black ground and is topped by a knobbed lid.

list.title: Caduceus
list.power: Reconciles enemies, puts people to sleep or wakes them, and leads the souls of the dead to the underworld.
list.summary: Hermes's staff wound with two serpents, a symbol of heralds and peace.
list.imageAlt: A Greek or Roman bronze statuette of Hermes from around the first century. A young Hermes stands with a cloak over his shoulder; the staff he once held does not survive.

list.title: Rod of Asclepius
list.power: A staff wound with a serpent, symbolizing healing skill that could revive even the dead.
list.summary: The staff of the god of medicine, wound with a single serpent and still a symbol of medicine today.
list.imageAlt: A marble head of Asclepius from the third to second century BCE, Roman. Blue glass eyes are set in a face framed by curly hair and beard.

list.title: Ark of the Covenant
list.power: The seat of God's presence. Carried before the people, it parted the Jordan and brought down the walls of Jericho.
list.summary: The golden chest holding the tablets of the Ten Commandments. It vanished after Babylon destroyed Jerusalem.
list.imageAlt: An English gilt-copper reliquary chest of 1207–13. The box with a roof-shaped lid and animal-paw feet is densely covered in round engraved plaques, with a lock on the front.

list.title: Aladdin's Lamp
list.power: Rub it, and the jinni of the lamp appears to grant its owner's wishes.
list.firstRecord: Antoine Galland, French Thousand and One Nights
list.summary: An old lamp hidden in a cave. Rubbing it brings out a jinni who will do anything.
list.imageAlt: A ninth-century bronze oil lamp from Iran, with a pointed spout, rounded body and a feather-shaped ornament rising above a ring handle.

list.title: Uchide no Kozuchi
list.owner: The god of fortune Daikokuten, Issun-bōshi
list.power: Shake it and whatever one desires pours out.
list.summary: A magic mallet that grants wishes when shaken. It made the thumb-sized Issun-bōshi grow into a man.
list.imageAlt: A woodblock print (surimono) by Yashima Gakutei of about 1828, Mallet of Daikoku and a Rat. A gray rat sits on a red mallet painted with a peony, with a poem written above.

list.title: Olifant
list.power: When Roland blew it at the pass of Roncevaux, the sound reached Charlemagne's army thirty leagues away.
list.summary: The ivory horn Roland blew with his last breath. He blew it so hard that his temples burst.
list.imageAlt: A South Italian ivory horn (oliphant) of the twelfth century. The long, curved elephant tusk is densely carved with roundels and animals, with metal bands for a strap at both ends.

list.title: Bayard
list.owner: The four sons of Aymon, Renaud de Montauban
list.power: His back lengthens to fit his riders, so he can carry all four brothers at once and still outrun any horse.
list.firstRecord: Renaut de Montauban (The Four Sons of Aymon)
list.summary: The magic horse that carried the four sons of Aymon at once. Even Charlemagne could not kill him.
list.imageAlt: A bronze horse made by the Florentine sculptor Giambologna around 1587–91. The dark brown horse walks with its head bowed and one foreleg and one hind leg raised, standing on an oval base.

list.title: Helmet of Mambrino
list.owner: Mambrino, a Moorish king; the knight Rinaldo; Don Quixote
list.power: A golden helmet that keeps its wearer from harm.
list.summary: The golden helmet the knight Rinaldo won from a Moorish king. Don Quixote believed a barber's brass basin was this helmet.
list.imageAlt: An eighteenth-century European pewter barber's basin. The broad basin has a wavy rim, and one edge is scooped out in a curve to fit against a customer's neck.

list.title: Hippogriff
list.owner: The sorcerer Atlante; the knights Ruggiero and Astolfo
list.maker: Born of a griffin father and a mare
list.power: Spreads its wings and carries its rider across the sea to the ends of the earth, even to the Earthly Paradise.
list.summary: A flying beast born of a griffin and a mare. The knight Astolfo rode it all the way to the Earthly Paradise.
list.imageAlt: The Griffin, an engraving by the German printmaker Martin Schongauer, about 1480–90. A winged beast stands in profile with a crested eagle's head, wings and taloned forelegs, and hind legs ending in hooves.

list.title: Gawain's Green Girdle
list.power: Whoever wears it, she said, cannot be slain by any blade on earth.
list.firstRecord: Sir Gawain and the Green Knight
list.summary: The green silk girdle the lady of the Green Knight's castle gave Gawain. She said it would keep him from death by any blade.
list.imageAlt: A lady's belt probably made in Siena, Italy, around 1375–1400. Silver plaques covered with translucent enamel are set along a narrow band of woven silver thread, with a gilt-silver buckle at the top.

list.title: Love Potion of Tristan and Iseult
list.titleOriginal: Love Potion of Tristan and Iseult
list.maker: The queen of Ireland, Iseult's mother
list.power: The two who drink it together fall into a love they can never escape.
list.firstRecord: Twelfth-century French Tristan romances (Thomas and Beroul)
list.summary: The love potion the queen of Ireland brewed for her daughter's wedding. Drinking it by mistake on board ship, Tristan and Iseult fell into an inescapable love.
list.imageAlt: A fifteenth-century German flask of green glass. Below a slender neck ringed with a collar, the body divides into several thin twisting tubes, and the base swells into a round bulb.

list.title: Scabbard of Excalibur
list.power: As long as one wears it, one loses no blood, however deep the wound.
list.summary: The scabbard the Lady of the Lake gave with Excalibur. Merlin said it was worth ten times more than the sword.
list.imageAlt: Fragment of a luxury dagger made by the Lombards around 600. Gold plaques and two gold bands, engraved with scrolls and animals, wrap the rusted, broken iron blade and scabbard.

list.title: The Round Table
list.owner: King Arthur and the Knights of the Round Table
list.maker: A Cornish carpenter (Layamon) or Merlin (Robert de Boron)
list.power: With no high or low place, every knight seated around it sits as an equal.
list.summary: A round table made to end quarrels over precedence. The Siege Perilous was kept empty for the one knight who would achieve the Grail.
list.imageAlt: Daniel Hopfer's etching Three Worthy Christians, about 1516. Charlemagne, King Arthur and Godfrey of Bouillon stand side by side in armor, with their names inscribed above.

list.title: Sword of the Strange Belt
list.maker: The sword of King David, remade by King Solomon
list.power: Only one destined man may draw it; anyone else who does comes to harm.
list.summary: King David's sword, carried on Solomon's ship to await the Grail knight. Perceval's sister wove a new belt for it from her own hair.
list.imageAlt: A French sword belt of the late eighteenth century. The white silk belt is embroidered with green and black flowers and set with spangles, and a U-shaped hanger for the scabbard hangs below.

list.title: Ring of Lunete
list.power: Turn the stone toward the palm and close the hand, and no one can see the wearer.
list.firstRecord: Chretien de Troyes, Yvain, the Knight of the Lion
list.summary: The ring the maid Lunete gave the knight Yvain. With the stone turned into the palm, he vanished from sight.
list.imageAlt: A German gold ring of the tenth to eleventh century. A plaque with a flower in green cloisonne enamel crowns a tall stepped setting decorated with gold granules and small arches.

list.title: Gleipnir
list.power: Thin and soft as a silk ribbon, yet no strength can break it.
list.summary: The fetter that bound the wolf Fenrir. Made of six things that no longer exist, it was as thin as silk.
list.imageAlt: A fragment of a band woven of silk and gold thread in Sicily, Italy, at the end of the eleventh century. Fine stripes run along the long, narrow dark-brown band, whose edges are worn.

list.title: Mistilteinn
list.owner: The blind god Hod (guided by Loki)
list.power: Pierced Baldr, whom everything in the world had sworn not to harm.
list.summary: Everything swore not to harm Baldr, but one sprig of mistletoe, passed over as too young, killed him.
list.imageAlt: Two arrows from sixteenth-century Turkey or Iran. Pointed steel arrowheads inlaid with gold scrolls are fixed to lacquered wooden shafts.

list.title: Gullinbursti
list.power: Runs through sky and sea faster than any horse, and its golden bristles light up the night.
list.summary: A boar with golden bristles made by a dwarf at his forge. Its glow lit the darkness as it drew Freyr's chariot.
list.imageAlt: A bronze wild boar made in the late seventeenth century by the Florentine sculptor Giovanni Francesco Susini. With bristles raised along its neck, the boar sits on its haunches with its mouth open.

list.title: Grotti
list.owner: King Frodi of Denmark; the sea-king Mysing
list.power: Grinds out whatever the one who turns it wishes for.
list.firstRecord: Snorri Sturluson, Prose Edda, "Song of Grotti"
list.summary: A mill that ground out anything. It sank into the sea while grinding salt, and that, they say, is why the sea is salty.
list.imageAlt: A stone grinding table (metate) from Costa Rica, about 1000–1550. A jaguar head is carved at the front of the broad, four-legged table, and patterns are carved in relief around the table and on the legs.

list.title: Mead of Poetry
list.power: Whoever drinks it becomes a poet or a scholar.
list.summary: Mead brewed from the blood of Kvasir, the wisest of men. Odin stole it from a giant in the shape of an eagle.
list.imageAlt: A German maple-wood double cup (mazer) of about 1530. Two round wooden cups are stacked one on the other, with gilt-silver mounts at the rims, the join and the foot, and a small handle at the side.

list.title: Idunn's Apples
list.power: Eaten by the gods as they grow old, they make them young again.
list.summary: Idunn's apples kept the gods young. When Idunn was carried off by a giant, the gods quickly grew old.
list.imageAlt: A sixteenth-century silver-gilt pomander. Round scenes are engraved on its apple-like body, with a ring at the top and a base hung with small balls below.

list.title: Naglfar
list.power: On the day of Ragnarok it crosses the sea packed with giants who will fight the gods.
list.summary: A huge ship built from the nails of the dead. On the day of Ragnarok it brings the giants.
list.imageAlt: A wooden model boat from Middle Kingdom Egypt (about 2040–1648 BCE). The yellow-painted boat carries a mast and a long steering oar, several painted figures of sailors, and a jar and a basket.

list.title: Thor's Goats
list.power: Eaten and their bones laid on their hides, they are blessed with Thor's hammer and live again the next day.
list.summary: The two goats that draw Thor's chariot. Even when eaten, they come back to life the next day.
list.imageAlt: A bronze nanny goat from Hellenistic Greece, late third century BCE. The goat, with horns curving back and a beard at its chin, stands on a white base with its long coat hanging down.

list.title: Dainsleif
list.power: Once drawn, it must kill before it is sheathed; it never misses, and its wounds never heal.
list.summary: A sword that returns to its scabbard only after drawing blood. Because of it, a battle began that is fought again every day.
list.imageAlt: An iron sword made by the Franks around 500–700. The straight, long double-edged blade lies vertically, rough with rust, and its grip no longer survives.

list.title: Hlidskjalf
list.power: Whoever sits in this seat sees everything that happens in the nine worlds.
list.summary: Odin's high seat. From it the whole world could be seen.
list.imageAlt: A child's throne made by Pierre-Marie Balny in Paris in 1822. The leather back of the gilded wooden chair is gold-tooled with a rooster in a laurel wreath and fleurs-de-lis, the crest is carved with cherubs, and the front legs are carved as winged beasts.

list.title: Lia Fail
list.owner: The kings of Ireland (the Hill of Tara)
list.maker: Unknown (brought by the Tuatha De Danann from Falias)
list.power: It cries out aloud when the rightful king of Ireland stands upon it.
list.firstRecord: Lebor Gabala Erenn (The Book of Invasions)
list.summary: The Stone of Destiny, one of the four treasures of the Tuatha De Danann. It cried out when the rightful king of Ireland stood on it.
list.imageAlt: A Celtic-style stone head from northern England under Roman rule, about 100–300. Large almond-shaped eyes, a straight nose and a thin, closed mouth are carved in red sandstone, with bulging locks of hair at both sides.

list.title: Harp of the Dagda
list.titleOriginal: Daur Dá Bláo (Harp of the Dagda)
list.owner: The Dagda, god of the Tuatha De Danann
list.power: It plays the three strains of weeping, laughter and sleep, and flies to its master's hands when called by name.
list.firstRecord: The Second Battle of Mag Tuired
list.summary: The harp the Dagda won back by calling its names. With the strains of sorrow, laughter and sleep he put the Fomorians to sleep.
list.imageAlt: A portable harp made by John Egan of Dublin, Ireland, in 1819. Many strings stretch between the gold-painted curved neck and the pillar, and the green soundbox is painted with gold leaves.

list.title: Moralltach
list.maker: Unknown (the sword of the sea god Manannan)
list.power: As its name, "Great Fury," says, one stroke cuts through anything.
list.firstRecord: The Pursuit of Diarmuid and Grainne
list.summary: The sword of the sea god Manannan. Aengus, god of love, passed it to his foster son Diarmuid.
list.imageAlt: A European long sword of about 1400. Below a round pommel, a wire-bound grip and a cross-guard spreading to both sides, a long, straight double-edged blade extends.

list.title: The Crane Bag
list.owner: The sea god Manannan, later Fionn mac Cumhaill
list.maker: The sea god Manannan (from the skin of Aoife, a woman turned into a crane)
list.power: When the sea is full, all the treasures of the gods appear in it; when the tide ebbs, it is empty.
list.firstRecord: Duanaire Finn (The Poem Book of Finn)
list.summary: Manannan's bag, made from the skin of a woman turned into a crane. It held all the treasures of the gods.
list.imageAlt: A purse-shaped reliquary from the Upper Rhine region of Germany, about 1320. Gilded copper is densely set with rock crystal, glass and gems, and a blue roundel at the center carries the Virgin holding the Christ Child.

list.title: Enbarr
list.owner: The sea god Manannan; Lugh, god of light
list.power: Runs faster than the spring wind over water and land alike, and no one on its back can be killed, it was said.
list.firstRecord: The Fate of the Children of Tuireann
list.summary: The horse of the sea god Manannan that runs over waves as if on land. Lugh, god of light, appeared before the king of the Tuatha De Danann riding it.
list.imageAlt: The two faces of a gold coin (stater) of the Catuvellauni of Britain, about 20 BCE–10 CE. The obverse at left bears the letters TASCIOV RICON in a band; the reverse at right shows a horse carrying a warrior with a sword.

list.title: Cormac's Cup of Truth
list.owner: Cormac mac Airt, high king of Ireland
list.power: Three lies spoken over it break it into three pieces; three truths make it whole again.
list.firstRecord: The Adventure of Cormac in the Land of Promise
list.summary: The golden cup Manannan gave King Cormac. It broke at falsehood and became whole again at the truth.
list.imageAlt: A Hungarian gilt-silver chalice of about 1450–80. Below the golden bowl, the cup's base and stem are filled with green and white enamel flowers, and square gems are set in the knop and the foot.

list.title: Cauldron of Ceridwen
list.power: Boiled for a year and a day, its first three drops hold all the wisdom of the world.
list.summary: The cauldron in which Ceridwen brewed wisdom for her son. The boy who tasted three drops became the poet Taliesin.
list.imageAlt: A ritual cauldron from Bronze Age Hungary, about 1000–900 BCE. A large looped handle in two strands rises above the round bronze body, and fine patterns are incised around the rim.

list.title: Dyrnwyn
list.power: When a man of noble birth draws it himself, flames blaze from hilt to point.
list.firstRecord: The Thirteen Treasures of the Island of Britain
list.summary: The sword of King Rhydderch, first of the Thirteen Treasures of the Island of Britain. When a worthy man drew it, the blade burst into flame.
list.imageAlt: A German two-handed sword of 1550–1600. Below a long grip, a cross-guard with rings spreads to both sides, and below it runs a long blade undulating like flames.

list.title: Gwyddbwyll Board of Gwenddoleu
list.power: Set out the pieces, and they move by themselves and play the game.
list.firstRecord: The Thirteen Treasures of the Island of Britain
list.summary: Set silver pieces on its gold board, and they played by themselves. It is one of the Thirteen Treasures of the Island of Britain.
list.imageAlt: An amber game board made in Konigsberg by Georg Schreiber in the seventeenth century. Inside the open box-shaped board, slices of red and yellow amber and ivory form the triangular points of backgammon.

list.title: Cloak of Manannan
list.owner: Manannan mac Lir, the sea god
list.power: Shaken between two people, it ensures they will never meet again in this world.
list.firstRecord: The Wasting Sickness of Cu Chulainn
list.summary: The sea god's cloak that keeps two people from ever meeting again. It parted Cu Chulainn and the fairy Fand forever.
list.imageAlt: A semicircular ecclesiastical cloak (cope) from late fifteenth-century Europe. Large pomegranates and flowers are woven in red velvet on a golden ground, and a gold-thread band is attached along the straight upper edge.

list.title: Lyre of Orpheus
list.maker: First made by Hermes and handed down by Apollo (by tradition)
list.power: When he plays, birds and beasts, trees and even stones follow, and the gods of the underworld are moved.
list.summary: When Orpheus played, beasts, trees and stones followed him. With his song he nearly brought his wife back from the underworld.
list.imageAlt: Orpheus and Cerberus, carved in sandstone by Ferdinand Tietz near Bamberg, Germany, about 1765. A young Orpheus stands with his head thrown back, playing a stringed instrument, while Cerberus, the dog of the underworld, crouches at his feet.

list.title: Bow of Odysseus
list.maker: Unknown (the bow of the archer Eurytus, given as a gift by his son Iphitus)
list.power: No one but its master can string it.
list.summary: The bow no one but Odysseus could string. Returning after twenty years, he used it to defeat the suitors.
list.imageAlt: An Ottoman Turkish composite bow of 1719–20 with two arrows. Unstrung, the bow curves deeply with its tips bent backward, and two long arrows stand beside it.

list.title: Chariot of Helios
list.power: Drawn by four fire-breathing horses, it carries the sun across the sky every day.
list.summary: The chariot of fire Helios drove across the sky carrying the sun. When his son Phaethon drove it, the world nearly burned.
list.imageAlt: An Athenian black-figure water jar (hydria) painted by the Antimenes Painter about 520 BCE. In the middle of the orange body, a chariot drawn by four horses is shown from the front, with a band of animals below.

list.title: Palladium
list.owner: The people of Troy, later Rome
list.power: As long as this statue remains within the walls, Troy will never fall.
list.summary: A small wooden image of Athena that fell from heaven. As long as it was inside the city, Troy would not fall.
list.imageAlt: A Greek bronze statuette of Athena, about 460 BCE. The helmeted goddess in a long robe raises her right arm high, releasing an owl from her hand.

list.title: Trojan Horse
list.power: A huge hollow wooden horse. The heroes hidden in its belly got inside the walls of Troy.
list.summary: The hollow wooden horse that ended the Trojan War. The heroes hidden in its belly opened the gates at night.
list.imageAlt: The Trojan Horse, a painted enamel plaque from Limoges, France, about 1530–40. Before Troy, lined with walls and towers, people pull a huge white horse into the city; the plaque is set in a red velvet frame.

list.title: Thyrsus
list.power: Strike a rock with it and water springs up; thrust it into the ground and wine gushes out.
list.summary: The staff of Dionysus, a fennel stalk tipped with a pine cone and wound with ivy. When it struck the ground, wine sprang up.
list.imageAlt: An Athenian red-figure mixing bowl (column krater) painted by the Naples Painter about 450–430 BCE. On the black ground, two satyrs with horse tails chase two women carrying leafy staffs (thyrsi), shown in red.

list.title: Bag of Aeolus
list.owner: Aeolus, master of the winds; Odysseus
list.maker: Aeolus (from the hide of a nine-year-old ox)
list.power: It holds every violent wind, so that a ship sails home with only a fair breeze.
list.summary: An oxhide bag holding all the violent winds. With home in sight, the sailors opened it.
list.imageAlt: An agate vessel (askos) of the Ptolemaic dynasty, 200–1 BCE. Agate with swirling brown and white bands is carved in the shape of a wineskin, with gold capping the slanted spout and the foot.

list.title: Cornucopia
list.owner: Tyche, goddess of fortune; Plutus, god of wealth
list.maker: Unknown (the horn of the goat Amalthea)
list.power: Food and drink of every kind flow from it without end.
list.summary: The horn of the goat that nursed the infant Zeus. It became the symbol of plenty, pouring out whatever one wishes without end.
list.imageAlt: Victory with Cornucopia, a Roman bronze chariot ornament of about 40–68 CE. The winged goddess soars upward with one arm raised above her head and the other holding a long horn of plenty.

list.title: Wings of Daedalus and Icarus
list.power: Wings of feathers bound with thread and wax. Strapped to the arms, they let a person fly like a bird.
list.summary: The wings Daedalus, builder of the Labyrinth, made to escape Crete with his son. Icarus flew too close to the sun.
list.imageAlt: Hendrick Goltzius's engraving Icarus, 1588. Within a round frame, a young man who has lost his wings falls headfirst with the sun behind him; far below, Daedalus flies small over the sea, and a Latin inscription runs around the border.

list.title: The Golden Bough
list.power: Whoever plucks it and carries it may enter the underworld alive and return.
list.summary: The golden bough that must be plucked before a living man can enter the underworld. Aeneas found it by following two doves.
list.imageAlt: Aeneas and the Sibyl in the Underworld, painted in oil on copper by Jan Brueghel the Younger in the 1630s. In the middle of a dark underworld where flames shoot up, the helmeted Aeneas follows the Sibyl, who points the way, surrounded by monsters and shades.

list.title: Rod of Moses
list.power: Thrown down it becomes a serpent; stretched over the sea it parts the waters; struck against a rock it brings forth water.
list.summary: The rod with which Moses led the Israelites out of Egypt. It parted the Red Sea and drew water from the rock.
list.imageAlt: A black-and-white photograph of the tapestry Moses Striking the Rock, woven in Florence, Italy, about 1650–57. In the center Moses strikes a rock with his rod as people gather around; at the top is a panel with a Latin inscription, and the sides are decorated with columns and cherubs.

list.title: Jawbone of Samson
list.power: With the jawbone of a newly dead donkey he struck down a thousand Philistines.
list.summary: The donkey's jawbone Samson snatched up from the ground. With it alone he struck down a thousand Philistines.
list.imageAlt: Samson, an oil painting by Valentin de Boulogne, about 1630–31. A young man with curly hair sits wrapped in a red cloak, his chin resting on his hand, with a donkey's jawbone beneath his arm, looking out at the viewer.

list.title: Sling of David
list.owner: David the shepherd (later king of Israel)
list.power: With one smooth stone chosen from a brook, it brought down the giant Goliath.
list.summary: The sling with which the shepherd boy David felled the giant Goliath. A single stone sank into the giant's forehead.
list.imageAlt: David Triumphant over Goliath, a bronze plaquette by the Italian sculptor Moderno, about 1490–1510. The naked boy David stands with his sling hanging down, and Goliath's head and fallen body lie at his feet.

list.title: Brazen Serpent
list.owner: Moses, later the people of Jerusalem
list.power: Whoever had been bitten by the fiery serpents lived when he looked at the bronze serpent on the pole.
list.summary: The bronze serpent Moses set on a pole in the wilderness. Anyone bitten by a snake who looked at it lived.
list.imageAlt: Moses Praying to End the Serpents' Attack on the Israelites, painted in Allahabad in the Mughal Empire, 1602–4. On a hillside Moses prays with both hands raised, while below him people bitten by snakes fall or writhe.

list.title: Crown of Thorns
list.power: A crown woven to mock a king, yet every one of its thorns came to be venerated as a relic.
list.summary: The crown of thorns Roman soldiers put on Jesus. King Louis IX of France built the Sainte-Chapelle to house it.
list.imageAlt: The right wing of a diptych painted in tempera and gold on oak in Styria, Austria, about 1400. Above, two men press the crown of thorns onto the head of the seated Christ with crossed staves; below, Christ prays in the garden while his disciples sleep.

list.title: The True Cross
list.owner: The church of Jerusalem, later many churches
list.power: When no one knew which was Christ's cross, it is said that a dying woman rose up when it touched her.
list.summary: The cross of Christ that Helena, mother of Emperor Constantine, is said to have found in Jerusalem. Its fragments were scattered to churches all over the world.
list.imageAlt: A reliquary of the True Cross. A double-armed cross from the Kingdom of Jerusalem, about 1214, is set in a thirteenth-century gilt-silver panel from the Rhine-Meuse region, amid rows of almond shapes pierced with quatrefoils and within a Latin inscription.

list.title: Gifts of the Magi
list.power: Gold was taken to signify a king, frankincense a god, and myrrh death.
list.summary: The gold, frankincense and myrrh that the Magi, following a star from the East, offered to the infant Jesus.
list.imageAlt: The Adoration of the Magi, painted by the Sienese artist Giovanni di Paolo about 1440–45. Before a stable the Virgin holds the infant Jesus on her lap, while a kneeling old king, two kings in golden robes and a mounted retinue have come to the child.

list.title: The Golden Calf
list.owner: The people of Israel in the wilderness
list.power: The idol the people worshiped as the god who had brought them out of Egypt.
list.summary: The calf Aaron cast from melted gold earrings while Moses was on the mountain. Moses ground it to powder.
list.imageAlt: Bull Calf Polemount, a Sumerian basalt ornament of about 2700 BCE. A black calf lies with its legs folded and its head raised, with a twisted cord around its neck and body.

list.title: Trumpets of Jericho
list.power: Blown long on the seventh day after circling the city seven times, they brought down the walls of Jericho with the people's shout.
list.summary: The rams' horn trumpets the priests blew as they circled Jericho. On the last day, with a great shout, the walls fell.
list.imageAlt: A Jewish shofar (horn trumpet) of the eighteenth or nineteenth century. A long, slender, pale horn turns upward and widens at one end, where the rim is carved into teeth.

list.title: Holy Ampulla
list.maker: Unknown (brought from heaven by a dove)
list.power: It held the oil with which French kings were anointed at their coronation, and it was said to refill itself after use.
list.firstRecord: Hincmar of Reims, Life of Remigius
list.summary: The flask of oil a dove is said to have brought from heaven at the baptism of Clovis. French kings were anointed with this oil at their coronations.
list.imageAlt: Both faces of a pilgrim's ampulla from Palestine, about 600. The flat, round flask is made of a lead and tin alloy, stamped with the Crucifixion on the front and the Ascension on the back, with lettering running around the edges.

list.title: Eye of Horus
list.maker: Restored by Thoth, god of wisdom
list.power: An amulet that heals what is hurt and keeps the body whole.
list.summary: The eye of Horus, torn out in his battle with Seth. Restored by Thoth, it became the most common protective amulet in Egypt.
list.imageAlt: A wedjat eye amulet from Egypt's Third Intermediate Period, about 1080–664 BCE. A white eye with a black pupil is inlaid in a sky-blue faience plaque, with a heavy brow above and the falcon's cheek markings worked in openwork below.

list.title: Tablet of Destinies
list.owner: Enlil, king of the gods, later Marduk
list.power: Whoever holds it decides the fates of gods, people and the world, and rules the universe.
list.firstRecord: The Epic of Anzu (Old Babylonian version)
list.summary: The tablet by which its holder decides the destiny of the universe. The monstrous bird Anzu stole it, and the war god Ninurta took it back.
list.imageAlt: A bronze tablet inscribed in cuneiform from Iran, about 850–750 BCE. A small tab rises from the top center of the dark, rectangular bronze plate, which is covered with incised cuneiform signs.

list.title: Gilgamesh's Plant of Rejuvenation
list.power: Eaten, it makes an old man young again.
list.summary: The plant called "the old man grows young" that Gilgamesh dug up from under the water. While he bathed, a snake carried it off.
list.imageAlt: An Assyrian shell inlay plaque of the ninth to eighth century BCE, in the shape of a tree with pointed leaves fanning out at the top and a trunk with chevron markings running downward.

list.title: Sharur
list.power: It speaks, flies off on its own to spy on the enemy, and reports back to its master.
list.summary: The talking mace of the god Ninurta. It flew off on its own to spy on enemies and brought back counsel from the king of the gods.
list.imageAlt: A pink limestone mace head from Predynastic Egypt, about 3650–3100 BCE. A face is carved on the front of the pear-shaped body, with a long nose, two drilled eyes and a thin mouth, and pierced knobs project from both sides.

list.title: Seven Ornaments of Inanna
list.power: Seven ornaments holding the goddess's powers. With each one she removes, she loses her strength.
list.firstRecord: Sumerian myth "Inanna's Descent to the Underworld"
list.summary: The ornaments Inanna gave up one by one at each of seven gates on her way down to the underworld. At the last gate she lost all her power.
list.imageAlt: A Sumerian headdress of about 2600–2500 BCE. Thin sheets of gold cut into leaf shapes hang in a row from a string of blue lapis lazuli and red carnelian beads.

list.title: The Jinni's Brass Bottle
list.titleOriginal: Qumqum of the Fisherman and the Jinni
list.maker: King Solomon (who imprisoned and sealed the jinni)
list.power: Sealed with Solomon's seal, it keeps the jinni inside from escaping.
list.firstRecord: The oldest Arabic manuscript of The Thousand and One Nights
list.summary: A brass bottle caught in a fisherman's net. When he opened the lid Solomon had sealed, a huge jinni rose out like smoke.
list.imageAlt: An inlaid brass container from northern Iraq, about 1250–1350. A round box with a knobbed lid is inlaid with silver and gold in dense patterns, Arabic lettering and a seated figure, with clasps on both sides to lock the lid.

list.title: Book of Thoth
list.power: Its first spell charms sky, earth and sea and reveals the speech of beasts; its second lets one see the gods even after death.
list.summary: A book of magic said to be written by Thoth, god of wisdom, himself. The princes who laid hands on it paid a heavy price.
list.imageAlt: A wooden scribe's palette from Egypt's New Kingdom, about 1540–1186 BCE. One end of the long wooden plank has two round wells for mixing ink, and a slot for reed pens runs along the middle.

list.title: Banner of Kaveh
list.owner: Kaveh the blacksmith, later the kings of Iran
list.power: The banner that rallied the people against a tyrant. Those who fought beneath it were believed to win.
list.summary: The leather apron of Kaveh the blacksmith, who rose against the tyrant Zahhak. Adorned with jewels, it became the banner of the Iranian kings.
list.imageAlt: A brass processional standard ('alam) of the late seventeenth to early eighteenth century. Below a top pointed like a spearhead, leaf-shaped blades spread out, and two dragons on either side curve around a round plaque pierced with lettering.

list.title: Cup of Jamshid
list.owner: King Kay Khosrow (Shahnameh); in later poetry, King Jamshid
list.power: Look into the cup and everything happening in the seven heavens and the whole world is reflected in it.
list.summary: A cup that reflects the whole world. With it King Kay Khosrow found the hero Bizhan imprisoned in a pit.
list.imageAlt: The Wade Cup, a brass cup inlaid with silver from Seljuq Iran, about 1200–1221. The outside of the footed round bowl is densely inlaid in silver with Arabic letters ending in human heads and with horsemen.

list.title: Feather of the Simurgh
list.owner: The hero Zal and his son Rostam
list.power: Burn it, and wherever you are, the Simurgh will fly to your aid.
list.summary: A feather left by the Simurgh, the divine bird that raised the abandoned baby Zal. When it was burned, the Simurgh came.
list.imageAlt: A page from a Shahnameh made in Iran about 1330–40, "Zal in the Simurgh's Nest." Persian verses fill several columns at the top and right; a small painting at lower left shows the great red-headed Simurgh, the naked child Zal on a rocky mountain and two white animals.

list.title: Brahmastra
list.power: Charged with a spell and loosed, it raises a fire terrible enough to set the sky ablaze and shake the earth.
list.summary: The ultimate weapon, imbued with the power of the creator god Brahma. Once loosed, it was hard to call back.
list.imageAlt: Rama and Lakshmana Fighting Ravana, painted in the kingdom of Chamba in northern India about 1765. Within a red border, blue-skinned Rama draws his bow, and before him stands Ravana in red, with ten heads and twenty arms holding weapons.

list.title: Pinaka
list.owner: Shiva, god of destruction, later the royal house of Mithila
list.power: A huge bow no one could lift. With it Shiva burned the three cities of the demons with a single arrow.
list.summary: Shiva's huge bow. Rama broke it while drawing it, and married Sita.
list.imageAlt: A black-and-white photograph of a composite bow from Italy or Indo-Persia, about 1500. Unstrung, the bow curves deeply like a letter C, and both tips are carved as animal heads.

list.title: Kaumodaki
list.maker: Unknown (given to Krishna by Varuna, god of the sea)
list.power: When hurled, it smashes demons with a sound like thunder.
list.summary: The mace Vishnu holds in one of his four hands. Varuna, god of the sea, gave it to Krishna in the Khandava forest.
list.imageAlt: An Indo-Persian steel mace (gada) of the seventeenth century. A ball-shaped fluted head sits at the end of a long, straight steel shaft, and the head and shaft are inlaid with gold designs here and there.

list.title: Panchajanya
list.maker: Unknown (the conch in which the demon Panchajana lived under the sea)
list.power: When blown, its sound shakes sky and earth and tears the hearts of the enemy.
list.summary: The conch Krishna blew to open the battle of Kurukshetra. He won it from a demon under the sea.
list.imageAlt: A ritual conch shell from the Khmer kingdom of Cambodia, twelfth century. The pointed conch is sheathed in carved bronze and stands on a three-legged stand decorated with serpent deities.

list.title: Pushpaka Vimana
list.owner: Kubera, god of wealth; the demon king Ravana; Rama
list.power: It flies wherever its master wishes, and however many ride it, there is always room for more.
list.summary: A heavenly chariot as beautiful as a flower. After defeating Ravana, Rama flew home to Ayodhya in it.
list.imageAlt: A Ramayana painting from the Pahari region of northern India, about 1765: Enthroned Rama and Sita Receive Homage from Their Monkey and Bear Allies. Rama and Sita sit on a throne under a pink canopy, with monkeys and a bear at left and courtiers at right.

list.title: Airavata
list.maker: Unknown (rose from the churning of the ocean of milk)
list.power: With its trunk it draws up the waters of the underworld and sprays them into the clouds, so that Indra can send rain.
list.summary: The white elephant Indra rides. It rose from the ocean of milk when the gods and demons churned it.
list.imageAlt: A sandstone elephant from the Champa kingdom of central Vietnam, about 900–950. The elephant stands with its ears spread wide and its trunk hanging down.

list.title: Syamantaka
list.power: It produces gold every day, and the land where it is kept knows neither drought nor sickness.
list.summary: The jewel the sun god gave to Satrajit. It produced gold every day, but suspicion and strife never ceased around it.
list.imageAlt: Akrura and Kritavarma Flee Dvaraka, a page from the "Large Basohli" Bhagavata Purana painted in the Pahari region of northern India about 1760–65. Two men gallop on horseback across fields of overlapping green hills.

list.title: Akshaya Patra
list.power: Every day, food flows from it without end until Draupadi has finished her meal.
list.summary: The vessel the sun god gave the Pandava brothers when they were banished to the forest. Food never ran out until Draupadi had eaten.
list.imageAlt: Draupadi Rescued from Abduction, a Mahabharata painting probably made at Bikaner in northern India about 1615. On a yellow ground two men grapple as if wrestling, with Draupadi behind them and onlookers standing at both sides.

list.title: Garuda
list.maker: Son of the sage Kashyapa and Vinata
list.power: On wings no god could stop, he seized the nectar of immortality from heaven.
list.summary: The king of birds, who carries Vishnu. To free his enslaved mother, he brought the nectar of immortality from heaven.
list.imageAlt: Vishnu Riding on Garuda, a schist sculpture from Bihar in eastern India, 300s CE. The crowned Vishnu sits astride Garuda, who has a human face and outspread wings, and tail feathers spread like rays behind his head.

list.title: Axe of Parashurama
list.maker: Given by Shiva, god of destruction
list.power: The axe given by Shiva. It cut off all the arms of a king who had a thousand.
list.summary: The axe Shiva gave Parashurama. With it he swept away the warrior class twenty-one times.
list.imageAlt: A steel battle axe from Sind, India, about 1800. A blade with a slanting edge sits at the end of a long, thin iron shaft, and the part joining the blade to the shaft is engraved with designs.

list.title: Yi's Red Bow
list.maker: Given by the heavenly emperor Di Jun
list.power: A red bow strong enough to shoot suns out of the sky.
list.firstRecord: Shan Hai Jing (Classic of Mountains and Seas)
list.summary: The red bow the heavenly emperor gave Yi the archer. Yi shot down nine of the ten suns that had risen in the sky at once.
list.imageAlt: An eight-lobed bronze mirror from the Tang dynasty, late seventh to early eighth century. Around the central knob, hunters on galloping horses aim their bows at fleeing animals, with flowers and butterflies in relief.

list.title: Chang'e's Elixir of Immortality
list.owner: Chang'e, wife of Yi the archer
list.maker: The Queen Mother of the West
list.power: Whoever takes it does not die; the body grows light and floats up to the sky.
list.summary: The elixir of immortality Yi obtained from the Queen Mother of the West. His wife Chang'e secretly took it and flew to the moon.
list.imageAlt: A bronze mirror with the Lunar Palace from the Jin dynasty, twelfth to thirteenth century. The back of the round mirror is cast in relief with a hall among clouds, a large tree, a bridge and waves, and standing figures, around a central knob.

list.title: Purple-Gold Red Gourd
list.owner: The Golden Horn and Silver Horn kings (servants of Laozi)
list.maker: Laozi, the Supreme Old Lord (a vessel for elixirs)
list.power: It sucks in anyone who answers when their name is called, and dissolves them within an hour and three quarters.
list.firstRecord: Wu Cheng'en, Journey to the West
list.summary: A gourd that sucks in whoever answers when called by name. Even Sun Wukong was trapped when he answered to a false name.
list.imageAlt: A celadon gourd vase from the Qianlong reign of the Qing dynasty, 1736–95. Above a lobed round body rise a large central double-gourd neck and four smaller gourds, covered in a clear sea-green glaze.

list.title: Qiankun Ring
list.power: Thrown, it flies to strike the enemy; dipped in the sea, it shakes the Dragon King's palace.
list.summary: The golden ring Nezha wore from birth. When he washed in the sea, the Dragon Palace shook, and he ended up fighting the Dragon King's son.
list.imageAlt: A jade ring of the Eastern Zhou dynasty, third century BCE. One end of a round ring patterned like twisted cord rises as an open-mouthed dragon's head, and the ring crosses over itself like a knot below.

list.title: Three-Pointed Double-Edged Blade
list.power: A three-pronged blade. Even after more than three hundred rounds with Sun Wukong, it never gave way.
list.firstRecord: Wu Cheng'en, Journey to the West
list.summary: The weapon of Erlang Shen, the god with a third eye in his forehead. With it he captured Sun Wukong, who had thrown heaven into turmoil.
list.imageAlt: A leaf, "Searching the Mountains," from a thirteenth-century Southern Song ink album of Daoist and Buddhist subjects. In fine ink lines, divine soldiers capture mountain demons and beasts, hanging them from spears or leading them on ropes.

list.title: Zhang Guolao's Paper Donkey
list.owner: Zhang Guolao, one of the Eight Immortals
list.power: It travels tens of thousands of li in a day; when resting it folds up like paper into a box, and a spray of water turns it back into a donkey.
list.summary: The white donkey the Daoist Zhang Guo rode. When resting, he folded it like paper and put it in a box.
list.imageAlt: The inside of a Qing porcelain dish of the Kangxi reign, 1662–1722, painted in colored enamels. On the white ground the old man Zhang Guolao, in green robes, stands beside a white donkey under the sun and red clouds, within a brocade-patterned border.

list.title: Wooden Ox and Gliding Horse
list.owner: Zhuge Liang, chancellor of Shu Han
list.power: Without eating or resting, it carries army provisions along steep plank roads.
list.firstRecord: Chen Shou, Records of the Three Kingdoms, "Biography of Zhuge Liang"
list.summary: The carts Zhuge Liang built to carry provisions over the rugged mountain roads of Shu. In the Romance of the Three Kingdoms they became mechanical oxen that stopped when their tongues were twisted.
list.imageAlt: A black-and-white photograph of a Tang dynasty earthenware ox cart, seventh to eighth century. A horned ox is harnessed to the shafts, and behind it are a cart compartment with a rounded roof and a large wheel with close-set spokes.

list.title: He Shi Bi
list.owner: Bian He of Chu, later the states of Zhao and Qin
list.maker: Unknown (an uncut jade found by Bian He on Mount Jing)
list.power: The finest jade under heaven, for which the king of Qin offered fifteen cities.
list.summary: The jade of Bian He, who lost both feet yet held to his uncut stone. Lin Xiangru risked his life to bring it back to Zhao.
list.imageAlt: A jade bi of the Warring States period, 475–221 BCE. A flat, pale-green jade disk with a round central hole is covered with a close-set grain pattern, crossed diagonally by a brown streak.

list.title: Brocade Kasaya
list.maker: Unknown (passed to Emperor Taizong of Tang by the bodhisattva Guanyin)
list.power: Whoever wears it will not fall into hell, and neither poisonous creatures, wild beasts nor demons can harm him.
list.firstRecord: Wu Cheng'en, Journey to the West
list.summary: The silk kasaya the bodhisattva Guanyin bestowed on Tang Sanzang. An old abbot who coveted it set fire to his own temple.
list.imageAlt: A Buddhist priest's ceremonial robe from the Ming dynasty, fifteenth century. Hundreds of small Buddhas are embroidered in gold and colored thread in compartments across a long red silk panel, with slightly larger Buddhas at the center and corners.

list.title: Hetu and Luoshu
list.maker: Unknown (borne out of the waters by a dragon-horse and a tortoise)
list.power: From the dot patterns on their backs came the eight trigrams and the nine great laws of government.
list.summary: The chart and the writing carried out of the Yellow River by a dragon-horse and out of the Luo River by a tortoise. They became the origin of the eight trigrams and the magic square.
list.imageAlt: A jade tortoise of the Ming dynasty, 1368–1644. A small tortoise carved from yellowish-green jade lies with its head raised, with brown markings here and there.

list.title: Tamatebako
list.power: As long as it stays closed it preserves youth, but opened, all the years that have passed fall upon you at once.
list.summary: The box Otohime gave Urashima Taro as he left the Dragon Palace. When he opened the box he had been told not to open, he became a white-haired old man.
list.imageAlt: A lacquered cosmetics box (tebako) of the Kamakura period, early fourteenth century. The round-cornered black box and its lid are decorated with golden chrysanthemums, and metal rings for a cord are fitted on the side.

list.title: Hagoromo
list.power: Wearing it, one can fly up and return to heaven.
list.summary: A heavenly maiden's feather robe left by the water. The maiden, held captive by the one who hid it, flew back to heaven when she got it back.
list.imageAlt: A Noh costume, a choken, from the Edo period, about 1800–1850. The loosely woven reddish silk robe is spread out on a pole, woven in gold and colored threads with hanging wisteria and fans.

list.title: Tide Jewels
list.power: One makes the tide rise; the other makes it ebb.
list.summary: The two jewels the sea god gave Hoori. With the flood-tide jewel and the ebb-tide jewel he subdued his brother.
list.imageAlt: Tide-Changing Jewel with Dragon, a decorative object of the Meiji period, early 1900s. A large crystal ball rests on a stand of rough waves wrought in silver and shakudo, a dragon twists among the waves, and another small crystal ball sits beside it.

list.title: The Buddha's Stone Begging Bowl
list.power: The true bowl the Buddha used was said to give off a soft light.
list.firstRecord: The Tale of the Bamboo Cutter
list.summary: The first impossible task Princess Kaguya set her suitors. Prince Ishitsukuri brought an old bowl from a country temple and was found out.
list.imageAlt: A gilt-bronze begging bowl from Heian-period Japan, around the tenth century. The outside of the round bowl, whose mouth curves slightly inward, is engraved with fine flowers and vines, and the gilding is worn in places.

list.title: Jeweled Branch of Mount Horai
list.maker: Unknown (the prince had six craftsmen make a fake)
list.power: A branch of the tree on the immortals' island in the eastern sea, with silver roots, a golden trunk and fruit of white jewels.
list.firstRecord: The Tale of the Bamboo Cutter
list.summary: Princess Kaguya's impossible task. Prince Kuramochi had craftsmen make a fake and was exposed by the craftsmen who came to collect their wages.
list.imageAlt: A long, narrow portable writing box from Edo-period Japan, nineteenth century. On gold lacquer sprinkled with gold flakes, Mount Horai, the island of the immortals, is raised in relief: a rocky peak soars in the middle, with round-leaved trees, tiled pavilions and rippling water.

list.title: Robe of Fire-Rat Fur
list.owner: Abe no Miushi, Minister of the Right
list.maker: Unknown (obtained through the Tang merchant Wang Qing)
list.power: Put into fire, it does not burn; rather, the dirt burns away and it comes out clean, it was said.
list.firstRecord: The Tale of the Bamboo Cutter
list.summary: A legendary fur robe said to come out of the fire cleaner than before. When Princess Kaguya put it in the fire to test it, it burned up.
list.imageAlt: A page from a hand-painted picture book of The Tale of the Bamboo Cutter made in Japan in the late seventeenth century. Between golden clouds a thatched house appears; on its veranda an old couple looks at a tiny child in a basket, and children play in the yard.

list.title: Princess Kaguya's Elixir of Immortality
list.power: Whoever takes it does not die. The emperor had it burned on the mountain nearest to heaven.
list.firstRecord: The Tale of the Bamboo Cutter
list.summary: The elixir of immortality Princess Kaguya left when she returned to the moon. Refusing eternal life without her, the emperor had it burned on a mountaintop: Mount Fuji.
list.imageAlt: A lacquered medicine case (inro) of the Edo period, about 1785. A rooster is painted on the outside of the small case of stacked compartments, with a cord and a round cord bead above and tassels hanging below.

list.title: Higekiri
list.owner: The Minamoto clan; the warrior Watanabe no Tsuna
list.maker: Unknown (one of two swords made for Minamoto no Mitsunaka)
list.power: Tested on a criminal, it cut cleanly through his beard and was named Beard-Cutter; after it cut off a demon's arm, it became Demon-Cutter.
list.firstRecord: The Tale of the Heike, "Book of Swords"
list.summary: The treasured sword of the Minamoto clan with which Watanabe no Tsuna cut off an oni's arm. From then on it was called Demon-Cutter.
list.imageAlt: Nakamura Nakazo I as Watanabe no Tsuna, a color woodblock print by Katsukawa Shunzan, 1781. A kabuki actor in a red outer robe stands glaring, with the hilt of a long sword rising behind his shoulder.

list.title: Ikutachi and Ikuyumiya
list.maker: Unknown (possessions of Susanoo, god of the underworld)
list.power: The great sword and bow of life. With them Okuninushi drove out his brother gods and founded a country.
list.summary: The sword and bow of life that Okuninushi stole from Susanoo, god of the underworld, as he fled. With them he founded a country.
list.imageAlt: A gilt-bronze sword pommel from Kofun-period Japan, sixth century. A phoenix head with a raised crest sits within a round ring, and below it extends the tang that fitted into the grip.

list.title: Bell of Mii-dera
list.maker: Unknown (given to Fujiwara no Hidesato by the dragon god of Lake Biwa)
list.power: A temple bell from the Dragon Palace. When the strongman Benkei dragged it away, it cried, they say, "I want to go back."
list.summary: The bell Tawara Toda is said to have brought back from the dragon god after defeating a giant centipede. It hangs at Mii-dera.
list.imageAlt: Evening Bell at Mii Temple, from the Eight Views of Omi, a color woodblock print by Utagawa Hiroshige, late 1830s. The roofs of Mii-dera show among the trees of a green mountain on Lake Biwa, with sailboats and far mountains, and the title and a poem at the top.

list.title: Dokkaebi Club
list.power: Strike it, saying "Out with gold!", and whatever one wishes comes pouring out.
list.firstRecord: Duan Chengshi, Youyang Zazu, "Tale of Bangi"
list.summary: The goblins' club that pours out whatever one wishes when struck. It was first recorded in a ninth-century Tang book as the tale of Bangi, a man of Silla.
list.imageAlt: A jade ogre mask (taotie) ornament from the Warring States period of China, 475–221 BCE. On a pale-green jade plaque, scrolling lines in relief form the face of a horned monster.

list.title: Jumong's Bow
list.maker: Jumong (made it himself at the age of seven)
list.power: Every arrow hit its mark, so that "jumong," meaning a fine archer, became his name.
list.summary: The bow of Goguryeo's founder, who shot so well that his very name became "Jumong." Fish and turtles made a bridge for him to cross.
list.imageAlt: A leather bow case, quiver and belt from Tibet or Mongolia, fifteenth to seventeenth century. A bow case and quiver of dark brown leather are fitted with round ornaments decorated in gold, joined by a belt.

list.title: King Suro's Golden Box
list.owner: The nine chiefs of Garak; King Suro
list.power: A box let down from heaven on a purple cord. From the six golden eggs inside were born the kings of the six Gaya states.
list.summary: The golden box that came down from heaven onto Gujibong Peak. From a golden egg inside it was born King Suro of Garak.
list.imageAlt: A Goryeo bronze lidded bowl of the thirteenth century. A bowl covered by a rounded lid with a knob stands on a high foot, its surface coated with green patina.

list.title: Seo-nyeo's Silk
list.titleOriginal: 細綃 (延烏郞 細烏女)
list.power: When a sacrifice was offered to heaven with this silk, the lost light of Silla's sun and moon returned.
list.summary: The silk woven by Seo-nyeo, who crossed the sea to Japan. When a sacrifice was offered with it, Silla's sun and moon regained their light.
list.imageAlt: A Joseon bridal robe (hwarot) of the late nineteenth century. The red silk robe with outspread sleeves is lavishly embroidered with lotuses, peonies, birds and butterflies, with multicolored stripes on the sleeves and white cuffs at the ends.

list.title: Princess Bari's Water of Life
list.maker: Unknown (the healing spring of the far western realm at the end of the underworld)
list.power: A healing water from the underworld that brings back the breath of the dead when poured into their mouths.
list.summary: The healing water fetched from the end of the underworld by Baridegi, the abandoned seventh princess. It brought her dead parents back to life.
list.imageAlt: A Goryeo celadon bottle of the twelfth to thirteenth century. A slender, long neck rises from the round body, which is incised with a floral design in fine lines.

list.title: Heungbu's Gourds
list.power: Sawn open, they pour out rice, money and silk. Gourds won through greed pour out misfortune.
list.summary: Gourds grown from a seed brought by the swallow whose leg was mended. From Heungbu's gourds came treasure; from Nolbu's, misfortune.
list.imageAlt: A Goryeo gourd-shaped celadon ewer of the thirteenth century. The body looks like a small gourd set on a large one, with a short spout and a long curving handle, covered in a soft green glaze.

list.title: Yuri's Broken Sword
list.maker: Unknown (Jumong broke it in two and hid one half)
list.power: Half of a sword broken in two. When fitted to the other half, blood flowed and the two became one sword again.
list.summary: The piece of sword Jumong hid under a pine on a seven-cornered stone when he left. His son Yuri found it and met his father.
list.imageAlt: A Joseon sword and scabbard of the sixteenth to nineteenth century. Beside a straight sword with a golden guard and a ring-pommeled grip lies a red-lacquered scabbard.

list.title: Haemosu's Five-Dragon Chariot
list.owner: Haemosu, son of the heavenly emperor
list.power: A chariot drawn by five dragons. In the morning it comes down to earth, and in the evening it returns to heaven.
list.summary: The chariot of five dragons in which Haemosu traveled between heaven and earth. He came down in the morning and rose to heaven in the evening.
list.imageAlt: A stoneware pedestal vessel shaped like a pair of chariot wheels from Gaya, fifth century. On a flaring pedestal stand a pair of spoked wheels, topped by two horn-shaped cups.

list.title: Mask of Cheoyong
list.owner: Cheoyong, son of the Dragon of the East Sea
list.power: Merely by posting a picture of Cheoyong's face, the spirit that spreads disease is kept from entering the house.
list.summary: The face of Cheoyong, who drove off the spirit of pestilence with song and dance. The people of Silla posted his face on their gates to keep evil away.
list.imageAlt: A Joseon wooden mask of an old man from the nineteenth century. The black-painted face is carved with a wrinkled brow, open eyes and a prominent nose, and a long beard of hair hangs from the chin.

list.title: Kim Yu-sin's Treasured Sword
list.owner: Kim Yu-sin, great general of Silla
list.power: Starlight came down from heaven and filled it with divine power.
list.summary: The sword that was filled with divine power when starlight came down as Kim Yu-sin prayed on Mount Yeolbak. He led the way in uniting the Three Kingdoms.
list.imageAlt: A Joseon sword and scabbard of the sixteenth to nineteenth century. Beside a straight sword with a grip and guard decorated in silver and gold lies a scabbard with silvery fittings.

list.title: Veillantif
list.power: Roland's warhorse, which carried him into the heart of the Saracen host.
list.summary: The warhorse Roland rode into his last battle at the pass of Roncevaux. Its name is read as 'the wakeful one.'
list.imageAlt: A woodcut printed on blue-washed paper by the German artist Hans Burgkmair in 1508, Equestrian Portrait of the Emperor Maximilian. Under an arch, the emperor in armor and a plumed helmet rides a horse in a patterned caparison toward the left, with a double-headed eagle banner behind.

list.title: Almace
list.power: With this sword the warrior-priest Turpin cut down Saracen after Saracen.
list.summary: The sword Archbishop Turpin of Reims wielded at Roncevaux. He fought with it until he fell.
list.imageAlt: A French double-edged sword of the thirteenth century. Below a disk-shaped pommel and a straight crossguard runs a long blade that tapers toward the point, darkened with age.

list.title: Babieca
list.power: Legend says that even after El Cid died, Babieca carried him out of the city gates and put the enemy to flight.
list.summary: El Cid's beloved warhorse. A legend tells that it carried the dead Cid out of the gates of Valencia.
list.imageAlt: Plate 11 of Francisco Goya's print series La Tauromaquia, El Cid Campeador Spearing Another Bull (1816 edition, printed 1876). A knight in a plumed helmet drives a lance down from the saddle while a bull charges the horse with lowered head.

list.title: Balisarda
list.power: Forged by magic, it could cut even enchanted armor and charmed things.
