list.summary: A sword the sorceress Falerina forged to kill Orlando. It could cut even what was enchanted.
list.imageAlt: A rapier made in Milan, Italy, about 1625–50. Below a wire-wrapped grip, curving iron bars and a pierced cup-shaped guard enclose the hand, and a long, slender blade extends below.

list.title: Ring of Angelica
list.power: Worn on the finger it made every enchantment fail; held in the mouth it made the wearer invisible.
list.summary: The ring of Angelica, princess of Cathay. Worn, it broke enchantments; held in the mouth, it made her invisible.
list.imageAlt: An engraving made about 1570 by the Italian brothers Giorgio and Teodoro Ghisi, Angelica and Medoro. Beneath dense trees the naked Angelica and Medoro embrace and carve their names on a tree trunk. A river and town appear at right.

list.title: Horn of Astolfo
list.maker: Unknown (given by the good fairy Logistilla)
list.power: One blast made every man and beast that heard it flee in terror.
list.summary: The horn the good fairy Logistilla gave Astolfo. Everything that heard it fled in fear.
list.imageAlt: An ivory horn carved in southern Italy or Sicily in the twelfth century, the so-called Horn of Saint Blaise. Bands of animals and scrolls encircle the wide mouth and the narrow tip, and the middle is left smooth.

list.title: Lancelot's Ring
list.power: Looking into its stone showed whether an enchantment before him was false.
list.firstRecord: Chrétien de Troyes, Lancelot, the Knight of the Cart
list.summary: The ring the Lady of the Lake, who raised Lancelot, gave him. Looking into it dispelled enchantments.
list.imageAlt: A side panel of an ivory casket made in France about 1330. Twisted columns divide it into scenes from knightly romances: at center left a knight fights a lion, at right Lancelot crosses a sword bridge over the waves, and at far right people watch from the battlements.

list.title: Merlin's Mirror
list.owner: King Ryence of Deheubarth and his daughter Britomart
list.power: It showed in perfect sight whatever thing the world contained.
list.summary: A round mirror Merlin made for a king of Britain. It showed whatever one wished to see.
list.imageAlt: A round bronze magic mirror made in Japan in the nineteenth century. The six characters of Namu Amida Butsu are raised down the center of the back. When light is reflected from the polished face, an image of the Buddha Amida appears in the reflection.

list.title: Balm of Fierabras
list.maker: Unknown (said to be the balm used to embalm Christ's body)
list.power: Drunk or applied, it healed any wound at once.
list.summary: The balm said to have embalmed the body of Christ. The Saracen prince Fierabras seized it in Rome.
list.imageAlt: The front of a pilgrim's flask for holy oil, cast in tin and lead in Palestine about 600, in the early Byzantine period. Below a narrow neck, the flat round body bears the Crucifixion, with a Greek inscription around the edge.

list.title: Shield of Galahad
list.maker: Josephus, son of Joseph of Arimathea (who drew the cross in his own blood)
list.power: Anyone but Galahad who bore it came to harm.
list.firstRecord: The Quest of the Holy Grail (Vulgate Cycle)
list.summary: A white shield with a red cross. Only Galahad, who would find the Grail, could bear it safely.
list.imageAlt: A tall wooden shield made in Erfurt, Germany, in the early fourteenth century. A large wheel in silver foil is painted on the upper part of the red, leather-covered ground, and the paint has flaked in places with age.

list.title: Balmung
list.power: The Nibelung kings gave it as payment for dividing their treasure, and with it Siegfried cut down those kings and their giants.
list.summary: The sword Siegfried won with the Nibelung treasure. After his death it passed to his enemy Hagen.
list.imageAlt: A sword probably made in Germany in the fifteenth century. Below a round pommel, a wood and leather grip and a straight crossguard, a long straight blade extends.

list.title: Svalinn
list.power: It stands before the sun so that its fire does not burn the earth and sea.
list.summary: The shield set before the sun. If it fell, mountains and sea would burn up.
list.imageAlt: A round steel shield made in northern Italy about 1550–1600. Etched panels radiate like sunbeams from a pointed central boss, and rivets are set close together along the rope-like border.

list.title: Freyr's Sword
list.owner: Freyr, god of plenty, later his servant Skírnir
list.power: When a wise man held it, it fought the giants by itself.
list.summary: Freyr's sword that fought by itself. He gave it to his servant to win the giant's daughter Gerd.
list.imageAlt: A fifteenth-century European steel sword. Below a round pommel is a crossguard with down-curved ends, and a long, straight blade tapers toward the point.

list.title: Sif's Golden Hair
list.power: Set on her head, it took root and grew like real hair.
list.summary: Hair the dwarves spun from gold to replace the hair Loki cut from Sif. It grew like real hair.
list.imageAlt: A pair of gold earrings or hair ornaments from ancient Greece. Hollow gold tubes are coiled into spirals with a palmette at the center, and each end finishes in a ram's head.

list.title: Freyja's Falcon Cloak
list.power: Whoever put it on became a falcon and could fly.
list.summary: Freyja's feather cloak that turned its wearer into a falcon. Loki borrowed it to fly to the land of the giants.
list.imageAlt: White Falcon, a sixteenth-century Korean hanging scroll on silk from the Joseon dynasty. Beneath a flowering tree a white falcon perches on a rock with wings spread and head bowed, painted feather by feather, while the trees and grasses are drawn with free, calligraphic lines.

list.title: Beowulf's Byrnie
list.power: It held even when Grendel's mother drove her blade down on him.
list.summary: The mail shirt Beowulf wore. Made by the legendary smith Wayland, it stopped even the blade of Grendel's mother.
list.imageAlt: A mail shirt probably made in Germany about 1400–1450. Steel and brass rings are linked one by one into a short-sleeved shirt fastened at the front with straps. In the photograph a helmet is placed above it.

list.title: Mimung
list.owner: The smith Velent, later his son Witege
list.power: So sharp it split even a tuft of wool drifting on the water.
list.summary: The sword the smith Velent forged for a contest on which his life depended. It split a tuft of wool floating on the water.
list.imageAlt: A hand-and-a-half sword made in Germany about 1540–80. Below a conical pommel is a long sharkskin grip, with straight quillons extending to either side and rings enclosing the hand, and the double-edged blade continues below.

list.title: Nibelung Hoard
list.owner: The kings of the Nibelungs, Siegfried, Kriemhild
list.power: So much gold and jewels that twelve wagons could not carry it in one trip; it brought strife and death to everyone who held it.
list.summary: The treasure Siegfried won from the Nibelungs. Hagen sank it in the Rhine, and no one ever found it.
list.imageAlt: Finale of the Rhinegold, a lithograph by the French artist Henri Fantin-Latour, 1877. Above, the gods rise through clouds; at lower left the Rhine maidens reach up from the waves. A bar of music and the title are written at the bottom.

list.title: Grani
list.maker: Of the line of Sleipnir, Odin's horse
list.power: He carried the dragon's gold and leaped the wall of fire with Sigurd on his back.
list.summary: The horse Sigurd chose with Odin's help. He carried the dragon Fafnir's gold and leaped the wall of fire.
list.imageAlt: A bronze horse made in Germany in the 1630s or later. It stands squarely on four legs with its head slightly lowered, its mane and muscles smoothly finished.

list.title: Eldhrímnir
list.power: A boar was boiled in it every day to feed the warriors of Valhalla, and each evening the boar was alive again.
list.summary: The cauldron of Odin's hall Valhalla. A boar was boiled in it every day for the warriors, and it came back to life.
list.imageAlt: An Etruscan bronze cauldron of about 550 BCE. The round, deep body is covered with green patina, and an arched iron handle hangs from rings on either side.

list.title: Horn of Brân Galed
list.power: Whatever drink one wished for was found in it.
list.firstRecord: The Thirteen Treasures of the Island of Britain
list.summary: One of the Thirteen Treasures of the Island of Britain. Whatever drink one wished for filled it.
list.imageAlt: A glass drinking horn of about 575–625, probably Lombard. Reddish-brown feather patterns are worked into the clear glass and fine white threads are wound around it in a spiral; part of the wide rim is broken.

list.title: Halter of Clydno Eiddyn
list.power: Fastened to a staple at the foot of his bed, it held whatever horse he wished for.
list.firstRecord: The Thirteen Treasures of the Island of Britain
list.summary: One of the Thirteen Treasures of the Island of Britain. Whatever horse one wished for would be found in this halter.
list.imageAlt: A horse bit made in Italy about 1580–1600. Curved iron bars, chains and rings for the reins form the bit, and gilt bronze bosses are set on each side.

list.title: Hamper of Gwyddno Garanhir
list.power: Put in food for one person, and food for a hundred came out.
list.firstRecord: The Thirteen Treasures of the Island of Britain
list.summary: One of the Thirteen Treasures of the Island of Britain. Put in food for one, and food for a hundred came out.
list.imageAlt: A silver fruit basket made in London, England, in 1729. The oval body is pierced with a lattice like woven wicker, with two twisted silver handles and a leaf-pattern rim.

list.title: Whetstone of Tudwal Tudglyd
list.power: If a brave man sharpened his sword on it, anyone it drew blood from would die; if a coward did, the sword would not cut at all.
list.firstRecord: The Thirteen Treasures of the Island of Britain
list.summary: One of the Thirteen Treasures of the Island of Britain. Sharpened by a brave man, a sword became deadly; by a coward, it went dull.
list.imageAlt: A whetstone handle cast in bronze in Luristan, Iran, about 1100–900 BCE. An ibex stretches its long neck, its horns curving into a loop above its head, and the whetstone fitted into the socket below.

list.title: Coat of Padarn Beisrudd
list.power: It fitted a man of noble blood perfectly and would not go on anyone else.
list.firstRecord: The Thirteen Treasures of the Island of Britain
list.summary: One of the Thirteen Treasures of the Island of Britain. It fitted the well-born perfectly and would not fit anyone else.
list.imageAlt: A mail cape, the so-called bishop's mantle, made in Germany or Switzerland about 1520–30. Riveted steel rings, some of brass, cover the shoulders and chest, with a stiff standing collar around the neck.

list.title: Chariot of Morgan Mwynfawr
list.power: Whoever sat in it and wished to be anywhere would be there at once.
list.firstRecord: The Thirteen Treasures of the Island of Britain
list.summary: One of the Thirteen Treasures of the Island of Britain. Whoever rode in it was carried at once wherever they wished.
list.imageAlt: A red-figure mixing bowl (calyx-krater) made in Lucania, southern Italy, about 400 BCE. In the center of the front, Medea flies up in a dragon-drawn chariot within a sunburst, with winged goddesses at the upper sides and fallen children on an altar below.

list.title: Cauldron of Rebirth
list.owner: The giant king Bendigeidfran, later the Irish king Matholwch
list.maker: Unknown (brought by a giant couple who came out of a lake in Ireland)
list.power: Dead warriors put into it rose the next day to fight again, but they could not speak.
list.firstRecord: The Four Branches of the Mabinogi, Branwen Daughter of Llŷr
list.summary: A cauldron that brought dead warriors back to life. It turned the war between Britain and Ireland into a slaughter.
list.imageAlt: A large bronze cauldron made by Greeks in Campania, southern Italy, in the fifth century BCE. A thick rim crowns the broad-shouldered, round-bottomed body, and green patina mottles the surface.

list.title: Rhiannon's Bag
list.owner: Rhiannon and Pwyll, prince of Dyfed
list.power: However much was put in, it was never full.
list.firstRecord: The Four Branches of the Mabinogi, Pwyll Prince of Dyfed
list.summary: A small bag Rhiannon gave Pwyll. Nothing could fill it, and it became a trap for her rival suitor.
list.imageAlt: A reliquary bag of silk woven with gold thread, made in Spain, probably Almería, in the late 1100s–1300s. The long bag is densely woven with a lozenge pattern, crossed by a horizontal stripe, and its edges are frayed.

list.title: Mac an Luin
list.owner: Fionn mac Cumhaill, leader of the Fianna
list.maker: The one-eyed smith Lon mac Liomtha
list.power: With this sword Fionn defeated countless enemies and monsters.
list.summary: The sword of Fionn mac Cumhaill, leader of the Fianna. Ballads say it was forged by the mysterious smith Lon.
list.imageAlt: A basket-hilted sword made in Britain about 1720–40. A gilded iron basket lined with red cloth encloses the whole hand, and a straight blade continues below.

list.title: Lúin of Celtchar
list.owner: Celtchar mac Uthechair, warrior of Ulster
list.power: When its lust for blood rose it blazed up of itself, and only a cauldron of dark poison could quench it.
list.firstRecord: The Destruction of Da Derga's Hostel
list.summary: The spear of Celtchar, warrior of Ulster. Before battle it blazed up of itself and had to be plunged into a cauldron of dark poison.
list.imageAlt: A parade spear probably made in Augsburg, Germany, about 1570–1600. The broad, leaf-shaped steel head is etched with ornament, with brass lugs on either side below it, and a woolen tassel hangs from the leather-strapped wooden shaft.

list.title: Talaria
list.owner: Hermes, messenger of the gods, later the hero Perseus
list.power: Bound on the feet, they carried their wearer as swift as the wind over the sea and the boundless earth.
list.summary: The immortal golden sandals of Hermes. Later painters and sculptors gave them wings.
list.imageAlt: A Roman bronze statuette of Mercury (Hermes) from the first century CE. A young god with small wings sprouting from his hair stands with a cloak over his left shoulder and sandals on his feet, holding a purse in his right hand.

list.title: Nepenthe
list.maker: Unknown (given by Polydamna, a woman of Egypt)
list.power: Mixed into wine, it banished grief so completely that for that day one shed no tears even at the loss of a parent or brother.
list.summary: An Egyptian drug Helen mixed into wine. Whoever drank it forgot every sorrow for that day.
list.imageAlt: A perfume flask (alabastron) carved from travertine in Ptolemaic Egypt about 305–222 BCE. Above a long, slender body are a narrow neck and small knob handles, and a thin disk lid covers the top.

list.title: Moly
list.maker: Unknown (Hermes pulled it from the ground and gave it to him)
list.power: Whoever carried it could drink the witch Circe's potion without being turned into a beast.
list.summary: The herb Hermes gave Odysseus. Its root was black and its flower white as milk, and it protected him from Circe's magic.
list.imageAlt: Circe Giving Drink to the Companions of Ulysses, a chiaroscuro woodcut by Antonio da Trento after Parmigianino, Italy, 1540s. In the round scene Circe holds out a cup at center, the companions take cups and drink at left, and animals appear at right and below.

list.title: Tripods of Hephaestus
list.power: With golden wheels beneath their legs, they rolled by themselves to the gathering of the gods and back home again.
list.summary: Twenty tripods made by Hephaestus. Fitted with golden wheels, they went to and from the gods' gathering by themselves.
list.imageAlt: A Greek bronze rod tripod stand of the early sixth century BCE. The round ring at the top is decorated with horse heads and animals, and three legs of crossed thin rods end in animal feet. The surface is covered with green corrosion.

list.title: Golden Maidens of Hephaestus
list.power: They thought and spoke like living girls and supported their lame master as he walked.
list.summary: Handmaidens Hephaestus made of gold. Like living girls, they had minds, voices and strength.
list.imageAlt: A bronze mirror made in Greece, probably Sicyon, about 470–460 BCE. A clothed woman stands holding a round mirror disk above her head, while winged Erotes fly in from either side. A ring for hanging is attached above the disk.

list.title: Net of Hephaestus
list.power: Fine as a spider's web, it was invisible even to the gods, and once caught, no one could loosen or break it.
list.summary: The net Hephaestus hung around his bed to catch his wife Aphrodite with Ares. Even the gods could not see it.
list.imageAlt: Mars and Venus Trapped by Vulcan, an octagonal gilt-bronze relief made in Italy in the late sixteenth century by Guglielmo della Porta. Below center the lovers lie caught in a net on a couch, while the gods gather around and above to watch.

list.title: Pelian Ash Spear
list.maker: The centaur Chiron (who cut the ash on Mount Pelion)
list.power: So heavy and huge that no one but Achilles could wield it.
list.summary: The spear Chiron made from an ash of Mount Pelion and gave to Peleus. Only Achilles could wield it.
list.imageAlt: Achilles Dragging the Body of Hector, an etching made in Italy in 1648. Achilles in a helmet stands in a chariot with Hector's body dragged behind; a winged goddess appears above, and the walls of Troy rise in the background.

list.title: Xanthus and Balius
list.maker: Born of Zephyrus, the west wind, and the Harpy Podarge
list.power: Horses swift as the wind that never aged or died. Xanthus foretold his master's death in a human voice.
list.summary: The two immortal horses that drew Achilles' chariot. Given a voice by Hera, Xanthus foretold his master's death.
list.imageAlt: A black-figure neck-amphora made in Athens about 520–510 BCE. On the body a warrior departs for battle with a chariot drawn by four horses; below run bands of meander and bud patterns, and palmettes decorate the neck.

list.title: Scepter of Agamemnon
list.power: The sign of kingship handed down from Zeus; whoever held it ruled many islands and all Argos.
list.summary: The scepter Hephaestus made, passed down from Zeus to Agamemnon. It was the sign of his kingship over the Greek army.
list.imageAlt: A tin-bronze scepter head made on Cyprus about 1450–1050 BCE. An animal head is attached to the end of a hollow tube, with red and blue inlays in its eyes and forehead. The surface is rough with corrosion.

list.title: Cup of Nestor
list.owner: Nestor, the old king of Pylos
list.power: When it was full, others could barely lift it, but old Nestor raised it with ease.
list.summary: The cup studded with golden nails that Nestor brought from home. On each of its four handles two golden doves were feeding.
list.imageAlt: A gold kantharos from Mycenaean Greece, about 1550–1500 BCE. Two tall handles rise on either side of a round-bellied cup hammered from sheet gold, which stands on a small foot.

list.title: Aaron's Rod
list.power: In a single night it sprouted, blossomed and bore ripe almonds.
list.summary: Of the rods of the twelve tribes, only Aaron's sprouted, blossomed and bore almonds overnight. It was kept before the Ark of the Covenant.
list.imageAlt: The Priest Aaron, a limestone figure carved in France about 1170. A bearded man in a hood sits holding a round object in both hands on his lap, his robe falling in layered folds.

list.title: Breastplate of the High Priest
list.owner: Aaron the high priest and the high priests after him
list.power: The high priest wore it on his chest before God, and with the Urim and Thummim placed in it he sought God's will.
list.summary: The high priest's breastpiece, set with twelve gems engraved with the names of the twelve tribes. The Urim and Thummim were placed inside it.
list.imageAlt: Alexander the Great and the High Priest of Jerusalem, an engraving made in Italy in the mid-1540s. Alexander in armor kneels, and the high priest in a tall headdress stands before him with a raised hand. A domed temple appears behind.

list.title: Menorah of the Temple
list.owner: The Tabernacle in the wilderness, later the Temple in Jerusalem
list.power: A seven-branched lampstand hammered from a talent of pure gold, which lit the sanctuary.
list.summary: A seven-branched lampstand hammered from pure gold. It lit the sanctuary of the Tabernacle in the wilderness and of the Temple in Jerusalem.
list.imageAlt: A silver Hanukkah lamp made in Rome in 1773–75 by the silversmith Gaspare Vanneschi. A branched menorah is embossed at the center of a backplate topped by a shell-shaped arch; a row of oil lamps is attached below, and a hanging cord with tassels is at the top.

list.title: Manna
list.owner: The people of Israel in the wilderness
list.power: It fell from heaven every morning and fed the Israelites wandering in the wilderness for forty years.
list.summary: The food that fell from heaven every morning in the wilderness. It was white like coriander seed and tasted like wafers made with honey.
list.imageAlt: Gathering of Manna, a woodcut from the devotional book Der Schatzbehalter (The Treasure Chest), printed in Nuremberg, Germany, in 1491. Round manna pours down from beneath the clouds, and in front of a camp of pointed tents people bend down to gather it into baskets.

list.title: Joseph's Coat
list.power: It showed his father Jacob's special love, and it stirred his brothers' envy.
list.summary: The long robe Jacob made for his beloved son Joseph. His brothers dipped it in goat's blood to deceive their father.
list.imageAlt: Jacob Is Shown Joseph's Coat, a maiolica (tin-glazed earthenware) plate painted by Gironimo Tomasi in Italy about 1560–75. Before old Jacob, seated in a chair at right, his sons hold out the robe, with arched buildings and a landscape behind.

list.title: Elijah's Mantle
list.owner: The prophet Elijah, later his disciple Elisha
list.power: Rolled up and struck on the water, it parted the Jordan so that one could cross on dry ground.
list.summary: The mantle with which Elijah parted the Jordan. It fell as he rose to heaven in a chariot of fire, and he left it to his disciple Elisha.
list.imageAlt: Elisha and Elijah's Chariot of Fire, an engraving by Jan Saenredam after Abraham Bloemaert, the Netherlands, 1604. Beneath a large tree in a forest Elisha kneels with both arms outstretched, looking up at the sky, where the chariot of fire rises in the distance.

list.title: Gideon's Fleece
list.power: Dew fell only on the fleece, and the next day only the fleece stayed dry, revealing God's will.
list.summary: The fleece Gideon laid on the threshing floor to confirm God's will. Dew fell only on the fleece, and the next day only the fleece was dry.
list.imageAlt: A page of a Biblia Pauperum blockbook, third edition, printed in the Netherlands about 1465. The Annunciation is at center, Eve and the serpent at left, and Gideon with the fleece at right, with prophets and Latin text above and below, printed in brown ink with traces of hand coloring.

list.title: Throne of Solomon
list.power: An ivory throne overlaid with pure gold, with lions on each of its six steps. Nothing like it was made in any kingdom.
list.summary: Solomon's ivory throne overlaid with pure gold. Twelve lions stood on either side of its six steps.
list.imageAlt: The Judgment of Solomon, stained glass made in the Southern Netherlands about 1530. Courtiers and two women gather before King Solomon, seated on an ornate golden throne. Silver stain gives a yellow tone to the colored and white glass, and lead lines cross the scene here and there.

list.title: Keys of Peter
list.owner: The apostle Peter, later the popes of Rome
list.power: Whatever is bound on earth is bound in heaven, and whatever is loosed on earth is loosed in heaven.
list.summary: The keys of the kingdom of heaven Jesus promised to Peter. They later became the symbol of papal authority.
list.imageAlt: A fire-gilt bronze statuette of Saint Peter made in Naples, Italy, in 1635–36. Peter, with a curly beard and a heavy cloak, stands holding a book in his left hand, his right hand lowered. The base set with red stone was made later.

list.title: Holy Nails
list.owner: Empress Helena and her son Constantine the Great
list.power: Nails of the Cross found by Helena; tradition says she had them set in the emperor's crown and his horse's bridle to protect him.
list.firstRecord: Ambrose, On the Death of Theodosius
list.summary: The nails that fastened Jesus to the Cross. Tradition says Empress Helena found them in Jerusalem and had them set in her son Constantine's crown and his horse's bridle.
list.imageAlt: Gold pendant and necklace parts from the eastern Mediterranean, probably Sirmium or Nicomedia, about 324–26. At the center of an octagonal pendant is a gold coin of Constantine the Great ringed by eight small busts, with two Corinthian-column spacers and a jeweled clasp above.

list.title: Pukku and Mikku
list.power: Gilgamesh's favorite plaything, which in the end fell into the netherworld and left Enkidu trapped there.
list.firstRecord: Sumerian poem Gilgamesh, Enkidu and the Netherworld
list.summary: A plaything Gilgamesh made from the huluppu tree. When it fell into the netherworld, Enkidu went down to fetch it.
list.imageAlt: A figurine plaque of a bearded man playing a drum, pressed in a mold and fired in Babylonia in the seventh–sixth century BCE. A long-bearded man stands holding a round drum against his chest; the clay is worn and the outlines are blurred.

list.title: Net of Marduk
list.power: With the four winds stationed at its four corners, it kept Tiamat, goddess of the sea, from escaping.
list.summary: The net Marduk made to capture Tiamat, goddess of the sea. He set the four winds at its corners so nothing could escape.
list.imageAlt: The top fragment of a kudurru (boundary stone) carved in limestone in Babylonia under the Second Dynasty of Isin, about 1156–1025 BCE. A horned dragon, the mushhushshu, sits beside a pointed spade-shaped symbol set on a pedestal, with cuneiform remaining below.

list.title: Etana's Eagle
list.power: It carried Etana on its back up to the heaven of Anu, god of the sky.
list.firstRecord: The Legend of Etana (Old Babylonian version)
list.summary: The eagle that flew up to heaven with Etana, king of Kish, on its back. Etana was seeking the 'plant of birth' that would give him a son.
list.imageAlt: A round ceramic jar from western Iran in the Early Bronze Age, about 2500–1900 BCE. An eagle with outspread wings is painted in black on the shoulder of the pale body, with a broad band of wavy lines below it.

list.title: Adapa's Bread and Water of Life
list.maker: Unknown (offered by Anu, god of the sky)
list.power: Whoever ate and drank them would live forever.
list.summary: The bread and water that Anu, god of the sky, offered the sage Adapa. Adapa refused them, thinking they were the food of death, and lost eternal life.
list.imageAlt: An apkallu (sage) figure modeled in clay in Assyria in the ninth–eighth century BCE. A man wearing a fish skin like a hood from his head down his back stands with both hands held before his chest; the surface is worn and the outlines are blurred.

list.title: Chest of Osiris
list.power: Made to fit the body of Osiris exactly, it floated down the Nile with him sealed inside.
list.summary: The chest Set made to trap his brother Osiris. It drifted across the sea and was enclosed in the trunk of a tree at Byblos.
list.imageAlt: The coffin of Bakenmut, a priest of the temple of Amun, made of gessoed and painted sycamore fig in Thebes, Egypt, about 1000–900 BCE. The lid at left shows a face, a wig, a broad collar and deities, and the inside of the coffin at right is densely painted with gods and symbols.

list.title: Webaoner's Wax Crocodile
list.power: Thrown into the water, a wax crocodile seven fingers long became a living crocodile seven cubits long.
list.summary: A small crocodile the priest Webaoner modeled in wax. Thrown into the water, it became a great crocodile and dragged his wife's lover under.
list.imageAlt: A small crocodile figure made of Egyptian blue in the late Middle Kingdom of Egypt, about 1850–1700 BCE. The sky-blue crocodile lies flat on its belly with scales incised along its back. A museum number in red writing is visible at right.

list.title: Babr-e Bayan
list.power: It is said that fire could not burn it, water could not soak it and no weapon could pierce it.
list.summary: The tiger-skin battle coat Rostam always wore over his armor. It is said to have warded off fire, water and weapons.
list.imageAlt: Rustam Meets the Challenge of Ashkabus, a page from a Shahnameh painted in Shiraz, Iran, about 1590–1600. On a purple field scattered with flowers, Rostam, on foot, shoots an arrow, an enemy champion falls at right, and armies with banners gather above.

list.title: Ox-Headed Mace of Fereydun
list.maker: Smiths (Fereydun drew its shape for them)
list.power: The ox-headed mace that struck down Zahhak, the serpent-shouldered tyrant.
list.summary: The ox-headed mace Fereydun had smiths make from a shape he drew. With it he overthrew the tyrant Zahhak.
list.imageAlt: A steel and gold mace made in Iran in the nineteenth century. The head is shaped like an ox head with horns and ears, its face inlaid with gold scrolling vines, and the long shaft is ringed with gold bands.

list.title: Flying Throne of Kay Kavus
list.power: Starving eagles chased the meat hung above them and hauled the throne up into the sky.
list.summary: The throne Kay Kavus launched by harnessing four eagles, to conquer the heavens. When the eagles tired, it fell into a forest.
list.imageAlt: Kai Kavus Ascends to the Sky, folio 134r of the Shahnameh made for Shah Tahmasp of Safavid Iran, about 1525–30. Between Persian verses above and below, Kay Kavus rises into the sky on a throne drawn by eagles as people look up from below. Gold is flecked in the margins.

list.title: Enmerkar's Clay Tablet
list.power: By writing on clay a message too long for his envoy to memorize, he sent words in writing for the first time.
list.firstRecord: Sumerian epic Enmerkar and the Lord of Aratta
list.summary: The clay tablet on which Enmerkar, king of Uruk, is said to have written for the first time. The lord of Aratta could not read the writing he had never seen before.
list.imageAlt: A clay tablet letter written in Babylonia about 1632 BCE. Cuneiform is pressed in dense horizontal lines across a palm-sized rectangular tablet.

list.title: Kaustubha
list.owner: Vishnu, the Preserver (and his avatar Krishna)
list.maker: Unknown (it rose when the Ocean of Milk was churned)
list.power: The most radiant jewel to rise from the Ocean of Milk, which Vishnu always wears on his chest.
list.summary: A jewel that rose when the gods and asuras churned the Ocean of Milk. Vishnu always wears it on his chest.
list.imageAlt: A granite figure of Vishnu carved in Tamil Nadu, South India, in the early Chola dynasty, about 900–950. The four-armed god in a tall crown stands on a base, holding a discus and a conch in his two rear hands, with layers of ornaments on his chest.

list.title: Uchchaihshravas
list.maker: Unknown (it rose from the Ocean of Milk)
list.power: A dazzling white horse born from the Ocean of Milk, the first of all horses.
list.summary: The white horse that rose when the Ocean of Milk was churned. It became the horse of Indra, king of the gods.
list.imageAlt: A Saddled Horse, painted on paper by an artist of the Pahari kingdoms of northern India about 1750. A bridled horse stands facing left, head lowered and neck arched, with a saddle and saddlecloth on its back. It is drawn in line and lightly colored.

list.title: Sharanga
list.owner: Vishnu, the Preserver, and his avatars Krishna and Rama
list.power: The bow of Vishnu, which only his avatar could string.
list.summary: The bow of Vishnu. His avatar Krishna was called 'the bearer of Sharanga.'
list.imageAlt: A page from a Ramayana painted in Malwa, central India, about 1650: Rama, Sita and Lakshmana visit the hermitage of the sage Bharadvaja. Against a red ground, blue-skinned Rama, holding a bow, bows with his companions to the sage; the yellow-doored hermitage is at right, trees above.

list.title: Vasavi Shakti
list.owner: Indra, king of the gods, later the hero Karna
list.power: It could be hurled only once, and whoever it was thrown at would surely die.
list.summary: The spear Indra gave Karna in exchange for his armor and earrings. It could be thrown only once and was sure to kill.
list.imageAlt: A male figure, possibly Indra, carved in schist in Gandhara (probably the Swat region of present-day Pakistan) in the 300s–400s CE. The figure, apparently unfinished with only its broad outlines carved, stands in a niche and wears a flat-topped crown.

list.title: Chandrahasa
list.owner: Ravana, the demon king of Lanka
list.power: The sword Shiva granted Ravana; its name means 'laughter of the moon.'
list.summary: The sword Shiva granted to the demon king Ravana. Its name means 'laughter of the moon.'
list.imageAlt: Ravana Shaking Mount Kailasa, a sandstone relief carved in Madhya Pradesh, central India, in the eighth century. Above, Shiva and Parvati sit side by side on the mountain; below, many-headed, many-armed Ravana lifts and shakes the mountain, surrounded by densely carved attendants.

list.title: Sita's Hair Jewel
list.power: As the token that Hanuman had found Sita, it told Rama she was still alive.
list.summary: The hair jewel the captive Sita gave Hanuman as a token when he found her. Rama wept when he saw it.
list.imageAlt: Hanuman Spies Sita in the Ashoka Grove, a page from the 'Shangri' Ramayana painted in Himachal Pradesh, northern India, about 1700–25. On a night with a crescent moon, Sita sits in a white pavilion surrounded by animal-faced demonesses, while Hanuman looks down from a tree.

list.title: Draupadi's Sari
list.owner: Draupadi, wife of the five Pandava brothers
list.power: However hard it was pulled, the cloth went on without end and saved Draupadi from disgrace.
list.summary: The garment of Draupadi, dragged into the gambling hall. However hard it was pulled, it went on without end and protected her.
list.imageAlt: A page from the Razmnama, the Persian Mahabharata, painted in Mughal India in 1598: Yaja and Upayaja perform a sacrifice for Dhrishtadyumna to emerge from the fire. From the flames of a roofed altar an armored youth appears, with Brahmins around and people gathered below.

list.title: Sanjeevani
list.maker: Unknown (it grew on the mountain of herbs in the Himalayas)
list.power: An herb that could revive even the dying.
list.summary: The Himalayan herb that saved the fallen Lakshmana. Unable to tell which herb it was, Hanuman carried back the whole mountain.
list.imageAlt: A bronze Flying Hanuman in the Koh Ker style of tenth-century Cambodia. The monkey god in a tall crown, mouth wide open and one knee bent, raises both arms high in the pose of taking flight.

list.title: Soma
list.owner: Indra, king of the gods, and the Vedic gods
list.maker: Unknown (pressed from the juice of the soma plant)
list.power: The hymns sing that whoever drinks it is filled with strength and inspiration and becomes immortal.
list.summary: The sacred drink of the Rigveda and the god of that drink. Indra drank soma and defeated the dragon Vritra.
list.imageAlt: Nine Celestial Bodies (Navagraha), carved in sandstone in central India in the eighth century. Gods stand in a row on a long stone: at far left the sun god in a tall crown with the goddess of dawn, then the moon and the planetary gods in similar poses, and at right Rahu with a huge head.

list.title: Parijata Tree
list.owner: Indra, king of the gods, later Krishna and his wife Satyabhama
list.power: A heavenly tree whose flowers never wither and whose fragrance spreads far.
list.summary: A heavenly flowering tree in Indra's paradise. Krishna brought it down to earth for his wife Satyabhama.
list.imageAlt: Krishna and Satyabhama Storm the Citadel of Naraka, folio 97 of a Bhagavata Purana painted in Kathmandu, Nepal, about 1775. Seen from above, the citadel is ringed by layers of walls like a mandala, and Krishna and Satyabhama fly in from the right to attack. Text is written below.

list.title: Golden Chain Mail
list.owner: Sun Wukong, the Great Sage Equal to Heaven
list.maker: Unknown (given by the Dragon King of the Western Sea)
list.power: Armor woven of golden chain links, which with a phoenix-feather cap and cloud-walking shoes became Sun Wukong's outfit.
list.firstRecord: Wu Cheng'en, Journey to the West
list.summary: The golden chain mail Sun Wukong pestered the Dragon Kings into giving him. With a phoenix-feather golden cap and cloud-walking shoes, it became his outfit.
list.imageAlt: A ceremonial uniform of the Qing dynasty (1644–1911). Brown silk lined with blue silk is closely studded with metal rivets and embroidered with gold thread, with a tasseled helmet, shoulder guards, a round metal plate on the chest and a skirt embroidered with dragons.

list.title: Nine-Ringed Monk's Staff
list.power: It was said that whoever leaned on this staff would come to no poisonous harm.
list.firstRecord: Wu Cheng'en, Journey to the West
list.summary: The monk's staff the bodhisattva Guanyin bestowed, with a cassock of gold brocade, on Tripitaka as he set out west for the scriptures. Whoever leaned on it came to no poisonous harm.
list.imageAlt: A Buddhist monk's staff (shakujō) made in Japan in the early nineteenth century. Several rings hang from the round loop of the bronze head, and below it runs a lacquered wooden shaft carved with patterns.

list.title: Eight Trigrams Furnace
list.owner: Taishang Laojun, the Supreme Old Lord
list.power: An elixir furnace whose fire was governed by the directions of the eight trigrams; it was said it could melt anything away.
list.firstRecord: Wu Cheng'en, Journey to the West
list.summary: The furnace in which Taishang Laojun brewed his elixirs. Sun Wukong endured forty-nine days in it and came out with eyes that could see through anything.
list.imageAlt: A tripod incense burner cast in copper alloy in 1346, in the Yuan dynasty. Animal-face motifs and the eight trigrams are cast in relief on a band around the round-bellied body, with characters inscribed below, and it stands on three short, thick legs.

list.title: Fahai's Alms Bowl
list.power: When it was clapped over the white snake spirit, she revealed her true form and shrank until she was trapped beneath it.
list.firstRecord: Feng Menglong, Stories to Caution the World (Madam White Under Leifeng Pagoda)
list.summary: The alms bowl in which the monk Fahai trapped Madam White, the white snake. Trapped beneath it, she was buried under Leifeng Pagoda.
list.imageAlt: A wide bronze alms bowl made in Korea in the early 1900s. A round sun, clouds and rocky mountains are incised in fine lines on the golden-toned body.

list.title: Shennong's Red Whip
list.owner: Shennong, god of agriculture and medicine
list.power: Striking every kind of plant with it, he learned whether each was warming or cooling and whether it was poisonous.
list.firstRecord: Gan Bao, In Search of the Supernatural
list.summary: The red whip with which Shennong is said to have struck every plant to tell medicine from poison.
list.imageAlt: Shennong, a hanging scroll painted in ink on paper in Muromachi-period Japan, late 1400s–early 1500s. Shennong, with small horns sprouting from his tousled head, holds a leaf in his mouth and stares wide-eyed, wearing a garment woven of leaves.

list.title: Twin Swords of Liu Bei
list.owner: Liu Bei, emperor of Shu Han
list.maker: Unknown (Liu Bei had a smith make them)
list.power: A pair of swords sheathed in one scabbard, which Liu Bei wielded one in each hand.
list.firstRecord: Luo Guanzhong, Romance of the Three Kingdoms
list.summary: The twin swords Liu Bei had made after the Oath of the Peach Garden. Guan Yu's Green Dragon Crescent Blade and Zhang Fei's long spear were made at the same time.
list.imageAlt: A Chinese double sword with its scabbard, eighteenth–nineteenth century. Two straight, double-edged swords with bronze guards and horn grips lie side by side, and at right is a single scabbard covered with sharkskin and fitted with bronze mounts.

list.title: Eight Steeds of King Mu
list.power: Eight fine horses that ran a thousand li a day and carried King Mu to the far west.
list.firstRecord: Mu Tianzi Zhuan (Account of King Mu, Son of Heaven)
list.summary: The eight fine horses that drew the chariot of King Mu of Zhou. With them King Mu went to meet the Queen Mother of the West at the far western edge of the world.
list.imageAlt: A blue-and-white porcelain seal-paste box fired at the Jingdezhen kilns in eighteenth-century China. Horses walking, galloping and rolling are painted in blue all around the round lid and body.

list.title: Hua Tuo's Mafeisan
list.owner: Hua Tuo, the famous physician of the Later Han
list.power: Mixed with wine and drunk, it left one insensible as if drunk, so that the belly could be opened for surgery.
list.firstRecord: Chen Shou, Records of the Three Kingdoms, Biography of Hua Tuo
list.summary: The anesthetic the famous physician Hua Tuo is said to have given before surgery. Whoever drank it felt nothing, as if drunk.
list.imageAlt: Operating on Guan Yu's Arm, a hanging scroll painted on silk by Katsushika Ōi of Japan in the 1840s. People gather around a table laid with objects as a physician operates on Guan Yu's arm, and at left an attendant holds up a tray filled with blood.

list.title: Su Wu's Envoy Staff
list.owner: Su Wu, envoy of the Han
list.power: The token proving him the emperor's envoy; Su Wu never let it go for nineteen years.
list.firstRecord: Ban Gu, Book of Han, Biography of Su Wu
list.summary: The envoy's staff that Su Wu, a Han envoy captured by the Xiongnu, never let go of for nineteen years. He held it until all its tassels had fallen off.
list.imageAlt: A rectangular inkstone of Duan stone made in Qing-dynasty China, eighteenth–nineteenth century. The grinding surface is cut low, and within it Su Wu herding sheep is engraved in fine lines.

list.title: Laozi's Five Thousand Characters
list.owner: Laozi, and Yin Xi, keeper of the pass
list.power: A text of some five thousand characters on the meaning of the Way and its virtue, later called the Daodejing.
list.firstRecord: Sima Qian, Records of the Grand Historian, Biographies of Laozi and Han Fei
list.summary: The text of some five thousand characters Laozi left at the pass as he departed west. It was later called the Daodejing.
list.imageAlt: Laozi Crossing the Han Pass, a pale jade (nephrite) boulder carved like a mountain in eighteenth-century Qing China. On a mountain path among trees and rocks are carved Laozi riding an ox and other figures; it rests on a wooden stand.

list.title: Sessho-seki (Killing Stone)
list.maker: Unknown (the dead fox turned to stone)
list.power: It breathed out poison that killed the birds and beasts that came near.
list.summary: The stone the nine-tailed fox became when it died on the plain of Nasu. It breathed out poison and killed every living thing that came near.
list.imageAlt: A surimono print by Yashima Gakutei, Japan, late 1820s: the warrior Miura-no-suke confronts the court lady Tamamo-no-Mae as she turns into a nine-tailed fox. Fox tails bloom behind the lady at left; at right a warrior with bow and arrows draws his sword. Verses fill the background.

list.title: Onimaru Kunitsuna
list.owner: Hōjō Tokimasa, later several warlords and the Japanese imperial household
list.power: When its rust was polished away, it toppled over by itself and cut down the little demon tormenting its master.
list.summary: A tachi forged by the Kamakura-period swordsmith Kunitsuna. When its rust was polished away, it fell over by itself and cut down a demon.
list.imageAlt: A mounting for a slung sword (itomaki-tachi koshirae) from Edo-period Japan, seventeenth–nineteenth century. The hilt and the upper scabbard are wrapped in silk braid, and the long scabbard, lacquered gold with round crests, carries hanging cords and crest-engraved fittings.

list.title: Umisachi's Fishhook
list.power: Umisachi's fishhook, which caught the fish of the sea; its loss led to the tale of the sea god's palace.
list.summary: The fishhook of the elder brother Umisachi, which his younger brother Hoori borrowed and lost in the sea. It was found caught in the throat of a sea bream in the sea god's palace.
list.imageAlt: A bone fishhook from Japan. Bone is carved into a J-shaped hook, with a barb left on the inside of the point.

list.title: Izanagi's Comb
list.power: Lit, one of its teeth lighted the darkness; thrown, it sprouted bamboo shoots that held back his pursuers.
list.summary: The comb Izanagi used as he fled the land of the dead. He lit a tooth of it to see his wife, and when he threw it, bamboo shoots sprang up.
list.imageAlt: A half-moon-shaped comb of lacquered wood made in Japan in the mid-nineteenth century, decorated in gold, silver and red maki-e with flower-shaped roundels. Fine teeth are closely cut below the golden spine.

list.title: Ame-no-Habaya
list.maker: Unknown (bestowed by the gods of heaven)
list.power: A feathered arrow given with the heavenly bow; shot upward, it flew all the way to heaven and came back.
list.summary: The feathered arrow the gods of heaven gave Ame-no-Wakahiko. When he shot heaven's messenger with it, the arrow came back and killed him.
list.imageAlt: A Japanese steel arrowhead (yanone) of the fifteenth–sixteenth century. A groove runs down the center of the long, pointed head shaped like a willow leaf, and a slender tang extends below to fit into the shaft.

list.title: Yashiori Sake
list.power: A strong sake brewed over and over, which made the eight-headed serpent Yamata no Orochi drunk.
list.summary: The strong sake Susanoo had brewed again and again. It made the eight-headed serpent drunk so that he could cut it down.
list.imageAlt: A Negoro lacquer sake bottle of the Muromachi period in Japan, late 1300s–late 1500s. A slender spout and a tall foot are attached to a body whose shoulders spread wide like a spinning top, and the red lacquer has worn away in places to show the black undercoat.

list.title: Murasamemaru
list.owner: Inuzuka Shino, a warrior of the Hakkenden
list.maker: Unknown (a treasured sword handed down in the Ashikaga shogun's house)
list.power: When drawn, drops of water beaded on the blade; swung, they scattered like a passing shower and could even put out fire.
list.firstRecord: Kyokutei Bakin, The Eight Dog Chronicles (Nansō Satomi Hakkenden)
list.summary: The treasured sword of Inuzuka Shino, a warrior of the Hakkenden. When drawn, water beaded on the blade, and when swung it scattered like a passing shower.
list.imageAlt: The Hōryūkaku from the Hakkenden, a woodblock triptych by Utagawa Kuniyoshi, Japan, 1840. Soldiers swarm up the steep tiled roof of the tall Hōryūkaku tower, two warriors grapple at the top of the roof, and an explanatory text is at upper right.

list.title: Eight Jewels of the Hakkenden
list.owner: The eight warriors of the Satomi clan (the Eight Dog Warriors)
list.maker: Unknown (scattered from Princess Fuse's prayer beads)
list.power: Each bore one of eight virtues, such as benevolence, loyalty and filial piety, and they bound the eight scattered warriors together.
list.firstRecord: Kyokutei Bakin, The Eight Dog Chronicles (Nansō Satomi Hakkenden)
list.summary: Eight jewels scattered from Princess Fuse's prayer beads. A character for a virtue appeared on each, linking the eight warriors who carried them.
list.imageAlt: A two-panel kabuki actor print made in Japan in 1834: Arashi Rikan II as Inuzuka Shino and Nakamura Utaemon III as Inukai Genpachi in battle. Two warriors with swords grapple on a tiled roof, with the roles and story written in the panels above.

list.title: Jewel from the Dragon's Neck
list.power: A jewel that hangs from a dragon's neck and shines in five colors.
list.firstRecord: The Tale of the Bamboo Cutter
list.summary: The dragon's jewel Princess Kaguya told her suitor, the Grand Counselor Ōtomo, to bring her. He met a storm at sea and was terrified out of his wits.
list.imageAlt: A blue-and-white porcelain stem cup fired at the Jingdezhen kilns in China in the fourteenth century, during the Yuan dynasty. A scaly dragon with flying mane circles the wide, flaring cup, which stands on a tall foot.

list.title: Swallow's Cowry Shell
list.power: A shell swallows were said to hold when laying eggs, believed to make childbirth easy.
list.firstRecord: The Tale of the Bamboo Cutter
list.summary: The swallow's shell Princess Kaguya told her suitor, the Middle Counselor Isonokami, to bring her. He fell while searching a nest and lost his life.
list.imageAlt: Calligraphy with Willow and Swallows, a hanging scroll written in ink on paper by the Zen monk Ikkyū in Muromachi-period Japan, fifteenth century. Behind the verse written in flowing vertical lines, willow branches and swallows painted in pale ink show through.

list.title: Talhae's Whetstone and Charcoal
list.owner: Seok Talhae, fourth king of Silla
list.power: With the whetstone and charcoal he had secretly buried as evidence, he claimed another man's house as the home of his blacksmith ancestors.
list.summary: The whetstone and charcoal young Talhae secretly buried to take over Hogong's house. He later became the fourth king of Silla.
list.imageAlt: A granite panel from a royal tomb of Unified Silla, late 700s–early 800s. A clothed, standing figure with a rat's head is carved in low relief on a long stone slab: the rat among the twelve animals of the zodiac.

list.title: Geotaji's Flower Branch
list.maker: Unknown (the daughter of the god of the Western Sea, transformed)
list.power: The daughter of the god of the Western Sea, turned into a flower branch; carried home in his bosom, she became a woman again.
list.firstRecord: Iryeon, Samguk Yusa, “Queen Jinseong and Geotaji”
list.summary: The tale of Geotaji, who carried home in his bosom the daughter of the Western Sea god, turned into a flower branch. Back in Silla, he lived with her.
list.imageAlt: An inlaid celadon bottle of the Goryeo dynasty, thirteenth–fourteenth century. A small loop is attached to the long, slender neck, and white wild chrysanthemums are inlaid on the pear-shaped body. The broken mouth was repaired with gold lacquer.

list.title: Peony Painting Without Fragrance
list.owner: King Jinpyeong of Silla and Princess Deokman (later Queen Seondeok)
list.power: Seeing no butterflies in the painting, she guessed that the flowers had no scent.
list.summary: A painting and seeds of peonies sent to Silla from Tang China. Princess Deokman guessed that, with no butterflies in the painting, the flowers had no fragrance.
list.imageAlt: An eight-panel folding screen of peonies painted on silk in Korea in the early 1900s. On every panel, red, pink, yellow and blue peonies bloom in layers on luxuriant branches.

list.title: Wonhyo's Muae Gourd
list.maker: Wonhyo (modeled on an entertainer's large gourd)
list.power: Dancing and singing with it, he taught even the poor and small children the name of the Buddha.
list.summary: The instrument Wonhyo made in the shape of an entertainer's great gourd. Carrying it, he danced and sang and spread the Buddha's teaching from village to village.
list.imageAlt: A bronze gourd-shaped bottle made in Goryeo in the twelfth century. A narrow spout rises long above a body that swells in two lobes, upper and lower, and the surface is covered with green corrosion.

list.title: Seonmyo's Floating Rock
list.owner: Uisang, monk of Silla, and Seonmyo, a woman of Tang
list.power: A great rock that Seonmyo became; it rose into the air and drove off the band that stood in Uisang's way.
list.firstRecord: Zanning, Song Biographies of Eminent Monks, “Biography of Uisang”
list.summary: The rock into which Seonmyo, a Tang woman who loved Uisang, transformed. Floating in the air, it won Uisang the site for his temple, which came to be called Buseoksa.
list.imageAlt: Orchids and Rocks, an eight-panel folding screen painted in ink on silk by Yi Ha-eung (the Heungseon Daewongun) in 1897–98. On every panel long, slender orchid leaves sweep vigorously around rocks drawn in ink, and some panels bear inscriptions and seals.

list.title: Seodong's Gold
list.owner: Seodong (later King Mu of Baekje) and Princess Seonhwa
list.power: Gold piled like clods of earth where he dug yams, carried to the Silla palace in a single night.
list.summary: The gold that Seodong, a yam digger, had heaped up like clods of earth. When Princess Seonhwa told him it was treasure, he sent it to the Silla palace.
list.imageAlt: A necklace of Unified Silla, eighth century. Faceted rock-crystal beads, dark beads and gold beads covered with gold granules are strung together, with comma-shaped amethyst jewels on either side and a comma-shaped jade jewel at the bottom center.

list.title: Cauldron of King Daemusin
list.power: Without any fire, it grew hot by itself and cooked enough rice to fill the whole army.
list.summary: The cauldron King Daemusin of Goguryeo found on his way to attack Buyeo. Without any fire it grew hot by itself and fed the whole army.
list.imageAlt: Still Life with Bronze Vessels and Flowering Plants, a ten-panel folding screen painted in ink on paper in Joseon Korea in 1894. Each panel shows ancient vessels such as bronze tripod cauldrons, censers and ewers with flowering branches and inscriptions. It is attributed to Jang Seung-eop.

list.title: Jakjegeon's Willow Staff
list.owner: Jakjegeon, grandfather of Wang Geon, founder of Goryeo
list.maker: Unknown (brought from the palace of the Dragon King of the Western Sea)
list.power: The willow staff and pig the dragon maiden had him ask for instead of seven treasures; they led him to the site where the Goryeo royal house would rise.
list.firstRecord: Goryeosa, “Genealogy of the Goryeo Royal House”
list.summary: The willow staff and pig Jakjegeon received along with the seven treasures after helping the Dragon King of the Western Sea. He became the ancestor of the Goryeo royal house.
list.imageAlt: An inlaid celadon ewer of the thirteenth-century Goryeo dynasty. A curved handle and a long spout are attached to the round body, and in a roundel two figures seated under a willow are inlaid in black and white. Bands of lotus petals ring the shoulder and base.

list.title: The Rabbit's Liver
list.owner: The daughter of the Dragon King of the Eastern Sea
list.power: The one medicine that could cure the Dragon King's daughter of her illness.
list.firstRecord: Kim Bu-sik, Samguk Sagi, “Biography of Kim Yu-sin”
list.summary: The rabbit's liver sought as medicine for the Dragon King's daughter. The rabbit tricked the turtle by saying he had left his liver on land, and returned alive.
list.imageAlt: A pair of openwork bronze ornaments made in Goryeo in the twelfth century. On each round-topped plaque, a heron above and a turtle below are pierced among scrolling vines, and the surface is covered with green corrosion.

list.title: Stone Chest of Tamna
list.owner: The three divine men of Tamna: Yang-eulna, Go-eulna and Bu-eulna
list.maker: Unknown (sent from a land across the sea)
list.power: A chest that came across the sea; three maidens, foals, calves and the seeds of the five grains came out of it, and Tamna began.
list.summary: The chest that drifted across the sea to the three divine men of Tamna. From a stone chest inside came three maidens, foals, calves and the seeds of the five grains.
list.imageAlt: An inlaid celadon box of the Goryeo dynasty (918–1392). A lid covers the round, flattish body; petal and phoenix designs are inlaid in black and white on the lid, and a patterned band circles the body.

artifact.title: Excalibur
artifact.maker: The smiths of Avalon (in some traditions, the Lady of the Lake)
artifact.power: Cuts through enemy armor, and whoever wears its scabbard does not bleed.
artifact.firstRecord: Geoffrey of Monmouth, History of the Kings of Britain
artifact.summary: The sword that proved the king of Britain. It came from a lake and returned to one.
artifact.story:
Excalibur first takes shape in Geoffrey of Monmouth's twelfth-century History of the Kings of Britain, where Arthur's sword is called Caliburnus and is said to have been forged on the isle of Avalon. Caledfwlch in Welsh tradition and Caladbolg in Irish heroic tales are counted as names from the same root.

The scene in which Arthur wins the sword comes down in two forms. In one he pulls it from a stone and becomes king; in the other he receives it from an arm rising out of a lake. Thomas Malory's Le Morte d'Arthur keeps both, explaining that the Lady of the Lake gave him Excalibur after the sword from the stone broke.

Merlin said the scabbard was worth more than the blade, because whoever wore it would not bleed however badly he was wounded. Having lost the scabbard, Arthur took a mortal wound at Camlann and ordered his last knight, Bedivere, to return the sword to the lake. Only at the third throw did a hand rise from the water, catch the sword and vanish.
artifact.imageAlt: A fifteenth-century European hand-and-a-half sword with a straight double-edged blade, cross guard and round pommel.

annotations.title: Round pommel
annotations.body: The round weight at the end of the hilt draws the balance toward the hand, making a long sword easier to wield with one hand.

annotations.title: Cross guard
annotations.body: The straight guard made a medieval knight's sword look like a cross. Arthur is often pictured planting this sword in the ground to receive oaths.

annotations.title: Straight double edge
annotations.body: The double edge tapers toward the tip, shaped for both cutting and thrusting. Legend says this blade parted enemy armor like cloth.

annotations.title: Tip
annotations.body: Malory writes that when Bedivere threw the sword into the lake, a hand rose from the water and caught it.

artifact.title: Holy Grail
artifact.owner: The Fisher King, Joseph of Arimathea
artifact.power: Grants those who see it the food they desire, and shows itself only to the pure knight.
artifact.firstRecord: Chrétien de Troyes, Perceval, the Story of the Grail
artifact.summary: The cup of the Last Supper and the vessel the knights of the Round Table searched for to the end.
artifact.story:
The word graal originally meant a wide, shallow dish. In Chrétien de Troyes's unfinished tale of the 1180s, the young knight Perceval watches a shining grail pass by in the Fisher King's castle, but fails to ask whom it serves and so loses his chance to heal the king.

A few decades later Robert de Boron turned the dish into the cup of the Last Supper. Joseph of Arimathea caught Christ's blood in it at the foot of the cross and carried it west to Britain. From then on the grail was the Holy Grail.

In the thirteenth-century prose Quest of the Holy Grail, the knights of the Round Table scatter to find it. Lancelot's sins keep him from coming near, while his son Galahad, with Percival and Bors, finally stands before it. Galahad dies on the spot, and the Grail is taken up to heaven.

The silver cup in this photograph, said to have been found near Antioch in Syria in the early twentieth century, was once presented as the true Grail and is known as the Antioch "Chalice." It is now thought more likely to be a lamp made in sixth-century Byzantium.
artifact.imageAlt: A gilded silver cup carved with figures among grapevines. Its rounded body sits on a low foot.

annotations.title: Rim of the cup
annotations.body: The inner silver cup is smooth and undecorated. The double structure once prompted the idea that the outer shell was made to honor a cup Christ himself had used.

annotations.title: Figures in the vine
annotations.body: The figures seated among the vines are read as Christ and the apostles. Grapes recall the wine of the Eucharist.

annotations.title: Foot
annotations.body: The low, wide foot is cited as evidence that this was a lamp to hang or stand rather than a cup.

artifact.title: Mjölnir
artifact.maker: The dwarf brothers Brokkr and Eitri
artifact.power: Smashes anything, and returns to its owner's hand when thrown.
artifact.summary: The hammer of the thunder god Thor. Its short handle is Loki's doing.
artifact.story:
As punishment for shearing off all the hair of Thor's wife Sif, Loki had to obtain new treasures from the dwarves. He staked his own head on a bet with the dwarf Brokkr that no one could make better treasures than the sons of Ivaldi.

While his brother Eitri worked at the forge, Brokkr could not stop pumping the bellows. Loki, changed into a fly, bit him on the eyelid until blood ran; Brokkr stopped for one moment, and so the last thing they made, a hammer, came out with a slightly short handle.

Even so, the gods judged Mjölnir the finest treasure. Nothing could break it however hard it struck, it came back to Thor's hand however far he threw it, and it could be made small enough to hide in his clothing. People of the Viking Age wore little hammer-shaped amulets around their necks.
artifact.imageAlt: A French war hammer of the mid-fifteenth century. One side of the steel head is a hammer, the other a pointed beak, on a wooden haft.

annotations.title: Hammer head
annotations.body: Loki turned into a fly to interfere, but the head of the hammer came out perfect. Only the handle was short.

annotations.title: Pointed beak
annotations.body: The beak on the far side is made to pierce armor. It recalls the hammer Thor used to fell giants.

annotations.title: Haft and rivets
annotations.body: Because Brokkr paused at the bellows for one moment, Mjölnir's handle was so short it could be gripped with only one hand.

artifact.title: Aegis
artifact.power: Shaken, it raises storms and sends enemy armies fleeing in terror.
artifact.summary: The shield borne by Zeus and Athena. The head of Medusa is set at its center.
artifact.story:
In the Iliad the aegis is a piece of war gear that raises thunder and dark clouds when Zeus shakes it. Athena and Apollo also borrow it and carry it into battle. A hundred golden tassels hung from its edges.

It is described sometimes as a goatskin cloak and sometimes as a shield. Athena on Greek vase paintings covers her shoulders with a leather cape fringed with snakes. When Perseus gave her Medusa's head, Athena set it in the center of the aegis, and from then on enemies who saw it froze where they stood.

The English phrase "under the aegis of," meaning under someone's protection, comes from this shield.
artifact.imageAlt: A black round Italian shield of about 1560. A tangled scene of figures occupies the center, with round medallions holding busts around it, all in relief.

annotations.title: Central scene
annotations.body: A tangle of figures is embossed at the center of the shield. Medusa's head was set at the center of the aegis.

annotations.title: Left medallion
annotations.body: A bust in profile sits inside a round medallion on the rim. Renaissance makers loved to transfer ancient myth onto shields.

annotations.title: Right medallion
annotations.body: A bust paired with the one on the left. The Iliad says a hundred golden tassels hung from the edge of the aegis.

annotations.title: Lower medallion
annotations.body: A reclining figure appears in the bottom medallion. The whole shield is composed like a single picture of a story.

artifact.title: Kusanagi-no-Tsurugi
artifact.maker: Found in the tail of Yamata-no-Orochi
artifact.power: Cuts the grass by itself and turns back fire.
artifact.summary: A sword from the tail of an eight-headed serpent, and one of the three sacred treasures of the Japanese imperial house.
artifact.story:
Cast out of heaven, the storm god Susanoo came to the land of Izumo and met Yamata-no-Orochi, a great serpent with eight heads and eight tails that devoured a daughter every year. He set out eight vats of strong liquor, got the serpent drunk and hacked it to pieces. When he cut the middle tail his blade struck something and chipped, and inside he found a sword.

Susanoo named it Ame-no-Murakumo-no-Tsurugi, the sword of the gathering clouds of heaven, and presented it to his sister, the sun goddess Amaterasu.

Later, when the hero Yamato Takeru campaigned in the east, enemies set fire to the fields around him. He drew the sword, cut away the grass around him and lit a counter-fire, and the flames turned on his enemies. From then on it was called Kusanagi, the grass-cutting sword. It is said to be enshrined at Atsuta Shrine in Nagoya, but it has never been shown to the public.

The photograph shows straight swords from Japan's Kofun period in the sixth century. Before the Kojiki was written, the swords carried by heroes of myth were straight like these rather than curved.
artifact.imageAlt: Seven straight iron swords from sixth-century Kofun-period Japan laid side by side, with rusted blades, gilt-bronze scabbard fittings and round ring pommels.

annotations.title: Round ring pommel
annotations.body: Swords with large ring pommels come from the tombs of the Kofun-period elite, showing that the sword was a symbol of power.

annotations.title: Gilt-bronze fittings
annotations.body: The scabbard and hilt are decorated in gilt bronze. Kusanagi too was revered as one of the three imperial treasures.

annotations.title: Straight blade
annotations.body: The rusted blade runs straight. The sword Yamato Takeru used to cut grass and stop the fire would have been a straight sword like this.

artifact.title: Manpasikjeok
artifact.maker: Bamboo sent by the dragon of the sea
artifact.power: When played, enemy armies retreat, illness is cured, drought brings rain and rough waves grow calm.
artifact.summary: The “flute that calms ten thousand waves,” a national treasure that protected Silla.
artifact.story:
In 682, King Sinmun of Silla received word that a small mountain was floating back and forth in the East Sea toward Gameunsa Temple. On it grew a bamboo that split in two by day and became one by night.

When the king sailed to the mountain a dragon appeared and offered him a black jade belt. The dragon said that bamboo makes sound only when joined, and that King Munmu, now a dragon of the sea, and Kim Yusin, now a god of heaven, had joined their hearts to send this treasure. The king cut the bamboo, made a flute and stored it in the Cheonjon storehouse of Wolseong.

When this flute was played, enemy armies withdrew, illness was cured, rain came in drought and skies cleared in floods, the wind died and the waves grew calm. So it was named Manpasikjeok, the flute that puts ten thousand waves to rest.

The photograph shows a shakuhachi, a nineteenth-century Japanese vertical bamboo flute. The thick root end and nodes recall the bamboo in the story of Manpasikjeok that sounds only when joined.
artifact.imageAlt: A nineteenth-century Japanese shakuhachi, a vertical bamboo flute. The golden, jointed bamboo tube has finger holes and a thick lower end at the root.

source.creditLine: The Crosby Brown Collection of Musical Instruments, 1889

annotations.title: Mouthpiece
annotations.body: The top end is cut at a slant so the lips can rest against it. Playing Manpasikjeok was said to calm violent waves.

annotations.title: Bamboo node
annotations.body: The natural nodes of the bamboo remain. The dragon had the flute made, saying bamboo sounds only when joined.

annotations.title: Finger holes
annotations.body: There are four holes on the front and one on the back. Covering and opening them alone produces five notes.

annotations.title: Root end
annotations.body: The lower end is the thick root of the bamboo. King Sinmun kept this flute in the Cheonjon storehouse of Wolseong.

artifact.title: Durendal
artifact.maker: Brought to Charlemagne by an angel
artifact.power: Never chips, even when struck against rock.
artifact.summary: The sword of Charlemagne's nephew Roland. It refused to break.
artifact.story:
In the late eleventh-century epic The Song of Roland, Durendal is the sword Charlemagne gave to his nephew Roland. Its golden hilt was said to hold a tooth of Saint Peter, the blood of Saint Basil, hair of Saint Denis and a piece of the Virgin's clothing.

Commanding the rearguard in the pass of Roncevaux, Roland is surrounded by an ambush. Facing death, he tries to shatter the sword on a rock so that it will not fall to the enemy, but the blade stays whole and the rock splits. The Brèche de Roland in the Pyrenees is said to have been made at that moment.

At last Roland lay down with the sword beneath him, facing the enemy, and died. A sword said to be Durendal is still lodged in the cliff at Rocamadour in France.
artifact.imageAlt: A two-handed Western European sword of the early fifteenth century with a long blade and a wide cross guard.

source.creditLine: Gift of Laird Landmann and Kathleen Kinney Landmann, in celebration of the Museum’s 150th Anniversary, 2023

annotations.title: Pommel
annotations.body: The Song of Roland says relics of the saints were sealed inside the golden hilt.

annotations.title: Cross guard
annotations.body: The long grip for two hands and the wide guard suggest the weight of this sword.

annotations.title: Blade
annotations.body: Just before his death Roland struck rock with this blade ten times without chipping it.

annotations.title: Tip
annotations.body: Roland's last pose, lying on his sword and facing the enemy, was painted throughout the Middle Ages.

artifact.title: Gungnir
artifact.power: Always strikes its target when thrown.
artifact.summary: The spear of the high god Odin. The first war of the gods began when it was thrown.
artifact.story:
Gungnir is one of the treasures Loki obtained while commissioning golden hair to replace Sif's. Along with the golden hair and the folding ship Skíðblaðnir, the sons of Ivaldi made this spear.

Runes were carved on its point, and once thrown it never missed. The Poetic Edda's Völuspá sings that the first war in the world began when Odin cast his spear over the host of the Vanir.

On the day of Ragnarök Odin takes up Gungnir to face the great wolf Fenrir. The spear does not miss, but Odin is swallowed by the wolf all the same.
artifact.imageAlt: A European steel spearhead of about 800 to 1000 with a willow-leaf blade and a socket decorated with silver.

source.creditLine: Purchase, Helmut Nickel Gift; Bequest of Stephen V. Grancsay and Gift of Carl Otto von Kienbusch, by exchange; and Rogers Fund, 1989

annotations.title: Spear point
annotations.body: Gungnir never missed when thrown. The long, slender point suits that story well.

annotations.title: Spiral pattern
annotations.body: A spiral inlaid in silver runs through the middle of the blade. Legend says runes were cut into Gungnir's point.

annotations.title: Silver band on the socket
annotations.body: A silver band wraps the socket that held the shaft, marking this as a weapon of the Viking Age elite.

artifact.title: Gram
artifact.maker: Given by Odin and reforged by the smith Regin
artifact.power: Splits an anvil in two and pierces a dragon's heart.
artifact.summary: A sword that waited in a tree for its owner. It broke, then was reborn as the sword that slew the dragon.
artifact.story:
A huge tree grew at the center of King Völsung's hall. On the night of a wedding feast, a one-eyed stranger came in, drove a sword deep into the trunk, said that whoever drew it would own it, and vanished. The stranger was Odin, and only Völsung's son Sigmund could pull the sword free.

In Sigmund's last battle Odin appeared again and held out his spear, and the sword snapped in two. Sigmund's wife kept the pieces and passed them to their son Sigurd.

The smith Regin melted the fragments into a new blade. When Sigurd tested it the anvil split down to its block, and a tuft of wool drifting on the river parted when it touched the edge. With this sword Sigurd stabbed the gold-guarding dragon Fafnir from below. In the German Nibelungenlied and Wagner's operas the same sword appears as Balmung and Nothung.
artifact.imageAlt: A tenth-century Scandinavian Viking sword with a straight double-edged blade, short guard, and a grip decorated with copper and silver.

annotations.title: Pommel
annotations.body: A rounded pommel divided into lobes is typical of Viking swords. It belongs to the age of the sword Sigurd would have held.

annotations.title: Short guard
annotations.body: The guard of a Viking sword is short and straight. Its job was less to protect the hand than to join blade and grip firmly.

annotations.title: Pattern in the blade
annotations.body: The faint pattern at the center of the blade is the trace of several irons forged together. It recalls Regin reforging the broken Gram.

artifact.title: Draupnir
artifact.maker: The dwarf brothers Brokkr and Eitri
artifact.power: Every ninth night it drops eight gold rings of equal weight.
artifact.summary: Odin's self-multiplying gold ring. Its name means “the dripper.”
artifact.story:
Draupnir was born on the same day and in the same forge as Mjölnir. In their wager with Loki, Brokkr and Eitri made in turn the golden boar Gullinbursti, the gold ring Draupnir and the hammer Mjölnir, and presented them to the gods.

Every ninth night, eight gold rings of exactly the same weight dripped from it. This endlessly growing wealth was the most kingly treasure in a northern society where rulers handed out rings to their followers.

When Odin's son Baldr died, Odin laid the ring on the funeral pyre to burn with him. Hermóðr, who rode down to the underworld, could not bring Baldr back, but Baldr sent Draupnir back to his father.
artifact.imageAlt: A Greek gold ring of the fourth to third century BCE. A face with flowing hair is embossed across the whole oval bezel.

annotations.title: Face on the bezel
annotations.body: A face in relief fills the bezel. Like Draupnir, gold was a symbol of authority that kings gave away.

annotations.title: Eyes and hair
annotations.body: Zoom in and you can see the pupils and rippling locks in fine detail. Imagine eight rings like this appearing every ninth night.

artifact.title: Golden Fleece
artifact.power: Brings prosperity and legitimate kingship to the land that holds it.
artifact.summary: A fleece guarded by a sleepless dragon. Jason and the Argonauts crossed the sea to bring it back.
artifact.story:
Phrixus and Helle, a brother and sister about to be sacrificed by their stepmother, escaped on a flying golden ram. Helle fell into the sea, which became the Hellespont, the "sea of Helle." Reaching Colchis at the far end of the Black Sea, Phrixus sacrificed the ram and gave its fleece to King Aeëtes.

The king hung the fleece on an oak in the grove of Ares and set a sleepless dragon to guard it. Jason, seeking to regain his throne, was ordered to fetch it, and he gathered heroes such as Heracles and Orpheus and launched the Argo.

The trials of yoking fire-breathing bulls and defeating warriors sprung from dragon's teeth were passed with the magic of the king's daughter Medea. When Medea lulled the dragon with herbs, Jason took the fleece and fled into the night sea.

The photograph shows a wild ram's head made of gold in Achaemenid Persia in the sixth to fourth century BCE. Its curling horns and thick neck recall the golden ram Chrysomallos that flew through the sky.
artifact.imageAlt: A Persian gold ornament of a ram's head from the sixth to fourth century BCE, with large curled horns, a long muzzle and patterned hair on the neck.

annotations.title: Curled horns
annotations.body: The great spiraling horns are the sign of the ram. They recall the golden ram Chrysomallos, which flew over the sea carrying Phrixus and Helle.

annotations.title: Eye and face
annotations.body: Zoom in and you can see even the wrinkles of the eyelid and muzzle hammered into the gold.

annotations.title: Hair on the neck
annotations.body: Thick locks are chased along the neck. The ram's fleece in the myth was pure gold, and the people of Colchis hung it on an oak.

artifact.title: Shield of Achilles
artifact.power: A shield of five layers forged by a god, with the whole world engraved on its face.
artifact.summary: A shield holding heaven and earth, war and peace on one face. It is counted the first description of a work of art in Western literature.
artifact.story:
When Achilles's friend Patroclus went out in his borrowed armor and fell to Hector, the armor passed into enemy hands. Seeing her son's grief, the sea goddess Thetis went to the forge of Hephaestus and asked for new arms.

Book 18 of the Iliad follows the making of the shield for more than a hundred and thirty lines. At the center are earth, sky and sea, the sun, moon and constellations. Around them a city at peace, with wedding feasts and a trial, faces a city at war, besieged and preparing an ambush.

Farmers plowing, children picking grapes, cattle attacked by lions and young people dancing in a circle follow one after another, and the river Oceanus runs around the outermost edge. Taking up the shield, Achilles returns to battle and kills Hector.

The photograph is a close view of the parade shield of Henry II of France. Scenes of cavalry combat are embossed on its steel surface and enriched with gold and silver.
artifact.imageAlt: A close view of the lower part of the steel shield of Henry II of France, about 1555. A cavalry battle fills the central oval, with figure medallions and floral relief around it and rivets along the edge.

source.objectTitle: Shield of Henry II of France (reigned 1547–59)

annotations.title: Central battle scene
annotations.body: Mounted soldiers grapple in battle. On the shield of Achilles, Hephaestus engraved a besieged 'city at war.'

annotations.title: Medallions around it
annotations.body: Figures also fill the round medallions around the battle. The shield in the Iliad likewise layered its scenes in concentric rings.

annotations.title: Rivets at the edge
annotations.body: Golden rivets run along the rim. On the Iliad's shield the river Oceanus encircled the outermost edge.

artifact.title: Holy Lance
artifact.power: Legend grew that whoever holds this spear holds the fate of the world.
artifact.summary: The spear that pierced the side of Christ on the cross. Kings and emperors sought it throughout the Middle Ages.
artifact.story:
The Gospel of John records that a soldier thrust a spear into the side of Jesus on the cross to confirm that he had died, and that blood and water flowed out. The Bible does not name the soldier. The name Longinus first appears around the fourth century in the apocryphal Gospel of Nicodemus.

In legend Longinus was a soldier with failing sight who regained it, along with faith, when blood running down the spear touched his eyes. From then on the spear itself became a relic.

In 1098, when the First Crusade was besieged at Antioch, the pilgrim Peter Bartholomew followed a vision and dug up a spearhead beneath the cathedral floor. Heartened, the crusaders broke the siege. Today Vienna's Hofburg, the Vatican in Rome and Etchmiadzin in Armenia each still keep a "Holy Lance."
artifact.imageAlt: A Bronze Age copper-alloy spearhead of 1200 to 800 BCE. The long leaf-shaped blade has a central ridge and part of its wooden shaft survives.

annotations.title: Spear point
annotations.body: The sharply tapered point. The Gospel of John says only that a soldier pierced the side with a spear and does not describe its shape.

annotations.title: Openings in the blade
