annotations.body: The holes on either side of the lower blade are found on Bronze Age spears, both as ornament and to lighten the weapon.

annotations.title: Socket
annotations.body: Part of the wooden shaft remains in the socket. Spears kept as relics also mostly survive as bare heads.

artifact.title: Seal of Solomon
artifact.maker: Brought from heaven by the archangel Michael
artifact.power: Its seal commands demons and lets the wearer understand beasts and birds.
artifact.summary: The signet ring of the wise king, said to have put demons to work building the Temple.
artifact.story:
According to the apocryphal Testament of Solomon, while the Temple in Jerusalem was being built a demon drained the strength of a young workman every night. When Solomon prayed, the archangel Michael brought him from heaven a ring engraved with a seal.

With the ring in hand Solomon summoned the demons one by one, forced out their names and weaknesses and set them to work on the Temple. The Talmud also tells how the demon king Asmodeus seized the ring, flung Solomon far away and posed as king.

In Islamic tradition the ring lives on as the Seal of Sulayman. Stories of commanding the winds and the jinn and understanding the speech of birds and ants flowed all the way into the Thousand and One Nights. The seal itself was drawn as a five- or six-pointed star.

The photograph shows a gold signet ring from Egypt's Amarna Period in the fourteenth century BCE.
artifact.imageAlt: A fourteenth-century BCE Egyptian gold signet ring. A flat engraved bezel is attached to a thick hoop.

annotations.title: Two seal faces
annotations.body: The bezel is divided into two ovals, or cartouches. Solomon's ring too was said to bind demons with a seal like a name.

annotations.title: Design in the seal
annotations.body: The figure cut into the oval prints in reverse like a stamp. Zoom in to see the depth of the incised lines.

annotations.title: Thick hoop
annotations.body: The hoop for the finger is thick and heavy. This was a signet for everyday use.

artifact.title: Yata-no-Kagami
artifact.power: Calls back the sun that hid in a cave.
artifact.summary: The bronze mirror that returned light to the world, most revered of the three sacred treasures.
artifact.story:
Hurt by Susanoo's violence, the sun goddess Amaterasu entered the rock cave Ama-no-Iwato in heaven and shut the door. The world sank into darkness and every sort of calamity arose.

The gods gathered before the cave and made a plan. Ishikoridome made a mirror, Tamanooya strung curved beads and hung them on a tree. The goddess Ame-no-Uzume danced on an upturned tub and the gods roared with laughter.

Curious about the merriment outside, Amaterasu opened the door a crack. The gods held up the mirror and told her a goddess more noble than she had come. At the moment she leaned out, drawn by her own reflected light, a strong god took her hand and pulled her out, and the sun shone on the world again. The mirror is said to have later been enshrined at Ise.

The photograph shows the back of a bronze mirror from Japan's Kofun period in the fourth to fifth century, carved after Han Chinese mirrors with immortals, beasts and the cosmos. Yata-no-Kagami is thought to have resembled mirrors of this era.
artifact.imageAlt: The back of a round Japanese bronze mirror of the fourth to fifth century. Squares, concentric circles, small bosses and animal designs ring a central knob, under a blue-green patina.

source.creditLine: The Harry G. C. Packard Collection of Asian Art, Gift of Harry G. C. Packard, and Purchase, Fletcher, Rogers, Harris Brisbane Dick, and Louis V. Bell Funds, Joseph Pulitzer Bequest, and The Annenberg Fund Inc. Gift, 1975
source.objectTitle: Mirror (Shinjūkyō) Based on Han Dynasty Prototype with Cosmological Design

annotations.title: Central knob
annotations.body: A round knob for threading a cord. This photo shows the back; the smooth opposite face was polished to reflect faces and light.

annotations.title: Square and bosses
annotations.body: The central square and small bosses around it stand for earth and heaven. A mirror was an object holding the cosmos.

annotations.title: Sawtooth band
annotations.body: The sawtooth pattern on the outer ring spreads like rays of sunlight, fitting for the mirror that called out the sun goddess Amaterasu.

artifact.title: Cheonbuin
artifact.power: Proves its bearer has received heaven's mandate, and commands wind, rain and clouds.
artifact.summary: Three heavenly tokens Hwanung received when he descended from heaven, commonly understood as a bronze sword, mirror and bell.
artifact.story:
According to the Gojoseon section of the Samguk Yusa, Hwanung, son of Hwanin the lord of heaven, often set his heart on the human world below. His father, knowing this, looked down on Samwi Taebaek, judged that it could bring wide benefit to humankind, and sent him down with three Cheonbuin.

Hwanung led three thousand followers to the sacred tree on the summit of Taebaek and called the place the City of God. With the wind lord Pungbaek, the rain master Usa and the cloud master Unsa, he took charge of grain and life, sickness and punishment, good and evil.

The record does not say what the Cheonbuin were. But because bronze swords, mirrors and bells are often buried together at Bronze Age sites on the Korean peninsula, the view that these three symbols of heavenly authority were the Cheonbuin is widely accepted.

This image is a composite made by the archive itself. Photographs of an ancient East Asian dagger, a bronze mirror in Han style and a Yayoi-period bronze bell are joined side by side to show "sword, mirror and bell" in one frame.
artifact.imageAlt: A composite of three photographs placed side by side: on the left an ancient East Asian dagger with a gold-decorated hilt, in the center a round bronze mirror with animal relief, on the right a bell-shaped bronze covered in blue-green patina.

parts.creditLine: Purchase, Bashford Dean Memorial Collection, Funds from various donors, by exchange, 1998

source.creditLine: Composited by Rizer Archive from three CC0 images
source.objectTitle: 검·거울·방울 합성 이미지 (Short Sword · Mirror in Han style · Dōtaku)

annotations.title: Sword
annotations.body: An ancient dagger with a gold-decorated hilt. Among the Cheonbuin, the sword is read as rule by heaven's authority.

annotations.title: Mirror
annotations.body: A bronze mirror with animal relief. Mirrors were regarded as sacred objects reflecting the light of heaven, that is, the sun.

annotations.title: Beasts in the mirror
annotations.body: Beasts romp around the central knob. The more you zoom, the more the relief of their bodies and legs comes alive.

annotations.title: Bell
annotations.body: A bell-shaped bronze. It was a ritual tool for calling the gods and gathering people with sound, and is thought to have led to the shaman's bell.

artifact.title: Clarent
artifact.power: A sword of peace used to dub knights, which became the blade that felled a king.
artifact.summary: Arthur's sword for ceremony rather than war. His nephew Mordred stole it and dealt Arthur a mortal wound.
artifact.story:
The late fourteenth-century English poem known as the Alliterative Morte Arthure says Arthur had another sword besides Excalibur. Clarent was a "sword of peace" used for dubbing knights and at feasts, and it was carefully stored in the treasury at Wallingford Castle.

While Arthur was away campaigning against Rome, his nephew Mordred, left in charge of the kingdom, seized the throne and took this sword as well. When the two met at the battle of Camlann, Mordred struck Arthur with Clarent, and Arthur fell from the wound.

That a sword made for peace became the sword that killed the king is counted among the bitterest touches at the end of the Arthurian story.
artifact.imageAlt: An Italian two-handed sword of the fifteenth to sixteenth century with a long straight blade, a wide cross guard with a ring-shaped hand guard, a black grip and a round pommel.

annotations.title: Cross guard
annotations.body: The guard extending straight on both sides made a knight's sword look like a cross. Clarent was a 'sword of peace' used at coronations and dubbing ceremonies.

annotations.title: Guard ring
annotations.body: The small ring below the guard protects the finger hooked over the blade. Mordred stole this ceremonial sword for his rebellion.

annotations.title: Long blade
annotations.body: A long blade held in two hands. At Camlann Mordred gave Arthur a mortal wound, and in some traditions that sword was Clarent.

artifact.title: Carnwennan
artifact.power: Thrown, it cleaves a witch in two.
artifact.summary: Arthur's dagger, “little white hilt,” one of his oldest weapons in Welsh tradition.
artifact.story:
In Culhwch and Olwen, a Welsh tale recorded around the eleventh century, Arthur lists his most prized possessions and names the dagger Carnwennan. The name means "little white hilt" in Welsh.

At the end of the tale Arthur goes to find the Very Black Witch in the uplands of Hell. When his men fall one after another, Arthur steps forward himself and throws Carnwennan, and the dagger splits the witch in two.

Modern games and novels often say this dagger hides its wielder in shadow. In the Welsh sources, however, the power of concealment belongs to Arthur's mantle, Gwenn.
artifact.imageAlt: A fourteenth-century roundel dagger, possibly British. A thin pointed blade is backed by a disk-shaped guard and pommel.

source.creditLine: Gift of Jean Jacques Reubell, in memory of his mother, Julia C. Coster, and of his wife, Adeline E. Post, both of New York City, 1926

annotations.title: Slender point
annotations.body: The awl-like point was made to pass between the rings of mail. Arthur split a witch in two with Carnwennan.

annotations.title: Disk guard
annotations.body: The round disk between blade and grip protects the hand. Daggers like this are called roundel daggers.

annotations.title: Disk pommel
annotations.body: A disk at the end of the grip keeps the hand from slipping. In Welsh the name means 'little white hilt.'

artifact.title: Rhongomyniad
artifact.power: Long and broad-bladed, said to thirst for enemy blood.
artifact.summary: King Arthur's spear. It first appears in Welsh tradition alongside Excalibur, there called Caledfwlch.
artifact.story:
In Culhwch and Olwen, the list of treasures Arthur says he will never give away includes the sword Caledfwlch, the dagger Carnwennan and the spear Rhongomyniad. The name is roughly interpreted as "cutting spear."

In the twelfth century Geoffrey of Monmouth's History of the Kings of Britain calls this spear Ron and describes it as long, broad-bladed and thirsty for blood in battle. Arthur fought the Saxons with it, together with Caliburnus and the shield Pridwen.

Though overshadowed by Excalibur's fame, it is a weapon never left out when describing Arthur fully armed.
artifact.imageAlt: A Carolingian or Ottonian winged lance head of the ninth to tenth century. Short wings project from either side below the long, slender steel blade.

annotations.title: Spear point
annotations.body: A long, sharply tapered point. Rhongomyniad is named in Culhwch and Olwen among Arthur's prized treasures.

annotations.title: Ridge of the blade
annotations.body: A ridge rising along the center of the blade gives firm support to the thin steel.

annotations.title: Wings
annotations.body: The wings projecting below the blade keep the spear from sinking too deep in a body. This is the winged spear of the Carolingian era.

artifact.title: Prydwen
artifact.power: With the Virgin painted inside, it guarded Arthur in battle.
artifact.firstRecord: Geoffrey of Monmouth, History of the Kings of Britain
artifact.summary: Arthur's shield and, in Welsh poetry, the name of the ship he sailed to the otherworld.
artifact.story:
Geoffrey of Monmouth writes that when Arthur set out for the battle of Bath he hung a round shield called Pridwen on his shoulder. The Virgin Mary was painted on its inner side, so that Arthur would keep her in mind throughout the fight.

In the older Welsh poem Preiddeu Annwfn, Prydwen is not a shield but a ship. Arthur and his men sail it to the otherworld of Annwfn to seize a magic cauldron, but only seven return.

Its two faces, shield and ship, are traces of a single name becoming different objects as it passed through different traditions.
artifact.imageAlt: An Italian parade shield from Milan, about 1570. Saint Paul falling from his horse amid soldiers is densely embossed on steel enriched with gold and silver.

source.objectTitle: Parade Shield Depicting the Conversion of Saint Paul

annotations.title: Upper medallion
annotations.body: Small round pictures run around the rim. Prydwen is both Arthur's shield and the ship that sailed to the otherworld.

annotations.title: Central scene
annotations.body: Saint Paul falling from his horse and startled soldiers are densely embossed here. Arthur is said to have had the Virgin Mary painted inside his shield.

annotations.title: Gold and silver
annotations.body: Gold and silver on the steel make the light alternate. It is a shield for processions and ceremony rather than combat.

artifact.title: Hauteclere
artifact.power: A “high and clear” blade to rival Roland's Durendal.
artifact.summary: The sword of prudent Oliver, one of Charlemagne's twelve peers, who fought beside Roland to the end.
artifact.story:
If Roland is brave in The Song of Roland, his friend Oliver is wise. Hauteclere, whose name means "high and clear," is Oliver's sword, with a golden hilt and a pommel of crystal.

When the great Saracen host poured into the pass of Roncevaux, Oliver asked three times that the horn be blown to call Charlemagne. Roland refused for honor's sake. Oliver fought with Hauteclere to the last and, blinded by blood, struck his friend Roland by mistake, then died begging forgiveness.

Named in the same poem with Roland's Durendal and Charlemagne's Joyeuse, it is one of the three swords of Frankish chivalry.
artifact.imageAlt: A Western European steel sword of about 1400 with a straight double-edged blade, a cross guard extending sideways and a round pommel.

source.creditLine: The Collection of Giovanni P. Morosini, presented by his daughter Giulia, 1932

annotations.title: Pommel
annotations.body: A round pommel. In The Song of Roland, Oliver's Hauteclere has a golden hilt set with crystal.

annotations.title: Down-curved guard
annotations.body: A guard whose ends curve slightly toward the blade, a common form on European swords around 1400.

annotations.title: Clear blade
annotations.body: Hauteclere means 'high and clear.' Oliver fought Roland for five days without a decision.

artifact.title: Joyeuse
artifact.power: Changes color thirty times a day, and holds the point of the Holy Lance in its hilt.
artifact.summary: Charlemagne's sword, named “joy,” which became the coronation sword of the kings of France.
artifact.story:
The Song of Roland sings that Charlemagne's sword Joyeuse changes color thirty times a day. The point of the lance that pierced Christ was set in its pommel, and the Frankish battle cry "Montjoie" was said to come from this sword.

After Roland fell, Charlemagne took this sword against the Saracen king Baligant. When the fight dragged on the angel Gabriel appeared and renewed his strength, and Charlemagne split his enemy's helmet with Joyeuse and won.

A coronation sword remade over several centuries is preserved in the Louvre in Paris under the name Joyeuse. The kings of France received it when they took the throne.
artifact.imageAlt: A cross-hilted sword with a hilt made in London and a blade from Solingen in the early seventeenth century. Silver-decorated guard, wire-wrapped grip and gold lettering on the upper blade are visible.

source.objectCulture: hilt, British, London; blade, German, Solingen

annotations.title: Pommel
annotations.body: A ball pommel patterned in silver. Legend says Joyeuse's pommel held the tip of the lance of Longinus.

annotations.title: Silver-mounted guard
annotations.body: Silver plaques run along the wide guard. Charlemagne's sword is sung of as changing color thirty times a day.

annotations.title: Blade with gold lettering
annotations.body: Gold letters are cut into the upper blade. The Joyeuse handed down as the coronation sword of French kings is also decorated on the blade.

artifact.title: Tizona
artifact.power: Enemies trembled at the mere sight of its blade.
artifact.summary: The sword the Castilian hero El Cid won in the fight for Valencia.
artifact.story:
In The Poem of the Cid, the oldest epic in Spanish literature, El Cid pursues and defeats the Moroccan king Búcar, who has marched on Valencia, and takes his sword Tizona.

El Cid later gave this sword and Colada to his two sons-in-law. But when they disgraced him by abandoning his daughters in a forest, he recovered both swords in a trial before the king and restored his honor by duel.

The Museum of Burgos holds a sword long handed down as El Cid's Tizona. Part of its blade has been analyzed as eleventh-century work from Islamic Spain.
artifact.imageAlt: A black-and-white photograph of a late fifteenth-century Spanish sword in its scabbard, standing vertically, with a densely decorated hilt and long scabbard.

annotations.title: Hilt and guard
annotations.body: A hilt decorated with gold and enamel. El Cid took Tizona after defeating the Moroccan king Búcar, who had marched on Valencia.

annotations.title: Scabbard fittings
annotations.body: Lozenge-shaped metal mounts run up and down the scabbard. The hilt of the Tizona preserved in the Museum of Burgos was also made later.

annotations.title: Scabbard tip
annotations.body: The tip of the scabbard is capped with metal to resist wear. In The Poem of the Cid, enemies who saw Tizona fled in terror.

artifact.title: Colada
artifact.power: A finely tempered sword worth a thousand marks.
artifact.summary: The sword El Cid seized from the Count of Barcelona, the partner of Tizona.
artifact.story:
Early in The Poem of the Cid, the exiled El Cid fights and captures Count Ramón of Barcelona. The sword he wins is Colada, and the poem stresses that it is worth a thousand marks.

The name Colada is interpreted as "well-cast" or tempered steel. El Cid carried it himself in battle, then passed it on with Tizona to his sons-in-law.

After their betrayal he recovered both swords, and his knights defeated the sons-in-law in single combat. The two swords are remembered as a pair symbolizing El Cid's honor.
artifact.imageAlt: A Spanish sword of about 1500 with a straight blade, a simple cross guard and a leather-wrapped grip.

annotations.title: Square pommel
annotations.body: A boxy, angular pommel, characteristic of Spanish swords around 1500.

annotations.title: Hooked guard
annotations.body: The ends of the guard bend toward the blade to catch an opponent's sword. El Cid took Colada from the Count of Barcelona.

annotations.title: Fuller in the blade
annotations.body: The shallow groove down the middle lightens the blade while keeping it firm. El Cid gave Colada and Tizona to his sons-in-law, then took them back.

artifact.title: Curtana
artifact.owner: Kings of England (in legend, Tristan or Ogier)
artifact.power: The broken-tipped “sword of mercy,” signifying a king's power to forgive rather than punish.
artifact.firstRecord: Record of the coronation of Queen Eleanor of England
artifact.summary: The pointless sword of English coronations. Legend says an angel broke off its tip.
artifact.story:
Curtana is a sword borne at the coronation of English monarchs; its name first appears in the record of the 1236 coronation of Eleanor, queen of Henry III. Its tip is cut blunt, and so it is also called the "sword of mercy."

Legend says it originally belonged to Tristan of the Round Table or to Ogier, a knight of Charlemagne. When Ogier in fury was about to strike Charlemagne's son, an angel came down from heaven, broke off the tip and told him mercy was better than justice.

The Curtana now in the Tower of London was remade in the seventeenth century, but it still keeps the form without a point.
artifact.imageAlt: The hilt of an English basket-hilted sword of the early seventeenth century. Steel bars embossed with silver scrolls are woven into a basket around the hand.

annotations.title: Pommel
annotations.body: A round pommel embossed with silver scrollwork.

annotations.title: Basket hilt
annotations.body: Steel bars are woven into a basket that encloses the whole hand, a type favored by English cavalry in the seventeenth century.

annotations.title: Base of the blade
annotations.body: The photograph ends at the base of the blade. The Curtana of the English coronation has a blunt, cut-off tip, read as a sign of mercy.

artifact.title: Tyrfing
artifact.power: Each time it is drawn someone must die, and it brings about three great evils.
artifact.summary: A sword cursed by dwarves forced to make it for a king. It destroyed its owners' family one by one.
artifact.story:
In the thirteenth-century Icelandic Hervarar Saga, King Svafrlami captured the dwarves Dvalin and Durin outside their rock and forced them to forge a sword that would never rust, would cut anything and would never miss.

The dwarves delivered a dazzling sword with a golden hilt, and laid a curse on it. Each time it left the scabbard a man must die, three great evils would be done with it, and at last it would kill its master.

Passed from generation to generation, the sword fulfilled the curse. His granddaughter Hervör won it from her father Angantýr in his grave, and it was present afterward at the tragedy of brothers killing each other.
artifact.imageAlt: A Sasanian sword and scabbard of about the seventh century, lying horizontally. The scabbard and hilt are covered entirely in gold sheet and set with garnets.

annotations.title: Golden hilt
annotations.body: The whole hilt is wrapped in gold sheet. Tyrfing in Hervarar Saga also has a golden hilt and shone even at sunset.

annotations.title: Garnet-set plaque
annotations.body: A plaque set with garnets and glass decorates the upper scabbard. Tyrfing had to kill each time it was drawn, and brought about three great evils.

annotations.title: Scabbard tip
annotations.body: Scale-patterned gold sheet continues to the end of the scabbard. Sasanian nobles wore such swords hung from two loops on a belt.

artifact.title: Hrunting
artifact.power: A patterned steel blade steeped in venom. It had never failed in battle.
artifact.summary: The famous sword Beowulf borrowed to fight Grendel's mother. It proved useless against the monster.
artifact.story:
In the Old English epic Beowulf, Unferth of the Danish court at first mocks Beowulf. But after Beowulf defeats the monster Grendel, Unferth lends him his own sword, Hrunting, for the fight against Grendel's mother.

The poem boasts that its blade is patterned steel steeped in venom and that no one who carried it ever failed in battle. Yet when Beowulf swings Hrunting in the underwater cave, the blade rebounds from the monster's head.

It was the first time the famous sword had failed. Beowulf throws Hrunting aside and ends the fight with a giant's sword hanging on the cave wall.
artifact.imageAlt: A bronze sword, probably Central European, of the thirteenth century BCE. Its slightly swelling leaf-shaped blade is covered in patina.

annotations.title: Round pommel
annotations.body: A disk-shaped bronze pommel. Bronze swords like this come from the graves of warriors in thirteenth-century BCE Central Europe.

annotations.title: Hilt shoulder
annotations.body: The hilt grips the blade in a half-moon. Hrunting was the sword Unferth lent to Beowulf.

annotations.title: Leaf-shaped blade
annotations.body: A blade slightly swollen at the middle. Hrunting had never failed in many fights, but it could not cut Grendel's mother.

artifact.title: Giant's Sword
artifact.power: So large an ordinary man could not lift it. Its blade melted in the monster's blood.
artifact.summary: An old sword of the giants hanging on an underwater cave wall, with which Beowulf slew Grendel's mother.
artifact.story:
With Hrunting useless and Beowulf cornered, his eye fell on an enormous sword hanging on the cave wall. The poem calls it an old sword made by giants, too large for any other man to carry into battle.

With it Beowulf cut down Grendel's mother and struck off the head of the dead Grendel. Then the blade melted like ice in the monster's hot blood, leaving only the hilt.

The golden hilt Beowulf carried back was said to be inscribed in runes with the ancient story of the giants destroyed by the great flood.
artifact.imageAlt: A German two-handed processional sword carried by the guard of Duke Julius of Brunswick, dated 1573, with a man-high blade and long grip.

source.objectTitle: Two-Handed Processional Sword carried by Guard of Duke Julius of Brunswick

annotations.title: Long grip
annotations.body: A long leather-wrapped grip for two hands. The 'giant's sword' Beowulf found in the cave of Grendel's mother was too large for an ordinary man to lift.

annotations.title: Guard and lugs
annotations.body: Short lugs project below the wide guard to protect the hand when gripping the base of the blade.

annotations.title: Blade
annotations.body: After Beowulf slew Grendel's mother, the blade melted like ice in the monster's blood and only the hilt remained.

artifact.title: Nægling
artifact.power: The gray blade at old Beowulf's last battle.
artifact.summary: The sword the aged king Beowulf carried against a fire-breathing dragon. It broke from his great strength.
artifact.story:
After ruling for fifty years as king, Beowulf in his old age had to face a dragon burning his land. The sword he carried then was Nægling, the "gray blade."

When Beowulf struck the dragon's head with all his might, Nægling snapped in two. The poem explains that Beowulf's hand was so strong no sword could withstand it.

Young Wiglaf came to help and stabbed the dragon in the belly, and Beowulf finished it with a dagger. But, wounded by the dragon's venom, Beowulf too died on that spot.
artifact.imageAlt: A long sword made in nineteenth-century Europe, possibly France, in fifteenth-century Gothic style, with a decorated straight blade, a down-curved guard and a round pommel.

annotations.title: Pommel
annotations.body: A round pommel with patterned decoration. This sword was made in the nineteenth century in the fifteenth-century Gothic style.

annotations.title: Down-curved guard
annotations.body: A thin guard curving toward the blade.

annotations.title: Patterned blade
annotations.body: Decoration runs along the whole blade. Nægling snapped the moment Beowulf struck the dragon; his hand was so strong no sword could withstand it.

artifact.title: Skofnung
artifact.power: It holds the spirits of twelve berserkers who guarded the king. Wounds from it do not heal.
artifact.summary: The sword of the legendary Danish king Hrólfr Kraki. It could not be drawn before women or have sunlight touch its hilt.
artifact.story:
Skofnung, sword of the legendary Danish king Hrólfr Kraki, appears in several Icelandic sagas. The spirits of the twelve berserkers who guarded the king were said to dwell in it.

The sword had rules. It could not be drawn in sight of a woman, and sunlight could not touch its hilt. A wound from it would not heal unless rubbed with the stone that came with the sword.

After Hrólfr died the sword was buried in his mound, until the Icelander Skeggi opened the grave and took it out, as the Laxdæla Saga relates.
artifact.imageAlt: A late ninth-century Anglo-Saxon sword pommel shaped like a triangular roof, in copper alloy inlaid with silver wire and niello in interlace patterns.

source.creditLine: Purchase, Gift of J. Pierpont Morgan, by exchange, 2005

annotations.title: Knotwork on the center panel
annotations.body: Round knotwork in silver wire and niello decorates the center panel, ornament from the ninth century when Anglo-Saxons and Vikings shared the same sea.

annotations.title: Wing-shaped ornament
annotations.body: The sides of the pommel slope down like a roof. Skofnung was the sword of the Danish king Hrólfr Kraki, inhabited by the spirits of his twelve champions.

annotations.title: Animal heads at the ends
annotations.body: The ends curl up into small heads. Skofnung was not to be drawn in the presence of women or when the sun shone on it.

artifact.title: Gjallarhorn
artifact.power: When blown it echoes through all the worlds, announcing Ragnarök.
artifact.summary: The horn of Heimdall, guardian of the rainbow bridge. It announces the last war of the gods.
artifact.story:
Heimdall is the watchman of Bifröst, the rainbow bridge leading to Asgard, world of the gods. He hardly sleeps, sees a hundred leagues even by night and can hear the grass and the wool grow.

Völuspá sings that when the end of the world comes, Heimdall lifts Gjallarhorn high and blows. The sound rings through the nine worlds, and the gods go out to Ragnarök, their last battle against the giants.

Snorri's Prose Edda also says that in ordinary times this horn lies beside Mímir's well of wisdom, and that Mímir drinks from the well with it and gains wisdom.
artifact.imageAlt: A nineteenth-century plaster cast of a fifteenth-century Danish drinking horn. The curving, tapering horn is densely covered in relief, with a band around the wide mouth.

annotations.title: Tip of the horn
annotations.body: A slender, curving tip. Heimdall stands guard at the edge of the gods' world and blows Gjallarhorn when the giants come.

annotations.title: Relief decoration
annotations.body: Vines and beasts cover the whole horn. This photograph shows a plaster copy of a fifteenth-century Danish drinking horn.

annotations.title: Band at the mouth
annotations.body: A band runs around the wide mouth. This horn's call, signaling the start of Ragnarök, is said to be heard in all nine worlds.

artifact.title: Megingjörð
artifact.power: Worn around the waist, it doubles the wearer's strength.
artifact.summary: The thunder god Thor's “belt of strength,” one of his three treasures with Mjölnir and the iron gloves.
artifact.story:
Snorri's Prose Edda says Thor has three most precious treasures: the hammer Mjölnir, the iron gloves Járngreipr and the belt of strength Megingjörð.

When Thor put on this belt his divine strength doubled. With it he took on the giants, and even hauled the great world-encircling serpent Jörmungandr up from the sea.

In another story the giantess Gríðr lends Thor this belt along with gloves and a staff. Thanks to them Thor manages to survive the palace of the giant Geirröd without his hammer.
artifact.imageAlt: A Frankish iron belt buckle of the late sixth to seventh century. Three rivets with copper-alloy heads are set in a plate inlaid with silver.

annotations.title: Three embossed heads
annotations.body: Three rivets with copper-alloy heads fix the plate. When Thor put on Megingjörð, his strength doubled.

annotations.title: Silver inlay
annotations.body: Silver wire set into the iron draws interlaced bands. This is a belt buckle of a Frankish noble of the sixth or seventh century.

annotations.title: Buckle loop and tongue
annotations.body: The loop and tongue lock the belt. Thor fought giants equipped with this belt, the iron gloves and Mjölnir.

artifact.title: Járngreipr
artifact.power: Lets a hand hold Mjölnir, hot as lightning, in place of a bare grip.
artifact.summary: Thor's iron gloves. Without them he could not grasp Mjölnir's handle.
artifact.story:
Járngreipr means "iron grippers." Thor always put on these iron gloves to wield Mjölnir.

Snorri notes briefly that the gloves were essential for gripping the hammer's handle. Later readers explained that this was because Mjölnir grew as hot as lightning and could not be held bare-handed.

When the giant Geirröd threw a red-hot lump of iron at Thor, Thor caught it in his gloved hand and hurled it back, killing Geirröd.
artifact.imageAlt: A locking steel gauntlet from Augsburg, Germany, about 1540. Plates covering the fingers bend into a fist, with gold bands in decoration.

annotations.title: Finger plates
annotations.body: Overlapping steel plates let the fingers bend. Járngreipr are the iron gloves Thor always wore to hold Mjölnir.

annotations.title: Gold bands
annotations.body: Gold bands and leaf patterns decorate the wrist and back of the hand, the skill of an Augsburg armorer around 1540.

annotations.title: Locking mechanism
annotations.body: When locked with a closed fist, the sword hilt cannot be lost. This is why it is called a locking gauntlet.

artifact.title: Brísingamen
artifact.power: A dazzling golden necklace that enchants all who see it.
artifact.summary: The necklace of Freyja, goddess of love, over which Loki and Heimdall fought.
artifact.story:
Brísingamen is the necklace of Freyja, goddess of love and beauty. In the Lay of Thrym, when the giant Thrym steals Thor's hammer and demands Freyja as his bride, she grows so furious that the necklace bursts.

The fourteenth-century Sörla þáttr tells its history. Freyja lost her heart to a necklace made by four dwarves, and won it at the price of spending a night with each of them.

When the trickster god Loki stole the necklace and fled, the watchman Heimdall is said to have changed into a seal, fought Loki and brought it back.
artifact.imageAlt: A Greek gold necklace made in Taranto in southern Italy, fourth to third century BCE. Fine gold chains hang in several layers with a disk bearing a face at the center.

annotations.title: Central disk
annotations.body: A face is carved on the large central disk. Freyja saw this necklace in the forge of four dwarves and paid with a night spent with each.

annotations.title: End plaques
annotations.body: Plaques that fasten at the back of the neck. This is goldwork from Taranto in southern Italy, of the fourth to third century BCE.

annotations.title: Hanging tassel
annotations.body: Small bell-like tassels swing at the ends of fine gold chains. Loki stole this necklace and Heimdall took it back.

artifact.title: Andvaranaut
artifact.power: Makes gold multiply but destroys everyone who owns it in turn.
artifact.summary: A gold ring cursed by the dwarf it was taken from. The tragedy of the dragon Fafnir and the hero Sigurd begins here.
artifact.story:
Loki accidentally killed the son of Hreidmar, who had taken the form of an otter, and as compensation had to pay enough gold to cover the otter's skin. Loki caught the dwarf Andvari, hiding in the form of a fish, and took all his gold.

Andvari begged to keep just one small gold ring, because it made gold multiply again. When Loki took the ring as well, Andvari cursed it, saying whoever held the ring and the gold would die.

The curse came true. Hreidmar was killed by his son Fafnir, Fafnir became a dragon guarding the gold and was killed by Sigurd, and Sigurd too lost his life in betrayal.
artifact.imageAlt: A Roman gold snake ring of the first century CE. A serpent winds several times around the finger, with head and tail projecting above and below.

source.creditLine: The Cesnola Collection, Purchased by subscription, 1874–76

annotations.title: Serpent's head
annotations.body: The upper end of the ring is a snake's head. Robbed of this ring, the dwarf Andvari cursed all who would own it.

annotations.title: Coiled body
annotations.body: The serpent winds several times around the finger. Andvaranaut made gold multiply, and for that gold Fafnir killed his father.

annotations.title: Tail
annotations.body: The lower end is a tightly curled tail. This is a Roman gold ring of the first century.

artifact.title: Skíðblaðnir
artifact.power: Large enough for all the gods, yet folds to fit a pocket. When its sail is raised a fair wind always blows.
artifact.summary: Best of all the ships of the gods. It could be folded like cloth and put in a pocket.
artifact.story:
Skíðblaðnir is one of the treasures made by the sons of Ivaldi, along with Gungnir and Sif's golden hair. Loki presented them to the gods and made a wager with the dwarf Brokkr.

The Prose Edda says this ship is large enough to carry all the gods in armor, and that when its sail is raised a fair wind always blows wherever it goes. When not in use it could be folded like cloth and carried in a pocket.

The ship was given to Freyr, god of fertility. The Lay of Grímnir calls it the best of ships.
artifact.imageAlt: A Cypriot terracotta ship model of about 600 to 480 BCE with a tall stem and stern and an openwork railing around the hull.

source.creditLine: The Cesnola Collection, Purchased by subscription, 1874–76

annotations.title: High stern
annotations.body: The end of the boat rises high. Skíðblaðnir was made for Freyr by the sons of the dwarf Ivaldi.

annotations.title: Openwork bulwark
annotations.body: The railing is pierced like a lattice. This ship could carry all the gods, yet folded into a pocket when not in use.

annotations.title: Hull
annotations.body: A rounded hull. This is a terracotta boat model of the kind placed in Cypriot tombs in the sixth and fifth centuries BCE.

artifact.title: Sleipnir
artifact.power: With eight legs it runs across sky, sea and the underworld.
artifact.summary: The eight-legged gray horse ridden by the high god Odin, finest of all horses.
artifact.story:
A mason offered to build the gods a wall in one winter and asked as payment the sun, the moon and the goddess Freyja. The gods agreed, thinking he could never do it, but his horse Svaðilfari hauled enormous stones and the wall was nearly done.

Desperate, the gods pressed Loki, who changed into a mare and lured Svaðilfari into the woods. The work went unfinished, and some time later Loki gave birth to a gray foal with eight legs.

Odin rode this horse, Sleipnir, across sky and earth. When Baldr died, Hermóðr borrowed Sleipnir and rode all the way to Hel to ask for Baldr's return.
artifact.imageAlt: A Greek bronze horse, possibly Corinthian, of the eighth century BCE. A long-legged, slim-bodied horse stands on an openwork base.

annotations.title: Head
annotations.body: A long muzzle and upright ears. This is a horse of the Greek Geometric style of the eighth century BCE.

annotations.title: Legs
annotations.body: Long, slender legs carry the body. Odin's horse Sleipnir, with eight legs, ran across earth, sky and even the underworld.

annotations.title: Pierced base
annotations.body: Triangular holes are cut in the base. Bronze horses like this were offerings to temples.

artifact.title: Helm of Awe
artifact.power: All who look on its wearer are seized by terror.
artifact.summary: The helm Fafnir wore as a dragon while guarding his gold. Sigurd took it after slaying the dragon.
artifact.story:
Having killed Hreidmar and seized the gold, Fafnir changed into a dragon and lay upon it. In the Lay of Fafnir he boasts that because he wore the Helm of Awe, no one dared come near.

Sigurd dug a pit, hid in it, and stabbed the dragon's belly from below as it went to drink. The dying Fafnir admits that the helm did not protect him after all.

Sigurd took the helm along with the gold. Among Icelandic magical symbols today there is a star-shaped design called the Helm of Awe, named after this story.
artifact.imageAlt: A Turkish helmet, probably from Istanbul, about 1560. A pointed steel bowl with gold and silver inlay carries ear and neck guards.

annotations.title: Pointed finial
annotations.body: A small finial at the top of an onion-shaped helmet.

annotations.title: Gold inlay band
annotations.body: Letters and patterns in gold run along the lower edge of the helmet, the skill of an Ottoman court workshop around 1560.

annotations.title: Cheek guards
annotations.body: Cheek guards with gold inlay hang down. Ægishjálmr is the 'Helm of Awe' that fills all who see the wearer with fear.

artifact.title: Tarnhelm
artifact.power: Its wearer can vanish, change into anything or travel far in an instant.
artifact.summary: The magic helmet of Wagner's Ring of the Nibelung, drawn from the medieval “cloak of invisibility.”
artifact.story:
In Wagner's Das Rheingold, the dwarf Alberich makes a ring from the gold of the Rhine and forces his brother Mime to forge a magic helmet, the Tarnhelm. Whoever wears it can vanish or turn into any shape.

Wotan, king of the gods, and Loge trick Alberich. When he boastfully changes into a great serpent and then a toad, they seize the toad and take the helmet, ring and gold.

Wagner drew this helmet from the invisibility cloak, or Tarnkappe, worn by Siegfried in the medieval German epic the Nibelungenlied. Siegfried later wins the helmet by killing the dragon Fafner.
artifact.imageAlt: A French close helmet made around 1850 in mid-sixteenth-century style. The steel covering the whole face is densely embossed with scrollwork.

source.objectDate: ca. 1850 in the style of the mid-16th century

annotations.title: Visor slit
annotations.body: The face is fully covered, leaving only a slit for the eyes. In Wagner's Ring, the Tarnhelm lets its wearer vanish or change shape.

annotations.title: Embossed ornament
annotations.body: Scrolls and faces are embossed all over. This helmet was made in nineteenth-century France in the style of the sixteenth century.

annotations.title: Neck guard
annotations.body: Overlapping plates wrap the neck. The dwarf Mime made the Tarnhelm on the orders of his brother Alberich.

artifact.title: Harpe
artifact.maker: Gaia (Cronus's sickle); given to Perseus by Hermes
artifact.power: A curved blade that can cut even the immortal.
artifact.summary: The curved sword of myth. Cronus castrated the sky with it, and Perseus took Medusa's head.
artifact.story:
In Hesiod's Theogony, the earth goddess Gaia, enraged at the sky god Uranus for imprisoning their children underground, made a great toothed sickle of hard metal. Her youngest, Cronus, cut his father down with it and separated sky from earth.

Later mythographers say Perseus was given a similar curved sword. With the harpe from Hermes, Perseus approached Medusa while watching her reflection in a mirror-bright shield, and took her head in one stroke.

Perseus in Greek vases and sculpture often holds this hooked sword, so that the harpe became the mark by which he is recognized.
artifact.imageAlt: Antonio Canova's marble statue Perseus with the Head of Medusa, 1804–6. The nude Perseus holds a curved sword in his right hand and Medusa's head in his left.

source.objectTitle: Perseus with the Head of Medusa

annotations.title: Curved sword
annotations.body: The sword in Perseus's right hand. The harpe lent by Hermes cut off Medusa's head with its sickle-shaped blade.

annotations.title: Head of Medusa
annotations.body: Medusa's head in his left hand. Even severed, it turned anyone who looked at it to stone.

annotations.title: Winged helmet
annotations.body: Perseus's helmet has small wings. Antonio Canova carved this marble statue in 1804–6.

artifact.title: Trident of Poseidon
artifact.power: When struck, the sea boils, the earth shakes and springs rise.
artifact.summary: The trident of Poseidon, god of sea and earthquakes.
artifact.story:
In thanks for help in the war against the Titans, the one-eyed Cyclopes made weapons for three divine brothers. Zeus received the thunderbolt, Hades the helmet and Poseidon the trident.

In the Iliad Poseidon uses this trident to tear down and sweep away the Greek wall on the shore of Troy. As his epithet Earthshaker suggests, when he struck rock with it the ground shook and springs rose.

Competing with Athena to be patron of Athens, Poseidon struck the rock of the Acropolis with his trident and raised a saltwater spring. But the people chose the olive tree Athena offered.
artifact.imageAlt: The reverse of a silver coin of King Demetrius of Macedon, about 300–295 BCE. A nude Poseidon with a cloak over his left arm strides forward aiming his trident, with Greek letters around him.

source.creditLine: Purchase from the J. H. Wade Fund

annotations.title: Trident
annotations.body: The trident held in his right hand points to the left. The one-eyed Cyclopes made this spear for Poseidon.

annotations.title: Striding god
annotations.body: With a cloak over his left arm, Poseidon advances aiming his spear. When he struck the ground with his trident, earthquakes shook and springs rose.

annotations.title: King's name
annotations.body: Greek letters around the edge read 'of King Demetrius.' A king who ruled the seas put Poseidon on his coins.

artifact.title: Thunderbolt of Zeus
artifact.power: Lightning that splits the sky. It felled the Titans and the monster Typhon.
artifact.summary: The lightning of Zeus, king of the gods, and the very emblem of his power.
artifact.story:
In the Theogony Zeus frees the Cyclopes whom his father Cronus had imprisoned, and in gratitude they make him thunder and lightning. Holding this lightning, Zeus ended the ten-year war against the Titans.

When Typhon, the most terrible of monsters, attacked the gods, Zeus hurled bolt after bolt, burned Typhon and cast him into Tartarus.

Zeus in Greek sculpture grasps lightning shaped like a rod pointed at both ends. For thousands of years afterward that form was how people drew the bolt of a god.
artifact.imageAlt: A Greek bronze statuette of the early fifth century BCE. A bearded god, Zeus or Poseidon, spreads his arms as if about to throw something. The lower legs are lost and it stands on a rod.

source.objectTitle: Bronze statuette of Zeus or Poseidon

annotations.title: Bearded face
annotations.body: A heavy beard and banded hair. It is not certain whether this statuette shows Zeus or Poseidon.

annotations.title: Raised arm
annotations.body: One arm extends and the other is drawn back. If Zeus, the hand holds a thunderbolt; if Poseidon, a trident, ready to throw.

annotations.title: Missing legs
annotations.body: The lower legs are lost, and a rod sets the figure on its base. This is a Greek bronze of the early fifth century BCE.

artifact.title: Helm of Hades
artifact.power: Its wearer cannot be seen even by the gods.
artifact.summary: The helmet of Hades, god of the underworld, which makes its wearer invisible.
artifact.story:
The helmet the Cyclopes made for Hades made its wearer visible to no one. In Book 5 of the Iliad Athena puts it on and enters battle, so that even Ares, god of war, cannot recognize her.

Perseus too borrowed this helmet from the nymphs when he went after Medusa. After beheading her he escaped the pursuing Gorgon sisters thanks to the helmet.

The Greek word kynee originally meant a cap of dogskin, a fitting name for the helmet of Hades, master of the hound Cerberus.
artifact.imageAlt: A Greek bronze helmet of Corinthian type, about 650–600 BCE. Only eye openings are cut, and guards for nose and cheeks extend downward.

annotations.title: Rounded bowl
annotations.body: A rounded bronze plate encloses the whole head. The helmet of Hades was made by the Cyclopes, and its wearer could be seen by no one.

annotations.title: Eye opening
annotations.body: A narrow opening shows only the eyes. A Corinthian helmet hid almost the whole face, so its wearer could not be recognized.

annotations.title: Holes along the edge
annotations.body: Small holes line the edge, where a leather or cloth lining was stitched inside.

artifact.title: Skin of the Nemean Lion
artifact.maker: Flayed by Heracles with the lion's own claws
artifact.power: No sword or arrow can pierce it.
artifact.summary: The lion skin won in the first labor of Heracles, which became his emblem.
artifact.story:
In the valley of Nemea lived a lion no weapon could wound. Sent to kill it as the first of his twelve labors, Heracles saw his arrows and sword bounce off, and so strangled the lion with his bare hands.

Skinning it remained. Since no blade would cut, Heracles slit the hide with the lion's own sharp claws.

After that he wore the lion's head as a helmet and the skin as a cloak. In Greek and Roman art a man in a lion skin is Heracles.
artifact.imageAlt: A Cypriot limestone head of the early fifth century BCE. Heracles wears a lion skin over his head, framing his face.

source.creditLine: The Cesnola Collection, Purchased by subscription, 1874–76
source.objectTitle: Limestone head of Herakles wearing the lion skin

annotations.title: Lion-skin hood
annotations.body: Heracles wore the lion's skin over his head. No weapon could pierce the hide of the Nemean lion.

annotations.title: Face
annotations.body: The face of Heracles shows beneath the skin. He strangled with bare hands the lion that arrows and clubs could not harm.

annotations.title: Fall of the mane
annotations.body: The lion's mane and forepaws hang at both sides. Heracles flayed the skin with the lion's own claws.

artifact.title: Golden Apples of the Hesperides
artifact.maker: Gaia gave them as a wedding gift
artifact.power: The fruit of the gods, said to give immortality.
artifact.summary: Golden apples guarded by a dragon in a garden at the western edge of the world. They were the eleventh labor of Heracles.
artifact.story:
To celebrate the marriage of Zeus and Hera, Gaia gave them a tree bearing golden apples. Hera planted it in a garden at the western end of the world and set the evening nymphs, the Hesperides, and the sleepless dragon Ladon to guard it.

Heracles had to bring back these apples as his eleventh labor. He asked the giant Atlas, who held up the sky, to pick them for him, and carried the sky on his own shoulders meanwhile.

A golden apple also sowed the seed of the Trojan War. When Eris, goddess of discord, tossed one inscribed "to the fairest," the quarrel of three goddesses began.
artifact.imageAlt: An Attic red-figure water jar (hydria) of the early fourth century BCE. Against the black ground, figures in red stand around a tree wound with a white snake.

annotations.title: Tree with the snake
annotations.body: A white snake winds around the tree: the dragon Ladon, who guarded the golden apples in the garden of the Hesperides.

annotations.title: Figures around it
annotations.body: Figures stand around the tree. As his eleventh labor, Heracles had to bring back the golden apples from this garden.

annotations.title: Neck and mouth
annotations.body: A narrow neck and wide mouth. A jar for drawing water (hydria), made in Athens in the early fourth century BCE.

artifact.title: Ambrosia and Nectar
artifact.power: Keeps the gods ageless and deathless.
artifact.summary: Ambrosia, food of the gods, and nectar, their drink. The very name means “not dying.”
artifact.story:
In Homer's epics the gods eat ambrosia and drink nectar rather than human bread and wine. The word ambrosia means "not dying," and ichor flows in the gods' veins instead of blood.

The Odyssey sings that doves bring ambrosia to Zeus from the ends of the earth. The gods also rub it on like perfumed oil; Hera washes and adorns herself with it.

Mortals who tried to steal it suffered greatly. Tantalus, for stealing the food of the gods and sharing it with people, was condemned to eternal hunger and thirst.
artifact.imageAlt: A Cypriot footed cup (kylix) of about 750–600 BCE, with scrolls and geometric designs in red and black on a pale ground.

source.creditLine: The Cesnola Collection, Purchased by subscription, 1874–76

annotations.title: Cup mouth
annotations.body: A wide, round mouth. At their feasts on Olympus the gods drank nectar and ate ambrosia.

annotations.title: Red scrollwork
annotations.body: Scrolls and geometric patterns are painted in red and black on this Cypriot cup of the eighth or seventh century BCE.

annotations.title: High foot
annotations.body: A slender foot holds up the cup. Tantalus stole the food of the gods, shared it with people and received everlasting punishment.

artifact.title: Necklace of Harmonia
artifact.owner: Harmonia and the royal house of Thebes
artifact.power: Keeps its wearer young and beautiful forever but brings misfortune for generations.
artifact.summary: A wedding gift forged with a curse by Hephaestus, enraged at his wife's infidelity.
artifact.story:
Harmonia was the daughter of Aphrodite and the war god Ares. Enraged at his wife's infidelity, Hephaestus gave Harmonia a beautiful necklace when she married Cadmus, founder of Thebes, and secretly put a curse in it.

The necklace kept women young and beautiful, but endless misery followed the Theban house that owned it. The tragedy of Oedipus unfolded in this family.

Later Polynices bribed Eriphyle, wife of a seer, with this necklace to send her husband to a war she knew would kill him. In the end the necklace is said to have left human hands only when dedicated at the temple at Delphi.
artifact.imageAlt: A Greek gold necklace of the fourth century BCE, with small spearhead-shaped gold ornaments packed closely along its length.

source.creditLine: The Cesnola Collection, Purchased by subscription, 1874–76

annotations.title: Clasp ends
annotations.body: The two ends that fasten behind the neck. Hating Harmonia, the daughter of Aphrodite and Ares, Hephaestus put a curse in this necklace.

annotations.title: Spear-shaped ornaments
annotations.body: Tiny gold ornaments crowd the strand. Harmonia's necklace kept its wearer young and beautiful, but also brought misfortune.

annotations.title: Lower part
annotations.body: The necklace brought tragedy down the generations of the Theban royal house. The photograph shows a Greek gold necklace of the fourth century BCE.

artifact.title: Arrows of Eros
artifact.power: A gold arrow makes one fall in love, a lead arrow makes one flee from it.
artifact.summary: The golden arrow that kindles love and the lead arrow that drives it away.
artifact.story:
In Ovid's Metamorphoses, Apollo, having shot the serpent Python, mocks young Eros's skill with the bow. Angered, Eros takes out two arrows: a sharp gold one that kindles love and a blunt lead one that puts it to flight.

He shoots Apollo with the gold arrow and the nymph Daphne with the lead. Apollo falls in love with Daphne, but she flees him and, praying to her river-god father, turns into a laurel tree.

Apollo wove a crown of laurel leaves to wear, and the laurel wreath became a symbol of victory and honor.
artifact.imageAlt: A Roman bronze statuette of the first to second century CE. A winged boy, Eros, strides forward holding what appears to be a long bow in his left hand with his right arm raised high.

annotations.title: Bow
annotations.body: He holds what appears to be a bow in his left hand. A gold arrow from Eros kindles love, and a lead arrow drives love away.

annotations.title: Wings
annotations.body: Small wings sprout from his back. This is a Roman bronze Eros of the first or second century.

annotations.title: Outstretched arm
annotations.body: His right arm reaches high. Eros shot Apollo with a gold arrow and Daphne with a lead one.

artifact.title: Pegasus
artifact.power: Flies on its wings, and raises springs by striking the ground with its hooves.
artifact.summary: The winged horse that sprang up when Perseus beheaded Medusa.
artifact.story:
The Theogony sings that when Perseus cut off Medusa's head, the winged horse Pegasus sprang from her body. When Pegasus kicked Mount Helicon with his hoof, the poets' spring Hippocrene gushed forth.

The hero Bellerophon tamed Pegasus with a golden bridle Athena gave him in a dream. Riding Pegasus through the sky, he shot down the fire-breathing monster Chimera.

When Bellerophon grew proud and tried to ride Pegasus up to Olympus, Zeus sent a gadfly to sting the horse. Bellerophon fell to earth, and Pegasus rose to heaven to carry the thunderbolts of Zeus.
artifact.imageAlt: A bronze statuette of Pegasus from the late sixteenth century. A horse with spread wings rears on its hind legs on a marble base.

annotations.title: Wings
annotations.body: Wings rising from the back. Pegasus was born from Medusa's blood when Perseus cut off her head.

annotations.title: Raised forelegs
annotations.body: He rears up on his hind legs. When Pegasus kicked Mount Helicon with his hoof, the poets' spring Hippocrene gushed out.

annotations.title: Marble base
annotations.body: The bronze dates from the late sixteenth century, and the marble base was added later.

artifact.title: The Argo
artifact.maker: The shipwright Argus, helped by Athena
artifact.power: Its prow, made of the sacred oak of Dodona, speaks like a person and tells the future.
artifact.summary: The ship that carried fifty heroes in search of the Golden Fleece, called “the Argo known to all.”
artifact.story:
The Odyssey says the only ship to pass safely between the clashing rocks was "the Argo known to all." The story of the Argo was already widely known in Homer's day.

The shipwright Argus built the vessel with Athena's help. Athena set in the prow a piece of the sacred oak of Dodona, where Zeus gave oracles, and the wood foretold the future in a human voice.

Jason sailed for Colchis with fifty heroes, including Heracles, Orpheus and the twins Castor and Polydeuces. When the voyage ended the ship was dedicated to the sea god Poseidon and is said to have become a constellation.
artifact.imageAlt: A wooden boat model from Middle Kingdom Egypt, about 1981–1975 BCE. Figures of rowers are packed on a green boat, their oars lowered into the water.

source.creditLine: Rogers Fund and Edward S. Harkness Gift, 1920

annotations.title: Rowers
annotations.body: Figures gripping oars sit close together. The Argo carried fifty heroes, among them Jason, Heracles and Orpheus.

annotations.title: Rows of oars

annotations.title: Steering oar

artifact.title: Girdle of Aphrodite
artifact.power: Embroidered with love, longing and beguiling words, it makes anyone fall in love.
artifact.summary: The embroidered band of Aphrodite that Hera borrowed to lull Zeus to sleep.
artifact.story:
In Book 14 of the Iliad, Hera schemes to distract Zeus, who favors the Trojans. She goes to Aphrodite, pretending she wishes to reconcile an estranged old couple, and borrows her embroidered band.

Homer sings that this band was stitched with love, longing and sweet words that steal even a wise man's mind.

Seeing Hera wearing it, Zeus was stirred as when he first fell in love. While he slept with the help of the god of Sleep, Poseidon aided the Greeks and turned the tide of battle.
artifact.imageAlt: A Roman marble statue of Aphrodite of the first to second century CE. The nude goddess, with hair tied up, stands with both arms broken away.

annotations.title: Face
annotations.body: The goddess's face with her hair tied up. This is a Roman statue of Aphrodite of the first or second century.

annotations.title: Waist
annotations.body: On Aphrodite's girdle were embroidered love, desire and beguiling words. Hera borrowed it to enchant Zeus.

annotations.title: Dolphin at her feet
annotations.body: A small figure is attached at her feet. Dolphins are often carved beside Aphrodite, who was born from the sea foam.

artifact.title: Ring of Gyges
artifact.power: Turning the bezel inward makes its wearer invisible.
artifact.summary: A ring of invisibility. Plato used it to ask whether one would be just if no one were watching.
artifact.story:
In Plato's Republic, Glaucon tells the story of Gyges, a shepherd of Lydia. In a chasm opened by an earthquake, Gyges found the corpse of a giant lying in a bronze horse and took a gold ring from its finger.

Gyges discovered that when he turned the bezel of the ring toward his palm, he became invisible. With this power he entered the palace, seduced the queen, killed the king and became ruler of Lydia.

Glaucon asks: would not even a just man commit injustice if he owned such a ring? In reply Socrates argues for the value of justice itself.
artifact.imageAlt: An Etruscan gold ring of the late fourth or early third century BCE. Letters are punched in dots across the front of the wide gold band.

annotations.title: Letters in dots
annotations.body: Letters are punched into the band with dots. This is an Etruscan gold ring of the fourth to third century BCE.

annotations.title: Ring bezel
annotations.body: A broad bezel. The shepherd Gyges found that turning the bezel toward his palm made him vanish.

annotations.title: Inside the ring
annotations.body: The inside of the thick gold band. In the Republic, Plato borrows this ring to ask whether one would be just if no one were watching.

artifact.title: Ascalon
artifact.maker: A one-eyed smith (in Richard Johnson's tale)
artifact.power: The dragon-slaying sword that cuts through any armor.
artifact.firstRecord: Richard Johnson, The Seven Champions of Christendom
artifact.summary: The sword of Saint George, who overcame the dragon. It is named after the Holy Land city of Ascalon.
artifact.story:
Saint George was a Roman soldier martyred early in the fourth century, who came to be portrayed in the Middle Ages as a dragon-slaying knight. The thirteenth-century Golden Legend tells how he overcame with a lance a dragon demanding maidens as sacrifice in a city of Libya.

In 1596 Richard Johnson's Seven Champions of Christendom gave his sword the name Ascalon, after a city of the Holy Land at the eastern end of the Mediterranean.

Saint George, who became England's patron saint, was painted countless times spearing the dragon, with his flag of a red cross on white.
artifact.imageAlt: A French walnut carving of Saint George and the Dragon from the early sixteenth century. A mounted knight drives down a lance while a dragon writhes beneath the horse's hooves.

annotations.title: Lance
annotations.body: The knight drives his lance downward. In 1596 Richard Johnson's tale gave Saint George's sword the name Ascalon.

annotations.title: Dragon underfoot
annotations.body: A dragon twists beneath the horse's hooves. In The Golden Legend, George overcame a dragon tormenting a city in Libya and saved a princess.

annotations.title: Knight's face
annotations.body: A young knight in a cap, carved from walnut in early sixteenth-century France.

artifact.title: Noah's Ark
artifact.maker: Built by Noah at God's command
artifact.power: Kept people and animals safe from the flood that covered the world.
artifact.summary: The great vessel that saved Noah's family and the animals from the flood.
artifact.story:
In Genesis, God sees the world filled with evil and resolves to wash it away with a flood. But he tells Noah, a righteous man, to build an ark of gopher wood three hundred cubits long, fifty wide and thirty high.

Noah took his family aboard with every kind of animal, male and female. Rain fell for forty days until the water covered the mountaintops, and when it drained away the ark came to rest on Mount Ararat.

When a dove Noah sent out came back with an olive leaf, he knew the land was dry. The rainbow that rose after the flood became a sign of the promise never again to destroy the world by water. The Mesopotamian Epic of Gilgamesh tells a similar story of flood and ship.
artifact.imageAlt: A sixteenth-century engraving, Noah Leaving the Ark. In front of the huge ark, Noah's family and many animals step down to the ground.

annotations.title: Ark
annotations.body: A huge ark lies at an angle behind. God told Noah to build an ark three hundred cubits long.

annotations.title: Noah and his family
annotations.body: The bearded old man with the staff is Noah. When the flood ended, his family came down from the ark.

annotations.title: Animals coming ashore
annotations.body: Lions, goats, porcupines, deer and other animals taken aboard in pairs step onto the land.

artifact.title: Sword of Saint Peter
artifact.power: Swung to defend his master, and rebuked with “Put your sword into its sheath.”
artifact.summary: The sword with which Peter cut off the ear of the high priest's servant Malchus on the night Jesus was arrested.
artifact.story:
On the night Jesus was arrested in the garden of Gethsemane, his disciple Peter drew a sword and cut off the right ear of Malchus, the high priest's servant. The Gospel of John names both the man who struck and the man who was struck.

Jesus rebuked Peter, saying, "Put your sword into its sheath." The Gospel of Luke adds that Jesus touched the servant's ear and healed him.

The cathedral museum in Poznań, Poland, keeps a sword said to be Peter's. In medieval art Peter is shown with the keys of heaven and sometimes also with this sword.
artifact.imageAlt: A falchion from Venice, about 1490. A hooked hand guard and round pommel sit above a broad single-edged blade.

annotations.title: Pommel
annotations.body: A round pommel with decorative projections.

annotations.title: Curved hand guard
annotations.body: The guard curves like a hook around the hand. Poznań Cathedral in Poland holds a falchion said to be the sword of Peter.

annotations.title: Single-edged blade
annotations.body: A wide single-edged blade. In Gethsemane Peter cut off the ear of Malchus, servant of the high priest, and Jesus told him to put away his sword.

artifact.title: Dhu al-Fiqar
artifact.power: A blade forked at the tip. “No youth like Ali, no sword like Dhu al-Fiqar.”
artifact.firstRecord: Ibn Ishaq, Life of the Prophet
artifact.summary: The sword of Ali, fourth caliph of Islam, depicted with a forked tip.
artifact.story:
Dhu al-Fiqar is said to have been a sword the Prophet Muhammad obtained after the battle of Badr, which passed at the battle of Uhud to Ali, his cousin and son-in-law. The name is interpreted as "having vertebrae."

Tradition relates that when Ali fought bravely with this sword at Uhud, a voice was heard from heaven: "There is no youth like Ali, no sword like Dhu al-Fiqar."

It is usually drawn as a sword forked in two at the tip. In Shi'a Islam especially it became an emblem of Ali and justice, used on banners, amulets and even the flags of Ottoman armies.
artifact.imageAlt: A Turkish kilij. A nineteenth-century gold guard and curved grip of nephrite are mounted on a blade inlaid with gold designs and letters.

source.objectDate: hilt and guard, 19th century; grip, possibly 18th century
source.objectCulture: hilt and guard, Turkish; grip, Indian

annotations.title: Nephrite grip
annotations.body: A curved grip carved from deep green nephrite. The nephrite handle is from India, and the hilt mounts and guard from Turkey.

annotations.title: Gold guard
annotations.body: A gold guard with ends curled like animal heads, set with rubies.

annotations.title: Gold-inlaid letters
annotations.body: Letters and patterns in gold are set into the blade. In Islamic tradition, Dhu al-Fiqar is drawn with a forked tip and praised as the sword of Ali.

artifact.title: Flying Carpet
artifact.power: Sit on it, think of a place, and it takes you there in an instant.
artifact.firstRecord: Galland, French Thousand and One Nights
artifact.summary: The magic carpet in the Thousand and One Nights tale of Prince Ahmed and the Fairy Peri Banu.
artifact.story:
An Indian sultan had three sons, all of whom wished to marry their cousin. The sultan declared he would give her to whichever son brought back the most marvelous thing after a year of traveling the world.

The eldest, Husain, bought in the market of Bisnagar a carpet that carried whoever sat on it to any place they imagined in an instant. The second obtained an ivory spyglass showing faraway things, and the youngest, Ahmed, an apple that cured any disease.

Seeing through the glass that their cousin was dying, the brothers flew home on the carpet and saved her with the apple. Antoine Galland heard this story from the Syrian Hanna Diyab early in the eighteenth century and put it in his French Thousand and One Nights.
artifact.imageAlt: The Seley Carpet from late sixteenth-century Iran, a long carpet with a round medallion at the center of a red ground, surrounded by flowers and vines.

source.creditLine: Presented in memory of Richard Ettinghausen, Gift of Louis E., Theresa S., Hervey, and Elliot Jay Seley, and Purchase, Harris Brisbane Dick and Fletcher Funds, 1978

annotations.title: Central medallion
annotations.body: Patterns spread from the round central medallion. Prince Husain of the Thousand and One Nights bought a carpet in the market of Bisnagar that flew wherever one wished.

annotations.title: Corner ornament
annotations.body: A quarter of the medallion sits in each of the four corners. This is a silk and wool carpet of late sixteenth-century Iran.

annotations.title: Border
annotations.body: Several layers of border enclose the field. Carpets like this covered palace floors or hung on walls.

artifact.title: Ring of the Jinn
artifact.power: Rub it and the jinni of the ring appears to grant your wishes.
artifact.firstRecord: Galland, French Thousand and One Nights
artifact.summary: The genie of the ring, who rescued Aladdin before the magic lamp did.
artifact.story:
In Aladdin and the Magic Lamp, the wicked sorcerer sends Aladdin into a cave to fetch a lamp and puts a ring on him for protection. When Aladdin will not hand over the lamp first, the sorcerer seals the cave entrance.

Wringing his hands in the dark, Aladdin rubs the ring, and the jinni of the ring appears and asks what he desires. Thanks to this jinni, Aladdin gets out of the cave and returns home.

Weaker than the jinni of the lamp, the jinni of the ring still carried Aladdin to the princess when the sorcerer later stole away the whole palace. This story too was told to Galland by Hanna Diyab and added to the Thousand and One Nights.
artifact.imageAlt: A gold ring from Iraq of the twelfth to thirteenth century. The hexagonal bezel is pierced with vines and script-like patterns, and animal-shaped ornaments sit on its shoulders.

annotations.title: Pierced bezel
annotations.body: The hexagonal bezel is cut through with vines and knots. In the Thousand and One Nights, Aladdin summons a genie by rubbing a ring in the cave.

annotations.title: Animal shoulders
annotations.body: Ornaments in animal form sit where bezel meets hoop.

annotations.title: Round bosses
annotations.body: A small gold boss marks each corner. This is a gold ring made in Iraq in the twelfth or thirteenth century.

artifact.title: Book of the Dead
artifact.titleOriginal: Book of the Dead (rw nw prt m hrw)
artifact.power: Reciting its spells carries one past the dangers of the underworld to the paradise of Osiris.
artifact.firstRecord: Funerary texts of the New Kingdom
artifact.summary: A guide to the afterlife buried with the dead. Its true title is “Spells for Going Forth by Day.”
artifact.story:
The ancient Egyptians believed a long journey continued after death. From the New Kingdom on they wrote on papyrus the spells needed to get past the gatekeepers and monsters of the underworld and buried them with the mummy. We call this writing the Book of the Dead, but its original name was "Spells for Going Forth by Day."

Its most famous scene is the weighing of the heart. The dead person's heart was placed on a scale against the feather of Maat, goddess of truth. If it was heavy the monster Ammit devoured it; if light, the dead could enter the paradise of Osiris.

The Book of the Dead was not one book but a selection from nearly two hundred spells. The wealthy commissioned copies with their own names and illustrations.
artifact.imageAlt: An Egyptian Book of the Dead papyrus of 664–30 BCE. Columns of hieroglyphs run across the yellowed sheet, with drawings of boats carrying gods.

source.objectTitle: Book of the Dead Papyrus with Chapters 100 and 129

annotations.title: Boat of the gods
annotations.body: At the top is a boat with gods in a line. The Book of the Dead is a collection of spells buried with the dead to carry them safely through the underworld.

annotations.title: Djed pillar and god
annotations.body: A tiered djed pillar and a god stand at the far left. The djed is the backbone of Osiris and means steadfastness.

annotations.title: Columns of hieroglyphs
annotations.body: On the right the spells run in vertical columns of hieroglyphs. This scroll contains Chapters 100 and 129.

artifact.title: Emerald Tablet
artifact.power: Holds the secret of all things and the foundation of alchemy in fourteen lines: “As above, so below.”
artifact.firstRecord: Arabic Book of the Secret of Creation
artifact.summary: The scripture of alchemy, said to be inscribed by “thrice-great Hermes” on a tablet of emerald.
artifact.story:
Hermes Trismegistus, "thrice-great Hermes," is a legendary sage in whom the Greek god Hermes and the Egyptian god of wisdom Thoth are merged. Many esoteric writings in his name were composed in Hellenistic Egypt.

The Emerald Tablet is a short text he is said to have engraved on a green stone. The Arabic Book of the Secret of Creation, of the eighth or ninth century, relates that a sage found the tablet in an underground chamber in Tyana, held by an old man seated beneath a statue of Hermes. It opens: "That which is above is like that which is below, and that which is below is like that which is above."

After its translation into Latin in the twelfth century, the text became a scripture for European alchemists. Isaac Newton himself wrote out a translation in English. There is no credible record of anyone having seen the tablet itself.
artifact.imageAlt: An Egyptian steatite magical stela (cippus of Horus) of about 300 BCE from the Ptolemaic period. The young Horus standing on crocodiles is carved in relief in the upper part of the dark slab, and spells are densely inscribed below.

annotations.title: Young Horus at the center
annotations.body: The boy Horus stands facing forward in the upper slab, grasping snakes and scorpions. Hermes Trismegistus is a figure merged with the Egyptian god of wisdom Thoth.

annotations.title: Feet on crocodiles
annotations.body: Horus stands on two crocodiles. Stelae like this are inscribed with magic spells to ward off poison and dangerous beasts.

annotations.title: Inscribed spells
annotations.body: Hieroglyphic spells crowd the lower part. The Emerald Tablet too survives as fourteen lines said to be engraved on stone, beginning 'As above, so below.'

artifact.title: Solar Barque of Ra
artifact.power: Crossing the sky by day and the underworld by night, it makes the sun rise again.
artifact.summary: The two ships in which the sun god Ra travels by day and by night.
artifact.story:
The ancient Egyptians believed the sun crossed the sky in a boat. In the morning the sun god Ra rose in the east in a boat called Mandjet, and in the evening he changed to Mesektet and entered the underworld beyond the western horizon.

In the night world the giant serpent Apep lay waiting to swallow the sun. The gods aboard, Set above all, had to fight off Apep so that the sun could rise again the next morning.

Pharaohs hoped after death to board this boat and travel the sky with Ra. The ship 43 meters long found beside the pyramid of Khufu is regarded as evidence of this belief.
artifact.imageAlt: A wooden boat model from Middle Kingdom Egypt. On a green boat with a raised sail stand figures of a rower, a seated person and a steersman.

annotations.title: Sail
annotations.body: A sail raised high. The sun god Ra crosses the sky by day in the 'Boat of Millions of Years' and passes through the underworld by night in another.

annotations.title: Seated figure
annotations.body: The figure seated in white is the owner of this boat. The model was placed in the tomb so the dead could travel by boat in the afterlife.

annotations.title: Steering oar
annotations.body: A long oar at the stern sets the course. Each night the serpent Apep of the underworld tried to swallow the sun's boat.

artifact.title: Rakhsh
artifact.power: Fights lions to protect its master, strong as an elephant and swift as the wind.
artifact.summary: The horse of Rustam, greatest hero of Persia, spotted red as if strewn with rose petals.
artifact.story:
In the Persian epic the Shahnameh (Book of Kings), young Rustam tested many horses to find one that could carry him. Horses sank to the ground when he merely pressed on them, but one colt, spotted red like rose petals, did not budge. That horse was Rakhsh.

On the first night of the Seven Trials undertaken by Rustam to rescue the king, Rakhsh alone killed a lion that was stalking his sleeping master. In the third trial, when a dragon drew near, the horse kept waking Rustam to warn him.

Rakhsh fought beside Rustam all his life and, at the end, fell with him into a pit dug by a traitor, and they died together.
artifact.imageAlt: A page from a Shahnameh manuscript painted in India around 1450, Rustam Lassos Rakhsh. Between Persian text above and below, a herd of horses runs on a meadow among people holding lassos.

source.objectTitle: "Rustam Lassos Rakhsh", Folio from a Shahnama (Book of Kings)

annotations.title: Herd of horses
annotations.body: A herd running on the meadow. The hero Rustam sought a strong young horse fit to carry him among many others.

annotations.title: Man with a lasso
annotations.body: Rustam throwing a lasso. Caught in that noose, Rakhsh became his lifelong companion.

annotations.title: Persian verse
annotations.body: Verses from Ferdowsi's Shahnameh are written above and below. This page comes from a manuscript painted in India around 1450.

artifact.title: Bucephalus
artifact.power: A wild horse no one could tame, afraid of its own shadow.
artifact.summary: The horse tamed by the boy Alexander, who rode it from Persia to India.
artifact.story:
According to Plutarch, a huge black horse brought for sale before Philip of Macedon would let no one ride it. Alexander, about twelve years old, noticed that it was startled by its own shadow, turned its head toward the sun, mounted and tamed it.

Philip is said to have told his son, "Macedon is too small for you; seek a kingdom that fits you." The name Bucephalus means "ox head."

Bucephalus carried Alexander through Persia as far as India. When the horse died of age by the river Hydaspes in 326 BCE, Alexander founded a city there and named it Bucephala.
artifact.imageAlt: A silver tetradrachm of Alexander the Great from the Seleucid dynasty, about 325–319 BCE, bearing a profile wearing a lion skin in the guise of Heracles.

annotations.title: Lion-skin helmet
annotations.body: He wears a lion skin on his head, the costume of Heracles. Alexander the Great is thought to be shown here as Heracles.

annotations.title: Profile
annotations.body: A straight nose and deep-set eye. Alexander noticed that Bucephalus, whom no one could tame, was startled by its own shadow, and mounted it facing the sun.

annotations.title: Edge of the coin
annotations.body: The thick rim of the silver coin, a tetradrachm struck by the Seleucid dynasty late in the fourth century BCE.

artifact.title: Sword of Light
artifact.owner: Nuada, king of the Tuatha Dé Danann
artifact.power: Once out of its sheath, no one can escape it.
artifact.summary: One of the four treasures of the Irish gods, a sword no one could evade once it was drawn.
artifact.story:
The divine people of Ireland, the Tuatha Dé Danann, are said to have brought four treasures from four cities across the northern sea: the Stone of Destiny from Falias, the Spear of Lugh from Gorias, the Sword of Nuada from Findias and the Cauldron of the Dagda from Murias.

Once the sword from Findias was drawn, no one could flee from it. In later folklore it came to be called the shining "sword of light."

Nuada lost an arm at the first battle of Mag Tuired and stepped down from the throne. When the healing god Dian Cécht made him an arm of silver, he became king again as Nuada of the Silver Arm.
