artifact.imageAlt: A Celtic sword and scabbard of about 60 BCE. The copper-alloy scabbard is covered in blue-green patina, and the end of the hilt splits into two curls.

annotations.title: Anthropoid hilt
annotations.body: The end of the hilt splits like a person spreading two arms, a common 'anthropoid' hilt of Celtic Iron Age swords.

annotations.title: Scabbard mouth
annotations.body: The bronze fitting at the mouth of the scabbard. Once Nuada's sword was drawn, no one could escape it.

annotations.title: Patinated scabbard
annotations.body: Blue-green patina covers the copper-alloy scabbard of this Celtic sword of about 60 BCE.

artifact.title: Spear of Lugh
artifact.owner: Lugh, god of light and skill
artifact.power: No battle can be won against the one who holds it.
artifact.summary: One of the four treasures of the Tuatha Dé Danann, the spear of victory from Gorias.
artifact.story:
Lugh is a god skilled in every art. When he first arrived at the Tuatha Dé Danann's palace at Tara and the doorkeeper asked what he could do, he named smith, poet, physician, warrior and sorcerer in turn, and entered because he alone possessed them all.

No battle could be won against the holder of his spear from Gorias. Later stories say the spear so thirsted for blood and shot out such flames that it had to be kept in water when not in use.

At the second battle of Mag Tuired Lugh faced Balor, one-eyed king of the Fomorians. When Balor opened the eye that killed everything it saw, Lugh pierced it and ended the fight.
artifact.imageAlt: An Etruscan bronze spearhead. Two barb-like wings extend behind a long triangular blade with a central ridge.

annotations.title: Spear point
annotations.body: A long, tapered point. No battle could be won against the bearer of Lugh's spear.

annotations.title: Barbs
annotations.body: Hook-like barbs extend behind the blade so that it does not slip easily from a wound.

annotations.title: Socket
annotations.body: The socket at the back held a wooden shaft. The photograph shows an Etruscan bronze spearhead.

artifact.title: Gáe Bulg
artifact.maker: Taught by the warrior woman Scáthach
artifact.power: Thrown with the foot, its barbs open inside the body so that it cannot be pulled out.
artifact.summary: The spear of Ireland's greatest hero, Cú Chulainn, given to him alone by his teacher Scáthach.
artifact.story:
Cú Chulainn learned the arts of war from the warrior woman Scáthach on the Isle of Skye across the sea. Having taught him every feat, Scáthach passed on the Gáe Bulg and its use to him alone.

The Gáe Bulg was cast from between the toes and kicked through the water. Inside an enemy's body thirty barbs opened, so that it could not be taken out without cutting the body open.

In The Cattle Raid of Cooley, Cú Chulainn fought for four days at a ford against Ferdiad, a friend as close as a brother. He finally brought Ferdiad down with the Gáe Bulg, and held him in long mourning.
artifact.imageAlt: An Indonesian spear of the eighteenth to nineteenth century. Three pairs of crescent-shaped barbs rise in tiers along both sides of a broad steel blade.

annotations.title: Spear tip
annotations.body: A broadly curving spearhead. The Gáe Bulg was the spear the warrior Scáthach gave only to Cú Chulainn.

annotations.title: Tiers of barbs
annotations.body: Crescent-shaped barbs rise in tiers on both sides. The legendary Gáe Bulg opened thirty barbs inside the body so it could not be removed.

annotations.title: Binding
annotations.body: The head is firmly bound to the shaft with cord and resin. The photograph shows an Indonesian spear of the eighteenth to nineteenth century.

artifact.title: Fragarach
artifact.owner: The sea god Manannán, later Lugh
artifact.power: Held to the throat, it prevents its victim from moving or lying. Wounds from it never heal.
artifact.firstRecord: The Fate of the Children of Tuireann
artifact.summary: The sword called “the Answerer,” given to Lugh by the sea god Manannán.
artifact.story:
Fragarach means "the answerer" or "the retaliator" in Irish. It was the sword of the sea god Manannán mac Lir and later passed to Lugh, god of light.

A person held at the throat by this sword could neither move nor lie. No one survived its wounds, and no armor could stop its blade.

In the later tale "The Fate of the Children of Tuireann," Lugh wore this sword to battle against the Fomorians. On the three sons of Tuireann, who had killed his father, he laid the penalty of gathering treasures from the ends of the earth.
artifact.imageAlt: A Cypriot iron sword of the sixth century BCE. A hilt end survives above a straight blade thick with rust, with one silver rivet gleaming.

source.creditLine: The Cesnola Collection, Purchased by subscription, 1874–76

annotations.title: Hilt end
annotations.body: A single silver rivet gleams on the rusted hilt end. The hilt was once decorated in silver and bronze. This is a Cypriot sword of the sixth century BCE.

annotations.title: Straight blade
annotations.body: A straight iron blade thick with rust. No armor could stop Fragarach, and wounds from it did not heal.

annotations.title: Point
annotations.body: A narrowly tapered point. Lugh held this sword to the throat so that a person could neither move nor lie.

artifact.title: Caladbolg
artifact.owner: The Ulster hero Fergus mac Róich
artifact.power: When swung it lengthens like a rainbow and shears off the tops of hills.
artifact.summary: The sword of Fergus. Its name shares a root with the Welsh Caledfwlch, that is, Excalibur.
artifact.story:
Fergus mac Róich was a former king of Ulster, driven from the throne, who fought for Connacht against Ulster. His sword Caladbolg was said to stretch out long like a rainbow when swung.

In the last great battle of The Cattle Raid of Cooley, Fergus swept through the Ulster army with Caladbolg. When his old comrade Cormac urged him to remember his homeland, Fergus turned the sword from men to hills and struck off the tops of the three hills of Meath.

Scholars regard Caladbolg as a name of the same root as the Welsh Caledfwlch, and so as Excalibur. The legend of a "shining sword" widespread in the Celtic world attached itself to different heroes in different places.
artifact.imageAlt: An iron sword from Roman Gaul of the second century BCE to first century CE. The blade, with its bronze hilt, is heavily rusted and uneven.

annotations.title: Pommel
annotations.body: A rusted lump of a pommel. Caladbolg is a name of the same root as the Welsh Caledfwlch, that is, Excalibur.

annotations.title: Bronze grip
annotations.body: A bronze grip with patina. This is a sword of Gaul of the second century BCE to the first century CE.

annotations.title: Rusted blade
annotations.body: The iron blade is rusted and uneven. Fergus turned Caladbolg from men to hills and struck the tops off three hills.

artifact.title: Cauldron of the Dagda
artifact.owner: The Dagda, god of the Tuatha Dé Danann
artifact.power: It never runs dry, however many eat. None left it unsatisfied.
artifact.summary: One of the four treasures of the Tuatha Dé Danann, the cauldron of plenty from Murias.
artifact.story:
The Dagda, "the good god," is a father-figure among the Tuatha Dé Danann. He owned a great club, one end of which killed and the other revived, and a cauldron that never ran dry.

The cauldron from Murias never emptied however many people ate from it, and no one is said to have left it unsatisfied.

When the Fomorians mockingly made him an enormous quantity of porridge and threatened to kill him if he failed to finish it, the Dagda ladled it all down. The Irish could not think of the cauldron of plenty apart from the Dagda.
artifact.imageAlt: An Etruscan bronze cauldron of about 550 BCE. The round body has a lid and hanging rings, with blotches of blue-green patina on its surface.

annotations.title: Lid
annotations.body: A round lid with a handle ring. The Dagda's cauldron was one of the four treasures the Tuatha Dé Danann brought from Murias.

annotations.title: Hanging rings
annotations.body: Rings on both sides let it hang over a fire.

annotations.title: Round body
annotations.body: A round body blotched with patina. The Dagda's cauldron never emptied however many ate. The photograph shows an Etruscan bronze cauldron of about 550 BCE.

artifact.title: Vajra
artifact.power: Unbreakable as diamond and striking like lightning. It slew Vritra, the serpent of drought.
artifact.summary: The thunderbolt of Indra, which became in Buddhism the ritual implement that shatters delusion.
artifact.story:
Indra, the god most praised in the Rigveda, fights with the vajra. When the great serpent Vritra imprisoned the world's waters and caused drought, Indra struck him down with the vajra and released the rivers.

Later stories say the weapon was made from the bones of the sage Dadhichi. When the gods were losing to the demons, Dadhichi gave up his life and the artisan god made the vajra from his bones.

Vajra means both "thunderbolt" and "diamond." In Buddhism and Tibetan esoteric practice it became the ritual implement called dorje, standing for wisdom nothing can break, and is used paired with a bell.
artifact.imageAlt: A twelfth-century Vietnamese bronze vajra. Hook-like prongs gather at both ends of a central grip.

source.creditLine: Gift of Steven Kossak, The Kronos Collections, 1992

annotations.title: Central grip
annotations.body: The central rounded section is held in the hand. Indra swung the vajra to bring down the serpent Vritra, who had imprisoned the waters.

annotations.title: Hooked prongs
annotations.body: The prongs at both ends curve like hooks and converge to a point. In Buddhism it became the ritual implement that shatters delusion.

annotations.title: Lotus base
annotations.body: Lotus petals surround the place between prongs and grip. The photograph shows a twelfth-century Vietnamese bronze vajra.

artifact.title: Trishula
artifact.owner: Shiva, god of destruction and renewal
artifact.power: Its three prongs govern creation, preservation and destruction, or past, present and future.
artifact.summary: Shiva's trident. Its three blades stand for three worlds and three powers.
artifact.story:
Trishula means "three spikes" and is the object most representative of Shiva. He is shown with this trident driving away demons.

The three prongs are interpreted in many ways: as the three powers of creation, preservation and destruction, as the three times of past, present and future, or as the three qualities of the human mind.

The goddess Durga too killed the buffalo demon Mahishasura with a trident received from Shiva. Even today a trident often stands in front of Shiva temples in India.
artifact.imageAlt: A hand-colored lithograph from Calcutta, India, 1878–1883, Shiva Mahadev. Shiva, wearing a tiger skin, walks a mountain path with a trident on his shoulder.

source.creditLine: Purchase, Friends of Asian Art Gifts, 2021

annotations.title: Trident
annotations.body: The trident Shiva carries on his shoulder. Its three prongs are read as creation, preservation and destruction.

annotations.title: Wild hair and beard
annotations.body: Tousled hair and a long beard. Shiva is often pictured as an ascetic practicing in the Himalayas.

annotations.title: Tiger skin
annotations.body: A tiger skin wraps his waist. This is a colored lithograph printed in Calcutta in 1878–1883.

artifact.title: Sudarshana Chakra
artifact.power: A disc with 108 teeth. Thrown, it cuts down enemies and returns to the hand.
artifact.summary: Vishnu's spinning disc, with which Krishna beheaded Shishupala.
artifact.story:
Vishnu holds in his four hands a conch, a mace, a lotus and the shining disc Sudarshana Chakra. This weapon, whose name means "beautiful to behold," spun on his fingertip, flew off to cut down enemies and returned.

In the Mahabharata, Krishna, an avatar of Vishnu, tolerates Shishupala's insults a hundred times, then at the hundred and first hurls this disc and takes off his head.

When gods and demons fought over the nectar of immortality, this was also the disc that beheaded Rahu, the demon who secretly drank it. Only his head survived, and it is said eclipses happen when Rahu tries to swallow the sun and moon.
artifact.imageAlt: A gilt-copper Vishnu from the Kathmandu Valley in Nepal, dated 1105. The four-armed Vishnu stands on a pedestal holding a wheel-shaped disc and a mace in his upper hands.

source.creditLine: Purchase, Louis V. Bell, Harris Brisbane Dick, Fletcher, and Rogers Funds and Joseph Pulitzer Bequest, Brooke Russell Astor Bequest, The Vincent Astor Foundation and Mr. and Mrs. Richard L. Chilton Jr. Gifts, and The Fred Eychaner Charitable Fund Gift, in honor of John Guy, 2015

annotations.title: Disc
annotations.body: The wheel-shaped disc in his upper left hand. The Sudarshana Chakra spins from the fingertip, flies out to cut down enemies and returns.

annotations.title: Mace
annotations.body: The mace in his upper right hand. Vishnu holds disc, mace, conch and lotus in his four hands.

annotations.title: Crown and halo
annotations.body: A tall crown and halo behind. This gilt-copper figure was made in the Kathmandu Valley of Nepal in 1105.

artifact.title: Gandiva
artifact.power: Paired with a quiver that never empties, its bowstring sounds like thunder.
artifact.summary: The bow of Arjuna, master archer of the Mahabharata, delivered to him by the fire god Agni.
artifact.story:
The fire god Agni wished to restore his strength by burning the Khandava forest, but Indra, its protector, kept sending rain to stop him. Agni asked Krishna and Arjuna for help and, in return, obtained from the water god Varuna the bow Gandiva and two inexhaustible quivers, which he gave to Arjuna.

Gandiva was made by Brahma and reached Arjuna through the hands of many gods and heroes. When Arjuna drew its string it sounded like thunder.

At the great war of Kurukshetra Arjuna felled countless enemies with Gandiva. When the time came for him to end his life, he cast the bow into the sea and returned it to Varuna.
artifact.imageAlt: A page from the Razmnama, the Persian translation of the Mahabharata, painted in Mughal India about 1616–17, Arjuna Battles Raja Tamradhvaja. Warriors on chariots, horses and elephants fight between blocks of text.

source.objectTitle: "Arjuna Battles Raja Tamradhvaja", Folio from a Razmnama

annotations.title: Chariot and warriors
annotations.body: A horse-drawn chariot and archers tangle in the central band. Arjuna took up Gandiva and rode in the chariot driven by Krishna.

annotations.title: Elephant corps
annotations.body: Warriors on elephants press forward below. The war of the Mahabharata was fought with chariots, elephants, cavalry and foot soldiers.

annotations.title: Persian text
annotations.body: The text of the Razmnama, the Persian translation of the Mahabharata, appears above. The Mughal emperor Akbar ordered this translation.

artifact.title: Amrita
artifact.maker: Obtained by churning the ocean of milk
artifact.power: Whoever drinks it does not die.
artifact.summary: The drink of immortality, won when gods and demons together churned the ocean of milk.
artifact.story:
When the gods lost their strength, Vishnu told them to join with the demons and churn the ocean of milk to obtain the drink of immortality. With Mount Mandara as the churning rod and the great serpent Vasuki as the rope, they pulled from both sides, and Vishnu became the tortoise Kurma to bear the mountain on his back.

Along with all sorts of treasures, the poison that could burn the world rose first. Shiva swallowed it and his throat turned blue, and last of all the divine physician Dhanvantari appeared with the jar of amrita.

When the demons seized the jar, Vishnu turned into the beautiful woman Mohini, beguiled them and served amrita to the gods alone. The demon Rahu, who slipped in and drank, had his head cut off by the disc, but his head did not die.
artifact.imageAlt: A painting from Mandi in the Punjab Hills of India, about 1780–90, The Churning of the Ocean of Milk. A serpent winds around a pillar set on a tortoise, with gods and demons pulling on either side; a many-armed Vishnu sits on a lotus above, among a white horse, an elephant, the sun and the moon.

source.creditLine: Gift of Mr. and Mrs. Alvin N. Haas, 1977
source.objectTitle: The Churning of the Ocean of Milk

annotations.title: Vishnu on the lotus
annotations.body: A many-armed Vishnu sits on the lotus atop the pillar. Vishnu had gods and demons churn the sea together to obtain the drink of immortality.

annotations.title: Gods and demons pulling the serpent
annotations.body: Gods pull from the left and demons from the right on Vasuki, the serpent wound around the pillar, Mount Mandara.

annotations.title: Tortoise
annotations.body: A tortoise holds up the mountain on its back beneath the pillar. This is Vishnu in the form of the tortoise Kurma.

artifact.title: Kavacha and Kundala
artifact.power: Golden armor and earrings one with his body. While he wears them, Karna cannot die.
artifact.summary: The armor and earrings Karna, son of the sun god, was born with, and gave away.
artifact.story:
While still a maiden, Kunti called on the sun god Surya with a spell she had received, and bore a son. The child Karna was born wearing golden armor and earrings attached to his body, and while he had them no one could kill him.

Before the great war of Kurukshetra, Indra, king of the gods and father of Arjuna, disguised himself as a Brahmin and went to Karna. Karna was famous for giving whatever anyone asked.

Surya warned him in a dream, but Karna cut the armor and earrings from his own skin and handed them to Indra. Moved, Indra gave him a spear he could use only once. Karna's generosity is still praised in India today.
artifact.imageAlt: A gold earring from the Kathmandu Valley in Nepal, seventeenth or eighteenth century. Red and blue gems set in a gold wire framework show Vishnu riding the bird Garuda, with pearls and gold disks hanging below.

source.creditLine: Gift of Mr. and Mrs. J. H. Wade

annotations.title: Vishnu on Garuda
annotations.body: Vishnu appears in blue stone at the center, with the bird Garuda's red face below. Karna, son of the sun god Surya, was born wearing golden earrings and armor.

annotations.title: Jeweled gold frame
annotations.body: Red and blue stones are set into a framework of gold wire. Earrings like this were hung on images of the gods in Nepalese temples.

annotations.title: Pearls and gold disks
annotations.body: Strands of pearls and gold disks sway below. Karna kept his vow to give whatever was asked, and cut his earrings and armor from his own skin for Indra.

artifact.title: Cintamani
artifact.owner: Bodhisattvas such as Kshitigarbha and Cintamanicakra
artifact.power: A jewel that grants whatever one wishes.
artifact.summary: The wish-fulfilling jewel, revered in both Buddhism and Hinduism.
artifact.story:
Cintamani means "thought-jewel" in Sanskrit. Whoever held this jewel could obtain anything desired; it gave light in the dark, removed poison and cured disease.

In Buddhism it symbolizes the Buddha's teaching and the compassion of bodhisattvas. Kshitigarbha and Cintamanicakra hold it in their hands and grant the wishes of living beings.

The jewel that dragons clutch or chase in East Asian paintings is also the cintamani. It was believed that only a dragon who obtained it could rise to heaven.
artifact.imageAlt: A tile from Ottoman Turkey of about 1560–70. On a deep blue ground it bears the cintamani pattern: three white orbs with red dots and rippling white stripes.

annotations.title: Three orbs
annotations.body: Orbs in groups of three form the 'cintamani' pattern, named after the jewel that grants any wish.

annotations.title: Wavy stripes
annotations.body: The rippling stripes beside the orbs are read as tiger stripes or clouds. This pattern was a favorite of the sixteenth-century Ottoman court.

artifact.title: Gan Jiang and Mo Ye
artifact.maker: The sword-making couple Gan Jiang and Mo Ye
artifact.power: A male and female pair of swords that cut iron like mud.
artifact.firstRecord: Spring and Autumn Annals of Wu and Yue
artifact.summary: A pair of swords named for the couple who forged them, the beginning of China's famous-sword legends.
artifact.story:
According to the Spring and Autumn Annals of Wu and Yue, King Helü of Wu ordered the smith Gan Jiang to forge famous swords. But after three months the metal would not melt.

Gan Jiang's wife Mo Ye, having heard that smiths of old had given themselves when iron would not melt, cut off her hair and fingernails and put them in the furnace. The iron melted and became two swords, and the couple named the male sword Gan Jiang and the female Mo Ye.

The Jin-dynasty Soushen Ji tells a different story, in which the king of Chu kills Gan Jiang after receiving his sword, and Gan Jiang's son gives his life for revenge. "Gan Jiang and Mo Ye" came to mean any famous sword.
artifact.imageAlt: A Chinese bronze sword of the fifth to fourth century BCE, with a ridge along the center of its straight double-edged blade and rings around the grip.

annotations.title: Ringed grip
annotations.body: Two ring bands circle the grip, the form of bronze swords of the states of Wu and Yue.

annotations.title: Writing on the blade
annotations.body: Faint characters are visible on the blade. After three months of failing to melt the iron, Gan Jiang and Mo Ye at last made a male and female pair.

annotations.title: Tip
annotations.body: A narrowly tapered point. This is a Chinese bronze sword of the fifth to fourth century BCE.

artifact.title: Ruyi Jingu Bang
artifact.maker: An iron pillar once used by King Yu to measure the sea
artifact.power: Weighs 13,500 catties. Grows and shrinks at will, down to a needle for tucking in the ear.
artifact.firstRecord: Wu Cheng'en, Journey to the West
artifact.summary: The staff Sun Wukong took from the palace of the Dragon King of the East Sea, capped with gold at each end.
artifact.story:
Sun Wukong went to the palace of the Dragon King of the East Sea in search of a weapon. When he rejected every spear and sword offered as too light, the Dragon King pointed to an iron pillar lodged at the bottom of the sea, once used by King Yu of Xia to measure the depths when he controlled the floods.

The pillar shone and shrank as Sun Wukong approached. Gold bands circled its ends, and it was inscribed "Ruyi Jingu Bang, weight 13,500 catties."

The staff grew as tall as heaven or shrank as small as a needle at his wish. Sun Wukong usually carried it reduced to a needle inside his ear.
artifact.imageAlt: A Japanese woodblock print of about 1824 by Yashima Gakutei, Sun Wukong. The monkey king in red robes stands on ground spread with clouds, a long staff on his back, blowing out a swarm of tiny monkeys.

source.creditLine: H. O. Havemeyer Collection, Bequest of Mrs. H. O. Havemeyer, 1929
source.objectTitle: The Monkey King Songokū, from the Chinese novel Journey to the West

annotations.title: Staff on his shoulder
annotations.body: A long staff carried at an angle behind the back. Ruyi Jingu Bang is an iron pillar of 13,500 catties that grows and shrinks at will.

annotations.title: Tiny monkeys blown out
annotations.body: A breath sends a swarm of tiny monkeys into the air. Sun Wukong plucks his hairs and blows on them to make countless copies of himself.

annotations.title: Clouds
annotations.body: Clouds spread at his feet. Sun Wukong rides the Somersault Cloud, 108,000 li to a leap. This woodblock print is by Yashima Gakutei, about 1824.

artifact.title: Green Dragon Crescent Blade
artifact.power: A great blade weighing 82 catties, also called “Cold Beauty.”
artifact.firstRecord: Luo Guanzhong, Romance of the Three Kingdoms
artifact.summary: The great crescent-shaped blade wielded by Guan Yu in the Romance of the Three Kingdoms.
artifact.story:
In the Romance of the Three Kingdoms, Liu Bei, Guan Yu and Zhang Fei swear brotherhood in a peach garden and then each prepare weapons. Guan Yu made the Green Dragon Crescent Blade, weighing 82 catties. Its edge was shaped like a reclining crescent moon and carved with a dragon.

With this blade Guan Yu cut down Dong Zhuo's fierce general Hua Xiong before his wine could cool, and felled Yuan Shao's generals Yan Liang and Wen Chou. Leaving Cao Cao to return to Liu Bei, he killed six generals at five passes.

The historical Records of the Three Kingdoms does not say Guan Yu used such a blade. It became his symbol through storytellers of the Song and Yuan. Today it stands beside him in temples dedicated to Guan Yu.
artifact.imageAlt: A nineteenth-century Jingdezhen porcelain figure of Guan Yu. Dressed in green armor and robes, Guan Yu sits stroking his long beard with one hand.

source.objectTitle: Figure of Guan Yu, a guardian deity

annotations.title: Hand stroking the beard
annotations.body: One hand strokes a long beard. Guan Yu was called 'Lord of the Beautiful Beard.'

annotations.title: Green armor
annotations.body: Armor and robes in green glaze. Guan Yu is pictured in a green battle robe holding the Green Dragon Crescent Blade.

annotations.title: Seated pose
annotations.body: A nineteenth-century porcelain figure of Guan Yu from Jingdezhen, China. Today Guan Yu is worshiped in temples as a god of war and wealth.

artifact.title: Sky Piercer
artifact.power: A halberd with a crescent blade beside the spear point. Lü Bu hit its small branch with an arrow at 150 paces.
artifact.firstRecord: Luo Guanzhong, Romance of the Three Kingdoms
artifact.summary: The halberd of Lü Bu, greatest warrior of the Romance of the Three Kingdoms.
artifact.story:
Lü Bu in the Romance of the Three Kingdoms fights in a red brocade robe, riding Red Hare and wielding the Sky Piercer. At Hulao Pass he took on the three brothers Liu Bei, Guan Yu and Zhang Fei all at once.

The Sky Piercer is a halberd with a crescent-shaped blade beside its spear point. To stop a fight between Yuan Shu's general Ji Ling and Liu Bei, Lü Bu planted the halberd 150 paces outside the camp gate and said they should stop fighting if he hit its small branch with an arrow. The arrow struck the branch exactly.

This episode of shooting at the halberd also appears in the historical Records of the Three Kingdoms, which says only that what he hit was the small branch of the halberd.
artifact.imageAlt: A Chinese bronze halberd head (ge) of the Zhou dynasty, 1122–255 BCE. A horizontal blade and the part inserted into the shaft form a T.

annotations.title: Horizontal blade
annotations.body: A bronze blade set crosswise on a shaft. Adding a spear point makes a ji, and Lü Bu's Sky Piercer gives the blade a crescent form.

annotations.title: Holes for binding
annotations.body: A cord through the holes at the base of the blade fixed it to the wooden shaft.

annotations.title: Downward extension
annotations.body: The long extension below the blade was used to hook and pull an opponent. This is a Zhou-dynasty bronze of the eleventh to third century BCE.

artifact.title: Red Hare
artifact.power: Runs a thousand li a day and crosses rivers and mountains as if on level ground.
artifact.firstRecord: Chen Shou, Records of the Three Kingdoms, Biography of Lü Bu
artifact.summary: A famous horse red as burning charcoal. “Among men Lü Bu, among horses Red Hare,” went the saying.
artifact.story:
The Biography of Lü Bu in the Records of the Three Kingdoms says he had a fine horse named Red Hare. Pei Songzhi's commentary records that people of the time said, "Among men Lü Bu, among horses Red Hare."

The Romance of the Three Kingdoms adds more. Dong Zhuo used Red Hare to lure Lü Bu into betraying his foster father Ding Yuan. After Lü Bu died Cao Cao gave the horse to Guan Yu to win his heart, and Guan Yu rejoiced that with it he could reach his elder brother Liu Bei in a single day if he learned where he was.

The Romance says that after Guan Yu's death Red Hare refused to eat and followed him in death.
artifact.imageAlt: A bronze horse of the late seventeenth century. Mane flying, it leaps with forelegs raised high on a black base.

source.creditLine: The Jack and Belle Linsky Collection, 1982

annotations.title: Head with flying mane
annotations.body: The head is raised and the mane flies. Red Hare was said to run a thousand li in a day.

annotations.title: Raised forelegs
annotations.body: He leaps with forelegs held high. After Lü Bu died, Cao Cao gave this horse to Guan Yu to win his heart.

annotations.title: Tail
annotations.body: A tail streaming behind. This is a bronze horse by the Italian sculptor Francesco Fanelli, of the late seventeenth century.

artifact.title: Nine Tripod Cauldrons
artifact.owner: The royal houses of Xia, Shang and Zhou
artifact.power: The legitimacy to rule all under heaven. They rest with dynasties of virtue.
artifact.summary: Nine cauldrons King Yu cast from metal sent by the nine provinces, signifying dynastic legitimacy.
artifact.story:
King Yu of Xia, who controlled the floods, divided the realm into nine provinces and cast nine great cauldrons from metal each province sent him. The mountains, rivers and monsters of each region are said to have been depicted on them, so that people would know what to avoid.

The Nine Tripods passed from Xia to Shang and then to Zhou. According to the Zuo Zhuan, when King Zhuang of Chu asked a Zhou envoy their size and weight, the envoy replied, "It depends on virtue, not on the tripods." To "ask the weight of the tripods" still means to covet another's power.

After the Zhou fell the Nine Tripods vanished. The Records of the Grand Historian says the First Emperor of Qin sent a thousand men into the Si River to retrieve a sunken cauldron, but they could not find it.
artifact.imageAlt: A thirteenth-century BCE Chinese bronze tripod cauldron (ding) of the Shang dynasty. A band of animal-face design rings the round vessel with two upright handles, under blue-green patina.

annotations.title: Upright handles
annotations.body: Handles rise on both sides of the mouth. A pole through them was used to lift and carry the cauldron.

annotations.title: Animal-face band
annotations.body: A band of animal faces and spirals rings the mouth. King Yu is said to have cast the mountains, rivers and monsters of each region onto his nine cauldrons.

annotations.title: Three legs
annotations.body: Three stout legs bear the cauldron. This is a Shang-dynasty bronze ding of the thirteenth century BCE.

artifact.title: Heirloom Seal of the Realm
artifact.owner: The First Emperor of Qin and later emperors
artifact.maker: Calligraphy by the Qin chancellor Li Si
artifact.power: “Having received the mandate of heaven, may it flourish forever.” Whoever holds this seal is emperor.
artifact.summary: The jade seal of the First Emperor, said to be made from the Jade of Bian He, the symbol of imperial legitimacy.
artifact.story:
Legend says this seal was made from the Jade of Bian He. Bian He of Chu found a piece of jade in the mountains and presented it to two kings, but had his feet cut off twice for offering a mere stone. Only when a third king had the stone split was it known to be the greatest jade under heaven.

The First Emperor had this jade made into a seal, and Chancellor Li Si wrote eight characters: "Having received the mandate of heaven, may it flourish forever." From then on the holder of this seal was regarded as the emperor recognized by heaven.

The Book of Han records that when Wang Mang seized the Han, the empress dowager hurled the seal to the ground, and later accounts say a corner broke off and was repaired with gold. The seal changed owners with each dynasty until it vanished around the Five Dynasties and Ten Kingdoms period.
artifact.imageAlt: An early twentieth-century Chinese jade seal. A rounded knob sits on a square body and is pierced for a cord.

annotations.title: Rounded knob
annotations.body: The rounded knob on the seal. The knob of the Heirloom Seal is said to have been carved with five intertwined dragons.

annotations.title: Cord hole
annotations.body: A hole pierces the knob for a cord, by which a seal was worn at the waist.

annotations.title: Square body
annotations.body: The square base where the characters are carved. The Heirloom Seal bore the eight characters 'Having received the mandate of heaven, may it flourish forever.'

artifact.title: Banana-Leaf Fan
artifact.power: One wave puts out fire, two bring wind, three bring rain.
artifact.firstRecord: Wu Cheng'en, Journey to the West
artifact.summary: The fan of Princess Iron Fan that extinguishes the Flaming Mountains. Sun Wukong fought three times to get it.
artifact.story:
On their way west, Tripitaka's party met the Flaming Mountains, where fire burned for eight hundred li. To put it out they needed the banana-leaf fan of Princess Iron Fan, wife of the Bull Demon King.

Holding a grudge because Sun Wukong had handed her son Red Boy over to Guanyin, the princess refused to lend it. Sun Wukong turned into an insect, got into her belly and forced her to hand it over, but it was a fake that only made the fire larger.

Disguised as the Bull Demon King he took the real one, then lost it again by trickery, and won it only after three fights. Waving the fan forty-nine times, he put out the fire of the Flaming Mountains forever.
artifact.imageAlt: A late nineteenth-century round fan painting by the Chinese painter Shu Hao, Zhou Dunyi Admiring Lotus Flowers. A scholar seated in a pavilion by a pond and lotus leaves are painted within a circular composition on silk.

source.creditLine: Gift of Robert Hatfield Ellsworth, in memory of La Ferne Hatfield Ellsworth, 1986

annotations.title: Scholar admiring lotuses
annotations.body: A scholar seated in a pavilion gazes at the lotuses. In 'On the Love of the Lotus,' the Song scholar Zhou Dunyi praised the lotus that rises unstained from mud.

annotations.title: Lotus leaves
annotations.body: Lotus leaves fill the pond, arranged to follow the round fan composition.

annotations.title: Writing and seals
annotations.body: The painter Shu Hao's writing and seals appear at upper left. Princess Iron Fan's banana-leaf fan put out fire at a single wave.

artifact.title: Peaches of Immortality
artifact.owner: Xiwangmu, Queen Mother of the West
artifact.power: Fruiting once in three thousand years, they make those who eat them immortal and ageless.
artifact.summary: The peaches of the Queen Mother of the West, which Sun Wukong secretly ate while guarding them.
artifact.story:
Xiwangmu, goddess of Mount Kunlun, grows peaches of immortality. In the Han Wu Gushi, she visits Emperor Wu of Han and shares her peaches; when the emperor tries to plant the stones, she laughs and says they fruit only once in three thousand years.

In Journey to the West the Jade Emperor puts Sun Wukong in charge of the peach orchard. The peaches ripen in three varieties, once every three, six or nine thousand years, and those who eat the ripe fruit become immortals or live as long as heaven and earth.

Learning he had not been invited to the banquet, Sun Wukong devoured all the peaches, setting off a great uproar in heaven.
artifact.imageAlt: A mid-eighteenth-century porcelain vase from Jingdezhen, China, painted in overglaze enamels. Branches with nine pink peaches are painted on a white ground.

source.creditLine: Mr. and Mrs. Isaac D. Fletcher Collection, Bequest of Isaac D. Fletcher, 1917

annotations.title: Peaches
annotations.body: Pink peaches hang from the branch. Xiwangmu's peaches fruit once in three thousand years and keep those who eat them from aging.

annotations.title: Branches and flowers
annotations.body: Peach branches and flowers climb the shoulder of the vase. Sun Wukong guarded the orchard and ate all the peaches.

annotations.title: Rounded body
annotations.body: A globular 'celestial sphere' shape. This is overglaze-enameled porcelain fired at Jingdezhen in the mid-eighteenth century.

artifact.title: Golden Headband
artifact.power: When a spell is recited it tightens around the head and subdues Sun Wukong.
artifact.firstRecord: Wu Cheng'en, Journey to the West
artifact.summary: The gold band Tripitaka placed on the unruly Sun Wukong.
artifact.story:
Soon after being freed from under the Five Elements Mountain and becoming Tripitaka's disciple, Sun Wukong killed some bandits and left his master in anger after being scolded.

Guanyin gave Tripitaka a flowered cap, a gold band and a spell called the Tightening Spell. When Sun Wukong came back and put on the cap, the band stuck fast to his head, and when Tripitaka recited the spell it squeezed as though to split his skull.

Sun Wukong tried to twist the band off with his staff, to no avail. From then on he protected his master on the whole journey west. When he became a Buddha in the West, the band vanished on its own.
artifact.imageAlt: A Japanese iron sword guard (tsuba) of the Edo period. Pierced monkeys link around the central sword opening, holding hands in a ring.

source.creditLine: Edward C. Moore Collection, Bequest of Edward C. Moore, 1891
source.objectTitle: Sword Guard (Tsuba) Depicting Group of Monkeys in a Peach Tree (猿猴摘桃透鐔)

annotations.title: Monkeys at the top
annotations.body: Monkeys hold each other's hands and tails, linked in a ring. Sun Wukong was king of the monkeys of Flower-Fruit Mountain.

annotations.title: Sword opening
annotations.body: The central opening holds the blade, and the small openings on either side take a small knife and a hairpin. This is a Japanese sword guard (tsuba).

annotations.title: Gold-lined opening
annotations.body: Gold lines the edge of the right opening, gleaming like the Golden Headband that tightened around Sun Wukong's head.

artifact.title: Somersault Cloud
artifact.power: One somersault carries him 108,000 li.
artifact.firstRecord: Wu Cheng'en, Journey to the West
artifact.summary: The cloud ridden by Sun Wukong. A single somersault flies 108,000 li.
artifact.story:
Sun Wukong learned magic from his master Subodhi, including how to ride clouds. Because he mounted a cloud with a tumbling motion instead of the elegance of other immortals, his master taught him the Somersault Cloud to suit him: one flip would carry him 108,000 li.

After causing an uproar in heaven, Sun Wukong made a wager with the Buddha. If he could leap out of the Buddha's palm, heaven would be his.

Sun Wukong flew on the cloud to the end of the world, wrote "The Great Sage Equal to Heaven was here" on five pillars and came back. But the pillars were the Buddha's five fingers. Sun Wukong was at once imprisoned under the Five Elements Mountain.
artifact.imageAlt: A Chinese hanging scroll of the sixteenth to seventeenth century, Cloud Rock. A strange rock billowing up like a cloud is painted in ink on silk.

source.creditLine: Bequest of John M. Crawford Jr., 1988

annotations.title: Cloud-like rock
annotations.body: A rock billowing up like a cloud is painted in ink on silk. Sun Wukong's Somersault Cloud flies 108,000 li at a single flip.

annotations.title: Inscription and seals
annotations.body: The painter's writing and seals appear at upper right. This is a hanging scroll of the Ming dynasty, sixteenth to seventeenth century.

artifact.title: Yasakani no Magatama
artifact.power: One of the three sacred treasures, holding the spirit of the gods and the legitimacy of the imperial line.
artifact.summary: The curved jewel used with the mirror to call Amaterasu out of the cave, one of Japan's three imperial treasures.
artifact.story:
When Amaterasu hid in the rock cave of heaven and the world grew dark, the gods hung a mirror and many curved beads on a sacred tree before the cave. The deity who made those beads was Tamanooya.

Yasakani no Magatama is said to be a necklace strung with those beads. Magatama are curved beads shaped like animal teeth or a fetus, found in great numbers in ancient tombs of Japan and the Korean peninsula.

It became one of the three imperial treasures, along with the mirror Yata no Kagami and the sword Kusanagi. While the mirror and sword are enshrined elsewhere with replicas kept in the palace, the jewel alone is said to remain in the palace in its original form.
artifact.imageAlt: A Japanese necklace of about the seventh century. Curved chalcedony beads (magatama) are strung among green jasper tube beads and laid in a circle.

annotations.title: Curved bead
annotations.body: A curved bead (magatama) cut from chalcedony. Yasakani no Magatama is one of Japan's three imperial treasures.

annotations.title: Tube beads
annotations.body: Green jasper tube beads are strung between them. This is a necklace of about the seventh century, Japan's Kofun period.

annotations.title: Ring of beads
annotations.body: The beads are joined into a circle. When Amaterasu hid in the cave, the gods hung beads and a mirror on a tree to call her out.

artifact.title: Ame-no-Nuboko
artifact.owner: The creator deities Izanagi and Izanami
artifact.maker: Bestowed by the gods of heaven
artifact.power: Churned the sea and made the first land.
artifact.summary: The jeweled spear that first made land in Japanese myth.
artifact.story:
According to the Kojiki, the gods of heaven gave the deities Izanagi and Izanami a jeweled spear, Ame-no-Nuboko, telling them to harden the land still drifting about.

Standing on the floating bridge of heaven, the two deities lowered the spear into the sea and stirred. When they lifted it, drops of brine falling from the tip piled up to form the first island, Onogoro.

The two descended to that island, married and gave birth to the islands of Japan and many gods. The spear is remembered in Japanese myth as the tool that first made the world.
artifact.imageAlt: A seventeenth-century Japanese hand spear (nage-yari) with its sheath. A black sheath lies beside the slender blade, and the shaft is wrapped with cord.

source.objectTitle: Hand Spear (Nage-yari) or Javelin (Te-yari) with Sheath

annotations.title: Spear blade
annotations.body: A slender, straight blade. Izanagi and Izanami stirred the sea with Ame-no-Nuboko from the bridge of heaven.

annotations.title: Sheath
annotations.body: A black sheath that covers the blade. When the spear was raised, brine dripping from its tip piled up to form the first island, Onogoro.

annotations.title: Cord-wrapped shaft
annotations.body: Cord wound around the shaft prevents slipping. This is a Japanese short hand spear of the seventeenth century.

artifact.title: Kurikara Sword
artifact.power: A sword wound by a dragon wreathed in flame. It severs delusion and evil.
artifact.firstRecord: Esoteric Buddhist scriptures and images of Fudō Myōō
artifact.summary: The sword in the right hand of Fudō Myōō, with the dragon Kurikara winding around it and swallowing its blade.
artifact.story:
Fudō Myōō, a guardian of esoteric Buddhism, sits with an angry face before flames, a sword in his right hand and a rope in his left. With the sword he cuts delusion, and with the rope he binds evil.

The Kurikara sword is drawn with a black dragon wreathed in flames winding around the blade and about to swallow its tip. The word Kurikara comes from a Sanskrit name for a dragon king.

When Kūkai brought esoteric Buddhism from Tang China in the early ninth century, devotion to Fudō Myōō spread through Japan. Even now many stone images in the shape of a sword wrapped by the Kurikara dragon stand at temples and along mountain paths in Japan.
artifact.imageAlt: A seated Japanese cypress statue of Fudō Myōō from the early thirteenth century. The angry-faced deity with inlaid crystal eyes sits cross-legged holding a golden sword in his right hand and a rope in his left.

source.creditLine: Mary Griggs Burke Collection, Gift of the Mary and Jackson Burke Foundation, 2015
source.objectTitle: Fudō Myōō, the Immovable Wisdom King (Achala Vidyaraja)

annotations.title: Sword in the right hand
annotations.body: Fudō Myōō holds a sword upright in his right hand. When a dragon wreathed in flame wraps around it, it becomes the Kurikara sword.

annotations.title: Angry face
annotations.body: An angry face with inlaid crystal eyes. Fudō Myōō overcomes delusion and evil in this wrathful form.

annotations.title: Rope in the left hand
annotations.body: The rope in his left hand binds wicked things. This is a Japanese cypress sculpture of the early thirteenth century.

artifact.title: Totsuka no Tsurugi
artifact.power: A great sword ten fists long, which cut the eight-headed serpent to pieces.
artifact.summary: The sword Susanoo used on Yamata-no-Orochi. Striking Kusanagi inside the serpent's tail, it chipped.
artifact.story:
Totsuka means "ten fists long." Many gods in the Kojiki carry such swords, but the most famous is Susanoo's.

Susanoo cut to pieces with this sword the great serpent Yamata-no-Orochi as it lay drunk. But when he cut the middle tail the blade chipped. Slitting open the tail he found another sword within, which was later called Kusanagi.

Susanoo's sword is said to have been enshrined at Isonokami Shrine and elsewhere under the name of "the sword that slew the Orochi."
artifact.imageAlt: A straight single-edged Japanese sword blade (chokutō) of the seventh century or earlier. Only the long, straight steel blade survives, with patches of rust.

source.objectTitle: Blade for a Straight Single-Edged Sword (Chokutō)

annotations.title: Tip
annotations.body: A tip cut at a slant. Susanoo cut the drunken eight-headed serpent Yamata-no-Orochi to pieces with Totsuka no Tsurugi.

annotations.title: Straight blade
annotations.body: A single-edged straight blade (chokutō), the form of the seventh century or earlier before Japanese swords began to curve.

annotations.title: Chipped section
annotations.body: Rust and nicks mark the edge in places. Susanoo's sword chipped when it struck Kusanagi inside the serpent's tail.

artifact.title: Futsu-no-Mitama
artifact.power: A single stroke revived soldiers felled by poisonous vapors.
artifact.summary: The sword with which the thunder god Takemikazuchi pacified the land, sent down to the first emperor, Jimmu.
artifact.story:
According to the Kojiki, when Emperor Jimmu reached Kumano on his eastern expedition, a great bear appeared and the emperor and his soldiers all collapsed from poisonous vapors.

Then a man named Takakuraji, receiving a revelation in a dream, came carrying a sword. It had been sent down from heaven by the thunder god Takemikazuchi, who had used it to pacify the land. When the emperor received it he recovered, and at a single stroke the evil gods of Kumano fell of themselves.

This sword, Futsu-no-Mitama, is enshrined as the chief deity at Isonokami Shrine in Nara Prefecture. A sword unearthed in 1874 from forbidden ground at the shrine is said to be this one.
artifact.imageAlt: A fifth-century Japanese double-edged sword blade (ken) of the Kofun period. The rusted iron blade stands vertically, and the tang for the hilt survives at the bottom.

source.creditLine: Gift of Bashford Dean, by exchange, 1906

annotations.title: Tip
annotations.body: The tip of a rusted double-edged sword. Takemikazuchi is said to have pacified the gods of the land with this sword.

annotations.title: Rusted blade
annotations.body: An iron blade from a fifth-century tomb. When Emperor Jimmu's soldiers fell to poisonous vapors, they all revived when he received this sword.

annotations.title: Tang
annotations.body: The tang that fit into the hilt survives at the bottom. Futsu-no-Mitama is enshrined at Isonokami Shrine in Nara Prefecture.

artifact.title: Jamyeonggo
artifact.power: Sounds by itself when enemies invade.
artifact.summary: The drum and horn of Nangnang that sounded by themselves when enemies came. A princess in love tore the drum open.
artifact.story:
According to the record of King Daemusin of Goguryeo in the Samguk Sagi, Prince Hodong of Goguryeo met Choe Ri, king of Nangnang, while traveling in Okjeo. Choe Ri made Hodong his son-in-law and gave him his daughter.

Nangnang had a drum and horn that sounded by themselves when enemy troops approached. After returning to Goguryeo, Hodong sent word to his wife that if she entered the armory, tore the drum and broke the horn, he would receive her with all honors.

The princess secretly broke the drum and horn, and on Hodong's word King Daemusin launched a surprise attack on Nangnang. Unprepared because the drum did not sound, Choe Ri killed his daughter and surrendered. Later people called this drum Jamyeonggo, the drum that sounds by itself.
artifact.imageAlt: A nineteenth-century Korean janggu drum. Hide is fitted to both ends of a red-lacquered wooden body with a narrow waist and tightened with cords. It is photographed against a blue background.

source.creditLine: The Crosby Brown Collection of Musical Instruments, 1889

annotations.title: Hide drumhead
annotations.body: Hide stretched over a wide drumhead. The Jamyeonggo of Nangnang sounded by itself when enemies invaded.

annotations.title: Narrow waist
annotations.body: The red-lacquered wooden body narrows at the waist. The photograph shows a nineteenth-century Korean janggu.

annotations.title: Tension cords
annotations.body: Cords lace together the two drumheads. The princess of Nangnang entered the armory and tore the drum for Prince Hodong.

artifact.title: Heavenly Jade Belt
artifact.owner: King Jinpyeong of Silla, later Taejo of Goryeo
artifact.maker: Delivered by a messenger from heaven
artifact.power: One of the three treasures of Silla. While it remained, no one dared attack the kingdom.
artifact.summary: The jade belt heaven gave King Jinpyeong, one of the three treasures of Silla.
artifact.story:
According to the Samguk Yusa, in the year King Jinpyeong of Silla took the throne a messenger from heaven came down to the palace courtyard and presented a jade belt, saying the Lord on High had ordered it given. The king received it on his knees and wore it at every great ceremony.

The Heavenly Jade Belt was counted among the three treasures of Silla, along with the great Buddha statue and nine-story pagoda of Hwangnyongsa Temple. It is told that a king of Goguryeo gave up a plan to invade Silla on hearing that no one could attack while these three treasures remained.

When Gyeongsun, the last king of Silla, surrendered his kingdom to Goryeo, this belt too was presented to Wang Geon, Taejo of Goryeo, who stored it in the royal treasury.
artifact.imageAlt: A twelfth-century gilt-bronze belt ornament from Goryeo Korea. A seated deer is embossed on a square plaque against a background of scrolls, with blue-green patina.

source.creditLine: Gift of the John Huntington Art and Polytechnic Trust

annotations.title: Seated deer
annotations.body: A deer with folded legs is embossed among scrolls. This is a gilt-bronze belt ornament of twelfth-century Goryeo.

annotations.title: Scroll background
annotations.body: Cloud-like scrolls fill the space around the deer. The Heavenly Jade Belt was given to King Jinpyeong of Silla by a messenger from heaven.

annotations.title: Square border
annotations.body: A border surrounds the plaque. Plaques like this were fixed in rows on a leather belt. The Heavenly Jade Belt was presented to Wang Geon when Silla surrendered to Goryeo.

artifact.title: Pandora's Box
artifact.maker: Zeus (all the gods shaped Pandora together)
artifact.power: Opened, it scatters every evil into the world, leaving only hope within.
artifact.summary: The vessel opened by Pandora. It was originally a large jar, and became a “box” in the sixteenth century.
artifact.story:
When Prometheus stole the fire of the gods and gave it to humankind, Zeus decided to punish them with evil in return. Hephaestus shaped a woman from earth, and each of the gods gave her a gift, so that she became Pandora, "she who received all gifts."

In Hesiod's Works and Days, Pandora opens the lid of a great jar (pithos). Sickness and suffering scatter across the world, and only hope remains beneath the jar's rim. Before that, it is said, people knew neither disease nor hard labor.

The jar became a "box" only when Erasmus retold the story in Latin in the sixteenth century, using pyxis, a word for a small casket. Since then "Pandora's box" has meant a source of trouble best left alone.
artifact.imageAlt: A lidded pottery container (pyxis) from Apulia in southern Italy, about 300 BCE. The round body has red spirals on a black ground and is topped by a knobbed lid.

annotations.title: Knobbed lid
annotations.body: A lid with a knob covers the body. A small lidded container like this is called a pyxis, and when Erasmus used the word for Pandora's jar it became a 'box.'

annotations.title: Spiral-painted body
annotations.body: Red spirals and floral motifs are painted on a black ground. Hesiod's Pandora opens a great jar and scatters sickness and suffering.

annotations.title: Foot
annotations.body: A low, wide foot. This pottery was fired in Apulia in southern Italy about 300 BCE. Only hope remained in the jar.

artifact.title: Caduceus
artifact.power: Reconciles enemies, puts people to sleep or wakes them, and leads the souls of the dead to the underworld.
artifact.summary: Hermes's staff wound with two serpents, a symbol of heralds and peace.
artifact.story:
According to the Homeric Hymn to Hermes, the newborn Hermes stole Apollo's cattle and was found out. He made peace by giving Apollo a lyre made from a tortoise shell, and Apollo gave him a golden staff in return.

Later stories tell that when Hermes held his staff between two fighting snakes, they stopped and wound around it. So the winged staff with two serpents became the emblem of heralds, truce and trade.

Hermes put people to sleep or awoke them with this staff, and led the souls of the dead to the underworld. Today it is sometimes mistakenly used as a symbol of medicine; the true symbol is the staff of Asclepius, wound with a single serpent.
artifact.imageAlt: A Greek or Roman bronze statuette of Hermes from around the first century. A young Hermes stands with a cloak over his shoulder; the staff he once held does not survive.

annotations.title: Young face
annotations.body: A young god with short curly hair. Hermes was clever enough to steal Apollo's cattle on the day he was born.

annotations.title: Cloak on the shoulder
annotations.body: A traveler's short cloak (chlamys) over the shoulder. Hermes is the messenger of the gods and protector of those on the road.

annotations.title: Winged sandals
annotations.body: Small wings are visible at the ankles. The caduceus he once held does not survive. With this staff Hermes reconciled two fighting serpents.

artifact.title: Rod of Asclepius
artifact.power: A staff wound with a serpent, symbolizing healing skill that could revive even the dead.
artifact.summary: The staff of the god of medicine, wound with a single serpent and still a symbol of medicine today.
artifact.story:
Asclepius, son of Apollo, learned medicine from the centaur Chiron. His skill was so great that he brought the dead back to life, and Zeus, fearing the order of the underworld would be overturned, struck him down with a thunderbolt.

He is portrayed leaning on a staff wound with a single serpent. The serpent, which sheds its skin, stood for rebirth and healing. At temples of Asclepius throughout Greece, such as Epidaurus, patients slept hoping for the god's cure in dreams, and harmless snakes were kept there.

This staff with one serpent is still used as a symbol of medicine, including on the flag of the World Health Organization.
artifact.imageAlt: A marble head of Asclepius from the third to second century BCE, Roman. Blue glass eyes are set in a face framed by curly hair and beard.

source.objectTitle: Head of a marble statuette of Asklepios

annotations.title: Glass eyes
annotations.body: Blue glass in the eyes gives them a living gaze. This is the head of a small marble statue of the third to second century BCE.

annotations.title: Thick hair
annotations.body: Curly hair frames the face. Asclepius was carved with a dignified middle-aged appearance like that of Zeus.

annotations.title: Beard
annotations.body: A beard covers the chin. He is shown leaning on a staff wound with a serpent, and this staff is still the symbol of medicine today.

artifact.title: Ark of the Covenant
artifact.power: The seat of God's presence. Carried before the people, it parted the Jordan and brought down the walls of Jericho.
artifact.summary: The golden chest holding the tablets of the Ten Commandments. It vanished after Babylon destroyed Jerusalem.
artifact.story:
In Exodus, God tells Moses to build a chest of acacia wood and overlay it inside and out with pure gold. On its lid two cherubim face each other with outspread wings, and inside are placed the two tablets of the Ten Commandments.

The Israelites carried the ark on poles through the wilderness. According to the Book of Joshua, the Jordan stopped flowing when the priests bearing it set foot in the river, and the walls of Jericho fell after the ark was carried around them for seven days. When the Philistines captured it, their idols toppled and calamity struck until they sent it back.

Solomon installed the ark in the Holy of Holies of the Temple in Jerusalem. After Babylon destroyed the Temple in 587 BCE, no one knows what became of it.
artifact.imageAlt: An English gilt-copper reliquary chest of 1207–13. The box with a roof-shaped lid and animal-paw feet is densely covered in round engraved plaques, with a lock on the front.

annotations.title: Openwork crest
annotations.body: The roof ridge is decorated with openwork scrolls. On the lid of the Ark of the Covenant, two cherubim faced each other with outspread wings.

annotations.title: Round plaques
annotations.body: Round plaques engraved with saints wrap the roof and body. This reliquary was made in England in 1207–13.

annotations.title: Animal-paw feet
annotations.body: Feet shaped like animal paws carry the chest. The Ark was carried on poles passed through rings, and before it the walls of Jericho fell.

artifact.title: Aladdin's Lamp
artifact.power: Rub it, and the jinni of the lamp appears to grant its owner's wishes.
artifact.firstRecord: Antoine Galland, French Thousand and One Nights
artifact.summary: An old lamp hidden in a cave. Rubbing it brings out a jinni who will do anything.
artifact.story:
The poor boy Aladdin followed a sorcerer posing as his uncle into an underground cave and brought out the old lamp the man wanted. When the sorcerer trapped him there, Aladdin rubbed the ring on his finger and escaped with the help of its jinni.

At home, when his mother rubbed the lamp to clean it, a huge jinni appeared. With its power Aladdin grew rich, married the sultan's daughter and built a palace overnight. The sorcerer stole the lamp by crying "New lamps for old," but Aladdin finally got it back.

This story is not in the Arabic manuscripts. The Frenchman Antoine Galland heard it from the Syrian storyteller Hanna Diyab and added it to his translation of the Thousand and One Nights.
artifact.imageAlt: A ninth-century bronze oil lamp from Iran, with a pointed spout, rounded body and a feather-shaped ornament rising above a ring handle.

annotations.title: Feather-shaped finial
annotations.body: A feather-shaped ornament rises above the handle of this ninth-century Iranian bronze oil lamp.

annotations.title: Ring handle
annotations.body: A round ring for the finger. When Aladdin's mother rubbed the lamp to clean it, an enormous jinni appeared.

annotations.title: Pointed spout
annotations.body: A long, pointed spout that holds the wick. The wick draws oil up from the body to burn.

artifact.title: Uchide no Kozuchi
artifact.owner: The god of fortune Daikokuten, Issun-bōshi
artifact.power: Shake it and whatever one desires pours out.
artifact.summary: A magic mallet that grants wishes when shaken. It made the thumb-sized Issun-bōshi grow into a man.
artifact.story:
Uchide no Kozuchi means "little mallet of striking out." Shaking or striking it was said to bring forth whatever one wished, gold, silver or rice.

In "Issun-bōshi," a story in the Edo-period Otogizōshi, the thumb-sized boy Issun-bōshi fought and defeated a demon from inside its belly, using a needle as his sword. When a princess shook the mallet the fleeing demon dropped, Issun-bōshi became a fine grown man.

The mallet is also famous as the object held by Daikokuten, one of the seven gods of fortune, standing on bales of rice. It is often pictured with the rat, Daikoku's messenger.
artifact.imageAlt: A woodblock print (surimono) by Yashima Gakutei of about 1828, Mallet of Daikoku and a Rat. A gray rat sits on a red mallet painted with a peony, with a poem written above.

source.creditLine: H. O. Havemeyer Collection, Bequest of Mrs. H. O. Havemeyer, 1929
source.objectTitle: Mallet of Daikoku, One of the Gods of Good Fortune, and a Rat

annotations.title: Magic mallet
annotations.body: The red head of a mallet painted with a peony. Shaking it brought forth whatever one wished, and it made Issun-bōshi a grown man.

annotations.title: Long handle
annotations.body: A handle extending at a slant. Daikokuten, god of fortune, holds this mallet while standing on bales of rice.

annotations.title: Rat
annotations.body: The rat on the mallet is Daikoku's messenger. This New Year's print (surimono) was made for the year of the rat in 1828.

artifact.title: Olifant
artifact.power: When Roland blew it at the pass of Roncevaux, the sound reached Charlemagne's army thirty leagues away.
artifact.summary: The ivory horn Roland blew with his last breath. He blew it so hard that his temples burst.
artifact.story:
In 778, as Charlemagne's army returned from Spain, Roland commanded the rearguard at the pass of Roncevaux. When a vast Saracen army fell on them through the treachery of his stepfather Ganelon, his friend Oliver urged him three times to sound his horn and call back the king. Roland refused, saying it would be shameful to ask for help.

Only when nearly all the knights had fallen did Roland blow the olifant. He blew so hard that blood burst from his mouth and his temples split, and the sound carried to Charlemagne thirty leagues away. Ganelon held the king back, saying Roland was probably just hunting a hare.

Dying, Roland struck down an enemy who tried to take Durendal with the olifant, and the gold and crystal set in the horn broke away. Charlemagne later filled the horn with gold coins and laid it on the altar of Saint-Seurin in Bordeaux. "Olifant" is Old French for elephant, that is, ivory.
artifact.imageAlt: A South Italian ivory horn (oliphant) of the twelfth century. The long, curved elephant tusk is densely carved with roundels and animals, with metal bands for a strap at both ends.

annotations.title: Narrow mouthpiece
annotations.body: The narrow end where the player blows. Roland blew this horn so hard that blood burst from his mouth and his temples split.

annotations.title: Carved roundels
annotations.body: The ivory surface is divided into round compartments carved with beasts and birds. Ivory horns carved like this in twelfth-century southern Italy are called oliphants.

annotations.title: Metal band
annotations.body: The metal band at the end held a strap so the horn could hang from the shoulder. Dying, Roland struck an enemy with the horn, and its gold and crystal fell away.

artifact.title: Bayard
artifact.owner: The four sons of Aymon, Renaud de Montauban
artifact.power: His back lengthens to fit his riders, so he can carry all four brothers at once and still outrun any horse.
artifact.firstRecord: Renaut de Montauban (The Four Sons of Aymon)
artifact.summary: The magic horse that carried the four sons of Aymon at once. Even Charlemagne could not kill him.
artifact.story:
Renaud de Montauban was the eldest of the four sons of Duke Aymon. During a game of chess with Charlemagne's nephew a quarrel broke out, and Renaud killed him with the chessboard; from then on the four brothers were hunted by the emperor. What protected them was Bayard, a horse found for them by their cousin, the enchanter Maugis.

Bayard's back grew longer to fit his riders, so he could carry all four brothers at once and still run faster than any horse. He understood human speech and could leap across a valley in a single bound. The "Bayard Rock" that towers beside the Meuse at Dinant in Belgium is said to have been split by his hoof as he leaped.

After a long war, Renaud gave Bayard to the emperor as the price of peace. Charlemagne had a millstone tied to Bayard's neck and threw him into the Meuse, but Bayard broke the stone with his hooves, swam ashore and fled into the Ardennes forest. They say he still runs somewhere in those woods.
artifact.imageAlt: A bronze horse made by the Florentine sculptor Giambologna around 1587–91. The dark brown horse walks with its head bowed and one foreleg and one hind leg raised, standing on an oval base.

annotations.title: Bowed head
annotations.body: The head is drawn in and bowed, with a neatly trimmed mane. Bayard was a clever horse that understood human speech.

annotations.title: Raised legs
annotations.body: One foreleg and one hind leg are raised together in a trot. Bayard could carry the four brothers at once and still outrun any horse.

annotations.title: Flowing tail
annotations.body: A long, flowing tail. Charlemagne threw Bayard into the river with a millstone around his neck, but he broke the stone, swam ashore and escaped into the Ardennes.

artifact.title: Helmet of Mambrino
artifact.owner: Mambrino, a Moorish king; the knight Rinaldo; Don Quixote
artifact.power: A golden helmet that keeps its wearer from harm.
artifact.summary: The golden helmet the knight Rinaldo won from a Moorish king. Don Quixote believed a barber's brass basin was this helmet.
artifact.story:
In Boiardo's Orlando Innamorato, the Moorish king Mambrino owns a golden helmet that keeps its wearer from harm. Charlemagne's knight Rinaldo defeats him and takes the helmet, and in Ariosto's Orlando Furioso it remains a treasure the knights covet.

What made the helmet most famous is Cervantes's Don Quixote, published in 1605. Seeing a barber riding a donkey with a brass basin on his head to keep off the rain, Don Quixote believes a knight in a golden helmet is approaching. He charges with his lance, drives off the barber and takes the basin.

Trying it on, Don Quixote declares that someone who did not know its worth must have melted down half of the helmet to sell and made the rest into something that looks like a barber's basin. However often Sancho Panza says it is a basin, he will not listen. Later, at an inn, the guests break into an uproar over whether it is a basin or a helmet.
artifact.imageAlt: An eighteenth-century European pewter barber's basin. The broad basin has a wavy rim, and one edge is scooped out in a curve to fit against a customer's neck.

annotations.title: Neck notch
annotations.body: One edge is scooped out in a curve. During a shave it fitted against the customer's neck to catch the lather. Don Quixote put a basin like this on his head and believed it was a golden helmet.

annotations.title: Wavy rim
annotations.body: A broad rim that curves like waves. This is a pewter (tin alloy) basin used in eighteenth-century Europe.

annotations.title: Deep well
annotations.body: The deep well that caught the lather. However often Sancho Panza said it was a basin, Don Quixote insisted someone had melted down half the helmet to make it.

artifact.title: Hippogriff
artifact.owner: The sorcerer Atlante; the knights Ruggiero and Astolfo
artifact.maker: Born of a griffin father and a mare
artifact.power: Spreads its wings and carries its rider across the sea to the ends of the earth, even to the Earthly Paradise.
artifact.summary: A flying beast born of a griffin and a mare. The knight Astolfo rode it all the way to the Earthly Paradise.
artifact.story:
The griffin was a beast that preyed on horses, so the Roman poet Virgil wrote "griffins shall mate with horses" to describe something impossible. In Orlando Furioso, Ariosto made that impossible beast real: the hippogriff, whose father was a griffin and whose mother was a mare.

Tamed by the sorcerer Atlante, the hippogriff carried the knight Ruggiero across the sea to the island of the witch Alcina. Ruggiero later swooped down on it to rescue Angelica, who had been offered to a sea monster.

The English knight Astolfo inherited the hippogriff and flew by way of Ethiopia to the Earthly Paradise at the top of the world. There he rode Elijah's chariot of fire up to the Moon and brought back the flask holding the wits of Orlando, who had gone mad.
artifact.imageAlt: The Griffin, an engraving by the German printmaker Martin Schongauer, about 1480–90. A winged beast stands in profile with a crested eagle's head, wings and taloned forelegs, and hind legs ending in hooves.

annotations.title: Eagle head
annotations.body: The front has a crested eagle's head, wings and talons. This is The Griffin, engraved by the German printmaker Martin Schongauer about 1480–90.

annotations.title: Hoofed hind legs
annotations.body: The hind legs are drawn like a horse's, ending in hooves. Ariosto created the hippogriff, a beast born of a griffin father and a mare.

annotations.title: Monogram
annotations.body: The letters M and S with a cross between them at the bottom are Schongauer's monogram. Tamed by the sorcerer Atlante, the hippogriff carried the knight Ruggiero across the sea to Alcina's island.

artifact.title: Gawain's Green Girdle
artifact.power: Whoever wears it, she said, cannot be slain by any blade on earth.
artifact.firstRecord: Sir Gawain and the Green Knight
artifact.summary: The green silk girdle the lady of the Green Knight's castle gave Gawain. She said it would keep him from death by any blade.
artifact.story:
At the height of the New Year feast in Camelot, a giant knight green from head to foot rode in with an axe and proposed a game. Anyone might strike his neck now, on condition that he receive the same blow a year and a day later. Gawain stepped forward and cut off his head, but the knight picked it up and rode away, saying he would wait at the Green Chapel.

The following year Gawain set out and stayed at a castle. For three days the lord's wife tried to seduce him, and on the last day she gave him a green silk girdle, saying that no one could kill the man who wore it. Gawain broke his promise to exchange all his day's winnings with the lord and hid the girdle.

At the Green Chapel the Green Knight twice stopped his axe, and on the third stroke only nicked Gawain's neck. He was the lord, Bertilak, and the small wound was the penalty for hiding the girdle. Ashamed, Gawain vowed to wear the girdle all his life, and Arthur's court resolved that everyone would wear a green band in his honor.
artifact.imageAlt: A lady's belt probably made in Siena, Italy, around 1375–1400. Silver plaques covered with translucent enamel are set along a narrow band of woven silver thread, with a gilt-silver buckle at the top.

source.creditLine: Gift of the John Huntington Art and Polytechnic Trust

annotations.title: Buckle
annotations.body: The gilt-silver buckle and strap end that fastened the belt. In late fourteenth-century Italy, ladies wore belts like this over their gowns.

annotations.title: Enamel plaques
annotations.body: Small silver plaques are set along the band of silver thread. Their engraved designs show through a coat of translucent enamel.

annotations.title: Hanging end
annotations.body: The end of the belt hung down after it was fastened at the waist. The lady untied her own girdle and gave it to Gawain, saying no one could kill its wearer.

artifact.title: Love Potion of Tristan and Iseult
artifact.titleOriginal: Love Potion of Tristan and Iseult
artifact.maker: The queen of Ireland, Iseult's mother
artifact.power: The two who drink it together fall into a love they can never escape.
artifact.firstRecord: Twelfth-century French Tristan romances (Thomas and Beroul)
artifact.summary: The love potion the queen of Ireland brewed for her daughter's wedding. Drinking it by mistake on board ship, Tristan and Iseult fell into an inescapable love.
artifact.story:
King Mark of Cornwall sent his nephew Tristan to Ireland to bring back the princess Iseult as his bride. The queen of Ireland, skilled in herbs, brewed a love potion for her daughter and her husband to drink together on their wedding night, so that they would live in love, and entrusted it to the maid Brangaine.

The voyage to Cornwall was hot. When Tristan and Iseult grew thirsty, a servant poured them the potion, thinking it was wine, and the two who shared the cup fell into a love they could never escape. In Beroul's story the potion's power lasts three years; in Thomas's it lasts for life.

Iseult became Mark's queen, but the love did not end. Far away in Brittany, Tristan, dying of a poisoned wound, waited for Iseult and died; Iseult arrived too late and died at his side. In 1865 the story was reborn as Wagner's music drama Tristan und Isolde.
artifact.imageAlt: A fifteenth-century German flask of green glass. Below a slender neck ringed with a collar, the body divides into several thin twisting tubes, and the base swells into a round bulb.

annotations.title: Collared neck
annotations.body: A ring-shaped collar circles the middle of the slender neck. This green glass flask was blown in fifteenth-century Germany.

annotations.title: Twisting tubes
annotations.body: Several thin glass tubes twist between the upper and lower body. Flasks like this were made so the drink gurgled out little by little through the tubes.

annotations.title: Round base
annotations.body: The round bulb that held the drink. On board ship, Tristan and Iseult shared the love potion, thinking it was wine.

artifact.title: Scabbard of Excalibur
artifact.power: As long as one wears it, one loses no blood, however deep the wound.
artifact.summary: The scabbard the Lady of the Lake gave with Excalibur. Merlin said it was worth ten times more than the sword.
artifact.story:
When Arthur's sword broke in a fight with King Pellinore, Merlin took him to a lake. An arm clothed in white samite rose from the water holding a sword, and the Lady of the Lake gave that sword, Excalibur, to Arthur together with its scabbard.

Merlin asked whether he liked the sword or the scabbard better, and Arthur said the sword. Merlin told him the scabbard was worth more than ten swords, for as long as he kept it on him he would lose no blood, however deep his wounds.

Morgan le Fay, Arthur's half-sister, who hated him, stole Excalibur and the scabbard and gave them to her lover Accolon to fight Arthur. Arthur barely won back the sword, but Morgan stole the scabbard again and threw it deep into a lake. Without it, Arthur fell gravely wounded at the last battle of Camlann.
artifact.imageAlt: Fragment of a luxury dagger made by the Lombards around 600. Gold plaques and two gold bands, engraved with scrolls and animals, wrap the rusted, broken iron blade and scabbard.

annotations.title: Gold plaque with animal
annotations.body: The gold plaque along the edge of the scabbard is engraved with a coiling animal. It decorated a dagger of the Lombards, who founded a kingdom in northern Italy around 600.

annotations.title: Upper gold band
annotations.body: A gold band that tightened the scabbard, edged with rows of gold granules and engraved with scrolls. It dates from the sixth century, the age in which Arthur is said to have lived.

annotations.title: Rusted iron
annotations.body: The rusted iron is what remains of the blade and scabbard. Having lost his scabbard, Arthur fell gravely wounded at the last battle of Camlann.

artifact.title: The Round Table
artifact.owner: King Arthur and the Knights of the Round Table
artifact.maker: A Cornish carpenter (Layamon) or Merlin (Robert de Boron)
artifact.power: With no high or low place, every knight seated around it sits as an equal.
artifact.summary: A round table made to end quarrels over precedence. The Siege Perilous was kept empty for the one knight who would achieve the Grail.
artifact.story:
In his Roman de Brut of 1155, the Norman poet Wace first wrote that Arthur had a round table made. It was a table at which no one sat higher or lower than anyone else, so that the barons would not quarrel over the place of honor. Some decades later Layamon added that after a quarrel over precedence at a Christmas feast turned bloody, a Cornish carpenter made a table that could seat sixteen hundred and still be carried about.

Robert de Boron told how Merlin made the Round Table for Arthur's father Uther. It was the third table, after the table of the Last Supper and the Grail table of Joseph of Arimathea, and it had an empty seat, the Siege Perilous, kept for the one knight who would achieve the Grail. Any unworthy man who sat there came to harm, and the seat finally went to Galahad.

In the great hall of Winchester Castle in England hangs an oak round table 5.5 meters across. It was made in the thirteenth century, and under Henry VIII it was painted with the Tudor rose and King Arthur on his throne.
artifact.imageAlt: Daniel Hopfer's etching Three Worthy Christians, about 1516. Charlemagne, King Arthur and Godfrey of Bouillon stand side by side in armor, with their names inscribed above.

source.creditLine: The Elisha Whittelsey Collection, The Elisha Whittelsey Fund, 1951
source.objectTitle: Three Worthy Christians: Charlemagne, King Arthur, and Geoffrey of Bouillon

annotations.title: Inscribed names
annotations.body: At the top are the German title "Three Good Christians" and the names of Emperor Carolus, King Artus and Duke Gotfrid.

annotations.title: King Arthur
annotations.body: The figure in the middle is King Arthur. Medieval people counted him among the Nine Worthies, the greatest heroes in history.

annotations.title: Charlemagne
annotations.body: The emperor on the left is Charlemagne. In 1155 Wace first wrote that Arthur had a round table made to end his knights' quarrels over precedence.

artifact.title: Sword of the Strange Belt
artifact.maker: The sword of King David, remade by King Solomon
artifact.power: Only one destined man may draw it; anyone else who does comes to harm.
artifact.summary: King David's sword, carried on Solomon's ship to await the Grail knight. Perceval's sister wove a new belt for it from her own hair.
artifact.story:
In the Queste del Saint Graal, Galahad, Perceval and Bors follow Perceval's sister aboard a ship with no crew. King Solomon had launched it long ago for the last knight of his line. On a bed inside lay a sword drawn a hand's breadth from its scabbard.

It was the sword of Solomon's father, King David. Solomon made a new hilt and scabbard, but his queen hung it from a mean belt of hemp. On the scabbard was written that a maiden would one day replace the belt with something precious, together with a warning that anyone but the one destined man who drew the sword would come to harm.

Perceval's sister cut off her long hair and wove it with gold thread into a new belt. The knight who girded on the sword was Galahad. Until the belt was changed, people called it the Sword of the Strange Belt.
artifact.imageAlt: A French sword belt of the late eighteenth century. The white silk belt is embroidered with green and black flowers and set with spangles, and a U-shaped hanger for the scabbard hangs below.

source.creditLine: Bashford Dean Memorial Collection, Funds from various donors, 1929

annotations.title: Belt fastening
