annotations.body: The fastening of the belt. In late eighteenth-century France, a belt like this was used to wear a sword at the waist.

annotations.title: Scabbard hanger
annotations.body: The scabbard slid into the U-shaped hanger. Perceval's sister replaced the mean hemp belt with a new one woven from her own hair and gold thread.

annotations.title: Embroidery
annotations.body: Flowers and vines are embroidered in green and black thread on white silk, edged with metallic thread and spangles.

artifact.title: Ring of Lunete
artifact.power: Turn the stone toward the palm and close the hand, and no one can see the wearer.
artifact.firstRecord: Chretien de Troyes, Yvain, the Knight of the Lion
artifact.summary: The ring the maid Lunete gave the knight Yvain. With the stone turned into the palm, he vanished from sight.
artifact.story:
Yvain, a knight of the Round Table, fought the knight who guarded a magic spring and dealt him a mortal wound. As he chased his fleeing enemy into the castle, iron portcullises came down before and behind him, and Yvain was trapped between the two gates.

He was saved by Lunete, a maid of the castle. Remembering that at Arthur's court only Yvain had treated her courteously, she gave him a ring. If he turned its stone toward his palm and closed his hand, no one could see him. The castle's people searched everywhere with clubs for their lord's killer, but they never found Yvain.

Watching from hiding, Yvain fell in love at first sight with the lord's widow, Laudine, and through Lunete's cleverness he married her. The same story survives in the Welsh Mabinogion as "Owain, or the Lady of the Fountain," where the maid who gives him the ring is called Luned.
artifact.imageAlt: A German gold ring of the tenth to eleventh century. A plaque with a flower in green cloisonne enamel crowns a tall stepped setting decorated with gold granules and small arches.

annotations.title: Cloisonne flower
annotations.body: Gold partitions on top of the ring are filled with green enamel to form a flower (cloisonne). Lunete's ring hid its wearer when the stone was turned toward the palm.

annotations.title: Stepped setting
annotations.body: The setting rises in tiers of gold granulation and small arches. This gold ring was made in Germany in the tenth or eleventh century.

annotations.title: Hoop
annotations.body: The hoop for the finger. Thanks to the ring, Yvain could stay hidden among the people searching the castle.

artifact.title: Gleipnir
artifact.power: Thin and soft as a silk ribbon, yet no strength can break it.
artifact.summary: The fetter that bound the wolf Fenrir. Made of six things that no longer exist, it was as thin as silk.
artifact.story:
The gods raised Fenrir, the wolf born of Loki, in Asgard. As the wolf grew larger every day and every prophecy warned that he would bring disaster, the gods bound him with the chains Leyding and Dromi, but both times Fenrir snapped them at once.

Odin sent the messenger Skirnir to the dwarves. They made a fetter from six things: the sound of a cat's footfall, the beard of a woman, the roots of a mountain, the sinews of a bear, the breath of a fish and the spittle of a bird. That, Snorri wrote, is why those things no longer exist. Gleipnir, made in this way, was as thin and soft as a silk ribbon.

Suspecting a trick, Fenrir agreed to be bound only if someone put a hand in his mouth as a pledge. Tyr, the god of war, offered his right hand, and when the fetter would not loosen, the wolf bit it off. Fenrir stays bound like this until Ragnarok.
artifact.imageAlt: A fragment of a band woven of silk and gold thread in Sicily, Italy, at the end of the eleventh century. Fine stripes run along the long, narrow dark-brown band, whose edges are worn.

annotations.title: Gold-thread stripes
annotations.body: Silk and gold thread are woven together in tablet weaving, turning cards threaded with yarn. The band was woven in Sicily at the end of the eleventh century.

annotations.title: Worn edge
annotations.body: It is worn and faded with age. The Normans who ruled Sicily at this time were descendants of the Vikings of the north.

annotations.title: Long, narrow band
annotations.body: A long, narrow band. Gleipnir was thin and soft as a silk ribbon, yet even the wolf Fenrir could not break it.

artifact.title: Mistilteinn
artifact.owner: The blind god Hod (guided by Loki)
artifact.power: Pierced Baldr, whom everything in the world had sworn not to harm.
artifact.summary: Everything swore not to harm Baldr, but one sprig of mistletoe, passed over as too young, killed him.
artifact.story:
When Baldr, the god of light, dreamed of his own death, his mother Frigg took an oath from everything in the world not to harm him. Fire and water, iron and stone, earth and trees, sicknesses, beasts and poisons all swore. For sport the gods threw stones and spears at Baldr, and he was not hurt at all.

Loki, disguised as a woman, learned the secret from Frigg: one sprig of mistletoe growing west of Valhalla had seemed too young to take the oath. Loki plucked it, put it into the hands of the god Hod, who was blind and could not join the game, and showed him where to throw.

The mistletoe pierced Baldr, and he fell dead on the spot. Snorri wrote that this was the greatest misfortune ever to befall gods and men. Mistilteinn means mistletoe in Old Norse, and Baldr's death was the first step toward Ragnarok.
artifact.imageAlt: Two arrows from sixteenth-century Turkey or Iran. Pointed steel arrowheads inlaid with gold scrolls are fixed to lacquered wooden shafts.

annotations.title: Gold-inlaid arrowhead
annotations.body: The steel head of the longer arrow is inlaid with gold scrolls. These arrows come from sixteenth-century Turkey or Iran.

annotations.title: Shorter arrowhead
annotations.body: The other arrow has a slightly shorter head. Everything swore not to harm Baldr, but the mistletoe that seemed too young to take the oath pierced him.

annotations.title: Shaft
annotations.body: A straight, lacquered wooden shaft. Loki plucked the mistletoe, put it into the hands of the blind god Hod and showed him where to throw.

artifact.title: Gullinbursti
artifact.power: Runs through sky and sea faster than any horse, and its golden bristles light up the night.
artifact.summary: A boar with golden bristles made by a dwarf at his forge. Its glow lit the darkness as it drew Freyr's chariot.
artifact.story:
As a prank, Loki cut off all the hair of the goddess Sif, and to escape Thor's anger he had dwarves make treasures for the gods. Then he bet his own head with the dwarf Brokk that Brokk's brother Eitri could make nothing as fine.

Eitri put a pigskin into the forge and told Brokk not to stop working the bellows until he took it out. Loki, turned into a fly, bit Brokk's hand, but Brokk kept pumping, and out of the forge came a boar with golden bristles. After it came the ring Draupnir and the hammer Mjolnir.

Gullinbursti means "golden bristles." The boar ran through sky and sea faster than any horse, and however dark the night, its bristles lit the way. Freyr rode to Baldr's funeral in a chariot drawn by this boar.
artifact.imageAlt: A bronze wild boar made in the late seventeenth century by the Florentine sculptor Giovanni Francesco Susini. With bristles raised along its neck, the boar sits on its haunches with its mouth open.

annotations.title: Tusks
annotations.body: Tusks show at the corners of the open mouth. This small bronze copies the ancient marble boar in the Uffizi in Florence.

annotations.title: Raised bristles
annotations.body: Coarse bristles stand up from the neck along the spine. Gullinbursti's golden bristles lit the way on even the darkest night.

annotations.title: Folded hind legs
annotations.body: The boar sits with its hind legs folded. Freyr rode to Baldr's funeral in a chariot drawn by Gullinbursti.

artifact.title: Grotti
artifact.owner: King Frodi of Denmark; the sea-king Mysing
artifact.power: Grinds out whatever the one who turns it wishes for.
artifact.firstRecord: Snorri Sturluson, Prose Edda, "Song of Grotti"
artifact.summary: A mill that ground out anything. It sank into the sea while grinding salt, and that, they say, is why the sea is salty.
artifact.story:
King Frodi of Denmark obtained Grotti, a mill that ground out whatever its turner wished. It was so heavy that no one could turn it, so the king bought two giantesses, Fenja and Menja, as slaves from Sweden and set them to grind gold, peace and happiness. In those days there were neither thieves nor strife in Denmark, and it was called the Peace of Frodi.

The king let the two rest only while the cuckoo was silent or while a single song was sung. Exhausted, the giantesses sang the "Song of Grotti" and this time ground out an army against the king. That night the sea-king Mysing attacked, killed Frodi and sailed away with the mill and the two women.

On board ship Mysing set them to grind salt. At midnight they asked whether they should stop, but he told them to grind on, and the ship, filling with salt, sank at last. Where the sea pours through the eye of the mill a whirlpool formed, and from then on the sea has been salty. In Korea, too, there is an old tale of a salt-grinding millstone that fell into the sea and made seawater salty.
artifact.imageAlt: A stone grinding table (metate) from Costa Rica, about 1000–1550. A jaguar head is carved at the front of the broad, four-legged table, and patterns are carved in relief around the table and on the legs.

source.creditLine: Gift of the Womens Council of the Cleveland Museum of Art

annotations.title: Jaguar head
annotations.body: A jaguar head is carved at the front of the grinding table. People in Costa Rica used such stones to grind maize, and also in rituals.

annotations.title: Grinding surface
annotations.body: Grain was placed on this surface and ground by pushing a hand stone across it. Grotti ground out whatever its turner wished.

annotations.title: Carved legs
annotations.body: The four legs are carved with patterns. Grotti was so heavy that King Frodi bought two giantesses to turn it.

artifact.title: Mead of Poetry
artifact.power: Whoever drinks it becomes a poet or a scholar.
artifact.summary: Mead brewed from the blood of Kvasir, the wisest of men. Odin stole it from a giant in the shape of an eagle.
artifact.story:
When the Aesir and the Vanir ended their long war, they sealed the peace by spitting into a single vat. From that spittle came Kvasir, the wisest man in the world. The dwarves Fjalar and Galar killed him and mixed his blood with honey, and whoever drank it became a poet or a scholar.

The mead passed into the hands of the giant Suttung, who hid it deep inside a mountain under the guard of his daughter Gunnlod. Odin bored a hole through the rock with an auger and crept in as a snake. After three nights with Gunnlod he was allowed three sips, and with those three sips he emptied all three vessels of mead.

Odin flew back to Asgard as an eagle, and Suttung pursued him, also as an eagle. As Odin spat the mead into the vessels the gods set out, a few drops escaped behind him. Snorri wrote that those drops became the share of bad poets.
artifact.imageAlt: A German maple-wood double cup (mazer) of about 1530. Two round wooden cups are stacked one on the other, with gilt-silver mounts at the rims, the join and the foot, and a small handle at the side.

source.creditLine: Purchase from the J. H. Wade Fund

annotations.title: Silver rim
annotations.body: A petal-edged silver mount circles the lip of the upper cup. The cup was turned from maple wood in Germany about 1530.

annotations.title: Two stacked cups
annotations.body: A double cup: the smaller cup sits upside down on the larger one like a lid, so that two people can share the drink.

annotations.title: Handle
annotations.body: A small handle projecting to the side. Inside the giant's mountain, Odin emptied all three vessels of the mead of poetry in three sips.

artifact.title: Idunn's Apples
artifact.power: Eaten by the gods as they grow old, they make them young again.
artifact.summary: Idunn's apples kept the gods young. When Idunn was carried off by a giant, the gods quickly grew old.
artifact.story:
The goddess Idunn kept apples in an ash-wood box. Whenever the gods began to grow old they ate these apples and became young again, and so they could keep their youth until Ragnarok.

One day Loki was caught by the giant Thjazi in the shape of an eagle, and to save his life he promised to bring Idunn out of Asgard. Telling her there were even finer apples in a forest, he lured her outside, and Thjazi snatched her away to the land of the giants. Without her apples the gods quickly turned gray and old.

When it came out that Loki was behind it, he borrowed the goddess Freyja's falcon cloak and flew to the land of the giants. He turned Idunn into a nut, carried her back in his claws, and Thjazi, chasing him as an eagle, fell when his wings caught fire in the flames the gods had lit on the walls.
artifact.imageAlt: A sixteenth-century silver-gilt pomander. Round scenes are engraved on its apple-like body, with a ring at the top and a base hung with small balls below.

source.creditLine: The Collection of Giovanni P. Morosini, presented by his daughter Giulia, 1932

annotations.title: Ring
annotations.body: A ring at the top so the pomander could be worn on the body. This silver scent container dates from the sixteenth century.

annotations.title: Apple-shaped body
annotations.body: Scent was kept in the round body. The name pomander comes from an old French word meaning "apple of amber." Idunn kept the apples that made the gods young again in an ash-wood box.

annotations.title: Base
annotations.body: A base hung with small balls. Whenever they grew old, the gods ate Idunn's apples and became young again.

artifact.title: Naglfar
artifact.power: On the day of Ragnarok it crosses the sea packed with giants who will fight the gods.
artifact.summary: A huge ship built from the nails of the dead. On the day of Ragnarok it brings the giants.
artifact.story:
When Ragnarok, the last day of the gods, comes, the earth will shake and everything that was bound will break loose. The great serpent of Midgard will thrash its way onto land, the sea will flood the earth, and on those waves the huge ship Naglfar will rise. The giant Hrym will steer it, packed with giants who will fight the gods.

Naglfar is built from the nails of the dead. Snorri wrote that anyone who dies with uncut nails adds material to the ship, which gods and men wish to be finished as late as possible. So the nails of the dead should be trimmed.

The "Prophecy of the Seeress" in the Poetic Edda also sings that a ship comes from the east and Naglfar is loosed. According to Snorri, the best of ships is Skidbladnir, the ship of the gods, but the largest is Naglfar, which belongs to Muspell, the land of fire.
artifact.imageAlt: A wooden model boat from Middle Kingdom Egypt (about 2040–1648 BCE). The yellow-painted boat carries a mast and a long steering oar, several painted figures of sailors, and a jar and a basket.

source.creditLine: Gift of the John Huntington Art and Polytechnic Trust

annotations.title: Steering oar
annotations.body: The long oar at the stern steers the boat. On the day of Ragnarok, the giant Hrym will take Naglfar's helm.

annotations.title: Mast
annotations.body: The mast and yard with the sail furled. Egyptians buried models of boats with the dead for the journey to the afterlife.

annotations.title: Sailors
annotations.body: Rowers and cargo on board. Naglfar is a ship built from the nails of the dead, bringing giants to fight the gods.

artifact.title: Thor's Goats
artifact.power: Eaten and their bones laid on their hides, they are blessed with Thor's hammer and live again the next day.
artifact.summary: The two goats that draw Thor's chariot. Even when eaten, they come back to life the next day.
artifact.story:
Thor, the god of thunder, raced across the sky in a chariot drawn by two goats, Tanngrisnir, "teeth-barer," and Tanngnjost, "teeth-grinder." They say thunder rolls when Thor's chariot passes.

Once, traveling with Loki, Thor stayed the night at a farmer's house. He slaughtered and cooked the two goats and shared them with the farmer's family, telling them to throw all the bones onto the hides. But the farmer's son Thjalfi split a thighbone with his knife to get at the marrow.

The next morning Thor raised his hammer Mjolnir and blessed the hides, and the goats came back to life, but one of them was lame in a hind leg. Before the furious Thor, the farmer begged forgiveness and gave him his son Thjalfi and daughter Roskva, who from then on followed Thor as his servants.
artifact.imageAlt: A bronze nanny goat from Hellenistic Greece, late third century BCE. The goat, with horns curving back and a beard at its chin, stands on a white base with its long coat hanging down.

annotations.title: Curved horns and beard
annotations.body: Horns curving back and a beard at the chin. This bronze goat comes from Hellenistic Greece in the late third century BCE.

annotations.title: Hanging coat
annotations.body: The long coat hanging from the body is modeled in waves. After eating the two goats, Thor had their bones gathered on the hides.

annotations.title: Legs
annotations.body: The goat stands on slender legs. When Thor blessed them with his hammer the next day, one of the revived goats was lame in a hind leg.

artifact.title: Dainsleif
artifact.power: Once drawn, it must kill before it is sheathed; it never misses, and its wounds never heal.
artifact.summary: A sword that returns to its scabbard only after drawing blood. Because of it, a battle began that is fought again every day.
artifact.story:
When King Hedin carried off Hild, the daughter of King Hogni, Hogni pursued him with an army and caught up with him on the island of Hoy in Orkney. Hild offered her father a necklace as a token of peace, but Hogni answered that it was too late.

He said he had already drawn Dainsleif, the sword made by the dwarf Dain. Once drawn, this sword had to kill a man; it never missed, and no wound it made ever healed. The two armies fought until sunset and all fell.

That night Hild walked the battlefield and raised all the dead by magic. The next day they fought again, and the battle is said to repeat every day until Ragnarok. This endless battle is called the Battle of the Hjadnings.
artifact.imageAlt: An iron sword made by the Franks around 500–700. The straight, long double-edged blade lies vertically, rough with rust, and its grip no longer survives.

annotations.title: Tang
annotations.body: The narrow iron tang onto which the grip was fitted. The grip, made of wood or horn, has rotted away.

annotations.title: Rusted blade
annotations.body: The broad, straight double-edged blade is rusted. This is a Frankish sword of about 500–700.

annotations.title: Tip
annotations.body: The rounded point. Once Dainsleif was drawn, it had to kill a man before it could return to its scabbard.

artifact.title: Hlidskjalf
artifact.power: Whoever sits in this seat sees everything that happens in the nine worlds.
artifact.summary: Odin's high seat. From it the whole world could be seen.
artifact.story:
In Odin's hall Valaskjalf stands a high seat called Hlidskjalf. When Odin sat in it he could look down on all nine worlds, and nothing anyone did escaped him.

One day Freyr, the god of fertility, secretly climbed into the seat and saw the beautiful Gerd in the land of the giants, and he fell sick with longing. He sent his servant Skirnir to woo her for him and gave away his sword that fought by itself, and for that reason, at Ragnarok, he will fight bare-handed and fall.

In the "Lay of Grimnir" in the Poetic Edda, Odin and his wife Frigg sit side by side in this seat, looking down on the two princes they each raised and making a wager. And when Loki, who caused Baldr's death, hid as a salmon in a waterfall, it was from Hlidskjalf that Odin found his hiding place.
artifact.imageAlt: A child's throne made by Pierre-Marie Balny in Paris in 1822. The leather back of the gilded wooden chair is gold-tooled with a rooster in a laurel wreath and fleurs-de-lis, the crest is carved with cherubs, and the front legs are carved as winged beasts.

annotations.title: Carved crest
annotations.body: Cherubs are carved and gilded at the top of the back. This throne was made in Paris in 1822 for a child.

annotations.title: Rooster and wreath
annotations.body: A rooster within a laurel wreath is tooled in gold on the leather back. Odin sat in the high seat Hlidskjalf and looked down on the nine worlds.

annotations.title: Winged-beast legs
annotations.body: The front legs are carved as winged beasts. Freyr secretly climbed into Odin's seat and fell sick with longing at the sight of the giantess Gerd.

artifact.title: Lia Fail
artifact.owner: The kings of Ireland (the Hill of Tara)
artifact.maker: Unknown (brought by the Tuatha De Danann from Falias)
artifact.power: It cries out aloud when the rightful king of Ireland stands upon it.
artifact.firstRecord: Lebor Gabala Erenn (The Book of Invasions)
artifact.summary: The Stone of Destiny, one of the four treasures of the Tuatha De Danann. It cried out when the rightful king of Ireland stood on it.
artifact.story:
The Tuatha De Danann came to Ireland bearing four treasures from four northern cities: from Gorias the spear of Lugh, from Findias the sword of Nuada, from Murias the cauldron of the Dagda, and from Falias the Lia Fail, the Stone of Destiny.

The Lia Fail cried out aloud when the rightful king of Ireland stood upon it. According to legend, the hero Cu Chulainn struck it with his sword when it would not acknowledge his protege Lugaid as king, and after that the stone fell silent. Only when Conn of the Hundred Battles stepped on it did it cry out once more.

Today a granite standing stone called the Lia Fail stands on the Hill of Tara in County Meath, Ireland. There is also a story that the Stone of Scone, on which the kings of Scotland sat to be crowned, was the Lia Fail.
artifact.imageAlt: A Celtic-style stone head from northern England under Roman rule, about 100–300. Large almond-shaped eyes, a straight nose and a thin, closed mouth are carved in red sandstone, with bulging locks of hair at both sides.

source.creditLine: Gift of Dr. and Mrs. Jacob Hirsch

annotations.title: Large eyes
annotations.body: Large almond-shaped eyes are shallowly carved. This stone head was made by Celtic people in northern England under Roman rule, about 100–300.

annotations.title: Closed mouth
annotations.body: A straight, closed mouth. The head was once painted red, and traces of the paint remain. The Lia Fail cried out when the rightful king of Ireland stood on it.

annotations.title: Locks of hair
annotations.body: Bulging locks of hair at both sides. The Celts are said to have held the human head sacred and to have carved heads in stone.

artifact.title: Harp of the Dagda
artifact.titleOriginal: Daur Dá Bláo (Harp of the Dagda)
artifact.owner: The Dagda, god of the Tuatha De Danann
artifact.power: It plays the three strains of weeping, laughter and sleep, and flies to its master's hands when called by name.
artifact.firstRecord: The Second Battle of Mag Tuired
artifact.summary: The harp the Dagda won back by calling its names. With the strains of sorrow, laughter and sleep he put the Fomorians to sleep.
artifact.story:
After the Tuatha De Danann defeated the Fomorians at the Second Battle of Mag Tuired, the fleeing Fomorians carried off the Dagda's harper and his harp. The Dagda, with Lugh and Ogma, followed them to the hall where they were feasting. The harp hung on the wall.

The Dagda had bound the music into the harp so that it would not sound until he called it. When he called out its names, "Come, Daur Da Blao; come, Coir Cetharchair; come, summer; come, winter," the harp leaped from the wall, killing nine men in its path, and came into its master's hands.

The Dagda played the three strains. At the strain of sorrow the women wept; at the strain of laughter the women and children laughed; at the strain of sleep all the Fomorians fell asleep, and the three gods escaped unharmed. The harp is also the national emblem of Ireland today.
artifact.imageAlt: A portable harp made by John Egan of Dublin, Ireland, in 1819. Many strings stretch between the gold-painted curved neck and the pillar, and the green soundbox is painted with gold leaves.

source.creditLine: The Crosby Brown Collection of Musical Instruments, 1889

annotations.title: Curved neck
annotations.body: The curved neck set with a row of tuning pins. This portable harp was made in Ireland in 1819.

annotations.title: Strings
annotations.body: The many strings. When the Dagda played the strains of sorrow, laughter and sleep, all the Fomorians fell asleep.

annotations.title: Green soundbox
annotations.body: A soundbox painted with gold leaves on a green ground. The harp is also the national emblem of Ireland today.

artifact.title: Moralltach
artifact.maker: Unknown (the sword of the sea god Manannan)
artifact.power: As its name, "Great Fury," says, one stroke cuts through anything.
artifact.firstRecord: The Pursuit of Diarmuid and Grainne
artifact.summary: The sword of the sea god Manannan. Aengus, god of love, passed it to his foster son Diarmuid.
artifact.story:
Diarmuid was one of the foremost warriors of the Fianna, the war band of Ireland. Grainne, who was to marry the aging leader Fionn mac Cumhaill, fell in love with Diarmuid at the wedding feast and laid on him a binding vow (geis) to run away with her. Diarmuid had no choice but to flee with Grainne, and for years Fionn pursued them all over Ireland.

Diarmuid carried two swords and two spears: the great sword Moralltach ("Great Fury") and the small sword Beagalltach ("Little Fury"), the red spear Gae Dearg and the yellow spear Gae Buidhe. Moralltach was the sword that the sea god Manannan gave to Aengus, god of love, and Aengus passed on to his foster son Diarmuid.

Years later, reconciled with Fionn, Diarmuid went hunting a boar on Ben Bulben. Grainne told him to take Moralltach and the red spear, but he took only the small sword and the yellow spear. Gored by an enchanted boar, Diarmuid lost his life.
artifact.imageAlt: A European long sword of about 1400. Below a round pommel, a wire-bound grip and a cross-guard spreading to both sides, a long, straight double-edged blade extends.

source.creditLine: Gift of Mr. and Mrs. John L. Severance

annotations.title: Round pommel
annotations.body: A round, disk-shaped pommel. This is a European long sword of about 1400.

annotations.title: Cross-guard
annotations.body: A cross-guard whose ends curve slightly toward the blade. Moralltach was the sword of the sea god Manannan.

annotations.title: Long blade
annotations.body: A long blade that gradually tapers. Ignoring Grainne's advice, Diarmuid went hunting with his small sword instead of this great one.

artifact.title: The Crane Bag
artifact.owner: The sea god Manannan, later Fionn mac Cumhaill
artifact.maker: The sea god Manannan (from the skin of Aoife, a woman turned into a crane)
artifact.power: When the sea is full, all the treasures of the gods appear in it; when the tide ebbs, it is empty.
artifact.firstRecord: Duanaire Finn (The Poem Book of Finn)
artifact.summary: Manannan's bag, made from the skin of a woman turned into a crane. It held all the treasures of the gods.
artifact.story:
Aoife loved Ilbrec, son of the sea god. Jealous of her, Iuchra turned Aoife into a crane by magic, and as a crane Aoife lived two hundred years in the house of Manannan, the sea god, before she died.

Manannan made a bag from her skin and put into it his most precious treasures: his own shirt and knife, the belt of Goibniu the smith god, the shears of the king of Scotland, the helmet of the king of the north, and a belt made from the back of a great whale. When the sea was full all those treasures could be seen, and when the tide ebbed the bag was empty.

The story comes from a poem in Duanaire Finn, compiled in the seventeenth century. The crane bag is said to have passed from Manannan to Lugh, god of light, and then to Fionn mac Cumhaill, leader of the war band.
artifact.imageAlt: A purse-shaped reliquary from the Upper Rhine region of Germany, about 1320. Gilded copper is densely set with rock crystal, glass and gems, and a blue roundel at the center carries the Virgin holding the Christ Child.

source.creditLine: Purchase from the J. H. Wade Fund
source.objectCulture: Germany, Upper Rhine, Southern Swabia, Gothic period, 14th century

annotations.title: Virgin and Child on blue
annotations.body: On the blue ground of the central roundel, the Virgin holding the Child is applied in gold. This reliquary was made in the Upper Rhine region of Germany about 1320.

annotations.title: Set stones
annotations.body: Polished rock crystal and gems are set all around. The sea god Manannan made a bag from the skin of a woman turned into a crane and kept the treasures of the gods in it.

annotations.title: Purse mouth
annotations.body: The top is shaped like the mouth of a purse. This reliquary imitates the purses medieval people wore at the waist.

artifact.title: Enbarr
artifact.owner: The sea god Manannan; Lugh, god of light
artifact.power: Runs faster than the spring wind over water and land alike, and no one on its back can be killed, it was said.
artifact.firstRecord: The Fate of the Children of Tuireann
artifact.summary: The horse of the sea god Manannan that runs over waves as if on land. Lugh, god of light, appeared before the king of the Tuatha De Danann riding it.
artifact.story:
Enbarr, "flowing mane," is the horse of the sea god Manannan. It ran faster than the cold spring wind, over water and land alike, and it is said that no one on its back was ever killed.

In "The Fate of the Children of Tuireann," Lugh, the god of light, borrowed Enbarr from Manannan and appeared on it before Nuada, king of the Tuatha De Danann. Equipped with Manannan's armor and sword as well, he struck down the envoys who had come to collect tribute for the Fomorians.

The three sons of Tuireann, as the price for killing Lugh's father, had to fetch treasures from the ends of the earth. When they asked to borrow Enbarr for the long journey, Lugh refused, saying he could not lend what was itself on loan, and gave them instead Manannan's boat, the "Wave-Sweeper," which crossed the sea by itself wherever its passengers wished.
artifact.imageAlt: The two faces of a gold coin (stater) of the Catuvellauni of Britain, about 20 BCE–10 CE. The obverse at left bears the letters TASCIOV RICON in a band; the reverse at right shows a horse carrying a warrior with a sword.

source.objectTitle: Tasciovanus Stater: Wreath (obverse); Horse and Armed Rider (reverse)

annotations.title: Mounted warrior
annotations.body: The reverse shows a warrior with a sword riding a galloping horse. This gold coin was struck by Tasciovanus, king of the Catuvellauni in Britain.

annotations.title: Inscribed letters
annotations.body: The obverse is inscribed TASCIOV RICON. Ricon is thought to mean "king" in a Celtic language.

annotations.title: Outstretched legs
annotations.body: The horse gallops with its legs outstretched. Enbarr, the horse of the sea god Manannan, ran faster than the spring wind over water and land alike.

artifact.title: Cormac's Cup of Truth
artifact.owner: Cormac mac Airt, high king of Ireland
artifact.power: Three lies spoken over it break it into three pieces; three truths make it whole again.
artifact.firstRecord: The Adventure of Cormac in the Land of Promise
artifact.summary: The golden cup Manannan gave King Cormac. It broke at falsehood and became whole again at the truth.
artifact.story:
One morning on the ramparts of Tara, King Cormac met a strange warrior holding a silver branch. When its three golden apples shook, the sick and the wounded forgot their troubles and fell asleep. To get the branch Cormac gave away his wife, son and daughter, but he soon set out to find his family.

Passing through a mist, he came to a palace in the Land of Promise, where the master showed him a golden cup. If three lies were spoken before it, it broke into three pieces, and if three truths were spoken, it became whole again. The master mended the broken cup by telling the truth that Cormac's wife and daughter had seen no other man in the meantime.

The master was the sea god Manannan. He gave Cormac back his family and the silver branch, and the golden cup as well, telling him to use it to tell truth from falsehood. When Cormac died, it is said, the cup vanished with him.
artifact.imageAlt: A Hungarian gilt-silver chalice of about 1450–80. Below the golden bowl, the cup's base and stem are filled with green and white enamel flowers, and square gems are set in the knop and the foot.

annotations.title: Golden bowl
annotations.body: A wide, flaring golden bowl. Cormac's cup, which broke into three at three lies and became whole again at three truths, was also made of gold.

annotations.title: Enamel flowers
annotations.body: On the base around the bowl, flowers are drawn in fine wire and filled with green and white enamel, the filigree enamel for which fifteenth-century Hungary was famous.

annotations.title: Jeweled foot
annotations.body: Square gems are set around the foot. Manannan told Cormac to use this cup to tell truth from falsehood.

artifact.title: Cauldron of Ceridwen
artifact.power: Boiled for a year and a day, its first three drops hold all the wisdom of the world.
artifact.summary: The cauldron in which Ceridwen brewed wisdom for her son. The boy who tasted three drops became the poet Taliesin.
artifact.story:
The witch Ceridwen had the ugliest son in the world, Morfran. To give him wisdom at least, she put herbs into a great cauldron and began to boil it for a year and a day. The first three drops to leap from the cauldron would hold all the wisdom of the world, and the rest would become poison.

The boy Gwion Bach was set to stir the cauldron. On the day the year was complete, three drops of the boiling brew splashed onto Gwion's thumb. He put the burning thumb in his mouth and at once knew everything in the world; the rest of the brew turned to poison, and the cauldron split in two.

Furious, Ceridwen chased the fleeing Gwion. He became a hare, a fish, a bird and a grain of wheat, and she became a greyhound, an otter, a hawk and a black hen, and at last she swallowed the grain. Nine months later the child was born again, put into a leather bag and thrown into the sea, and the man who found him cried "a radiant brow!", which gave Taliesin, the greatest poet of Wales, his name.
artifact.imageAlt: A ritual cauldron from Bronze Age Hungary, about 1000–900 BCE. A large looped handle in two strands rises above the round bronze body, and fine patterns are incised around the rim.

source.creditLine: Purchase from the J. H. Wade Fund

annotations.title: Looped handle
annotations.body: A large handle bent in two strands, so the cauldron could hang over a fire. This cauldron comes from Bronze Age Hungary, about 1000–900 BCE.

annotations.title: Handle attachment
annotations.body: The handle hangs from fittings riveted to the body. Ceridwen boiled the brew of wisdom in her cauldron for a year and a day.

annotations.title: Round body
annotations.body: A round body of hammered bronze. After three drops splashed onto Gwion's thumb, the rest of the brew turned to poison and the cauldron split in two.

artifact.title: Dyrnwyn
artifact.power: When a man of noble birth draws it himself, flames blaze from hilt to point.
artifact.firstRecord: The Thirteen Treasures of the Island of Britain
artifact.summary: The sword of King Rhydderch, first of the Thirteen Treasures of the Island of Britain. When a worthy man drew it, the blade burst into flame.
artifact.story:
In Wales there survives "The Thirteen Treasures of the Island of Britain," a list of thirteen treasures of the old kingdoms of northern Britain. At its head stands Dyrnwyn, "white hilt," the sword of Rhydderch Hael, a sixth-century king of Strathclyde.

When a man of noble birth drew this sword himself, flames blazed from its hilt to its point. True to his name, "the Generous," Rhydderch gave the sword to anyone who asked for it, but because of those flames everyone who received it gave it back.

Later tradition says the wizard Merlin gathered all thirteen treasures and took them to a house of glass. Rhydderch was a real king, and his name also appears in the Merlin legends and in the life of Saint Kentigern.
artifact.imageAlt: A German two-handed sword of 1550–1600. Below a long grip, a cross-guard with rings spreads to both sides, and below it runs a long blade undulating like flames.

source.creditLine: Gift of Mr. and Mrs. John L. Severance

annotations.title: Wavy blade
annotations.body: The blade undulates like flames; such a blade is called a flame blade (flamberge). Dyrnwyn burst into flame from hilt to point when a worthy man drew it.

annotations.title: Small wings
annotations.body: The small lugs projecting near the top of the blade caught an enemy's blade and protected the hand when gripping the blade below the guard.

annotations.title: Ringed guard
annotations.body: A long cross-guard with rings on both sides. This is a German two-handed sword of the late sixteenth century.

artifact.title: Gwyddbwyll Board of Gwenddoleu
artifact.power: Set out the pieces, and they move by themselves and play the game.
artifact.firstRecord: The Thirteen Treasures of the Island of Britain
artifact.summary: Set silver pieces on its gold board, and they played by themselves. It is one of the Thirteen Treasures of the Island of Britain.
artifact.story:
Gwyddbwyll, "wood-sense," was a board game enjoyed by the medieval Welsh. According to "The Thirteen Treasures of the Island of Britain," King Gwenddoleu's board was made of gold and its pieces of silver, and once the pieces were set out they moved by themselves and played the game.

Gwenddoleu was a king of northern Britain who fell at the Battle of Arfderydd in 573. In Welsh tradition his poet, Myrddin, that is Merlin, went mad with grief at losing his lord and wandered in the forest.

Boards that play by themselves appear in other stories too. In "Peredur," Peredur finds a board in a castle on which the game plays by itself, and when the side he favors loses, he angrily throws the board into a lake. In "The Dream of Rhonabwy," Arthur and Owain play the game while their men and a flock of ravens fight.
artifact.imageAlt: An amber game board made in Konigsberg by Georg Schreiber in the seventeenth century. Inside the open box-shaped board, slices of red and yellow amber and ivory form the triangular points of backgammon.

annotations.title: Triangular points
annotations.body: The side with rows of long triangles is a backgammon board. When the board is folded shut, the outside becomes a chessboard.

annotations.title: Amber slices
annotations.body: Red and yellow amber is cut thin and laid over gold foil so the light shines through. Seventeenth-century Konigsberg was famous for its Baltic amber work.

annotations.title: Folding hinge
annotations.body: Folded in the middle, the board becomes a box for carrying the pieces. On Gwenddoleu's board, the pieces played the game by themselves once they were set out.

artifact.title: Cloak of Manannan
artifact.owner: Manannan mac Lir, the sea god
artifact.power: Shaken between two people, it ensures they will never meet again in this world.
artifact.firstRecord: The Wasting Sickness of Cu Chulainn
artifact.summary: The sea god's cloak that keeps two people from ever meeting again. It parted Cu Chulainn and the fairy Fand forever.
artifact.story:
The hero Cu Chulainn, trying to shoot magical birds on a lake, was whipped by two women in a dream and lay sick for a year. The one who called him to the Otherworld was Fand, who had parted from her husband, the sea god Manannan. Cu Chulainn crossed into the Otherworld and fought on Fand's side, and the two fell in love.

When Cu Chulainn's wife Emer learned of it, she went to find Fand with fifty women armed with knives. But seeing how much Emer loved her husband, Fand withdrew of her own accord and said she would return to Manannan. Manannan came across the sea to take Fand away, and shook his cloak between Cu Chulainn and Fand.

Whoever Manannan shook his cloak between would never meet again in this world. When Cu Chulainn, having lost Fand, wandered the mountains in grief, the druids gave him and Emer a drink of forgetfulness so that they would forget it all.
artifact.imageAlt: A semicircular ecclesiastical cloak (cope) from late fifteenth-century Europe. Large pomegranates and flowers are woven in red velvet on a golden ground, and a gold-thread band is attached along the straight upper edge.

source.creditLine: Brooklyn Museum Costume Collection at The Metropolitan Museum of Art, Gift of the Brooklyn Museum, 2009; Gift of The Rembrandt Club, 1911

annotations.title: Pomegranate pattern
annotations.body: Leaving the golden ground showing between areas of red velvet, large pomegranates and flowers are woven in. This pattern was a favorite of fifteenth-century European silks.

annotations.title: Upper band
annotations.body: A band woven with gold thread is attached along the straight edge that rests on the shoulders. The cope was fastened at the front and worn like a cloak.

annotations.title: Curved hem
annotations.body: The hem forms a half circle when spread out. When the sea god Manannan shook his cloak between Cu Chulainn and Fand, the two could never meet again.

artifact.title: Lyre of Orpheus
artifact.maker: First made by Hermes and handed down by Apollo (by tradition)
artifact.power: When he plays, birds and beasts, trees and even stones follow, and the gods of the underworld are moved.
artifact.summary: When Orpheus played, beasts, trees and stones followed him. With his song he nearly brought his wife back from the underworld.
artifact.story:
Orpheus was the son of the Muse Calliope and is said to have received his lyre from Apollo. When he sang to the lyre, birds and fish gathered, and even trees and rocks moved after him. On the voyage of the Argo his song drowned out the song of the Sirens, so that the sailors passed by unharmed.

When his wife Eurydice died of a snakebite, Orpheus went down to the underworld with his lyre. Moved by his song, Hades and Persephone gave her back on condition that he not look back until they reached the world above. But just short of the exit he turned around, and Eurydice vanished back into the underworld.

Later Orpheus was torn apart by Thracian women who followed Dionysus. His head and lyre, thrown into a river, floated all the way to the island of Lesbos without ceasing to sing, and the lyre is said to have risen into the sky as the constellation Lyra.
artifact.imageAlt: Orpheus and Cerberus, carved in sandstone by Ferdinand Tietz near Bamberg, Germany, about 1765. A young Orpheus stands with his head thrown back, playing a stringed instrument, while Cerberus, the dog of the underworld, crouches at his feet.

annotations.title: Stringed instrument
annotations.body: The stringed instrument Orpheus holds against his chest. The eighteenth-century sculptor gave him an instrument of his own day instead of an ancient lyre.

annotations.title: Singing face
annotations.body: A young man singing with his head thrown back. When he sang, birds and beasts, trees and stones moved after him.

annotations.title: Cerberus
annotations.body: Crouching at his feet is Cerberus, the dog that guards the gates of the underworld. Even the gods of the underworld were moved by Orpheus's song.

artifact.title: Bow of Odysseus
artifact.maker: Unknown (the bow of the archer Eurytus, given as a gift by his son Iphitus)
artifact.power: No one but its master can string it.
artifact.summary: The bow no one but Odysseus could string. Returning after twenty years, he used it to defeat the suitors.
artifact.story:
Twenty years after Odysseus left for the Trojan War, his palace on Ithaca was overrun by men wooing his wife Penelope and wasting his wealth. Unable to hold out any longer, Penelope brought out her husband's bow and said she would marry the man who could string it and shoot an arrow through the holes of twelve axes at once.

Odysseus had received the bow in his youth from Iphitus, son of the great archer Eurytus, as a token of friendship. He treasured it so much that he did not take it to war but kept it at home. The suitors tried one after another, but none could even bend the bow to string it.

Odysseus, who had come home disguised as a beggar, offered to try. He strung the bow as easily as stringing a lyre, and when he plucked the string it sang like a swallow. His arrow passed through all twelve axes, and Odysseus revealed himself and turned the bow on the suitors.
artifact.imageAlt: An Ottoman Turkish composite bow of 1719–20 with two arrows. Unstrung, the bow curves deeply with its tips bent backward, and two long arrows stand beside it.

annotations.title: Reflexed tips
annotations.body: When unstrung, the tips bend sharply the other way. Made of wood, horn and sinew glued in layers, a composite bow takes great strength to string.

annotations.title: Grip
annotations.body: The middle of the bow where the archer holds it is painted with designs. The bow was made in the Ottoman Empire in 1719–20.

annotations.title: Arrows
annotations.body: Two of the forty arrows that came with the bow. Odysseus's arrow passed through the holes of twelve axes set in a row.

artifact.title: Chariot of Helios
artifact.power: Drawn by four fire-breathing horses, it carries the sun across the sky every day.
artifact.summary: The chariot of fire Helios drove across the sky carrying the sun. When his son Phaethon drove it, the world nearly burned.
artifact.story:
Every day the sun god Helios rose at the eastern edge of the world in a golden chariot drawn by four horses, crossed the sky and went down into the western sea. The horses breathed fire from their nostrils, and at night Helios sailed back east on a golden cup across the river that encircles the world.

Helios's son Phaethon was mocked by his friends, who said he was not truly the son of the Sun. He went to his father, won a promise to grant him anything, and begged to drive the chariot for just one day. Helios tried to dissuade him, but he could not take back an oath sworn by the Styx, the river of the underworld.

The horses knew their master was not driving and ran wild off their course. When the chariot climbed too high the earth froze, and when it came too low the rivers dried and the land burned. Seeing that the world would burn up, Zeus struck Phaethon down with a thunderbolt. His sisters, weeping on the riverbank, turned into poplars, and their tears became amber.
artifact.imageAlt: An Athenian black-figure water jar (hydria) painted by the Antimenes Painter about 520 BCE. In the middle of the orange body, a chariot drawn by four horses is shown from the front, with a band of animals below.

source.creditLine: Purchase from the J. H. Wade Fund
source.objectTitle: Black-Figure Hydria (Water Vessel): Frontal Quadriga (Body); Theseus and Minotaur (Shoulder)

annotations.title: Four horses from the front
annotations.body: A chariot drawn by four horses is painted as if seen from the front. Helios's chariot was also drawn by four fire-breathing horses.

annotations.title: Charioteer
annotations.body: Between the horses, the charioteer standing in the chariot can be seen. The jar was painted in Athens by the artist known as the Antimenes Painter.

annotations.title: Animal frieze
annotations.body: Animals march in a row in the lower band. The chariot Phaethon drove left its course and nearly set the earth on fire.

artifact.title: Palladium
artifact.owner: The people of Troy, later Rome
artifact.power: As long as this statue remains within the walls, Troy will never fall.
artifact.summary: A small wooden image of Athena that fell from heaven. As long as it was inside the city, Troy would not fall.
artifact.story:
When Ilus, the founder of Troy, prayed for a sign of the gods' will, a small wooden statue fell from heaven in front of his tent. It was the Palladium, an image of the goddess Athena with a spear raised in her right hand and a distaff and spindle in her left. Some say Athena made it in memory of her young friend Pallas, whom she had killed by accident.

An oracle declared that Troy would never fall as long as this image stayed within its walls. In the tenth year of the war, the Trojan seer Helenus, captured by the Greeks, revealed this secret. Odysseus and Diomedes slipped into the city by night and stole the Palladium, and soon afterward the wooden horse passed through the gates.

The Romans believed that Aeneas had rescued the true Palladium from burning Troy and brought it to Italy. In Rome it was kept deep inside the Temple of Vesta, where the undying fire was guarded.
artifact.imageAlt: A Greek bronze statuette of Athena, about 460 BCE. The helmeted goddess in a long robe raises her right arm high, releasing an owl from her hand.

source.objectTitle: Bronze statuette of Athena flying her owl

annotations.title: Owl
annotations.body: An owl is about to fly from her raised right hand. The owl is the bird of Athena, goddess of wisdom.

annotations.title: Helmet
annotations.body: The helmeted head of the goddess. The Palladium is said to have been a small wooden image of Athena raising a spear in her right hand.

annotations.title: Long robe
annotations.body: A robe (peplos) that falls straight from the shoulders to the feet. The Trojans believed Troy would not fall as long as the Palladium was inside the city.

artifact.title: Trojan Horse
artifact.power: A huge hollow wooden horse. The heroes hidden in its belly got inside the walls of Troy.
artifact.summary: The hollow wooden horse that ended the Trojan War. The heroes hidden in its belly opened the gates at night.
artifact.story:
After besieging Troy for ten years without victory, the Greeks devised a trick. The carpenter Epeius, with Athena's help, built a huge hollow wooden horse, and Odysseus and other heroes hid in its belly. The rest of the army pretended to sail away and hid behind a nearby island.

In the Odyssey, the Trojans drag the horse into the city and then argue over whether to cut open its belly, throw it from a cliff or keep it as an offering to the gods. Helen walks around the horse imitating the voices of the heroes' wives, but Odysseus stops the mouths of his comrades, who are about to leap out.

The Roman poet Virgil sang in the Aeneid that the priest Laocoon struck the horse with a spear, saying he feared the Greeks even when they bore gifts. That night the heroes came out of the horse and opened the gates, and Troy burned and fell.
artifact.imageAlt: The Trojan Horse, a painted enamel plaque from Limoges, France, about 1530–40. Before Troy, lined with walls and towers, people pull a huge white horse into the city; the plaque is set in a red velvet frame.

source.creditLine: Andrew R. and Martha Holden Jennings Fund
source.objectTitle: Plaque Depicting the Trojan Horse from the Aeneid

annotations.title: White horse
annotations.body: People drag a huge white horse into the city. This plaque is one of a series made in Limoges, France, about 1530–40, picturing scenes from the Aeneid in enamel.

annotations.title: City of Troy
annotations.body: Above the city crowded with walls and towers, the word TROIA can be seen. That night the heroes who came out of the horse opened the gates.

annotations.title: Priam and Sinon
annotations.body: Labels reading PRIAMVS and SINON float above the heads of the people at upper left. Deceived by the lies of the Greek Sinon, King Priam of Troy let the horse into the city.

artifact.title: Thyrsus
artifact.power: Strike a rock with it and water springs up; thrust it into the ground and wine gushes out.
artifact.summary: The staff of Dionysus, a fennel stalk tipped with a pine cone and wound with ivy. When it struck the ground, wine sprang up.
artifact.story:
The thyrsus is a staff made from a giant fennel stalk tipped with a pine cone and wound with ivy. Dionysus, god of wine and revelry, and the women who followed him, the maenads, carried it as they roamed the mountains and fields.

In Euripides's Bacchae, the women of Thebes worship Dionysus on Mount Cithaeron. One woman strikes a rock with her thyrsus and clear water springs up; another plunges hers into the ground and wine gushes out. Scraping the earth with their fingertips they draw out milk, and honey drips from their thyrsi.

When villagers come to seize them, the women drive the men off by throwing their thyrsi. The men's spears cannot wound them, but the thyrsi wound the men. Pentheus, king of Thebes, who scorned Dionysus, disguises himself as a woman to spy on them and is torn apart by the maenads, led by his own mother.
artifact.imageAlt: An Athenian red-figure mixing bowl (column krater) painted by the Naples Painter about 450–430 BCE. On the black ground, two satyrs with horse tails chase two women carrying leafy staffs (thyrsi), shown in red.

source.objectTitle: Red-Figure Column Krater (Mixing Vessel): Satyrs Pursuing Maenads

annotations.title: Maenad with thyrsus
annotations.body: The woman on the right flees holding a leafy staff, the thyrsus. She is a maenad, a woman who follows Dionysus.

annotations.title: Satyr
annotations.body: A satyr with a horse's tail chases a woman. Satyrs are spirits of the wild who follow Dionysus.

annotations.title: Thyrsus on the shoulder
annotations.body: The woman on the left also carries a thyrsus on her shoulder. In the Bacchae, the maenads strike rocks with their thyrsi to bring forth water and pierce the ground to bring forth wine.

artifact.title: Bag of Aeolus
artifact.owner: Aeolus, master of the winds; Odysseus
artifact.maker: Aeolus (from the hide of a nine-year-old ox)
artifact.power: It holds every violent wind, so that a ship sails home with only a fair breeze.
artifact.summary: An oxhide bag holding all the violent winds. With home in sight, the sailors opened it.
artifact.story:
Aeolus, master of the winds, lived on a floating island ringed with bronze walls. When Odysseus stopped there on his way home from Troy, Aeolus entertained him for a month and gave him a gift when he left: a bag made from the hide of a nine-year-old ox, in which he had bound all the violent winds, tied with a silver cord.

Outside the bag he left only the west wind, to carry the ship straight to Ithaca. They sailed for nine days and nights, and on the tenth, when they were so close that the fires of home were in sight, Odysseus, who had held the helm the whole time, fell asleep.

The sailors, thinking the bag must be full of gold and silver, secretly untied it. The imprisoned winds rushed out all at once, and the ship was driven back to Aeolus's island. Aeolus, declaring him a man hated by the gods, never helped him again.
artifact.imageAlt: An agate vessel (askos) of the Ptolemaic dynasty, 200–1 BCE. Agate with swirling brown and white bands is carved in the shape of a wineskin, with gold capping the slanted spout and the foot.

source.creditLine: Andrew R. and Martha Holden Jennings Fund

annotations.title: Gold-capped spout
annotations.body: The end of the slanted spout is capped with gold. The vessel dates from the Ptolemaic period, 200–1 BCE.

annotations.title: Banded agate
annotations.body: It is carved from a single piece of agate with swirling brown and white bands. An askos is a vessel modeled on a leather wineskin.

annotations.title: Handle
annotations.body: A loop handle is carved at the top. Aeolus shut all the violent winds in an oxhide bag and tied it with a silver cord.

artifact.title: Cornucopia
artifact.owner: Tyche, goddess of fortune; Plutus, god of wealth
artifact.maker: Unknown (the horn of the goat Amalthea)
artifact.power: Food and drink of every kind flow from it without end.
artifact.summary: The horn of the goat that nursed the infant Zeus. It became the symbol of plenty, pouring out whatever one wishes without end.
artifact.story:
To hide him from his father Cronus, who swallowed his children, Rhea hid the newborn Zeus in a cave on Crete. The infant was nursed by the she-goat Amalthea. One day, while playing, Zeus broke off one of her horns, and from then on food and drink of every kind flowed from it without end.

There is another story. Heracles, wrestling the river god Achelous, who had turned himself into a bull, broke off one of his horns, and the water nymphs filled it with fruit and fragrant flowers. Ovid sang that by this horn Plenty became plentiful.

The horn overflowing with fruit and grain became the attribute of Tyche and Fortuna, goddesses of fortune, and of Plutus, god of wealth. The Latin name cornucopia, "horn of plenty," still lives on in harvest decorations and in the coats of arms of many countries.
artifact.imageAlt: Victory with Cornucopia, a Roman bronze chariot ornament of about 40–68 CE. The winged goddess soars upward with one arm raised above her head and the other holding a long horn of plenty.

annotations.title: Horn of plenty
annotations.body: The long horn resting on her arm is the cornucopia. Food of every kind flowed without end from the horn of Amalthea.

annotations.title: Wings
annotations.body: Victoria, goddess of victory, with great wings on her back. This bronze ornament decorated a Roman chariot about 40–68 CE.

annotations.title: Flying drapery
annotations.body: Her robe streams in the wind. The horn overflowing with fruit and grain came to be held by Fortuna, goddess of fortune, and by Victory.

artifact.title: Wings of Daedalus and Icarus
artifact.power: Wings of feathers bound with thread and wax. Strapped to the arms, they let a person fly like a bird.
artifact.summary: The wings Daedalus, builder of the Labyrinth, made to escape Crete with his son. Icarus flew too close to the sun.
artifact.story:
Daedalus, the master craftsman of Athens, built a labyrinth for King Minos of Crete to imprison the Minotaur. But after Theseus escaped from it, Daedalus was imprisoned with his son Icarus for having shown the way out. Land and sea alike were in Minos's hands.

Daedalus reasoned that the sky alone was open. He laid out feathers from small to large, bound them in the middle with thread and at the ends with wax, and curved them like a bird's wings. Fitting the wings on his son, he warned him: fly too low and the sea spray will weigh your wings down; fly too high and the sun's heat will melt them; keep to the middle.

Drunk with the joy of flight, Icarus climbed higher and higher. The sun melted the wax, the feathers scattered, and he fell into the sea. That sea is called the Icarian Sea, and the island nearby Icaria. Daedalus reached Sicily alone.
artifact.imageAlt: Hendrick Goltzius's engraving Icarus, 1588. Within a round frame, a young man who has lost his wings falls headfirst with the sun behind him; far below, Daedalus flies small over the sea, and a Latin inscription runs around the border.

annotations.title: Falling Icarus
annotations.body: Icarus, who flew too close to the sun, falls headfirst. Hendrick Goltzius engraved this print in 1588 as part of the series The Four Disgracers.

annotations.title: Daedalus in the distance
annotations.body: Far below, Daedalus flies over the sea on his wings. The father had told his son to fly neither too high nor too low, but in the middle.

annotations.title: Latin inscription
annotations.body: The round border carries a Latin inscription meaning that knowledge is a gift of God, but one must keep within one's limits. The sea where Icarus fell is named the Icarian Sea after him.

artifact.title: The Golden Bough
artifact.power: Whoever plucks it and carries it may enter the underworld alive and return.
artifact.summary: The golden bough that must be plucked before a living man can enter the underworld. Aeneas found it by following two doves.
artifact.story:
Having reached Italy after the fall of Troy, Aeneas wished to meet his father Anchises in the underworld. The Sibyl of Cumae told him that a living man who wishes to enter the underworld must first pluck a golden bough hidden in a dark tree in the forest and offer it to Proserpina, queen of the dead. Only for one whom fate allows does the bough come away, and in its place a new golden bough soon grows.

As Aeneas stood helpless before the vast forest, two doves, the birds of his mother Venus, flew down before him. Following them, he found the gleaming golden bough in a tree beside Lake Avernus and plucked it.

At the river of the underworld the ferryman Charon barred the way, saying he could not carry the living, but at the sight of the golden bough he silently gave up his boat. Aeneas offered the bough at the threshold of the palace of the dead and met his father. In 1890 the British anthropologist James Frazer took the title of his book on myth and magic, The Golden Bough, from this story.
artifact.imageAlt: Aeneas and the Sibyl in the Underworld, painted in oil on copper by Jan Brueghel the Younger in the 1630s. In the middle of a dark underworld where flames shoot up, the helmeted Aeneas follows the Sibyl, who points the way, surrounded by monsters and shades.

source.creditLine: Gift of Mrs. Erna S. Blade, in memory of her uncle, Sigmund Herrmann, 1991
source.objectTitle: Aeneas and the Sibyl in the Underworld

annotations.title: Aeneas and the Sibyl
annotations.body: The helmeted Aeneas and the Sibyl, who points the way. Only after plucking the golden bough could Aeneas enter the underworld alive.

annotations.title: Burning underworld
annotations.body: Flames of the underworld shoot up at upper right. On a small copper plate, Jan Brueghel the Younger painted every monster and punishment of the underworld in close detail.

annotations.title: Shades and monsters
annotations.body: Naked shades and monsters swarm together. The ferryman Charon carried the living man across only after seeing the golden bough.

artifact.title: Rod of Moses
artifact.power: Thrown down it becomes a serpent; stretched over the sea it parts the waters; struck against a rock it brings forth water.
artifact.summary: The rod with which Moses led the Israelites out of Egypt. It parted the Red Sea and drew water from the rock.
artifact.story:
While tending sheep in the land of Midian, Moses saw on Mount Horeb a bush that burned but was not consumed. God called him to lead the Israelites out of Egypt and asked what was in his hand. When Moses threw down his shepherd's staff it became a serpent, and when he caught it by the tail it became a staff again.

Before Pharaoh, the staff Aaron threw down became a serpent and swallowed the serpents of the Egyptian magicians. When Moses struck the Nile with the staff its water turned to blood, and ten plagues fell on Egypt. Standing at the Red Sea with the Egyptian army behind them, Moses raised his staff and stretched his hand over the sea, and the waters parted to open a dry path.

In the wilderness, when the people were thirsty, Moses struck a rock with his staff and water came out. In the Book of Numbers, Aaron's staff sprouted, blossomed and bore almonds overnight, and it was kept before the Ark of the Covenant.
artifact.imageAlt: A black-and-white photograph of the tapestry Moses Striking the Rock, woven in Florence, Italy, about 1650–57. In the center Moses strikes a rock with his rod as people gather around; at the top is a panel with a Latin inscription, and the sides are decorated with columns and cherubs.

source.creditLine: Gift of the family of Frederic W. Rhinelander, 1920
source.objectTitle: Moses Striking the Rock from a set of the Life of Moses

annotations.title: Moses with the rod
annotations.body: The figure in the center stretching out his rod to strike the rock is Moses. Water gushed from the rock and saved the thirsty people.

annotations.title: Latin inscription
annotations.body: The upper panel is woven with Latin meaning: let the heart of man, stubborn against God's kindness, blush before the rock that obeyed the blows of Moses.

annotations.title: Border decoration
annotations.body: A border of columns and cherubs. This is one tapestry of a Life of Moses series woven in Florence after designs by Agostino Melissi.

artifact.title: Jawbone of Samson
artifact.power: With the jawbone of a newly dead donkey he struck down a thousand Philistines.
artifact.summary: The donkey's jawbone Samson snatched up from the ground. With it alone he struck down a thousand Philistines.
artifact.story:
Samson was a Nazirite, dedicated to God from birth, and as long as his hair was never cut, no one could match his strength. He tore apart a lion with his bare hands and set the Philistines' wheat fields on fire by tying torches to the tails of three hundred foxes.

When the Philistines invaded, the frightened men of Judah bound Samson with two new ropes and handed him over. At Lehi, as the Philistines rushed at him shouting, the ropes that bound him melted like flax burned in fire. Samson picked up the fresh jawbone of a donkey lying on the ground and with it struck down a thousand Philistines.

"With the jawbone of a donkey, heaps upon heaps; with the jawbone of a donkey I have slain a thousand men." So Samson sang, threw the jawbone away and named the place Jawbone Hill. When he was parched with thirst, God split open a hollow at Lehi and water came out.
artifact.imageAlt: Samson, an oil painting by Valentin de Boulogne, about 1630–31. A young man with curly hair sits wrapped in a red cloak, his chin resting on his hand, with a donkey's jawbone beneath his arm, looking out at the viewer.

source.creditLine: Mr. and Mrs. William H. Marlatt Fund

annotations.title: Donkey's jawbone
annotations.body: Beneath his arm lies the jawbone of a donkey. With this jawbone alone, Samson struck down a thousand Philistines.

annotations.title: Thoughtful face
annotations.body: Samson rests his chin on his hand, lost in thought. The French painter Valentin de Boulogne, who worked in Rome, painted it about 1630–31.

annotations.title: Red cloak
annotations.body: A red cloak over his shoulders. Samson's strength came from his hair, which had never been cut.

artifact.title: Sling of David
artifact.owner: David the shepherd (later king of Israel)
artifact.power: With one smooth stone chosen from a brook, it brought down the giant Goliath.
artifact.summary: The sling with which the shepherd boy David felled the giant Goliath. A single stone sank into the giant's forehead.
artifact.story:
The armies of the Philistines and of Israel faced each other across the Valley of Elah. From the Philistine camp came the giant Goliath, six cubits and a span tall, in a bronze helmet and coat of scale armor, and for forty days, morning and evening, he challenged Israel to single combat, but no one dared to come forward.

The shepherd boy David, who had brought food to his brothers, came forward. King Saul put his own armor on him, but David took it off, saying he was not used to it, and took up his shepherd's staff and his sling, chose five smooth stones from the brook and put them in his bag. Goliath, seeing a boy coming at him with a stick, mocked him, asking whether he took him for a dog.

David cried, "You come to me with sword and spear, but I come in the name of the Lord of hosts," and slung a single stone. It sank into Goliath's forehead, and the giant fell face down on the ground. David drew Goliath's own sword and ended the fight.
artifact.imageAlt: David Triumphant over Goliath, a bronze plaquette by the Italian sculptor Moderno, about 1490–1510. The naked boy David stands with his sling hanging down, and Goliath's head and fallen body lie at his feet.

source.creditLine: Seventy-fifth anniversary gift of Dr. and Mrs. Sherman E. Lee

annotations.title: Hanging sling
annotations.body: The cord and pouch hanging from his hand are a sling. David brought down the giant with one smooth stone chosen from the brook.

annotations.title: Goliath's head
annotations.body: The giant Goliath's head lies at David's feet. When the stone sank into Goliath's forehead and he fell, David finished him with the giant's own sword.

annotations.title: Fallen giant
annotations.body: The headless body of the fallen giant. This small bronze plaquette was made by the Italian sculptor Moderno in the late fifteenth or early sixteenth century.

artifact.title: Brazen Serpent
artifact.owner: Moses, later the people of Jerusalem
artifact.power: Whoever had been bitten by the fiery serpents lived when he looked at the bronze serpent on the pole.
artifact.summary: The bronze serpent Moses set on a pole in the wilderness. Anyone bitten by a snake who looked at it lived.
artifact.story:
Wandering in the wilderness, the Israelites complained against God and Moses that they had neither food nor water. Then fiery serpents appeared and bit the people, and many died. When the people repented, Moses prayed for them.

God told him to make a fiery serpent and set it on a pole. Moses made a serpent of bronze and set it on a pole, and whoever had been bitten lived when he looked at the bronze serpent. The Gospel of John recalls it: "As Moses lifted up the serpent in the wilderness, even so must the Son of Man be lifted up."

The bronze serpent remained in Jerusalem for centuries. According to the Book of Kings, when the people called it Nehushtan and burned incense before it, King Hezekiah of Judah broke it in pieces to put an end to idol worship.
artifact.imageAlt: Moses Praying to End the Serpents' Attack on the Israelites, painted in Allahabad in the Mughal Empire, 1602–4. On a hillside Moses prays with both hands raised, while below him people bitten by snakes fall or writhe.

source.objectTitle: Moses praying to end the serpents’ attack on the Israelites (folio 63 verso), from a Mirror of Holiness (Mir’at al-quds) of Father Jerome Xavier
source.objectCulture: Mughal India, Allahabad, made for Prince Salim (1569–1627)

annotations.title: Praying Moses
annotations.body: The old man praying to heaven with both hands raised is Moses. God told him to make a serpent of bronze and set it on a pole.

annotations.title: People bitten by snakes
annotations.body: Below, people bitten by snakes fall and writhe. This is a page from the Mirror of Holiness, a book of Christian stories made in 1602–4 for the Mughal prince Salim.

annotations.title: Snakes
annotations.body: Thin snakes slither among the people. Whoever had been bitten lived when he looked at the bronze serpent on the pole.

artifact.title: Crown of Thorns
artifact.power: A crown woven to mock a king, yet every one of its thorns came to be venerated as a relic.
artifact.summary: The crown of thorns Roman soldiers put on Jesus. King Louis IX of France built the Sainte-Chapelle to house it.
artifact.story:
According to the Gospel of Mark, the Roman soldiers who took Jesus clothed him in purple, wove a crown of thorns and put it on him. They saluted him, "Hail, King of the Jews!", struck his head with a reed and spat on him. It was a crown meant to mock a king.

The crown later became one of the most precious relics. There are records of pilgrims venerating it in Jerusalem in the early fifth century, and later it was kept in the imperial palace of Constantinople. In 1238, when Baldwin II, the impoverished emperor of the Latin Empire, pawned it to Venetian merchants, King Louis IX of France paid the debt and brought it to Paris.

Louis IX built the Sainte-Chapelle, enclosed in stained glass, within his palace to house the crown. Thorns taken from it were distributed among reliquaries all over Europe. The crown, kept in the Cathedral of Notre-Dame, was rescued from the flames of the 2019 fire.
artifact.imageAlt: The right wing of a diptych painted in tempera and gold on oak in Styria, Austria, about 1400. Above, two men press the crown of thorns onto the head of the seated Christ with crossed staves; below, Christ prays in the garden while his disciples sleep.

source.creditLine: Mr. and Mrs. William H. Marlatt Fund
source.objectTitle: Diptych with the Passion of Christ (right wing): Crowning with Thorns and Agony on the Garden

annotations.title: Crown of thorns
annotations.body: Christ sits wearing the crown of thorns and a red robe. The soldiers plaited a crown of thorns, put a reed in his hand and mocked him as King of the Jews.

annotations.title: Men with staves
annotations.body: Two men on either side press the crown onto his head with crossed staves, a scene often painted in late medieval northern Europe. Louis IX of France built the Sainte-Chapelle in his Paris palace to house the crown of thorns.

annotations.title: Garden of Gethsemane
annotations.body: The lower panel shows Christ praying in the Garden of Gethsemane on the night before his arrest, while his disciples sleep. It is the right wing of a diptych painted in Styria, Austria, about 1400.

artifact.title: The True Cross
artifact.owner: The church of Jerusalem, later many churches
artifact.power: When no one knew which was Christ's cross, it is said that a dying woman rose up when it touched her.
artifact.summary: The cross of Christ that Helena, mother of Emperor Constantine, is said to have found in Jerusalem. Its fragments were scattered to churches all over the world.
artifact.story:
In the fourth century, Bishop Cyril of Jerusalem wrote that the wood of the cross on which Christ was crucified had been divided into fragments and spread throughout the world. A little later, Bishop Ambrose of Milan told how Helena, mother of Emperor Constantine, had found that cross in Jerusalem.

According to legend, Helena dug at Golgotha and found three crosses. Since no one could tell which was Christ's, they touched each one to a dying woman, and the moment the third cross touched her, she rose up. On that spot Constantine built the Church of the Holy Sepulchre.

In 614 a Persian army took Jerusalem and carried off the cross, and the Byzantine emperor Heraclius brought it back in 630. Fragments of the cross were placed in cross-shaped reliquaries adorned with gold and gems and kept in churches throughout Europe.
artifact.imageAlt: A reliquary of the True Cross. A double-armed cross from the Kingdom of Jerusalem, about 1214, is set in a thirteenth-century gilt-silver panel from the Rhine-Meuse region, amid rows of almond shapes pierced with quatrefoils and within a Latin inscription.

source.creditLine: Purchase from the J. H. Wade Fund
source.objectCulture: Cross: Latin Kingdom of Jerusalem; Panel: Rhine-Meuse region, Gothic period, 13th century

annotations.title: Double-armed cross
annotations.body: A fragment of the True Cross is enshrined in the double-armed cross set in the center. The cross was made about 1214 in the Kingdom of Jerusalem, founded by the crusaders.

annotations.title: Quatrefoil openings
annotations.body: Almond-shaped frames with quatrefoil openings are set in rows across the panel. The panel was made in the Rhine and Meuse region in the thirteenth century.

annotations.title: Inscribed border
annotations.body: A Latin inscription in black niello runs along the border. The fragments of the cross Helena is said to have found were enshrined in caskets like this, adorned with gold and silver, all over Europe.

artifact.title: Gifts of the Magi
artifact.power: Gold was taken to signify a king, frankincense a god, and myrrh death.
artifact.summary: The gold, frankincense and myrrh that the Magi, following a star from the East, offered to the infant Jesus.
artifact.story:
According to the Gospel of Matthew, when Jesus was born, Magi from the East saw a star and came to Jerusalem asking where the child born king of the Jews was. King Herod asked them to let him know when they found the child. The star went ahead of the Magi and stopped over the place in Bethlehem where the child was.

The Magi bowed down before the child, opened their treasure chests and offered gold, frankincense and myrrh. In the second century, Irenaeus explained that gold befits a king, frankincense a god, and myrrh one who is to die. Warned in a dream not to return to Herod, the Magi went home by another road.

The Gospel does not say how many Magi there were, but because there were three gifts they came to be counted as three, and later they were pictured as kings. A sixth-century mosaic in Ravenna, Italy, names them Caspar, Melchior and Balthasar. Cologne Cathedral in Germany houses a great golden shrine said to contain their relics.
artifact.imageAlt: The Adoration of the Magi, painted by the Sienese artist Giovanni di Paolo about 1440–45. Before a stable the Virgin holds the infant Jesus on her lap, while a kneeling old king, two kings in golden robes and a mounted retinue have come to the child.

source.creditLine: Delia E. Holden and L. E. Holden Funds

annotations.title: King kissing the child's foot
annotations.body: The oldest of the Magi kneels and kisses the foot of the infant Jesus. The Sienese painter Giovanni di Paolo painted this about 1440–45.

annotations.title: King removing his crown
annotations.body: The second king bows and takes off his crown. The Magi offered the child gold, frankincense and myrrh.

annotations.title: Young king
annotations.body: The youngest king, in golden robes, waits his turn. A sixth-century mosaic in Ravenna names the three Magi Caspar, Melchior and Balthasar.

artifact.title: The Golden Calf
artifact.owner: The people of Israel in the wilderness
artifact.power: The idol the people worshiped as the god who had brought them out of Egypt.
artifact.summary: The calf Aaron cast from melted gold earrings while Moses was on the mountain. Moses ground it to powder.
artifact.story:
When Moses had been on Mount Sinai for forty days receiving the law from God and still did not come down, the people crowded around Aaron and asked him to make a god to go before them. Aaron collected the people's gold earrings, melted them and cast the image of a calf.

The people said, "These are your gods, O Israel, who brought you up out of the land of Egypt," offered sacrifices before the calf, and ate, drank and danced. Coming down from the mountain, Moses saw them and in his anger threw down the two stone tablets in his hands and broke them at the foot of the mountain.

Moses burned the golden calf, ground it to powder, scattered it on water and made the people drink it. The bull was an image of divine strength and fertility in ancient Egypt and Canaan. The Book of Kings records that King Jeroboam of northern Israel later set up golden calves at Bethel and Dan.
artifact.imageAlt: Bull Calf Polemount, a Sumerian basalt ornament of about 2700 BCE. A black calf lies with its legs folded and its head raised, with a twisted cord around its neck and body.

source.creditLine: Purchase from the J. H. Wade Fund

annotations.title: Calf's head
annotations.body: The calf's raised head. Sumerians carved it from hard basalt about 2700 BCE.

annotations.title: Twisted cord
annotations.body: A twisted cord is wrapped around the neck and body. It seems to have been an ornament fixed to the top of a pole.

annotations.title: Folded legs
annotations.body: The calf lies with its legs folded. Aaron melted the people's gold earrings and cast an image of a calf.

artifact.title: Trumpets of Jericho
