artifact.power: Blown long on the seventh day after circling the city seven times, they brought down the walls of Jericho with the people's shout.
artifact.summary: The rams' horn trumpets the priests blew as they circled Jericho. On the last day, with a great shout, the walls fell.
artifact.story:
Joshua, who succeeded Moses, led the people of Israel across the Jordan to Jericho, the first city of the land of Canaan. Jericho shut its gates tight and let no one go in or out.

God told Joshua: for six days let the soldiers march around the city once a day, and let seven priests carrying seven rams' horn trumpets walk before the Ark. On the seventh day, march around the city seven times, and when the priests sound a long blast, let the people raise a great shout. They did so, and the walls of Jericho fell down.

A trumpet made from a ram's horn is called a shofar in Hebrew. The shofar is still blown in synagogues on Rosh Hashanah, the Jewish New Year, and at the end of Yom Kippur, the Day of Atonement.
artifact.imageAlt: A Jewish shofar (horn trumpet) of the eighteenth or nineteenth century. A long, slender, pale horn turns upward and widens at one end, where the rim is carved into teeth.

source.creditLine: The Crosby Brown Collection of Musical Instruments, 1889

annotations.title: Upturned bell
annotations.body: The wide end where the sound comes out is turned upward and its rim carved like teeth. This shofar was used by a Jewish community in the eighteenth or nineteenth century.

annotations.title: Mouthpiece
annotations.body: The narrow end where the player blows. On the seventh day, when the priests sounded a long blast on their shofars and the people shouted, the walls of Jericho fell.

annotations.title: Long body
annotations.body: A long body shaped from an animal's horn. The shofar is still blown on the Jewish New Year and the Day of Atonement.

artifact.title: Holy Ampulla
artifact.maker: Unknown (brought from heaven by a dove)
artifact.power: It held the oil with which French kings were anointed at their coronation, and it was said to refill itself after use.
artifact.firstRecord: Hincmar of Reims, Life of Remigius
artifact.summary: The flask of oil a dove is said to have brought from heaven at the baptism of Clovis. French kings were anointed with this oil at their coronations.
artifact.story:
On Christmas Day around 496, Clovis, king of the Franks, was baptized by Bishop Remigius at Reims. According to legend, the crowd was so dense that the cleric carrying the holy oil could not get through, so Remigius prayed, and a white dove came down from heaven carrying a small flask of oil.

After Hincmar, archbishop of Reims in the ninth century, wrote this story into his life of Remigius, the flask was kept in the Abbey of Saint-Remi in Reims. From then on French kings were crowned in Reims Cathedral after being anointed with chrism mixed with a drop of oil from this flask. The oil was said to refill itself after use.

In 1793, during the French Revolution, Ruhl, a member of the National Convention, smashed the flask in a square in Reims. A new flask holding fragments and oil that had been secretly saved was used at the coronation of Charles X in 1825, the last coronation in France.
artifact.imageAlt: Both faces of a pilgrim's ampulla from Palestine, about 600. The flat, round flask is made of a lead and tin alloy, stamped with the Crucifixion on the front and the Ascension on the back, with lettering running around the edges.

source.objectTitle: Pilgrim's Ampulla with Scenes of the Crucifixion (front) and the Ascension (back)
source.objectCulture: Byzantium, Palestine, early Byzantine period, early 7th Century

annotations.title: Crucifixion on the front
annotations.body: The front is stamped with the Crucifixion and encircled by Greek lettering. Pilgrims in the Holy Land carried holy oil home in small flasks like this around 600.

annotations.title: Ascension on the back
annotations.body: The back is stamped with Christ rising to heaven. The flask was cast in an alloy of lead and tin.

annotations.title: Neck
annotations.body: The narrow neck that held the oil. According to legend, on the day Clovis was baptized, a dove came down from heaven carrying a small flask of oil.

artifact.title: Eye of Horus
artifact.maker: Restored by Thoth, god of wisdom
artifact.power: An amulet that heals what is hurt and keeps the body whole.
artifact.summary: The eye of Horus, torn out in his battle with Seth. Restored by Thoth, it became the most common protective amulet in Egypt.
artifact.story:
When Osiris was killed by his brother Seth, his son Horus, the falcon god, fought a long battle with Seth for his father's throne. During the fight Seth tore out Horus's eye and ripped it to pieces.

Thoth, god of wisdom, gathered the scattered pieces and restored the eye. The eye brought back to life in this way was called the wedjat, "the sound one." In the Pyramid Texts, Horus offers his recovered eye to his dead father Osiris to bring him back to life. The moon, which wanes and waxes again, was seen as the eye of Horus being hurt and healed.

The wedjat eye, drawn with a brow and the markings of a falcon's cheek, became the most common amulet in Egypt. The living wore it to ward off sickness and bad luck, and it was placed between the wrappings of mummies to keep the bodies of the dead whole.
artifact.imageAlt: A wedjat eye amulet from Egypt's Third Intermediate Period, about 1080–664 BCE. A white eye with a black pupil is inlaid in a sky-blue faience plaque, with a heavy brow above and the falcon's cheek markings worked in openwork below.

annotations.title: Eye
annotations.body: The eye is made of inlaid white and black stone. It is the wedjat, the eye of Horus torn out by Seth and restored by Thoth.

annotations.title: Brow
annotations.body: A heavy brow with slanting lines runs above the eye. This amulet dates from Egypt's Third Intermediate Period, about 1080–664 BCE.

annotations.title: Openwork
annotations.body: Below, the falcon's cheek markings and small figures are worked in openwork. Amulets like this were placed between the wrappings of mummies to keep the bodies of the dead whole.

artifact.title: Tablet of Destinies
artifact.owner: Enlil, king of the gods, later Marduk
artifact.power: Whoever holds it decides the fates of gods, people and the world, and rules the universe.
artifact.firstRecord: The Epic of Anzu (Old Babylonian version)
artifact.summary: The tablet by which its holder decides the destiny of the universe. The monstrous bird Anzu stole it, and the war god Ninurta took it back.
artifact.story:
The people of Mesopotamia believed that the king of the gods held the Tablet of Destinies and with it decided the fates of gods, people and the world. In the Epic of Anzu the tablet belonged to Enlil, god of heaven and earth.

One day, while Enlil laid down his crown and the tablet to bathe, Anzu, the lion-headed eagle who kept his door, stole the tablet and flew off to the mountains. All the commands of the gods stopped, and arrows shot at Anzu, who held the tablet, turned back at a single word: "Reed, return to your canebrake." With the advice of Ea, god of wisdom, the war god Ninurta cut off Anzu's wings and recovered the tablet.

In the Babylonian creation epic Enuma Elish, Tiamat, goddess of the sea, gave the tablet to her champion Kingu. The young god Marduk defeated them, took the tablet, fastened it on his own breast and so became king of the gods.
artifact.imageAlt: A bronze tablet inscribed in cuneiform from Iran, about 850–750 BCE. A small tab rises from the top center of the dark, rectangular bronze plate, which is covered with incised cuneiform signs.

annotations.title: Upper tab
annotations.body: A small tab rises at the top. This bronze tablet was made in Iran about 850–750 BCE.

annotations.title: Incised cuneiform
annotations.body: Cuneiform signs are incised into the bronze. The Mesopotamians believed that the fate of the world was written on the Tablet of Destinies held by the king of the gods.

annotations.title: Faded lower part
annotations.body: The signs at the bottom are blurred under corrosion. The monstrous bird Anzu stole the tablet and fled to the mountains, but the war god Ninurta took it back.

artifact.title: Gilgamesh's Plant of Rejuvenation
artifact.power: Eaten, it makes an old man young again.
artifact.summary: The plant called "the old man grows young" that Gilgamesh dug up from under the water. While he bathed, a snake carried it off.
artifact.story:
When his friend Enkidu died, Gilgamesh, king of Uruk, terrified of death, set out in search of eternal life. At the end of the world he met Utnapishtim, who had survived the great flood and been granted immortality by the gods, but immortality could not be granted again.

As Gilgamesh was leaving empty-handed, Utnapishtim told him a secret: deep under the water grows a plant like a thornbush, and whoever eats it becomes young again. Gilgamesh tied heavy stones to his feet, sank to the bottom and dug up the plant, though its thorns pricked his hands. He named it "the old man grows young" and said he would take it home and give it to the old men to eat.

On the way back, while Gilgamesh was bathing in a cool spring, a snake smelled the plant, came up and carried it off, shedding its skin as it went. Gilgamesh sat down and wept. They say snakes shed their skins and are born anew because they ate that plant.
artifact.imageAlt: An Assyrian shell inlay plaque of the ninth to eighth century BCE, in the shape of a tree with pointed leaves fanning out at the top and a trunk with chevron markings running downward.

source.objectTitle: Plaque in the form of a tree

annotations.title: Fanned leaves
annotations.body: A tree with pointed leaves spread like a fan is carved in shell. Plaques like this decorated furniture in ninth- to eighth-century BCE Assyria.

annotations.title: Chevron trunk
annotations.body: A trunk carved with chevrons. The Assyrians loved to carve such sacred trees on palace walls and furniture.

annotations.title: Side branch
annotations.body: A short branch at the lower part. The plant Gilgamesh dug up from under the water is said to have been like a thornbush.

artifact.title: Sharur
artifact.power: It speaks, flies off on its own to spy on the enemy, and reports back to its master.
artifact.summary: The talking mace of the god Ninurta. It flew off on its own to spy on enemies and brought back counsel from the king of the gods.
artifact.story:
Ninurta, the Sumerian god of war, carried a mace called Sharur, meaning "smasher of multitudes." Sharur could speak, and it flew off on its own to spy on the enemy and came back to report to its master.

In Lugal-e, Sharur tells Ninurta that Asag, a monster born in the mountains, is ravaging the land with an army of stone warriors. When Ninurta is driven back in the first battle, Sharur flies to Enlil, king of the gods, and returns with his counsel, and Ninurta at last defeats Asag.

After the battle Ninurta piled up stones to make the mountains and gathered the waters flowing down from them into the Tigris to water the fields. He cursed the stones that had sided with Asag and blessed those that had sided with him, giving each kind of stone its use.
artifact.imageAlt: A pink limestone mace head from Predynastic Egypt, about 3650–3100 BCE. A face is carved on the front of the pear-shaped body, with a long nose, two drilled eyes and a thin mouth, and pierced knobs project from both sides.

annotations.title: Face on the front
annotations.body: Two eyes are drilled above a long nose, with a thin mouth incised below. Ninurta's mace Sharur could speak, flew off on its own to spy on the enemy and reported back to its master.

annotations.title: Side knobs
annotations.body: Pierced knobs are carved on both sides of the body. The mace head is small: 4 cm high and 5.6 cm wide.

annotations.title: Pink limestone body
annotations.body: Pink limestone is carved into a pear shape and polished smooth. It dates from Predynastic Egypt, about 3650–3100 BCE, and is among the very early real mace heads.

artifact.title: Seven Ornaments of Inanna
artifact.power: Seven ornaments holding the goddess's powers. With each one she removes, she loses her strength.
artifact.firstRecord: Sumerian myth "Inanna's Descent to the Underworld"
artifact.summary: The ornaments Inanna gave up one by one at each of seven gates on her way down to the underworld. At the last gate she lost all her power.
artifact.story:
Inanna, queen of heaven, decided to descend to the underworld ruled by her sister Ereshkigal. She put on seven divine powers: on her head the shugurra crown, at her neck small lapis lazuli beads, on her breast a double strand of beads, a breastplate, a gold ring on her hand, a lapis lazuli measuring rod and line in her hand, and a royal robe. She told her servant Ninshubur to seek help from the gods if she did not return in three days.

The underworld had seven gates. At each gate the gatekeeper Neti made her take off one ornament, and whenever Inanna asked why, he only answered, "Quiet, Inanna. The ways of the underworld are perfect." Passing the seventh gate, Inanna stood naked before Ereshkigal, and when the judges of the underworld fixed on her the eye of death, she became a corpse hung on a hook.

Hearing Ninshubur's plea, Enki, god of wisdom, fashioned two beings from the dirt under his fingernails and sent them with the food and water of life, and Inanna came back to life. But by the law of the underworld she had to give up someone to take her place, and she gave up her husband Dumuzi, who had not mourned for her.
artifact.imageAlt: A Sumerian headdress of about 2600–2500 BCE. Thin sheets of gold cut into leaf shapes hang in a row from a string of blue lapis lazuli and red carnelian beads.

annotations.title: Gold leaves
annotations.body: Thin sheet gold is cut into leaf shapes and hung on the string. This headdress came from the royal tombs of Ur in Sumer, about 2600–2500 BCE.

annotations.title: Lapis and carnelian
annotations.body: Blue lapis lazuli and red carnelian beads are strung in alternation. Inanna, too, wore lapis lazuli beads at her neck when she went down to the underworld.

annotations.title: Crescent ornament
annotations.body: A small crescent-shaped gold ornament at the end. At each of the seven gates of the underworld, Inanna had to take off one ornament.

artifact.title: The Jinni's Brass Bottle
artifact.titleOriginal: Qumqum of the Fisherman and the Jinni
artifact.maker: King Solomon (who imprisoned and sealed the jinni)
artifact.power: Sealed with Solomon's seal, it keeps the jinni inside from escaping.
artifact.firstRecord: The oldest Arabic manuscript of The Thousand and One Nights
artifact.summary: A brass bottle caught in a fisherman's net. When he opened the lid Solomon had sealed, a huge jinni rose out like smoke.
artifact.story:
A poor fisherman had resolved to cast his net only four times a day. One day his fourth cast brought up a heavy brass bottle. Its mouth was sealed with lead, stamped with the seal of King Solomon.

When the fisherman pried off the lead with his knife, smoke poured out of the bottle and reached the sky, then became a gigantic jinni. It was a jinni who had defied Solomon and been shut in the bottle and thrown into the sea. For the first hundred years, he said, he had sworn to make whoever freed him rich, but when no one came for centuries he changed his oath and swore to kill whoever freed him, and he told the fisherman to choose how he would die.

The fisherman, thinking fast, said he could not believe such a huge body had fitted into this little bottle. The angry jinni turned into smoke and went back into the bottle to show him, and the fisherman quickly shut the lid and sealed it again. In The Thousand and One Nights, this story becomes the first link in a chain of tales that follow.
artifact.imageAlt: An inlaid brass container from northern Iraq, about 1250–1350. A round box with a knobbed lid is inlaid with silver and gold in dense patterns, Arabic lettering and a seated figure, with clasps on both sides to lock the lid.

source.creditLine: Purchase from the J. H. Wade Fund

annotations.title: Knobbed lid
annotations.body: A ring knob tops the lid. The jinni's bottle had a lid sealed with lead and stamped with the seal of Solomon.

annotations.title: Seated figure
annotations.body: In the round panel at the center, a cross-legged figure is inlaid in silver. This box was hammered from sheet brass in northern Iraq about 1250–1350.

annotations.title: Band of lettering
annotations.body: Arabic lettering is inlaid in gold and silver in the band around the body. The jinni's bottle caught in the fisherman's net was also made of brass.

artifact.title: Book of Thoth
artifact.power: Its first spell charms sky, earth and sea and reveals the speech of beasts; its second lets one see the gods even after death.
artifact.summary: A book of magic said to be written by Thoth, god of wisdom, himself. The princes who laid hands on it paid a heavy price.
artifact.story:
Setne Khaemwaset, son of Ramesses II, was a renowned scholar and magician. In search of a book of magic said to have been written by Thoth, god of wisdom, himself, he entered the tomb of the ancient prince Naneferkaptah at Memphis. Inside, the book was glowing, and the spirits of Naneferkaptah and his wife Ahwere stood in his way.

Ahwere told him the story. Naneferkaptah had taken the book from the middle of the river at Coptos, where it lay in nested boxes of iron, copper, wood, ivory and ebony, silver and gold, guarded by snakes and scorpions. Reading its first spell, one could charm the sky, the earth and the sea and understand the speech of birds, fish and beasts; reading the second, one could see the gods of the sun and moon even after death. But through the anger of Thoth, Ahwere and her son drowned in the river, and Naneferkaptah threw himself into the water.

Setne carried off the book after a contest at a board game, but only after suffering terrible things did he return it to the tomb. The story survives in Demotic script on a papyrus of about the third century BCE.
artifact.imageAlt: A wooden scribe's palette from Egypt's New Kingdom, about 1540–1186 BCE. One end of the long wooden plank has two round wells for mixing ink, and a slot for reed pens runs along the middle.

source.creditLine: Gift of the John Huntington Art and Polytechnic Trust

annotations.title: Ink wells
annotations.body: Two round wells for mixing black and red ink. Thoth, god of wisdom, presided over writing and records.

annotations.title: Pen slot
annotations.body: A long slot for keeping reed pens. This palette was used by a scribe in New Kingdom Egypt, about 1540–1186 BCE.

annotations.title: Wooden plank
annotations.body: A long plank of carved wood. The Book of Thoth lay in the middle of a river in nested boxes of iron, copper, wood, ivory and ebony, silver and gold.

artifact.title: Banner of Kaveh
artifact.owner: Kaveh the blacksmith, later the kings of Iran
artifact.power: The banner that rallied the people against a tyrant. Those who fought beneath it were believed to win.
artifact.summary: The leather apron of Kaveh the blacksmith, who rose against the tyrant Zahhak. Adorned with jewels, it became the banner of the Iranian kings.
artifact.story:
In the Shahnameh, two serpents grew from the shoulders of the tyrant Zahhak where a demon had kissed him. The serpents were calmed only by eating the brains of young men every day, and the people lost their sons one after another. Kaveh the blacksmith lost seventeen of his eighteen sons.

When even his last son was to be taken, Kaveh stormed into the palace and tore up the document declaring Zahhak just. He hung the leather apron he wore at his forge on the tip of a spear, held it high and went into the streets, and the people gathered beneath it. They went to Fereydun, a prince living in hiding, and overthrew Zahhak.

Fereydun adorned Kaveh's leather apron with silk and jewels and made it the royal banner. This "Banner of Kaveh" was kept by generations of Iranian kings, each adding more jewels, until, it is said, it was captured by the Arab army in 636 and cut into pieces.
artifact.imageAlt: A brass processional standard ('alam) of the late seventeenth to early eighteenth century. Below a top pointed like a spearhead, leaf-shaped blades spread out, and two dragons on either side curve around a round plaque pierced with lettering.

source.creditLine: Purchase, Friends of Islamic Art Gifts, 2013

annotations.title: Spear-shaped top
annotations.body: A blade pointed like a spearhead rises at the top. This is a standard ('alam) carried high at the head of processions in the Islamic world in the late seventeenth or early eighteenth century.

annotations.title: Dragon heads
annotations.body: Dragons rear their heads on both sides. Kaveh hung the leather apron from his forge on the tip of a spear, held it high and rallied the people.

annotations.title: Pierced lettering
annotations.body: Lettering is pierced through the central round plaque. Adorned with jewels, Kaveh's apron became the banner of the Iranian kings for generations.

artifact.title: Cup of Jamshid
artifact.owner: King Kay Khosrow (Shahnameh); in later poetry, King Jamshid
artifact.power: Look into the cup and everything happening in the seven heavens and the whole world is reflected in it.
artifact.summary: A cup that reflects the whole world. With it King Kay Khosrow found the hero Bizhan imprisoned in a pit.
artifact.story:
The Iranian hero Bizhan fell in love with Manizheh, princess of Turan, and was caught by her father, King Afrasiyab of Turan, and thrown into a deep pit. Its mouth was blocked with a huge boulder. Bizhan's father Giv went to Kay Khosrow, king of Iran, and begged him in tears for help.

When Nowruz, the New Year, came, Kay Khosrow prayed to God and looked into a cup. In it the seven heavens and every land on earth were reflected. In the cup the king found Bizhan imprisoned in the pit in the land of Turan, and he sent the hero Rostam to rescue him.

In the Shahnameh this cup belongs to Kay Khosrow, but later Persian poets called it the cup of Jamshid, the ancient sage-king: the Jam-e Jam. The fourteenth-century poet Hafez sang, "For years my heart sought the cup of Jam from me, begging from strangers what it held itself."
artifact.imageAlt: The Wade Cup, a brass cup inlaid with silver from Seljuq Iran, about 1200–1221. The outside of the footed round bowl is densely inlaid in silver with Arabic letters ending in human heads and with horsemen.

source.creditLine: Purchase from the J. H. Wade Fund
source.objectTitle: The Wade Cup with Animated Script

annotations.title: Letters with heads
annotations.body: In the band below the rim, the ends of the Arabic letters turn into human heads. Such writing is called animated script.

annotations.title: Horsemen
annotations.body: Horsemen and animals are inlaid in silver on the body. This brass cup was made in Iran under the Seljuqs about 1200–21.

annotations.title: Foot
annotations.body: A wide, flaring foot. On New Year's Day, Kay Khosrow looked into his cup and found Bizhan imprisoned in a pit in the land of Turan.

artifact.title: Feather of the Simurgh
artifact.owner: The hero Zal and his son Rostam
artifact.power: Burn it, and wherever you are, the Simurgh will fly to your aid.
artifact.summary: A feather left by the Simurgh, the divine bird that raised the abandoned baby Zal. When it was burned, the Simurgh came.
artifact.story:
A son was born to the Iranian hero Sam, but the baby's hair was white like an old man's. Thinking him the child of a demon, Sam abandoned him on Mount Alborz. The Simurgh, a divine bird that nested on the summit, carried the baby off and raised him with her own young, and he grew into the gallant young Zal.

When the repentant Sam came looking for his son, the Simurgh gave Zal some of her feathers as she let him go. If trouble came, she told him, he should burn a feather and she would fly to help him at once. Later, when Zal's wife Rudabeh was near death in childbirth, Zal burned a feather. The Simurgh came and showed how to deliver the child by cutting open her belly and how to heal the wound, and the child so born was Rostam, the greatest hero of Iran.

When Rostam was gravely wounded fighting the invincible prince Esfandiyar, Zal burned a feather again. The Simurgh healed Rostam's wounds and told him to make an arrow from a tamarisk branch and shoot Esfandiyar in the eyes.
artifact.imageAlt: A page from a Shahnameh made in Iran about 1330–40, "Zal in the Simurgh's Nest." Persian verses fill several columns at the top and right; a small painting at lower left shows the great red-headed Simurgh, the naked child Zal on a rocky mountain and two white animals.

source.objectTitle: "Zal in the Simurgh's Nest", Folio from a Shahnama (Book of Kings)

annotations.title: Simurgh
annotations.body: A great bird with a red head and many-colored wings looks down at the child on the rocky mountain. The Simurgh carried the baby Zal, abandoned because he was born white-haired, to her nest and raised him.

annotations.title: Young Zal
annotations.body: The naked child Zal stands on the mountaintop. The painting is tiny, 5.6 cm wide and 8.1 cm high. It was painted in Iran about 1330–40.

annotations.title: Text of the poem
annotations.body: Ferdowsi's verses are written in several columns. Sending Zal back to his father, the Simurgh gave him her feather, saying she would come if he burned it in time of trouble.

artifact.title: Brahmastra
artifact.power: Charged with a spell and loosed, it raises a fire terrible enough to set the sky ablaze and shake the earth.
artifact.summary: The ultimate weapon, imbued with the power of the creator god Brahma. Once loosed, it was hard to call back.
artifact.story:
The brahmastra is a divine weapon imbued with the power of Brahma, the creator god. When a spell was breathed into an arrow or a blade of grass and it was loosed, a fire arose terrible enough to set the sky ablaze and shake the earth. So a teacher taught the spell only to his finest pupil.

As the great war of the Mahabharata neared its end, Ashwatthama, son of the teacher Drona, loosed a brahmastra at the Pandava brothers. Arjuna answered with the same weapon, and as the two were about to collide, sages fearing that the world would burn stood between them. Arjuna withdrew his weapon, but Ashwatthama did not know how to withdraw his, and turned its power against the unborn child of a Pandava woman. Krishna brought the child back to life, and Ashwatthama was stripped of the jewel in his forehead and cursed to wander for ages.

In the Ramayana, Rama pierced the chest of the demon king Ravana with the brahmastra he had received from the sage Agastya, and so ended the war.
artifact.imageAlt: Rama and Lakshmana Fighting Ravana, painted in the kingdom of Chamba in northern India about 1765. Within a red border, blue-skinned Rama draws his bow, and before him stands Ravana in red, with ten heads and twenty arms holding weapons.

source.objectTitle: Rama and Lakshmana Fighting Ravana, from a Dashavatara (Ten Incarnations [of Vishnu]) series
source.objectCulture: Northern India, Pahari Region, Himachal Pradesh, Rajput Kingdom of Chamba, Court of Raj Singh (reigned 1764–94)

annotations.title: Rama drawing his bow
annotations.body: Blue-skinned Rama aims an enchanted arrow. Rama pierced Ravana's chest with the brahmastra he had received from a sage.

annotations.title: Ten-headed Ravana
annotations.body: Ravana, the demon king with ten heads and twenty arms. Each hand holds a weapon, and a donkey's head sits at the very top.

annotations.title: Lakshmana
annotations.body: Behind him, holding a bow, is Rama's brother Lakshmana. This is a page from a series on the ten avatars of Vishnu painted in the kingdom of Chamba, northern India, about 1765.

artifact.title: Pinaka
artifact.owner: Shiva, god of destruction, later the royal house of Mithila
artifact.power: A huge bow no one could lift. With it Shiva burned the three cities of the demons with a single arrow.
artifact.summary: Shiva's huge bow. Rama broke it while drawing it, and married Sita.
artifact.story:
Pinaka is the bow of Shiva, god of destruction. With it Shiva burned the three cities the demons had built in heaven, in the air and on earth with a single arrow, at the moment the three cities stood in a line, and he was called Destroyer of the Three Cities.

Shiva later entrusted the bow to the royal house of Mithila. According to the Ramayana, it was so heavy that it was carried on an eight-wheeled cart pulled by five thousand strong men. King Janaka of Mithila promised his daughter Sita to whoever could string the bow, but no king could even lift it.

The young prince Rama, who came to Mithila with his teacher, lifted the bow easily, strung it and drew it. At that moment the bow broke in the middle with a sound like thunder, and Rama married Sita. Parashurama, a devotee of Shiva, came in anger when he heard the news, but withdrew when he saw Rama draw even the bow of Vishnu.
artifact.imageAlt: A black-and-white photograph of a composite bow from Italy or Indo-Persia, about 1500. Unstrung, the bow curves deeply like a letter C, and both tips are carved as animal heads.

annotations.title: Animal-head tip
annotations.body: The tip of the bow is carved as an animal's head. This bow was made in Italy or Indo-Persia about 1500.

annotations.title: Grip
annotations.body: The grip where the archer holds the bow. Wood, horn and sinew are glued in layers to give it spring.

annotations.title: Lower tip
annotations.body: The lower tip is also shaped as an animal's head. Shiva's bow had to be pulled on a cart by five thousand men, but Rama lifted it easily and strung it.

artifact.title: Kaumodaki
artifact.maker: Unknown (given to Krishna by Varuna, god of the sea)
artifact.power: When hurled, it smashes demons with a sound like thunder.
artifact.summary: The mace Vishnu holds in one of his four hands. Varuna, god of the sea, gave it to Krishna in the Khandava forest.
artifact.story:
Vishnu is shown holding a conch, a discus, a mace and a lotus in his four hands. The mace is called Kaumodaki. Krishna, an avatar of Vishnu, also carried this mace.

According to the Mahabharata, Agni, god of fire, wanted to consume the Khandava forest, but Indra, who protected it, thwarted him every time with rain. When Krishna and Arjuna agreed to help Agni, Varuna, god of the sea, gave Arjuna the bow Gandiva and Krishna the mace Kaumodaki, and Agni gave Krishna the discus Sudarshana. When hurled, Kaumodaki smashed demons with a sound like thunder.

In Indian sculpture and painting, Kaumodaki sometimes stands beside Vishnu in the form of a woman, Gadadevi, "goddess of the mace."
artifact.imageAlt: An Indo-Persian steel mace (gada) of the seventeenth century. A ball-shaped fluted head sits at the end of a long, straight steel shaft, and the head and shaft are inlaid with gold designs here and there.

annotations.title: Round head
annotations.body: The ball-shaped head is fluted and decorated with gold. This is an Indo-Persian steel mace, or gada, of the seventeenth century.

annotations.title: Gold inlay
annotations.body: Gold scrolls are inlaid where the shaft meets the head.

annotations.title: Long shaft
annotations.body: A long, straight steel shaft. Vishnu's mace Kaumodaki smashed demons with a sound like thunder when hurled.

artifact.title: Panchajanya
artifact.maker: Unknown (the conch in which the demon Panchajana lived under the sea)
artifact.power: When blown, its sound shakes sky and earth and tears the hearts of the enemy.
artifact.summary: The conch Krishna blew to open the battle of Kurukshetra. He won it from a demon under the sea.
artifact.story:
As boys, Krishna and his brother Balarama studied under the teacher Sandipani. When they finished and offered to repay him, the teacher asked for the return of his son, who had drowned in the sea. Krishna went down beneath the waves, defeated the demon Panchajana, who lived in a conch shell, and brought back the conch. Since the boy was in the realm of the dead, Krishna retrieved him from Yama, god of death, and returned him to his teacher.

That conch is Panchajanya, named after the demon. At the opening of the Bhagavad Gita, as the battle of Kurukshetra begins, Krishna blows Panchajanya and Arjuna blows Devadatta. The sound, it is said, echoed through sky and earth and tore the hearts of the enemy.

In Hinduism the conch is still blown to begin rituals. A conch that spirals to the right is especially rare and prized as belonging to Vishnu.
artifact.imageAlt: A ritual conch shell from the Khmer kingdom of Cambodia, twelfth century. The pointed conch is sheathed in carved bronze and stands on a three-legged stand decorated with serpent deities.

source.objectTitle: Conch Shell with a Figure of Hevajra

annotations.title: Conch
annotations.body: A conch blown at the start of rituals, sheathed in carved bronze. It comes from the twelfth-century Khmer kingdom of Cambodia and was probably used at the royal temple of Banteay Chhmar.

annotations.title: Hevajra
annotations.body: The dancing Buddhist deity Hevajra is carved on the lower part.

annotations.title: Serpent stand
annotations.body: A three-legged stand decorated with naga serpent deities. Krishna won the conch Panchajanya after defeating a demon under the sea.

artifact.title: Pushpaka Vimana
artifact.owner: Kubera, god of wealth; the demon king Ravana; Rama
artifact.power: It flies wherever its master wishes, and however many ride it, there is always room for more.
artifact.summary: A heavenly chariot as beautiful as a flower. After defeating Ravana, Rama flew home to Ayodhya in it.
artifact.story:
Pushpaka is a heavenly chariot whose name means "flower." Vishwakarma, craftsman of the gods, built it for Brahma, the creator, and Brahma gave it to Kubera, god of wealth. Kubera's half-brother, the demon king Ravana, drove him out and seized the chariot along with the island of Lanka.

Pushpaka was like a golden palace shining like the sun, adorned with jeweled windows and banners. It flew wherever its master wished, and however many people rode in it, it is said, there was always room.

After Rama defeated Ravana, Ravana's brother Vibhishana gave Pushpaka to Rama. Rama flew to Ayodhya with Sita, Lakshmana, Hanuman and the monkey army, pointing out to Sita, one by one, the battlefields and forests they had passed. Diwali, India's festival of lights, is said to come from the lamps people lit to welcome Rama home that day.
artifact.imageAlt: A Ramayana painting from the Pahari region of northern India, about 1765: Enthroned Rama and Sita Receive Homage from Their Monkey and Bear Allies. Rama and Sita sit on a throne under a pink canopy, with monkeys and a bear at left and courtiers at right.

source.creditLine: Purchase and partial gift from the Catherine and Ralph Benkaim Collection; Severance and Greta Millikin Purchase Fund

artifact.title: Airavata
artifact.maker: Unknown (rose from the churning of the ocean of milk)
artifact.power: With its trunk it draws up the waters of the underworld and sprays them into the clouds, so that Indra can send rain.
artifact.summary: The white elephant Indra rides. It rose from the ocean of milk when the gods and demons churned it.
artifact.story:
To obtain amrita, the nectar of immortality, the gods and demons churned the ocean of milk, using Mount Mandara as the rod and Vasuki, king of serpents, as the rope. Treasures of every kind rose from the ocean, among them Airavata, a white elephant with four tusks. Indra, king of the gods, made the elephant his mount.

Airavata's name is understood to mean "born of the waters." According to legend, Airavata drew up the waters of the underworld with his long trunk and sprayed them into the clouds, and Indra sent rain from those clouds. He is also the elephant who guards the eastern sky.

Airavata was loved beyond India as well. In Thailand and Laos he was pictured as Erawan, a white elephant with three heads, and until 1975 the flag of the Kingdom of Laos bore a three-headed white elephant.
artifact.imageAlt: A sandstone elephant from the Champa kingdom of central Vietnam, about 900–950. The elephant stands with its ears spread wide and its trunk hanging down.

artifact.title: Syamantaka
artifact.power: It produces gold every day, and the land where it is kept knows neither drought nor sickness.
artifact.summary: The jewel the sun god gave to Satrajit. It produced gold every day, but suspicion and strife never ceased around it.
artifact.story:
Satrajit, a devotee of Surya, the sun god, received the jewel Syamantaka from the god. It shone like the sun, so that when he entered Dvaraka wearing it, people thought the sun god himself was coming. The jewel produced gold every day, and the land where it was kept knew neither drought nor sickness.

Satrajit's brother Prasena went hunting wearing the jewel and was killed by a lion; the lion was killed by Jambavan, king of the bears, and the jewel went into Jambavan's cave. People whispered that Krishna, who had coveted the jewel, had killed Prasena. To clear his name Krishna went into the forest, fought Jambavan for twenty-eight days and won back the jewel, and Jambavan, recognizing him as an avatar of Vishnu, gave him his daughter Jambavati in marriage.

Krishna returned the jewel to Satrajit, and the ashamed Satrajit gave his daughter Satyabhama to Krishna. But the strife over the jewel did not end, and Satrajit was killed by men who wanted it. In India there is still a saying that whoever looks at the moon on the night of the Ganesha festival will, like Krishna, be falsely accused.

artifact.title: Akshaya Patra
artifact.power: Every day, food flows from it without end until Draupadi has finished her meal.
artifact.summary: The vessel the sun god gave the Pandava brothers when they were banished to the forest. Food never ran out until Draupadi had eaten.
artifact.story:
Having lost everything at a game of dice, the five Pandava brothers and their wife Draupadi had to live in the forest for twelve years. When they had no way to feed even the Brahmins who followed them, the eldest brother, Yudhishthira, prayed to Surya, the sun god. Surya sent down a copper vessel.

Every day, food came from this vessel without end until Draupadi had finished her meal. So it was called Akshaya Patra, "the inexhaustible vessel." Once Draupadi had eaten, no more came that day.

Some versions tell another story. Duryodhana, who hated the Pandavas, sent the irascible sage Durvasa and his disciples to them after Draupadi had eaten, and Draupadi turned to Krishna for help. Krishna ate a single leaf of greens stuck to the vessel, and the sage and his disciples, bathing in the river, all felt full and went away.
artifact.imageAlt: Draupadi Rescued from Abduction, a Mahabharata painting probably made at Bikaner in northern India about 1615. On a yellow ground two men grapple as if wrestling, with Draupadi behind them and onlookers standing at both sides.

artifact.title: Garuda
artifact.maker: Son of the sage Kashyapa and Vinata
artifact.power: On wings no god could stop, he seized the nectar of immortality from heaven.
artifact.summary: The king of birds, who carries Vishnu. To free his enslaved mother, he brought the nectar of immortality from heaven.
artifact.story:
Garuda's mother Vinata and Kadru, mother of serpents, made a wager on the color of the tail of the divine horse Uchchaihshravas. Kadru won by trickery, having her serpent children cling to the tail to make it look black, and Vinata became Kadru's slave. Garuda, who hatched from his egg blazing like fire, was told that the price of his mother's freedom was amrita, the nectar of immortality, from heaven.

Garuda flew to heaven, defeated the gods, passed an ever-spinning wheel of blades and two serpents breathing fire from their eyes, and seized the amrita. He did not drink a single drop, and Vishnu, seeing this, made him his mount. When Indra hurled his thunderbolt, Garuda let fall a single feather out of respect.

Garuda gave the amrita to the serpents and freed his mother, but while the serpents went to bathe, Indra took the amrita back. Licking the kusha grass where the vessel had stood, the serpents split their tongues in two, it is said. Garuda is the national emblem of Indonesia and Thailand today.
artifact.imageAlt: Vishnu Riding on Garuda, a schist sculpture from Bihar in eastern India, 300s CE. The crowned Vishnu sits astride Garuda, who has a human face and outspread wings, and tail feathers spread like rays behind his head.

artifact.title: Axe of Parashurama
artifact.maker: Given by Shiva, god of destruction
artifact.power: The axe given by Shiva. It cut off all the arms of a king who had a thousand.
artifact.summary: The axe Shiva gave Parashurama. With it he swept away the warrior class twenty-one times.
artifact.story:
Parashurama, "Rama with the axe," is the sixth avatar of Vishnu. Born the son of the sage Jamadagni, he practiced austerities in devotion to Shiva, and Shiva gave him the sharp axe called parashu.

When Kartavirya Arjuna, the thousand-armed king of the Haihayas, carried off a sacred wish-granting cow from Jamadagni's hermitage, Parashurama pursued him with his axe, cut off all his thousand arms and killed him. When the king's sons killed Jamadagni in revenge, Parashurama swept the warrior class, the Kshatriyas, from the earth twenty-one times.

In the Mahabharata, Parashurama also appears as the teacher who trained Bhishma, Drona and Karna in the arts of war. There is a legend, too, that when he threw his axe into the sea, the sea drew back and land appeared, which became Kerala on India's west coast.
artifact.imageAlt: A steel battle axe from Sind, India, about 1800. A blade with a slanting edge sits at the end of a long, thin iron shaft, and the part joining the blade to the shaft is engraved with designs.

source.creditLine: Gift of Mr. and Mrs. J. H. Wade

artifact.title: Yi's Red Bow
artifact.maker: Given by the heavenly emperor Di Jun
artifact.power: A red bow strong enough to shoot suns out of the sky.
artifact.firstRecord: Shan Hai Jing (Classic of Mountains and Seas)
artifact.summary: The red bow the heavenly emperor gave Yi the archer. Yi shot down nine of the ten suns that had risen in the sky at once.
artifact.story:
In the time of Emperor Yao, ten suns rose in the sky at once. The ten suns were the sons of the heavenly emperor Di Jun and Xihe, who were supposed to rise one at a time, day by day. Crops and grass withered and burned, the people had nothing to eat, and all kinds of monsters appeared and preyed on them.

According to the Shan Hai Jing, the heavenly emperor Di Jun gave Yi the archer a red bow and white arrows to relieve the sufferings of the earth. The Huainanzi records that, at Yao's command, Yi shot down nine suns and killed the monsters, saving the people. Each time a sun fell, the three-legged crow that lived inside it fell dead too.

But the heavenly emperor, having lost his sons, would not take Yi back into heaven. Left on earth, Yi obtained the elixir of immortality from the Queen Mother of the West, but it fell into the hands of his wife Chang'e. Mencius records that Yi was finally killed by Feng Meng, his own pupil in archery.
artifact.imageAlt: An eight-lobed bronze mirror from the Tang dynasty, late seventh to early eighth century. Around the central knob, hunters on galloping horses aim their bows at fleeing animals, with flowers and butterflies in relief.

artifact.title: Chang'e's Elixir of Immortality
artifact.owner: Chang'e, wife of Yi the archer
artifact.maker: The Queen Mother of the West
artifact.power: Whoever takes it does not die; the body grows light and floats up to the sky.
artifact.summary: The elixir of immortality Yi obtained from the Queen Mother of the West. His wife Chang'e secretly took it and flew to the moon.
artifact.story:
Yi the archer went to the Queen Mother of the West on Mount Kunlun and obtained a medicine against death. But Yi's wife Chang'e secretly took the elixir and fled to the moon. The Huainanzi, compiled in 139 BCE, records it briefly: "Yi asked the Queen Mother of the West for the elixir of immortality, and Chang'e stole it and fled to the moon."

Zhang Heng of the Eastern Han said that Chang'e entrusted herself to the moon and became a toad, and later stories say she lives alone in the cold palace of the moon, the Guanghan Palace. On the moon live the Jade Rabbit, pounding the elixir of immortality, and Wu Gang, chopping at a cassia tree that grows back whole however often it is cut.

On the Mid-Autumn Festival, the fifteenth day of the eighth lunar month, Chinese people look at the moon and remember Chang'e. Since 2007 China has launched its lunar probes under the name Chang'e.
artifact.imageAlt: A bronze mirror with the Lunar Palace from the Jin dynasty, twelfth to thirteenth century. The back of the round mirror is cast in relief with a hall among clouds, a large tree, a bridge and waves, and standing figures, around a central knob.

source.creditLine: Gift of Drs. Thomas and Martha Carter in Honor of Sherman E. Lee

artifact.title: Purple-Gold Red Gourd
artifact.owner: The Golden Horn and Silver Horn kings (servants of Laozi)
artifact.maker: Laozi, the Supreme Old Lord (a vessel for elixirs)
artifact.power: It sucks in anyone who answers when their name is called, and dissolves them within an hour and three quarters.
artifact.firstRecord: Wu Cheng'en, Journey to the West
artifact.summary: A gourd that sucks in whoever answers when called by name. Even Sun Wukong was trapped when he answered to a false name.
artifact.story:
As the monk Tang Sanzang and his companions passed Flat-Top Mountain, the Golden Horn and Silver Horn kings of Lotus Cave seized Sanzang. The two demon kings had five treasures, and the chief of them was a gourd of reddish gold, the Purple-Gold Red Gourd.

If someone's name was called with the gourd's mouth turned downward and he answered, he was sucked inside in an instant. With a talisman of the Supreme Old Lord stuck on the stopper, whoever was trapped inside would melt into liquid within an hour and three quarters. Sun Wukong answered, thinking he was safe because the name called was a false one, not "Sun Xingzhe" but "Zhe Xingsun," and he was trapped all the same.

Pretending to melt, Wukong slipped out and in turn called the Silver Horn King's name and trapped him in the gourd. The gourd turned out to be a vessel in which Laozi, the Supreme Old Lord, kept his elixirs, and the two demon kings were the boys who tended his furnace. Laozi appeared and took back his treasures and his servants.
artifact.imageAlt: A celadon gourd vase from the Qianlong reign of the Qing dynasty, 1736–95. Above a lobed round body rise a large central double-gourd neck and four smaller gourds, covered in a clear sea-green glaze.

artifact.title: Qiankun Ring
artifact.power: Thrown, it flies to strike the enemy; dipped in the sea, it shakes the Dragon King's palace.
artifact.summary: The golden ring Nezha wore from birth. When he washed in the sea, the Dragon Palace shook, and he ended up fighting the Dragon King's son.
artifact.story:
The wife of Li Jing, a general at Chentang Pass, carried a child for three years and six months and then gave birth to a round ball of flesh. When Li Jing split it with his sword, a boy leaped out with a golden ring on his right arm and a red silk sash around his waist. The immortal Taiyi Zhenren came to be the boy's teacher and named him Nezha. The ring was called the Qiankun Ring, the sash the Huntian Sash.

One summer day when he was seven, Nezha was bathing in the Eastern Sea and rinsed the Huntian Sash in the water. The sea boiled red and the Dragon Palace shook. Nezha killed the yaksha who came out to see what was happening with the Qiankun Ring, and then struck down Ao Bing, the Dragon King's third son, who came after him.

When the furious Dragon King threatened to punish Li Jing's family, Nezha cut away his flesh and bones, returned them to his parents and took his own life. Taiyi Zhenren remade Nezha's body from lotus flowers and lotus roots and brought him back to life, giving him a fire-tipped spear and the Wind Fire Wheels.
artifact.imageAlt: A jade ring of the Eastern Zhou dynasty, third century BCE. One end of a round ring patterned like twisted cord rises as an open-mouthed dragon's head, and the ring crosses over itself like a knot below.

annotations.title: Twisted-cord pattern

annotations.title: Knot
annotations.body: Below, the ring crosses over itself like a knot. Nezha wore the golden Qiankun Ring on his arm from birth.

artifact.title: Three-Pointed Double-Edged Blade
artifact.power: A three-pronged blade. Even after more than three hundred rounds with Sun Wukong, it never gave way.
artifact.firstRecord: Wu Cheng'en, Journey to the West
artifact.summary: The weapon of Erlang Shen, the god with a third eye in his forehead. With it he captured Sun Wukong, who had thrown heaven into turmoil.
artifact.story:
Erlang Shen, Yang Jian, was the nephew of the Jade Emperor and had a third eye in his forehead that saw through everything. He carried the three-pointed double-edged blade and was accompanied by his heavenly hound, Xiaotian.

In Journey to the West, when none of the generals of heaven could capture Sun Wukong, who had thrown the heavenly palace into turmoil, the bodhisattva Guanyin recommended Erlang. Erlang and Wukong fought more than three hundred rounds with the blade and the golden-banded staff, and then a battle of transformations began. When Wukong became a sparrow, Erlang became a hawk; when Wukong became a fish, Erlang became a cormorant. Wukong turned himself into a temple and raised his tail as a flagpole, but Erlang saw through it.

At last the diamond ring hurled by Laozi struck Wukong on the head, the hound Xiaotian bit his leg, and Wukong was captured. From the Song dynasty on, paintings of "Searching the Mountains" showed Erlang leading his divine soldiers to hunt out the demons of the mountains, and Erlang is still worshiped as a god who tames waters and subdues demons.
artifact.imageAlt: A leaf, "Searching the Mountains," from a thirteenth-century Southern Song ink album of Daoist and Buddhist subjects. In fine ink lines, divine soldiers capture mountain demons and beasts, hanging them from spears or leading them on ropes.

artifact.title: Zhang Guolao's Paper Donkey
artifact.owner: Zhang Guolao, one of the Eight Immortals
artifact.power: It travels tens of thousands of li in a day; when resting it folds up like paper into a box, and a spray of water turns it back into a donkey.
artifact.summary: The white donkey the Daoist Zhang Guo rode. When resting, he folded it like paper and put it in a box.
artifact.story:
Zhang Guo was a Daoist who lived in seclusion on Mount Heng in the Tang dynasty and claimed to be several hundred years old. He always rode a white donkey that could travel tens of thousands of li in a day. When he rested, he folded the donkey up layer upon layer like paper and put it in a box, and when he wanted to ride, he sprayed it with a mouthful of water and it became a donkey again.

Emperor Xuanzong of Tang heard of him and summoned him to court. Before the emperor, Zhang Guo drank poisoned wine until his teeth turned black and then grew a new set of white teeth, among other marvels. Xuanzong gave him an official title and the name "Master of Penetrating Mystery," but he returned to the mountains.

Later Zhang Guo became one of the Eight Immortals and was called Zhang Guolao. He is often pictured as an old man riding his donkey backward, holding a fish drum, a musical instrument made of a bamboo tube.

artifact.title: Wooden Ox and Gliding Horse
artifact.owner: Zhuge Liang, chancellor of Shu Han
artifact.power: Without eating or resting, it carries army provisions along steep plank roads.
artifact.firstRecord: Chen Shou, Records of the Three Kingdoms, "Biography of Zhuge Liang"
artifact.summary: The carts Zhuge Liang built to carry provisions over the rugged mountain roads of Shu. In the Romance of the Three Kingdoms they became mechanical oxen that stopped when their tongues were twisted.
artifact.story:
In 231, Zhuge Liang, chancellor of Shu Han, set out north to attack the state of Wei and built "wooden oxen" to carry his army's provisions. In his last northern campaign in 234, he moved provisions with "gliding horses." Chen Shou's Records of the Three Kingdoms notes this briefly, and in the fifth century Pei Songzhi, in his commentary, quoted Zhuge Liang's collected writings to give the size and construction of the wooden ox and gliding horse in detail.

The road north from Shu was a perilous route of plank roads built out from cliff faces. The wooden oxen and gliding horses carried provisions along it without eating or resting. Scholars today guess they were one-wheeled barrows or four-wheeled carts.

In the Romance of the Three Kingdoms they become mechanical oxen and horses. When Sima Yi captured a few and copied them for his own use, Zhuge Liang had his soldiers twist the tongues of the Wei army's oxen and horses. With their tongues twisted, the oxen and horses would not budge, and the Shu army hauled them away, provisions and all.
artifact.imageAlt: A black-and-white photograph of a Tang dynasty earthenware ox cart, seventh to eighth century. A horned ox is harnessed to the shafts, and behind it are a cart compartment with a rounded roof and a large wheel with close-set spokes.

artifact.title: He Shi Bi
artifact.owner: Bian He of Chu, later the states of Zhao and Qin
artifact.maker: Unknown (an uncut jade found by Bian He on Mount Jing)
artifact.power: The finest jade under heaven, for which the king of Qin offered fifteen cities.
artifact.summary: The jade of Bian He, who lost both feet yet held to his uncut stone. Lin Xiangru risked his life to bring it back to Zhao.
artifact.story:
Bian He of Chu found a stone with jade inside on Mount Jing and presented it to King Li. When the jade carver said it was just a stone, the king cut off Bian He's left foot for deceiving his ruler. He presented it again to the next king, King Wu, and when he again heard it was only a stone, his right foot was cut off too.

When King Wen came to the throne, Bian He clasped the stone and wept at the foot of Mount Jing for three days and nights, until his tears ran out and he wept blood. When the king asked why, he answered that he grieved not for his lost feet, but because a precious jade was called a stone and an honest man was called a liar. When King Wen had the stone cut, a jade without equal under heaven emerged, and people called it "Mr. He's jade."

When He Shi Bi later came into the hands of Zhao, King Zhaoxiang of Qin offered fifteen cities for it. Lin Xiangru, sent as envoy, saw that Qin had no intention of giving up the cities, threatened to smash the jade together with his own head against a pillar, and finally sent the jade back to Zhao intact. The Korean word wanbyeok, "perfect," comes from this story. It is also said that the First Emperor of Qin carved the Heirloom Seal of the Realm from this jade.
artifact.imageAlt: A jade bi of the Warring States period, 475–221 BCE. A flat, pale-green jade disk with a round central hole is covered with a close-set grain pattern, crossed diagonally by a brown streak.

annotations.title: Central hole
annotations.body: A flat jade disk with a round hole in the center is called a bi. He Shi Bi was also such a jade bi. This one dates from the Warring States period, 475–221 BCE.

annotations.title: Grain pattern

annotations.title: Brown streak
