artifact.title: Brocade Kasaya
artifact.maker: Unknown (passed to Emperor Taizong of Tang by the bodhisattva Guanyin)
artifact.power: Whoever wears it will not fall into hell, and neither poisonous creatures, wild beasts nor demons can harm him.
artifact.firstRecord: Wu Cheng'en, Journey to the West
artifact.summary: The silk kasaya the bodhisattva Guanyin bestowed on Tang Sanzang. An old abbot who coveted it set fire to his own temple.
artifact.story:
In Journey to the West, the bodhisattva Guanyin came to Chang'an, the Tang capital, disguised as a shabby monk, and offered a silk kasaya and a nine-ringed staff for sale. Whoever wore this kasaya, the bodhisattva said, would not fall into hell, and neither poisonous creatures, wild beasts nor demons could harm him. Emperor Taizong of Tang bought them and gave them to Tang Sanzang, who was setting out for the West to bring back scriptures.

On their way, Sanzang and his companions stayed at a temple called Guanyin Chan Monastery. The old abbot, Elder Jinchi, two hundred and seventy years old, was blinded by greed for the kasaya and plotted to burn Sanzang and his companions to death and take it. Sun Wukong borrowed a fire-proof cover from heaven to protect Sanzang and, in turn, blew on the flames until the temple burned down.

Amid the confusion, a black bear demon from Black Wind Mountain, who had come to watch the fire, stole the kasaya. With the bodhisattva Guanyin's help, Wukong captured the bear demon and recovered the kasaya. The bear demon afterward became the guardian of the bodhisattva's mountain.
artifact.imageAlt: A Buddhist priest's ceremonial robe from the Ming dynasty, fifteenth century. Hundreds of small Buddhas are embroidered in gold and colored thread in compartments across a long red silk panel, with slightly larger Buddhas at the center and corners.

annotations.title: Rows of Buddhas
annotations.body: Small Buddhas are embroidered in compartments on the red silk ground. This is a robe a monk wore for ceremonies in the fifteenth-century Ming dynasty.

annotations.title: Larger Buddha
annotations.body: In the upper center compartment, a slightly larger Buddha is embroidered.

annotations.title: Gold-thread border
annotations.body: Buddhas and flowers embroidered in gold thread run along the border. The bodhisattva Guanyin bestowed a splendid silk kasaya like this on Tang Sanzang.

artifact.title: Hetu and Luoshu
artifact.maker: Unknown (borne out of the waters by a dragon-horse and a tortoise)
artifact.power: From the dot patterns on their backs came the eight trigrams and the nine great laws of government.
artifact.summary: The chart and the writing carried out of the Yellow River by a dragon-horse and out of the Luo River by a tortoise. They became the origin of the eight trigrams and the magic square.
artifact.story:
The "Great Treatise" of the Book of Changes says, "The Yellow River brought forth a chart and the Luo River brought forth a writing, and the sages took them as models." According to legend, in the time of Fuxi a dragon-horse, with a dragon's head and a horse's body, rose from the Yellow River bearing a pattern of dots on its back. From this Hetu, "River Chart," Fuxi drew the eight trigrams.

When Yu the Great was taming the floods, a divine tortoise rose from the Luo River with another dot pattern on its shell. This is the Luoshu, "Luo Writing." From it, it is said, Yu established the nine great laws for governing the realm.

Song dynasty scholars drew the Hetu and Luoshu as diagrams of dots. The Luoshu arranges the numbers one to nine in a three-by-three grid so that every line adds up to fifteen: a magic square. The four trigrams on the Korean flag also come from Fuxi's eight trigrams.
artifact.imageAlt: A jade tortoise of the Ming dynasty, 1368–1644. A small tortoise carved from yellowish-green jade lies with its head raised, with brown markings here and there.

annotations.title: Raised head
annotations.body: The tortoise raises its head. In the time of Yu the Great, a divine tortoise rose from the Luo River bearing a dot pattern on its shell.

annotations.title: Shell
annotations.body: The rounded shell. The Luoshu arranges the numbers one to nine in a three-by-three grid so that every line adds up to fifteen, a magic square.

annotations.title: Brown markings
annotations.body: Brown markings run through the yellowish-green jade. This small tortoise was carved in jade in the Ming dynasty, 1368–1644.

artifact.title: Tamatebako
artifact.power: As long as it stays closed it preserves youth, but opened, all the years that have passed fall upon you at once.
artifact.summary: The box Otohime gave Urashima Taro as he left the Dragon Palace. When he opened the box he had been told not to open, he became a white-haired old man.
artifact.story:
The fisherman Urashima rescued a turtle that children were tormenting on the beach. In gratitude the turtle carried him on its back to the Dragon Palace under the sea, where Otohime entertained him lavishly. After three dreamlike years, Urashima began to long for his parents at home.

As he left, Otohime gave him a lacquered box, the tamatebako, and told him never to open it. When he got home the village was strange and he knew no one: three years in the Dragon Palace had been three hundred years on land. In despair Urashima opened the box, white smoke rose from it, and he instantly became a white-haired old man.

In the oldest version, recorded in the early-eighth-century Tango no Kuni Fudoki, Urashima follows a maiden who had appeared as a five-colored turtle to the land of the immortals across the sea. When he opens the box, her fragrant form flies away on the clouds, and he can never return.
artifact.imageAlt: A lacquered cosmetics box (tebako) of the Kamakura period, early fourteenth century. The round-cornered black box and its lid are decorated with golden chrysanthemums, and metal rings for a cord are fitted on the side.

annotations.title: Chrysanthemums
annotations.body: Chrysanthemums are drawn by sprinkling gold powder on black lacquer (maki-e). This cosmetics box dates from the Kamakura period, early fourteenth century.

annotations.title: Metal ring
annotations.body: A cord threaded through the metal rings on the side tied the lid shut.

annotations.title: Lid
annotations.body: The lid that covers the box. Otohime told Urashima never to open the box she gave him. When he opened it, he instantly became a white-haired old man.

artifact.title: Hagoromo
artifact.power: Wearing it, one can fly up and return to heaven.
artifact.summary: A heavenly maiden's feather robe left by the water. The maiden, held captive by the one who hid it, flew back to heaven when she got it back.
artifact.story:
According to the Tango no Kuni Fudoki, long ago eight heavenly maidens came down to bathe in the Manai spring on the summit of Mount Hiji. An old couple secretly hid one maiden's feather robe, and without it she could not return to heaven and became their daughter. The sake she brewed cured any illness and the old couple grew rich, but after ten years or so they drove her out.

The most famous version is the Noh play Hagoromo. The fisherman Hakuryo finds a beautiful robe hanging on a pine in the pine grove of Miho. When a heavenly maiden appears and weeps that without it she cannot return to heaven, he says he will give it back if she shows him a heavenly dance. When he suspects she will fly away without dancing if he returns it first, she answers, "Doubt belongs to the human world; in heaven there is no deceit."

Ashamed, the fisherman returns the robe, and the maiden puts it on, dances and vanishes into the sky beyond Mount Fuji. Stories of capturing a heavenly maiden by hiding her feather robe are told all over the world, including the Korean tale "The Fairy and the Woodcutter."
artifact.imageAlt: A Noh costume, a choken, from the Edo period, about 1800–1850. The loosely woven reddish silk robe is spread out on a pole, woven in gold and colored threads with hanging wisteria and fans.

annotations.title: Wisteria
annotations.body: Hanging wisteria is woven in gold and colored threads. This Noh costume dates from the Edo period, about 1800–1850.

annotations.title: Fans
annotations.body: Open fans are set among the flowers in gold.

annotations.title: Wide sleeves
annotations.body: Wide sleeves hang from the shoulders. In the Noh play Hagoromo, the heavenly maiden dances wearing a sheer outer robe like this choken as her feather robe.

artifact.title: Tide Jewels
artifact.power: One makes the tide rise; the other makes it ebb.
artifact.summary: The two jewels the sea god gave Hoori. With the flood-tide jewel and the ebb-tide jewel he subdued his brother.
artifact.story:
Hoderi, the elder brother, who fished the sea, and Hoori, the younger, who hunted in the mountains, exchanged their tools for a day. Hoori lost his brother's fishhook in the sea, and though he broke his own sword to make a thousand hooks for him, his brother refused them, demanding the original.

As Hoori wept on the shore, the god of sea paths helped him reach the palace of Watatsumi, god of the sea, where he married the god's daughter Toyotama-hime. Three years later, hearing his story, the sea god found the fishhook caught in the throat of a sea bream and gave him, along with it, the shiomitsu-tama, which makes the tide rise, and the shiofuru-tama, which makes it ebb.

When Hoori returned to land and his brother attacked him, he raised the waters with the flood-tide jewel and drowned his brother, and when his brother begged for his life, he drew the waters back with the ebb-tide jewel. His brother swore to serve him. The Kojiki records that Hoori's grandson was Jimmu, the first emperor.
artifact.imageAlt: Tide-Changing Jewel with Dragon, a decorative object of the Meiji period, early 1900s. A large crystal ball rests on a stand of rough waves wrought in silver and shakudo, a dragon twists among the waves, and another small crystal ball sits beside it.

annotations.title: Large crystal ball
annotations.body: A large crystal ball rests on the waves. This ornament, Tide-Changing Jewel with Dragon, was made in the Meiji period, early 1900s.

annotations.title: Small ball
annotations.body: Beside it is another small ball. The sea god gave Hoori two jewels, one for the flood tide and one for the ebb.

annotations.title: Waves and dragon
annotations.body: Rough waves and a dragon within them are wrought in silver and shakudo. Hoori drowned his brother with the flood-tide jewel and drew back the water with the ebb-tide jewel.

artifact.title: The Buddha's Stone Begging Bowl
artifact.power: The true bowl the Buddha used was said to give off a soft light.
artifact.firstRecord: The Tale of the Bamboo Cutter
artifact.summary: The first impossible task Princess Kaguya set her suitors. Prince Ishitsukuri brought an old bowl from a country temple and was found out.
artifact.story:
An old bamboo cutter found a girl no bigger than a finger inside a shining stalk of bamboo. In three months she grew into a beautiful young woman and was called Kaguya-hime, "the shining princess," and five nobles wooed her persistently. The princess told each of them she would marry him if he brought her a treasure not to be found in this world.

The task she set Prince Ishitsukuri was the Buddha's stone begging bowl, said to be in Tenjiku, that is, India. A legend says that when the Buddha attained enlightenment, the four heavenly kings each offered him a stone bowl, and the Buddha stacked the four into one. The true bowl was said to give off a soft light.

Not daring to go all the way to India, the prince waited about three years and then presented a soot-blackened old bowl from a mountain temple in Yamato, wrapped in a brocade bag. Seeing that it gave off no light at all, the princess sent it back, and the prince threw the bowl away at her gate and went on pleading. The Tale of the Bamboo Cutter jokes that a Japanese expression for shamelessness comes from this.
artifact.imageAlt: A gilt-bronze begging bowl from Heian-period Japan, around the tenth century. The outside of the round bowl, whose mouth curves slightly inward, is engraved with fine flowers and vines, and the gilding is worn in places.

source.creditLine: Purchase from the J. H. Wade Fund

annotations.title: Inward-curving rim
annotations.body: A round begging bowl whose mouth curves slightly inward. It was made of gilt bronze in the Heian period, around the tenth century.

annotations.title: Engraved scrolls
annotations.body: Flowers and vines are engraved in fine lines all over the outside. The gilding is worn in places, showing the bronze.

annotations.title: Rounded lower body
annotations.body: The rounded lower part. Prince Ishitsukuri passed off a soot-blackened bowl from a mountain temple as the Buddha's stone bowl, but it gave off no light and he was found out.

artifact.title: Jeweled Branch of Mount Horai
artifact.maker: Unknown (the prince had six craftsmen make a fake)
artifact.power: A branch of the tree on the immortals' island in the eastern sea, with silver roots, a golden trunk and fruit of white jewels.
artifact.firstRecord: The Tale of the Bamboo Cutter
artifact.summary: Princess Kaguya's impossible task. Prince Kuramochi had craftsmen make a fake and was exposed by the craftsmen who came to collect their wages.
artifact.story:
Princess Kaguya asked Prince Kuramochi to bring her a branch of a tree said to grow on Mount Horai, the island of the immortals in the eastern sea. It was a tree with silver roots, a golden trunk and fruit of white jewels.

The crafty prince pretended to set sail and then went into hiding, gathered six skilled craftsmen and had them spend more than a thousand days making a branch that looked real. He presented it with a false tale of overcoming monsters and starvation at sea to reach Mount Horai, and the princess was left with no choice but to marry him.

Just then the craftsmen arrived, complaining that they had not yet been paid for their thousand days of work. With the lie exposed, the princess joyfully sent the branch back, and the prince vanished into the mountains in shame. Mount Horai is an island from Chinese tales of immortals, where the First Emperor of Qin is said to have sent Xu Fu to search for the elixir of immortality.
artifact.imageAlt: A long, narrow portable writing box from Edo-period Japan, nineteenth century. On gold lacquer sprinkled with gold flakes, Mount Horai, the island of the immortals, is raised in relief: a rocky peak soars in the middle, with round-leaved trees, tiled pavilions and rippling water.

source.creditLine: Gift of Mr. and Mrs. Gilbert P. Schafer

annotations.title: Peaks of Mount Horai
annotations.body: The rocky peaks are raised in gold and silver lacquer so they soar upward. Mount Horai is the island of the immortals said to lie in the eastern sea.

annotations.title: Jewel-like trees
annotations.body: Clusters of round leaves bulge like jewels. Prince Kuramochi had craftsmen make a fake of the branch from Mount Horai, with silver roots, a golden trunk and fruit of white jewels.

annotations.title: Pavilions by the water
annotations.body: Tiled pavilions stand by the water. Inside, clouds, birds and water plants are painted, with a space for a tiny inkstone. The box was made in nineteenth-century Edo-period Japan.

artifact.title: Robe of Fire-Rat Fur
artifact.owner: Abe no Miushi, Minister of the Right
artifact.maker: Unknown (obtained through the Tang merchant Wang Qing)
artifact.power: Put into fire, it does not burn; rather, the dirt burns away and it comes out clean, it was said.
artifact.firstRecord: The Tale of the Bamboo Cutter
artifact.summary: A legendary fur robe said to come out of the fire cleaner than before. When Princess Kaguya put it in the fire to test it, it burned up.
artifact.story:
Princess Kaguya asked Abe no Miushi, Minister of the Right, to bring her a robe of fire-rat fur said to be found in Tang China. Old Chinese books told of cloth woven from the fur of rats that live in the mountains of fire in the south, which, when soiled, could be put in the fire and washed as if burned, coming out as good as new.

Abe, a very rich man, sent a great deal of gold to the Tang merchant Wang Qing and asked him to find the robe. Some time later Wang Qing sent a robe he said an Indian monk had brought, and asked for more gold. It was a beautiful robe whose dark-blue fur shone gold at the tips.

When Abe presented the robe, the princess said they should test whether it was genuine by putting it in the fire. The robe burned up in flames, and Abe went home with a face as green as a leaf. The cloth that people of old said could be washed in fire was probably cloth woven from asbestos, a mineral fiber.
artifact.imageAlt: A page from a hand-painted picture book of The Tale of the Bamboo Cutter made in Japan in the late seventeenth century. Between golden clouds a thatched house appears; on its veranda an old couple looks at a tiny child in a basket, and children play in the yard.

source.objectTitle: The Tale of the Bamboo Cutter

annotations.title: Child in the basket
annotations.body: The tiny child in the basket is Princess Kaguya, found inside a stalk of bamboo. In three months she grew into a beautiful young woman.

annotations.title: Old couple
annotations.body: The old bamboo cutter and his wife look at the child. This hand-painted picture book of The Tale of the Bamboo Cutter was made in Japan in the late seventeenth century.

annotations.title: Golden clouds
annotations.body: Clouds of gold leaf frame the scene above and below. The princess asked Minister Abe to bring her a robe of fire-rat fur that would not burn in fire.

artifact.title: Princess Kaguya's Elixir of Immortality
artifact.power: Whoever takes it does not die. The emperor had it burned on the mountain nearest to heaven.
artifact.firstRecord: The Tale of the Bamboo Cutter
artifact.summary: The elixir of immortality Princess Kaguya left when she returned to the moon. Refusing eternal life without her, the emperor had it burned on a mountaintop: Mount Fuji.
artifact.story:
Princess Kaguya was in truth a person of the moon. As the full moon of the eighth month drew near, she wept as she gazed at the moon and confessed that on that night the people of the moon would come for her. The emperor sent two thousand soldiers to guard the old man's house, but before the people of the moon, who came down from the sky riding on clouds, the soldiers could not even draw their bows.

Before she left, the princess wrote a letter to the emperor and left him, with it, a jar of the elixir of immortality the people of the moon had brought. When she put on the heavenly feather robe, she forgot all her earthly sorrows and rose into the sky.

Reading her letter, the emperor asked what use a medicine against death was if he could never see her again, and had the letter and the elixir burned on the summit of the mountain in Suruga nearest to heaven. Because a great many soldiers climbed it, the mountain came to be called Fuji, "rich in soldiers," and the smoke, they say, still rises into the clouds.
artifact.imageAlt: A lacquered medicine case (inro) of the Edo period, about 1785. A rooster is painted on the outside of the small case of stacked compartments, with a cord and a round cord bead above and tassels hanging below.

annotations.title: Rooster
annotations.body: A rooster is painted in gold lacquer on the outside of the stacked compartments of the medicine case (inro). It dates from the Edo period, about 1785.

annotations.title: Cord bead
annotations.body: The bead (ojime) that tightens the cord. An inro was a small case for carrying medicine, hung from the sash.

annotations.title: Cord
annotations.body: The cord from which the inro hangs. As she returned to the moon, Princess Kaguya left the emperor a jar of the elixir of immortality.

artifact.title: Higekiri
artifact.owner: The Minamoto clan; the warrior Watanabe no Tsuna
artifact.maker: Unknown (one of two swords made for Minamoto no Mitsunaka)
artifact.power: Tested on a criminal, it cut cleanly through his beard and was named Beard-Cutter; after it cut off a demon's arm, it became Demon-Cutter.
artifact.firstRecord: The Tale of the Heike, "Book of Swords"
artifact.summary: The treasured sword of the Minamoto clan with which Watanabe no Tsuna cut off an oni's arm. From then on it was called Demon-Cutter.
artifact.story:
The Heian warrior Minamoto no Yorimitsu had four retainers called the Four Heavenly Kings. One night, as the foremost of them, Watanabe no Tsuna, crossed the Ichijo Modoribashi bridge in Kyoto, a beautiful woman asked him to escort her. When Tsuna put her on his horse, she turned into a terrible oni, seized his topknot and flew off toward Mount Atago.

Tsuna drew Higekiri, the treasured sword of the Minamoto at his waist, and cut off the oni's arm. The sword had been called Beard-Cutter because, when tested on a criminal, it cut cleanly even through his beard; after this it was called Demon-Cutter.

Tsuna kept the severed arm in a box and, on the advice of the yin-yang master Abe no Seimei, shut himself in for seven days. On the sixth night his foster mother came to visit and Tsuna let her in; asking to see the arm, she turned into the oni, snatched it and flew out through the smoke hole in the roof.
artifact.imageAlt: Nakamura Nakazo I as Watanabe no Tsuna, a color woodblock print by Katsukawa Shunzan, 1781. A kabuki actor in a red outer robe stands glaring, with the hilt of a long sword rising behind his shoulder.

source.objectTitle: Nakamura Nakazo I as Watanabe no Tsuna

annotations.title: Actor's face
annotations.body: The glaring kabuki actor Nakamura Nakazo I plays Watanabe no Tsuna. This is one sheet of a triptych printed by Katsukawa Shunzan in 1781.

annotations.title: Sword hilt
annotations.body: The hilt of a long sword rises behind his shoulder. Tsuna cut off the oni's arm with Higekiri, the treasured sword of the Minamoto.

annotations.title: Red robe
annotations.body: A large crest is printed on the red outer robe. The oni who lost its arm came disguised as Tsuna's foster mother and took the arm back.

artifact.title: Ikutachi and Ikuyumiya
artifact.maker: Unknown (possessions of Susanoo, god of the underworld)
artifact.power: The great sword and bow of life. With them Okuninushi drove out his brother gods and founded a country.
artifact.summary: The sword and bow of life that Okuninushi stole from Susanoo, god of the underworld, as he fled. With them he founded a country.
artifact.story:
Okuninushi was first called Onamuji. His eighty jealous brother gods killed him twice, and, brought back to life at his mother's pleading, he fled from them to Susanoo in the underworld, Ne-no-kuni. There he and Susanoo's daughter Suseri-hime fell in love at first sight.

Susanoo made him sleep in a room swarming with snakes and in another full of centipedes and wasps, sent him to fetch an arrow shot into a field and then set the field on fire. Saved by a scarf Suseri-hime gave him and by a mouse, Onamuji, while Susanoo slept, tied the god's hair to the rafters, blocked the door with a great rock, took the great sword of life, Ikutachi, the bow and arrows of life, Ikuyumiya, and the heavenly koto, and fled with Suseri-hime.

The koto brushed against a tree and sounded, waking Susanoo, but at the edge of the underworld slope he shouted after them: "With that sword and bow, drive out your brothers and become Okuninushi." Onamuji did as he said, defeated his brother gods and founded a country.
artifact.imageAlt: A gilt-bronze sword pommel from Kofun-period Japan, sixth century. A phoenix head with a raised crest sits within a round ring, and below it extends the tang that fitted into the grip.

source.creditLine: Purchase from the J. H. Wade Fund
source.objectTitle: Sword-hilt with Phoenix Head Ring Pommel

annotations.title: Phoenix head

annotations.title: Ring
annotations.body: A gilt-bronze ring. Ring-pommel great swords like this came to Japan from the Korean peninsula and were carried by kings and chieftains.

annotations.title: Tang
annotations.body: The tang that fitted into the grip. Okuninushi fled from Susanoo, god of the underworld, carrying Ikutachi, the great sword of life.

artifact.title: Bell of Mii-dera
artifact.maker: Unknown (given to Fujiwara no Hidesato by the dragon god of Lake Biwa)
artifact.power: A temple bell from the Dragon Palace. When the strongman Benkei dragged it away, it cried, they say, "I want to go back."
artifact.summary: The bell Tawara Toda is said to have brought back from the dragon god after defeating a giant centipede. It hangs at Mii-dera.
artifact.story:
According to the Taiheiki, as the warrior Fujiwara no Hidesato was about to cross the Seta bridge over Lake Biwa, a huge serpent lay across it. Hidesato calmly stepped over it, and that night a visitor came to him, saying he was the dragon god of the lake and was being tormented by the giant centipede of Mount Mikami, and begged for his help.

Hidesato shot arrows at the great centipede coiled around the mountain. His first arrows bounced off, but the last one pierced the centipede's head. In gratitude the dragon god took him to the Dragon Palace and gave him all kinds of treasures, among them a great temple bell. Hidesato offered the bell to Mii-dera. People called him Tawara Toda.

Later a story arose that the strongman Benkei dragged the bell to Mount Hiei, and when he struck it, it cried, "I want to go back, I want to go back," so he threw it into a ravine in anger. The evening bell of Mii-dera is counted among the Eight Views of Omi, the eight scenic sights of Lake Biwa.
artifact.imageAlt: Evening Bell at Mii Temple, from the Eight Views of Omi, a color woodblock print by Utagawa Hiroshige, late 1830s. The roofs of Mii-dera show among the trees of a green mountain on Lake Biwa, with sailboats and far mountains, and the title and a poem at the top.

source.objectTitle: Evening Bell at Mii Temple, from the series Eight Views of Omi Province

annotations.title: Title
annotations.body: The title reads "Evening Bell at Mii." This is a sheet from the Eight Views of Omi printed by Utagawa Hiroshige in the late 1830s.

annotations.title: Temple in the mountains
annotations.body: The roofs of Mii-dera appear among the trees on the green mountainside. The temple keeps a bell said to have been brought back from the Dragon Palace by Tawara Toda.

annotations.title: Lake Biwa
annotations.body: Lake Biwa with sailboats. Fujiwara no Hidesato shot down the giant centipede that had been tormenting the dragon god of the lake.

artifact.title: Dokkaebi Club
artifact.power: Strike it, saying "Out with gold!", and whatever one wishes comes pouring out.
artifact.firstRecord: Duan Chengshi, Youyang Zazu, "Tale of Bangi"
artifact.summary: The goblins' club that pours out whatever one wishes when struck. It was first recorded in a ninth-century Tang book as the tale of Bangi, a man of Silla.
artifact.story:
"Out with gold, knock! Out with silver, knock!" The dokkaebi club is a treasure that pours out whatever one wishes when it is struck. A widely told tale says that when a kind woodcutter cracked a hazelnut, the startled goblins ran away and left their club behind, while a greedy neighbor who tried to copy him got a sound thrashing.

The oldest record of the tale is the story of Bangi, a man of Silla, in the Youyang Zazu, written by Duan Chengshi of Tang in the ninth century. Poor Bangi saw children in red clothes in the mountains striking a golden awl to bring out food and wine. When the children left the awl behind, Bangi took it home and became very rich.

His greedy younger brother imitated him and went into the mountains, but the children caught him. Calling him the thief who had stolen their awl, they stretched his nose out long like an elephant's trunk. The story of Bangi lives on in old tales of a kind man and a greedy one, such as "The Old Man with a Lump."
artifact.imageAlt: A jade ogre mask (taotie) ornament from the Warring States period of China, 475–221 BCE. On a pale-green jade plaque, scrolling lines in relief form the face of a horned monster.

source.objectCulture: China, Eastern Zhou dynasty (770–256 BCE), Warring States period (475–221 BCE)

annotations.title: Curled horns
annotations.body: Horns curling like whorls are carved at both upper sides. This jade ornament comes from the Warring States period of China, 475–221 BCE.

annotations.title: Scrolling face
annotations.body: The scrolling lines in the middle form the eyes and nose of a beast's face. Such a beast face is called a taotie.

annotations.title: Divided lower edge
annotations.body: The lower edge divides like a beast's legs. The patterns of the demon-face roof tiles that Koreans call "dokkaebi faces" are linked to beast faces like this.

artifact.title: Jumong's Bow
artifact.maker: Jumong (made it himself at the age of seven)
artifact.power: Every arrow hit its mark, so that "jumong," meaning a fine archer, became his name.
artifact.summary: The bow of Goguryeo's founder, who shot so well that his very name became "Jumong." Fish and turtles made a bridge for him to cross.
artifact.story:
Sunlight shone on Yuhwa, daughter of the water god Habaek, who was confined in the palace of Buyeo, and she laid a great egg. When the king threw the egg to dogs and pigs they would not eat it; when he cast it on the road, oxen and horses stepped around it; when he left it in a field, birds covered it with their wings. The boy who hatched from the egg made his own bow and arrows at the age of seven, and every arrow hit its mark.

In the language of Buyeo a fine archer was called "jumong," and so the boy was named Jumong. The Chinese history Book of Wei, completed in 554, records this story as the founding legend of Goguryeo. The princes of Buyeo, jealous of Jumong's skill, plotted to kill him.

Fleeing south, Jumong came to a river with no bridge and cried, "I am the son of the sun and the grandson of Habaek," and fish and turtles rose up to form a bridge. When he had crossed, the bridge scattered, and his pursuers could not cross. Jumong came to Jolbon and founded Goguryeo.
artifact.imageAlt: A leather bow case, quiver and belt from Tibet or Mongolia, fifteenth to seventeenth century. A bow case and quiver of dark brown leather are fitted with round ornaments decorated in gold, joined by a belt.

source.objectTitle: Bow Case, Quiver, and Belt (gzhu shubs dang mda' shubs)

annotations.title: Bow case
annotations.body: A leather case for carrying a bow at the waist, used by mounted archers of Tibet or Mongolia in the fifteenth to seventeenth century.

annotations.title: Quiver
annotations.body: The quiver for arrows carries round ornaments decorated with gold. This was the gear of northern peoples who shot from horseback.

annotations.title: Belt
annotations.body: The belt from which the bow case and quiver hang. In the language of Buyeo, a fine archer was called "jumong."

artifact.title: King Suro's Golden Box
artifact.owner: The nine chiefs of Garak; King Suro
artifact.power: A box let down from heaven on a purple cord. From the six golden eggs inside were born the kings of the six Gaya states.
artifact.summary: The golden box that came down from heaven onto Gujibong Peak. From a golden egg inside it was born King Suro of Garak.
artifact.story:
In the third month of the year 42, the nine chiefs of the land of Garak and several hundred people gathered on Gujibong Peak. A voice from heaven said, "I am coming down to found a kingdom here; dig the earth on the peak, sing and dance." The people danced, singing the "Gujiga": "Turtle, turtle, put out your head; if you do not, we will roast and eat you."

Then a purple cord came down from the sky and touched the ground, and at its end hung a golden box wrapped in red cloth. When they opened it, there were six golden eggs, round as the sun. The next morning all the eggs had hatched into boys, and the first to emerge became Suro, king of Garak. The other five, it is said, became kings of the five Gaya states.

This story is Iryeon's abridgment, in the Samguk Yusa, of the "Record of Garak" written by a local official of Geumgwan in the reign of King Munjong of Goryeo. King Suro later took as his queen Heo Hwang-ok, a princess from the land of Ayuta, who came across the sea in a ship with red sails.

artifact.title: Seo-nyeo's Silk
artifact.titleOriginal: 細綃 (延烏郞 細烏女)
artifact.power: When a sacrifice was offered to heaven with this silk, the lost light of Silla's sun and moon returned.
artifact.summary: The silk woven by Seo-nyeo, who crossed the sea to Japan. When a sacrifice was offered with it, Silla's sun and moon regained their light.
artifact.story:
In the fourth year of King Adalla of Silla (157), Yeono-rang, who lived on the shore of the East Sea, was gathering seaweed on a rock when the rock carried him across to Japan. The people there thought him an extraordinary man and made him their king. His wife Seo-nyeo, searching for him, saw his shoes on the rock and stepped onto it, and the same rock carried her to Japan, where she became queen.

Then in Silla the sun and moon lost their light. The official who watched the sun and moon reported that their essence had gone away to Japan. When the king sent envoys to bring the couple back, Yeono-rang said it was the will of heaven and he could not return, but he gave them fine silk woven by Seo-nyeo, saying that a sacrifice offered to heaven with it would suffice.

When the sacrifice was offered with the silk the envoys brought, the sun and moon shone again. The king kept the silk in the royal storehouse as a national treasure, named the storehouse Gwibigo, and called the place of the sacrifice Yeongil-hyeon, "the county that welcomes the sun." It is today's Yeongil Bay in Pohang, North Gyeongsang Province.
artifact.imageAlt: A Joseon bridal robe (hwarot) of the late nineteenth century. The red silk robe with outspread sleeves is lavishly embroidered with lotuses, peonies, birds and butterflies, with multicolored stripes on the sleeves and white cuffs at the ends.

annotations.title: Floral embroidery
annotations.body: Lotuses, peonies and butterflies are lavishly embroidered on red silk. This is a hwarot, a Joseon bridal robe of the late nineteenth century.

annotations.title: Striped sleeves
annotations.body: The sleeves are pieced from silks of many colors in stripes (saekdong).

annotations.title: Waves and rocks
annotations.body: Waves and rocks are embroidered near the hem. When a sacrifice was offered to heaven with the fine silk Seo-nyeo had woven, Silla's sun and moon shone again.

artifact.title: Princess Bari's Water of Life
artifact.maker: Unknown (the healing spring of the far western realm at the end of the underworld)
artifact.power: A healing water from the underworld that brings back the breath of the dead when poured into their mouths.
artifact.summary: The healing water fetched from the end of the underworld by Baridegi, the abandoned seventh princess. It brought her dead parents back to life.
artifact.story:
Long ago King Ogu had six daughters, and when the seventh was also a girl, he angrily put the baby in a jade box and cast it into the river. Because she was thrown away she was called Baridegi, Princess Bari. Saved by a turtle and an immortal, the child grew up in the care of an old couple by the sea.

Years later the king and queen fell mortally ill. A diviner said only the healing water of the far western realm could save them, but the six pampered daughters all made excuses and refused. Only Princess Bari set out for the parents who had abandoned her. Crossing rugged mountains and the hells, she met Mujangseung, who guarded the healing water at the end of the underworld, and only after years of drawing water, gathering firewood and tending the fire as he bade, marrying him and bearing seven sons, did she obtain the water.

Returning with the water and the flowers that revive bones and flesh, Princess Bari met her parents' funeral bier. When she restored their bones and flesh with the flowers and poured the water into their mouths, the king and queen breathed again. Princess Bari became the goddess who guides the souls of the dead to the other world, and her story is still sung at shamanic rituals for the dead.
artifact.imageAlt: A Goryeo celadon bottle of the twelfth to thirteenth century. A slender, long neck rises from the round body, which is incised with a floral design in fine lines.

source.objectTitle: Long-necked Bottle with Incised Floral Design

annotations.title: Long neck
annotations.body: A slender, long neck. One side of the lip is pressed in to make pouring easy. This celadon bottle was made in Goryeo in the twelfth to thirteenth century.

annotations.title: Incised flowers
annotations.body: A floral design is incised in fine lines on the body and covered with a bluish-green glaze.

annotations.title: Round body
annotations.body: The round body that holds the water. Princess Bari revived her dead parents by pouring the healing water she had fetched from the end of the underworld into their mouths.

artifact.title: Heungbu's Gourds
artifact.power: Sawn open, they pour out rice, money and silk. Gourds won through greed pour out misfortune.
artifact.summary: Gourds grown from a seed brought by the swallow whose leg was mended. From Heungbu's gourds came treasure; from Nolbu's, misfortune.
artifact.story:
Nolbu, the greedy elder brother, took everything their parents had left and drove his kind younger brother Heungbu out of the house. Heungbu and his children lived in a hut, barely able to get a meal. One spring Heungbu found a baby swallow whose leg had broken when it fell fleeing a snake; he bound the leg with care and let it fly away.

The next spring, when he planted the gourd seed the swallow brought him, gourds big enough to cover the roof grew. As he sawed them open, singing "Saw, saw, back and forth," out poured rice and money, silk, and carpenters who built him a house, one after another, and Heungbu became very rich.

Hearing of this, Nolbu broke a swallow's leg on purpose and then bound it up. When he sawed open the gourds grown from the seed the swallow brought, a band of beggars and goblins came out and carried off all his wealth, and from the last gourd poured filth. Heungbu gladly took in his penniless brother. In 1843, Song Man-jae included this story as "Bak Taryeong" in Gwanuhui, his verses on the twelve pansori.
artifact.imageAlt: A Goryeo gourd-shaped celadon ewer of the thirteenth century. The body looks like a small gourd set on a large one, with a short spout and a long curving handle, covered in a soft green glaze.

annotations.title: Two gourds
annotations.body: A gourd-shaped ewer that looks like a small gourd stacked on a large one. It is Goryeo celadon of the thirteenth century.

annotations.title: Handle
annotations.body: A long handle curving down to the body.

annotations.title: Spout
annotations.body: A short spout for pouring wine. When Heungbu sawed open his gourds, singing "Saw, saw, back and forth," rice, money and silk came pouring out.

artifact.title: Yuri's Broken Sword
artifact.maker: Unknown (Jumong broke it in two and hid one half)
artifact.power: Half of a sword broken in two. When fitted to the other half, blood flowed and the two became one sword again.
artifact.summary: The piece of sword Jumong hid under a pine on a seven-cornered stone when he left. His son Yuri found it and met his father.
artifact.story:
Driven out by the princes of Buyeo and leaving for the south, Jumong told his pregnant wife, Lady Ye: "If you bear a son, tell him that I have hidden something under a pine on a seven-cornered stone. The child who finds it and brings it to me is my son."

Yuri, growing up without a father, broke a woman's water jar while shooting at birds and was cursed as a fatherless child. Hearing his father's words from his mother, Yuri searched every mountain valley but could not find a seven-cornered stone. One day, sitting on the floor of his house, he heard a sound between a pillar and its foundation stone. The pillar was pine, and the foundation stone had seven corners. Beneath it he found a piece of a broken sword.

Yuri took the piece to Goguryeo and presented it to his father, King Dongmyeong. When the king brought out the other piece he kept and fitted them together, blood flowed and they joined into a single sword. Overjoyed, the king made Yuri crown prince, and Yuri became the second king of Goguryeo.
artifact.imageAlt: A Joseon sword and scabbard of the sixteenth to nineteenth century. Beside a straight sword with a golden guard and a ring-pommeled grip lies a red-lacquered scabbard.

annotations.title: Ring pommel
annotations.body: A ring is fitted at the end of the grip. This is a Joseon sword of the sixteenth to nineteenth century.

annotations.title: Blade
annotations.body: A straight, slender blade. When the piece Yuri brought was fitted to Jumong's piece, blood flowed and they joined into a single sword.

annotations.title: Red scabbard
annotations.body: A red-lacquered scabbard fitted with a ring and strap for wearing at the waist. Yuri found the piece of sword beneath a pine pillar on a seven-cornered foundation stone.

artifact.title: Haemosu's Five-Dragon Chariot
artifact.owner: Haemosu, son of the heavenly emperor
artifact.power: A chariot drawn by five dragons. In the morning it comes down to earth, and in the evening it returns to heaven.
artifact.summary: The chariot of five dragons in which Haemosu traveled between heaven and earth. He came down in the morning and rose to heaven in the evening.
artifact.story:
After reading the story of King Dongmyeong, founder of Goguryeo, in the Old History of the Three Kingdoms, Yi Gyu-bo of Goryeo composed the long narrative poem "Lay of King Dongmyeong" in 1193. It opens with Haemosu, son of the heavenly emperor, descending from the sky.

Haemosu came down in the Oryonggeo, a chariot drawn by five dragons. His hundred or more followers all rode white swans, colored clouds floated in the sky, and music sounded within the clouds. Haemosu wore a crown of crow feathers and at his waist a sword shining with dragon light. In the morning he came down to earth to attend to affairs of state, and in the evening he rose to heaven, so people called him the Heavenly King's Son.

Haemosu wished to take Yuhwa, daughter of the water god Habaek, as his wife. After he won a contest of transformations with Habaek, Habaek put the drunken Haemosu with Yuhwa into a leather palanquin and set it on the five-dragon chariot. Before the chariot left the water, Haemosu woke from his drunkenness, tore the leather with Yuhwa's golden hairpin and rose to heaven alone. The son born to Yuhwa, left behind, was Jumong.
artifact.imageAlt: A stoneware pedestal vessel shaped like a pair of chariot wheels from Gaya, fifth century. On a flaring pedestal stand a pair of spoked wheels, topped by two horn-shaped cups.

annotations.title: Two cups
annotations.body: Two horn-shaped cups stand on the chariot. This pedestal vessel was fired in Gaya in the fifth century.

annotations.title: Spoked wheel
annotations.body: A chariot wheel with each spoke cut out individually. Haemosu traveled between heaven and earth in the Oryonggeo, a chariot drawn by five dragons.

annotations.title: Pedestal
annotations.body: A pedestal that flares like a trumpet. The people of Gaya and Silla buried vessels shaped like chariots, boats and horses with the dead.

artifact.title: Mask of Cheoyong
artifact.owner: Cheoyong, son of the Dragon of the East Sea
artifact.power: Merely by posting a picture of Cheoyong's face, the spirit that spreads disease is kept from entering the house.
artifact.summary: The face of Cheoyong, who drove off the spirit of pestilence with song and dance. The people of Silla posted his face on their gates to keep evil away.
artifact.story:
When King Heongang of Silla went out to Gaeunpo on the shore of the East Sea, clouds and fog suddenly rolled in and he lost his way. Told that it was the work of the Dragon of the East Sea, the king ordered a temple built for the dragon, and the fog cleared; the delighted dragon appeared with his seven sons and danced. One of them, Cheoyong, followed the king to the capital, received an official post and married a beautiful wife.

One night Cheoyong came home to find the spirit of pestilence lying beside his wife. Cheoyong sang a song beginning, "Under the bright moon of the capital, I roamed far into the night," danced and withdrew. Moved, the spirit knelt and swore that from then on he would not enter any house where he saw even a picture of Cheoyong's face.

From then on the people of Silla posted Cheoyong's face on their gates to drive away evil. The music treatise Akhak Gwebeom, compiled in 1493, pictures the Cheoyong mask with a red face and a samo hat adorned with peony flowers and peaches, and the Cheoyong dance is still performed as a court dance.
artifact.imageAlt: A Joseon wooden mask of an old man from the nineteenth century. The black-painted face is carved with a wrinkled brow, open eyes and a prominent nose, and a long beard of hair hangs from the chin.

source.creditLine: The Severance and Greta Millikin Purchase Fund

annotations.title: Wrinkled brow
annotations.body: A mask of an old man with deep wrinkles carved in the brow. It was carved in wood in nineteenth-century Joseon.

annotations.title: Open eyes
annotations.body: The eyes are cut through so the wearer can see. Cheoyong sang and danced and withdrew before the spirit of pestilence.

annotations.title: Long beard
annotations.body: A long beard of hair hangs from the chin. The Cheoyong mask in the Akhak Gwebeom has a red face and a samo hat adorned with peonies and peaches.

artifact.title: Kim Yu-sin's Treasured Sword
artifact.owner: Kim Yu-sin, great general of Silla
artifact.power: Starlight came down from heaven and filled it with divine power.
artifact.summary: The sword that was filled with divine power when starlight came down as Kim Yu-sin prayed on Mount Yeolbak. He led the way in uniting the Three Kingdoms.
artifact.story:
At seventeen, seeing Goguryeo, Baekje and the Malgal invading his country, Kim Yu-sin of Silla resolved to drive out the enemy. He went alone into a stone cave on Jungak, purified himself and prayed, making a vow to heaven, and on the fourth day an old man named Nanseung appeared and taught him secret arts.

The next year, as the invasions of the neighboring countries grew fiercer, Kim Yu-sin went alone with his treasured sword into a deep valley of Mount Yeolbak, burned incense and prayed to heaven. On the third night, rays of light from two stars, Heo and Gak, came down brightly and touched the sword, and the sword trembled as if moving by itself. Heaven had filled the treasured sword with divine power.

Kim Yu-sin later became the great general of Silla and, with King Taejong Muyeol and King Munmu, led the way in overthrowing Baekje and Goguryeo and uniting the Three Kingdoms. The Samguk Sagi devotes three of its ten volumes of biographies to his life.
artifact.imageAlt: A Joseon sword and scabbard of the sixteenth to nineteenth century. Beside a straight sword with a grip and guard decorated in silver and gold lies a scabbard with silvery fittings.

annotations.title: Decorated grip
annotations.body: Silver scrolls decorate the grip and guard. This is a Joseon sword of the sixteenth to nineteenth century.

annotations.title: Straight blade
annotations.body: A straight blade. When Kim Yu-sin prayed on Mount Yeolbak, starlight came down and filled his treasured sword with divine power.

annotations.title: Scabbard and rings
annotations.body: A silver-decorated scabbard with two rings for wearing at the waist. Kim Yu-sin later led the way in uniting the Three Kingdoms.

artifact.title: Veillantif
artifact.power: Roland's warhorse, which carried him into the heart of the Saracen host.
artifact.summary: The warhorse Roland rode into his last battle at the pass of Roncevaux. Its name is read as 'the wakeful one.'
artifact.story:
In The Song of Roland every knight's sword and horse has a name. If Roland's sword is Durendal, the warhorse he rides is Veillantif. When the vast Saracen army pours into the pass of Roncevaux, Roland mounts Veillantif, ties a white pennon with golden fringes to his lance, and rides up and down before the Frankish knights to rouse them.

The name is read as coming from the Old French word for 'to be awake.' The poem sings again and again of Roland driving Veillantif through the enemy ranks and striking down their champions with Durendal. In the chansons de geste a horse was the knight's companion in his deeds.

The battle of Roncevaux rests on a real event of 778, when Charlemagne's rearguard was ambushed by Basques in the Pyrenees. In a poem written some three hundred years later the enemy became a Saracen army, and Roland and Veillantif became the model of a knight and horse who never gave ground.
artifact.imageAlt: A woodcut printed on blue-washed paper by the German artist Hans Burgkmair in 1508, Equestrian Portrait of the Emperor Maximilian. Under an arch, the emperor in armor and a plumed helmet rides a horse in a patterned caparison toward the left, with a double-headed eagle banner behind.

source.objectTitle: Equestrian Portrait of the Emperor Maximilian

annotations.title: Armored knight
annotations.body: Maximilian I in a plumed helmet and plate armor. In this 1508 woodcut Hans Burgkmair presents knight and warhorse as one, like an ancient equestrian statue.

annotations.title: Caparisoned warhorse
annotations.body: The horse wears a patterned caparison and steps forward with a raised foreleg. In the chansons de geste the horse was the knight's companion in his deeds, as Roland's warhorse Veillantif was.

annotations.title: The emperor's titles
annotations.body: The Latin abbreviations at the top mean 'August Emperor Caesar Maximilian.' The double-headed eagle on the banner below is the arms of the Habsburg family.

artifact.title: Almace
artifact.power: With this sword the warrior-priest Turpin cut down Saracen after Saracen.
artifact.summary: The sword Archbishop Turpin of Reims wielded at Roncevaux. He fought with it until he fell.
artifact.story:
Turpin in The Song of Roland is both archbishop of Reims and a knight who bears a sword. At the pass of Roncevaux he has the knights confess their sins and blesses them, then spurs his own horse into the Saracen army. The sword he swings is Almace.

The poem tells how Turpin drew Almace and cut down one Saracen warrior after another. Pierced by lances all over his body, he did not stop fighting until he fell, and he gave a last blessing to the bodies of his fellow knights that Roland gathered before him.

The real Turpin was archbishop of Reims in the eighth century. In the twelfth century a Latin chronicle claiming to be his work, the Pseudo-Turpin Chronicle, spread the story of Charlemagne's Spanish campaigns across Europe.
artifact.imageAlt: A French double-edged sword of the thirteenth century. Below a disk-shaped pommel and a straight crossguard runs a long blade that tapers toward the point, darkened with age.

annotations.title: Disk pommel
annotations.body: A disk-shaped pommel at the end of the hilt keeps the hand from slipping and balances the sword. This is a thirteenth-century French sword.

annotations.title: Straight crossguard
annotations.body: A straight crossguard sits between blade and grip. The knights of the chansons de geste fought with cross-shaped swords like this.

annotations.title: Double-edged blade
annotations.body: A double-edged blade tapering to the point. Archbishop Turpin drew Almace and cut down one Saracen warrior after another.

artifact.title: Babieca
artifact.power: Legend says that even after El Cid died, Babieca carried him out of the city gates and put the enemy to flight.
artifact.summary: El Cid's beloved warhorse. A legend tells that it carried the dead Cid out of the gates of Valencia.
artifact.story:
In The Poem of the Cid, after taking Valencia, El Cid welcomes his wife Jimena and their daughters by riding his warhorse Babieca before them. Babieca is a horse named together with the Cid's deeds, and this poem is the first to record its name.

Later chronicles and legends added more. When the Cid died in 1099, it is said, Jimena had his body armored and set on Babieca and sent out of the city gates, and the Moorish army, believing the Cid had returned alive, fled.

Legend also says Babieca let no one ride him after the Cid's death and was buried at the monastery of San Pedro de Cardeña near Burgos. The real El Cid was an eleventh-century Castilian knight who served Christian and Muslim kings alike.
artifact.imageAlt: Plate 11 of Francisco Goya's print series La Tauromaquia, El Cid Campeador Spearing Another Bull (1816 edition, printed 1876). A knight in a plumed helmet drives a lance down from the saddle while a bull charges the horse with lowered head.

source.objectTitle: Bullfights:  El Cid Campeador Spearing Another Bull

annotations.title: El Cid
annotations.body: A knight in a plumed helmet thrusts a lance from the saddle. Goya included in his series on the history of bullfighting a tale that the medieval hero El Cid speared bulls.

annotations.title: Horse
annotations.body: The horse twists away from the bull's horns. El Cid's horse Babieca is first named in The Poem of the Cid.

annotations.title: Charging bull
annotations.body: A bull charges with lowered head. This is plate 11 of Francisco Goya's Tauromaquia, published in 1816; this impression was printed in 1876.

artifact.title: Balisarda
artifact.power: Forged by magic, it could cut even enchanted armor and charmed things.
artifact.summary: A sword the sorceress Falerina forged to kill Orlando. It could cut even what was enchanted.
artifact.story:
In Boiardo's Orlando Innamorato, the sorceress Falerina forged a sword in her enchanted garden to kill the knight Orlando. Made by magic, it could cut through enchanted armor and charmed things. Its name was Balisarda.

Orlando broke the spells of the garden and won the sword, but it passed through several hands and became the sword of Ruggiero, a young knight on the Moorish side. In Ariosto's Orlando Furioso, Ruggiero fights battle after battle with it.

Ruggiero was portrayed as the ancestor of the Este family whom Ariosto served. The poet made the love of Ruggiero and the warrior maiden Bradamante a main thread of his story, singing the glory of the Este who ruled Ferrara.
artifact.imageAlt: A rapier made in Milan, Italy, about 1625–50. Below a wire-wrapped grip, curving iron bars and a pierced cup-shaped guard enclose the hand, and a long, slender blade extends below.

source.creditLine: Gift of Mr. and Mrs. John L. Severance

annotations.body: Below the round pommel, wire is wound around the grip so the hand will not slip.

annotations.title: Guard around the hand
annotations.body: Curving bars and a pierced cup-shaped guard enclose the hand. This rapier was made in Milan about 1625–50.

annotations.title: Long, slender blade
annotations.body: A long, slender blade suited to thrusting. Balisarda, forged by the sorceress Falerina, could cut even enchanted armor.

artifact.title: Ring of Angelica
artifact.power: Worn on the finger it made every enchantment fail; held in the mouth it made the wearer invisible.
artifact.summary: The ring of Angelica, princess of Cathay. Worn, it broke enchantments; held in the mouth, it made her invisible.
artifact.story:
Boiardo's tale begins when Angelica, princess of Cathay (China), appears at Charlemagne's court. Orlando, Rinaldo and the other knights all lose their hearts to her, and Angelica often flees from the knights who pursue her. Her protection is a magic ring.

On her finger, the ring made every enchantment fail; held in her mouth, it made her invisible. In Ariosto's Orlando Furioso the ring passes through the hands of the thief Brunello and the sorceress Melissa and is used to free Ruggiero from the castle of the wizard Atlante and the island of the sorceress Alcina.

In the end Angelica fell in love not with any famous knight but with Medoro, a wounded Moorish soldier she nursed, married him and left for home. At this news Orlando went mad, and that is the meaning of the title Orlando Furioso.
artifact.imageAlt: An engraving made about 1570 by the Italian brothers Giorgio and Teodoro Ghisi, Angelica and Medoro. Beneath dense trees the naked Angelica and Medoro embrace and carve their names on a tree trunk. A river and town appear at right.

source.creditLine: Gift of The Print Club of Cleveland

annotations.title: Names carved on the tree
annotations.body: The names Angelica and Medoro are carved on the trunk. In Orlando Furioso the two carved each other's names on every tree and stone.

annotations.title: Angelica and Medoro
annotations.body: Angelica and Medoro embrace. Angelica owned a ring that broke enchantments when worn and made her invisible when held in the mouth.

annotations.title: Distant landscape
annotations.body: A river and a town spread out at right. This engraving was made about 1570 by the Italian brothers Giorgio and Teodoro Ghisi.

artifact.title: Horn of Astolfo
artifact.maker: Unknown (given by the good fairy Logistilla)
artifact.power: One blast made every man and beast that heard it flee in terror.
artifact.summary: The horn the good fairy Logistilla gave Astolfo. Everything that heard it fled in fear.
artifact.story:
In Ariosto's Orlando Furioso, the English knight Astolfo is bewitched by the sorceress Alcina and turned into a myrtle tree before he is set free. Alcina's sister, the good fairy Logistilla, sends him home with two gifts: a book telling how to break enchantments, and a horn.

When the horn was blown, every man and beast that heard it was seized with terror and fled. With it Astolfo defeated the man-eating giant Caligorante, and he drove the Harpies that fouled the Ethiopian king's table all the way to the mouth of Hell.

Later Astolfo rode the hippogriff to the Earthly Paradise, then went up to the Moon in Elijah's chariot of fire and brought back the lost wits of the mad Orlando in a flask.
artifact.imageAlt: An ivory horn carved in southern Italy or Sicily in the twelfth century, the so-called Horn of Saint Blaise. Bands of animals and scrolls encircle the wide mouth and the narrow tip, and the middle is left smooth.

source.creditLine: Gift of the John Huntington Art and Polytechnic Trust
source.objectTitle: The So-called Horn of Saint Blaise

annotations.title: Band at the mouth
annotations.body: A band of animals and scrolls encircles the wide mouth. This ivory horn was carved in southern Italy or Sicily in the twelfth century.

annotations.title: Smooth body
annotations.body: The middle is left plain to show the grain of the ivory. The horn the good fairy Logistilla gave Astolfo made men and beasts flee at its sound alone.

annotations.title: Band at the tip
annotations.body: Another decorated band encircles the narrowing tip. The horn has come down under the name Horn of Saint Blaise.

artifact.title: Lancelot's Ring
artifact.power: Looking into its stone showed whether an enchantment before him was false.
artifact.firstRecord: Chrétien de Troyes, Lancelot, the Knight of the Cart
artifact.summary: The ring the Lady of the Lake, who raised Lancelot, gave him. Looking into it dispelled enchantments.
artifact.story:
In Chrétien de Troyes' Lancelot, the Knight of the Cart, Lancelot sets out for the land of Gorre to rescue the abducted Queen Guinevere. On his finger is a ring given him by the Lady of the Lake, who raised him as a child. When he looked into its stone, anything enchanted showed its true nature.

The way into Gorre lay across a bridge made of a sword blade. Before Lancelot crossed it, gripping the blade with bare hands and feet, two lions seemed to wait at the far end. Once over, he looked into his ring, and the lions were nowhere to be seen.

In this story, where Lancelot even climbs into a prisoner's cart, a disgrace for a knight, to save the queen, the love of Guinevere and Lancelot is told in full for the first time. Chrétien said that Countess Marie of Champagne gave him the matter and meaning of the tale.
artifact.imageAlt: A side panel of an ivory casket made in France about 1330. Twisted columns divide it into scenes from knightly romances: at center left a knight fights a lion, at right Lancelot crosses a sword bridge over the waves, and at far right people watch from the battlements.

source.objectTitle: Panel from a Casket with Scenes from Courtly Romances

annotations.title: Lancelot crossing the sword bridge
annotations.body: Lancelot crosses a great blade laid over the waves. When he reached the other side and looked at the ring the Lady of the Lake had given him, the lions on the far bank vanished.

annotations.title: Gawain fighting the lion
annotations.body: A knight with a sword faces a lion: Sir Gawain in the adventure of the Perilous Bed at the Castle of Marvels.

annotations.title: Watchers in the castle
annotations.body: People watch the adventures from the battlements. This is a side panel of an ivory casket carved with knightly tales in France about 1330.

artifact.title: Merlin's Mirror
artifact.owner: King Ryence of Deheubarth and his daughter Britomart
artifact.power: It showed in perfect sight whatever thing the world contained.
artifact.summary: A round mirror Merlin made for a king of Britain. It showed whatever one wished to see.
artifact.story:
In Book III of Edmund Spenser's The Faerie Queene, the wizard Merlin made a mirror as round as a glass globe for Ryence, king of Deheubarth (today South Wales). It showed whatever the world contained, so the king could know in advance what his enemies plotted.

The king's daughter Britomart looked into the mirror and saw a knight's image and fell in love. He was Artegall, the knight of Justice. With her old nurse Britomart sought out Merlin's cave to learn who the knight was, then put on armor and set out to find him.

Merlin prophesied that a line of British kings would descend from Britomart and Artegall. Britomart, the maiden knight of Chastity, is a figure who recalls Elizabeth I, to whom Spenser dedicated the poem.
artifact.imageAlt: A round bronze magic mirror made in Japan in the nineteenth century. The six characters of Namu Amida Butsu are raised down the center of the back. When light is reflected from the polished face, an image of the Buddha Amida appears in the reflection.

source.objectTitle: Magic Mirror with Image of the Buddha Amida

annotations.title: Namu Amida Butsu
annotations.body: The phrase Namu Amida Butsu is raised vertically down the center: the prayer of devotion to the Buddha Amida.

annotations.title: Mirror with a hidden image
annotations.body: This is a magic mirror: when sunlight is reflected from its polished face, a hidden image of Amida appears in the reflected light. It was made in nineteenth-century Japan.

annotations.title: Round bronze mirror
annotations.body: The whole round bronze mirror. In Spenser's poem, the mirror Merlin made was round as a glass globe and showed whatever the world contained.

artifact.title: Balm of Fierabras
artifact.maker: Unknown (said to be the balm used to embalm Christ's body)
artifact.power: Drunk or applied, it healed any wound at once.
artifact.summary: The balm said to have embalmed the body of Christ. The Saracen prince Fierabras seized it in Rome.
artifact.story:
The hero of the twelfth-century French chanson de geste Fierabras is the giant Saracen prince Fierabras. Sacking Rome, he carried off the balm said to have been used to embalm the body of Jesus. Whoever drank it or put it on a wound was healed at once.

When Charlemagne's knight Oliver fought Fierabras in single combat, Fierabras healed his wounds with the balm as they fought. Only after Oliver seized the balm and threw it into the river could he win. Fierabras became a Christian and one of Charlemagne's knights.

The balm won fame again in Cervantes' Don Quixote. Don Quixote brewed his own 'balm of Fierabras' from oil, wine, salt and rosemary, drank it and was violently ill, and Sancho, who drank it too, fared even worse.
artifact.imageAlt: The front of a pilgrim's flask for holy oil, cast in tin and lead in Palestine about 600, in the early Byzantine period. Below a narrow neck, the flat round body bears the Crucifixion, with a Greek inscription around the edge.

source.objectCulture: Byzantium, Palestine, early Byzantine period, early 7th Century

annotations.title: Narrow neck
annotations.body: The narrow neck for holding and pouring oil. Pilgrims to the Holy Land about 600 carried oil from the holy places home in flasks of tin and lead like this.

annotations.title: The Crucifixion
annotations.body: The Crucifixion fills the center of the body, and the Ascension is on the back. The balm Fierabras seized in Rome was said to have embalmed the body of Christ.

annotations.title: Inscription at the edge
annotations.body: A Greek inscription runs around the edge. Such pilgrim flasks often bore words declaring that the oil came from the holy places of Christ.

artifact.title: Shield of Galahad
artifact.maker: Josephus, son of Joseph of Arimathea (who drew the cross in his own blood)
artifact.power: Anyone but Galahad who bore it came to harm.
artifact.firstRecord: The Quest of the Holy Grail (Vulgate Cycle)
artifact.summary: A white shield with a red cross. Only Galahad, who would find the Grail, could bear it safely.
artifact.story:
In The Quest of the Holy Grail, Galahad comes to a white abbey and hears of a shield no one may take away. King Bademagu, who took the white shield with its red cross before him, came back gravely wounded by a knight in white armor.

The White Knight told the shield's history. When Joseph of Arimathea came west bearing the vessel that held Christ's blood, Joseph's son Josephus drew a cross on the shield in his own blood for Evalach, king of Sarras. Josephus said that only the last knight of his lineage could bear it.

Galahad bore the shield through many adventures and at last, in Sarras, beheld the mysteries of the Grail and died. The Quest of the Holy Grail is one volume of the cycle of Arthurian prose romances written in France in the early thirteenth century.
artifact.imageAlt: A tall wooden shield made in Erfurt, Germany, in the early fourteenth century. A large wheel in silver foil is painted on the upper part of the red, leather-covered ground, and the paint has flaked in places with age.

annotations.title: Silver wheel
annotations.body: A large wheel is painted in silver foil on the red ground. The archbishops of Mainz, who ruled Erfurt, also bore a white wheel on red.

annotations.title: Standing shield
annotations.body: A tall shield long enough to cover the body, of wood covered with leather and painted over gesso. Galahad's shield was white with a red cross.

annotations.title: Rivets
annotations.body: The round rivets in the middle probably once held the grip and straps on the inside.

artifact.title: Balmung
artifact.power: The Nibelung kings gave it as payment for dividing their treasure, and with it Siegfried cut down those kings and their giants.
artifact.summary: The sword Siegfried won with the Nibelung treasure. After his death it passed to his enemy Hagen.
artifact.story:
In the medieval German epic The Nibelungenlied, the young hero Siegfried is asked by Schilbung and Nibelung, two kings of the Nibelungs, to divide their treasure. As payment they give him the sword Balmung, but unhappy with their shares they turn on him. With Balmung Siegfried cuts down both kings and their men and takes the whole treasure.

He also took from the dwarf Alberich a cloak that made the wearer invisible. With Balmung, the treasure and a body hardened by bathing in dragon's blood, Siegfried became a hero no one could defeat. Only the spot between his shoulders, where a linden leaf had stuck as he bathed, could be wounded.

Siegfried was killed on a hunt by the spear of Hagen, who had learned his weakness. Hagen took Balmung too, but at the end of the poem Siegfried's wife Kriemhild seized the sword and struck off Hagen's head.
artifact.imageAlt: A sword probably made in Germany in the fifteenth century. Below a round pommel, a wood and leather grip and a straight crossguard, a long straight blade extends.

source.creditLine: Gift of Mr. and Mrs. John L. Severance

annotations.title: Round pommel
annotations.body: The round pommel at the end of the hilt. This sword was probably made in Germany in the fifteenth century.

annotations.title: Crossguard and grip
annotations.body: Above the straight crossguard is a wooden grip wrapped in leather. In the Nibelungenlied, Siegfried felled the kings of the Nibelungs with Balmung.

annotations.title: Long blade
annotations.body: A long, straight blade. After Siegfried's death his wife Kriemhild beheaded his enemy Hagen with this sword.

artifact.title: Svalinn
artifact.power: It stands before the sun so that its fire does not burn the earth and sea.
artifact.summary: The shield set before the sun. If it fell, mountains and sea would burn up.
artifact.story:
In Grímnismál in the Poetic Edda, Odin, disguised as Grímnir, sits bound between two fires and reveals the secrets of the world. One stanza sings of a shield called Svalinn, which stands before the shining goddess, the sun.

The poem says that if the shield fell from its place, mountains and sea would burn up. Its name is read as 'the cooling one': the shield screens the earth from the burning light of the sun as it crosses the sky.

According to Snorri Sturluson's Prose Edda, the sun is a chariot driven by the goddess Sól, and the wolf Sköll runs behind it. When the last days of Ragnarök come, the wolf will swallow the sun.
artifact.imageAlt: A round steel shield made in northern Italy about 1550–1600. Etched panels radiate like sunbeams from a pointed central boss, and rivets are set close together along the rope-like border.

source.creditLine: Gift of Mr. and Mrs. John L. Severance

annotations.title: Central boss
annotations.body: A pointed boss rises at the center. Like Svalinn, the shield that stands before the sun, a round shield resembles the sun.

annotations.title: Panels like sunbeams
annotations.body: Etched panels radiate from the center like sunbeams. This steel shield was made in northern Italy about 1550–1600.

annotations.title: Rivets at the rim
annotations.body: Rivets along the edge held the lining and grip inside.

artifact.title: Freyr's Sword
artifact.owner: Freyr, god of plenty, later his servant Skírnir
artifact.power: When a wise man held it, it fought the giants by itself.
artifact.summary: Freyr's sword that fought by itself. He gave it to his servant to win the giant's daughter Gerd.
artifact.story:
In Skírnismál in the Poetic Edda, Freyr, god of plenty, secretly sits on Odin's high seat Hlidskjalf, sees the beautiful Gerd in the land of the giants and falls in love. He asks his servant Skírnir to win her heart for him, and Skírnir asks for Freyr's sword as his price.

When a wise man held that sword, it fought the giants by itself. Skírnir took it, crossed the flames into the land of the giants and persuaded Gerd, who agreed to meet Freyr in the grove of Barri after nine nights.

Snorri's Prose Edda tells the cost of the bargain. Without his sword Freyr had to kill the giant Beli with a stag's antler, and at Ragnarök, facing the fire giant Surtr without his sword, he falls.
artifact.imageAlt: A fifteenth-century European steel sword. Below a round pommel is a crossguard with down-curved ends, and a long, straight blade tapers toward the point.

source.creditLine: Gift of Mr. and Mrs. John L. Severance

annotations.title: Round pommel
annotations.body: The round pommel at the end of the hilt draws the sword's weight toward the hand.

annotations.title: Down-curved crossguard
annotations.body: The ends of the crossguard curve down to catch an opponent's blade. This fifteenth-century European sword descends from the straight, double-edged Viking sword of the ninth century.

annotations.title: Straight double-edged blade
annotations.body: A straight double-edged blade for both cutting and thrusting. Freyr's sword fought the giants by itself when a wise man held it.

artifact.title: Sif's Golden Hair
artifact.power: Set on her head, it took root and grew like real hair.
artifact.summary: Hair the dwarves spun from gold to replace the hair Loki cut from Sif. It grew like real hair.
artifact.story:
According to Snorri Sturluson's Prose Edda, the trickster god Loki once cut off all the hair of Sif, Thor's wife. When the furious Thor threatened to break every bone in his body, Loki swore to go to the dwarves and have new hair made of gold.

The dwarves called the sons of Ivaldi spun hair from gold. Set on Sif's head, it took root and grew like real hair. At the same time the dwarves made Freyr's ship Skidbladnir and Odin's spear Gungnir.

Not stopping there, Loki bet the dwarf brothers Brokk and Eitri that they could not make better treasures. From that wager came Draupnir, Gullinbursti and Mjölnir. Some read Sif's golden hair as the ripe fields of grain.
artifact.imageAlt: A pair of gold earrings or hair ornaments from ancient Greece. Hollow gold tubes are coiled into spirals with a palmette at the center, and each end finishes in a ram's head.

source.creditLine: Norman O. Stone and Ella A. Stone Memorial Fund
source.objectTitle: Pair of Earrings or Hair Ringlets with Ram Head

annotations.title: Ram's heads
annotations.body: Each end of the coil finishes in a ram's head above an elaborate collar.

annotations.title: Palmette
annotations.body: A double palmette is set at the center of the coil. The hollow gold tube was coiled without a visible seam.

annotations.title: Golden spiral
annotations.body: The coiled gold tube looks like a lock of hair. The golden hair the dwarves made for Sif grew from her head like real hair.

artifact.title: Freyja's Falcon Cloak
artifact.power: Whoever put it on became a falcon and could fly.
artifact.summary: Freyja's feather cloak that turned its wearer into a falcon. Loki borrowed it to fly to the land of the giants.
artifact.story:
In Þrymskviða in the Poetic Edda, Thor wakes one morning to find his hammer Mjölnir gone. Loki borrows Freyja's falcon cloak, flies as a falcon to the land of the giants, and learns that the giant Thrym has buried the hammer deep in the earth. Thrym will return it only if he is given Freyja as his wife.

Freyja flew into a rage, and in the end Thor dressed as the bride, with Loki as his maid, and won back the hammer. In Snorri's Prose Edda too, Loki borrows this cloak to rescue the goddess Idun, carried off by the giant Thiazi.

Freyja is the goddess of love and magic, and she receives half of those who die in battle into her own hall. She rode in a chariot drawn by two cats.
artifact.imageAlt: White Falcon, a sixteenth-century Korean hanging scroll on silk from the Joseon dynasty. Beneath a flowering tree a white falcon perches on a rock with wings spread and head bowed, painted feather by feather, while the trees and grasses are drawn with free, calligraphic lines.

source.creditLine: Purchase from the Karl B. Goldfield Trust

annotations.title: White falcon
annotations.body: A white falcon painted feather by feather. Whoever put on Freyja's cloak became a falcon and could fly.

annotations.title: Head and beak
annotations.body: The falcon's bowed head and hooked beak. White gyrfalcons were also prized hunting birds sent from Iceland and Norway as gifts to the kings of Europe.

annotations.title: Flowering branches
annotations.body: The flowering branches and grasses above are drawn with free, calligraphic lines, contrasting with the finely painted falcon. This is a sixteenth-century Korean painting.

artifact.title: Beowulf's Byrnie
artifact.power: It held even when Grendel's mother drove her blade down on him.
artifact.summary: The mail shirt Beowulf wore. Made by the legendary smith Wayland, it stopped even the blade of Grendel's mother.
artifact.story:
In the Old English epic Beowulf, Beowulf, hero of the Geats, crosses the sea to help the Danish king Hrothgar, tormented by the monster Grendel. The poem calls his armor 'the work of Weland,' meaning that the legendary smith Wayland made it.

After killing Grendel with his bare hands, Beowulf pursued Grendel's mother, who had come to avenge her son, into a cave beneath a lake. She pinned him down and drove her knife at him, but the close-linked mail turned the point. Beowulf killed her with a giant's sword that hung in the cave.

Beowulf survives in a single manuscript of about 1000. In 1731 a fire in the library that held it scorched its edges, but the poem survived.
artifact.imageAlt: A mail shirt probably made in Germany about 1400–1450. Steel and brass rings are linked one by one into a short-sleeved shirt fastened at the front with straps. In the photograph a helmet is placed above it.

annotations.title: Linked rings
annotations.body: Small iron rings are linked and riveted one by one. Until about 1350 European knights mostly wore mail like this.

annotations.title: Front fastenings
annotations.body: The front closes with straps and buckles, which were added later.

annotations.title: Helmet
annotations.body: A helmet shown with the mail shirt. Beowulf's mail held even when Grendel's mother drove her blade down on him.

artifact.title: Mimung
artifact.owner: The smith Velent, later his son Witege
artifact.power: So sharp it split even a tuft of wool drifting on the water.
artifact.summary: The sword the smith Velent forged for a contest on which his life depended. It split a tuft of wool floating on the water.
artifact.story:
In Þiðreks saga, compiled in thirteenth-century Norway from German legends, appears the smith Velent (Wayland). He competes with the king's smith Amilias, and the loser is to forfeit his life. The sword Velent forges is Mimung.

To test the sword, Velent floated a tuft of wool down the river, and the wool split where it touched the blade. On the day of the contest Amilias sat wearing the armor and helmet he had made, and when Velent struck with Mimung, the blade cut through armor and man alike.

Mimung later passed to Velent's son Witege and was used in many battles in the tales of Dietrich of Bern.
artifact.imageAlt: A hand-and-a-half sword made in Germany about 1540–80. Below a conical pommel is a long sharkskin grip, with straight quillons extending to either side and rings enclosing the hand, and the double-edged blade continues below.

source.creditLine: Gift from the Bascom Little Estate

annotations.title: Conical pommel
annotations.body: The pommel is shaped like a cone. This hand-and-a-half sword was made in Germany about 1540–80.

annotations.title: Sharkskin grip
annotations.body: A long grip of sharkskin over a wooden core, long enough to hold with both hands when needed, hence the name hand-and-a-half sword.

annotations.title: Quillons and rings
annotations.body: Long straight quillons and rings enclose the hand. Mimung, forged by the smith Velent, split even a tuft of wool floating on the water.

artifact.title: Nibelung Hoard
artifact.owner: The kings of the Nibelungs, Siegfried, Kriemhild
artifact.power: So much gold and jewels that twelve wagons could not carry it in one trip; it brought strife and death to everyone who held it.
