artifact.summary: The treasure Siegfried won from the Nibelungs. Hagen sank it in the Rhine, and no one ever found it.
artifact.story:
In The Nibelungenlied the Nibelung hoard was so vast that twelve wagons hauling for four days and nights could not carry it all. Siegfried won it by defeating the kings of the Nibelungs, and when he married Kriemhild it became her portion.

After Siegfried's death Kriemhild brought the treasure to Worms and gathered followers by giving it away. Fearing this, Hagen seized the treasure and sank it in the Rhine. Only Hagen and the kings he served knew where.

Later Kriemhild married Etzel, king of the Huns, and took her revenge by inviting the Burgundians to his court. The captured Hagen refused to tell where the treasure lay while his king lived, and its resting place was buried with him forever. Richard Wagner drew on this tradition for The Ring of the Nibelung.
artifact.imageAlt: Finale of the Rhinegold, a lithograph by the French artist Henri Fantin-Latour, 1877. Above, the gods rise through clouds; at lower left the Rhine maidens reach up from the waves. A bar of music and the title are written at the bottom.

annotations.title: Rhine maidens
annotations.body: At lower left, in the waves, the Rhine maidens lament and beg for their stolen gold. This is the final scene of Wagner's Das Rheingold.

annotations.title: Gods going to Valhalla
annotations.body: Above, the gods ascend to their new fortress Valhalla. Wagner wove the tradition of the Nibelung hoard together with Norse myth in The Ring of the Nibelung.

annotations.title: Music and title
annotations.body: A bar of music and the words Rheingold (R. Wagner) appear below. This lithograph was made by the French artist Henri Fantin-Latour in 1877.

artifact.title: Grani
artifact.maker: Of the line of Sleipnir, Odin's horse
artifact.power: He carried the dragon's gold and leaped the wall of fire with Sigurd on his back.
artifact.summary: The horse Sigurd chose with Odin's help. He carried the dragon Fafnir's gold and leaped the wall of fire.
artifact.story:
In the Völsunga saga, young Sigurd goes to choose a horse and meets an old man with a long beard. The old man drives the horses into a river and tells him to choose the one that swims across. That horse was Grani, and the old man told Sigurd that Grani was of the line of Sleipnir, Odin's horse. The old man was Odin himself.

After killing the dragon Fafnir, Sigurd loaded its treasure on Grani's back. Later, in place of his brother-in-law Gunnar, Sigurd rode Grani through the wall of fire surrounding Brynhild's dwelling. Gunnar's horse shied at the flames, and Grani would not carry Gunnar.

When Sigurd died, the Poetic Edda says, Grani hung his head. Snorri's Prose Edda also records the poets' habit of calling gold 'Grani's burden.' Medieval carvings of Sigurd and Grani survive across Scandinavia, such as the portal of Hylestad church in Norway.
artifact.imageAlt: A bronze horse made in Germany in the 1630s or later. It stands squarely on four legs with its head slightly lowered, its mane and muscles smoothly finished.

annotations.title: Horse's head
annotations.body: The horse's head and mane, slightly lowered. This bronze horse was made in Germany in the 1630s or later.

annotations.title: Powerful body
annotations.body: A deep chest and muscular body. It was once published as a model for an equestrian monument of Emperor Maximilian, but recent scholars question the connection.

annotations.title: Legs and hooves
annotations.body: Four straight legs and hooves. Sigurd's horse Grani leaped the wall of fire to carry his master to Brynhild.

artifact.title: Eldhrímnir
artifact.power: A boar was boiled in it every day to feed the warriors of Valhalla, and each evening the boar was alive again.
artifact.summary: The cauldron of Odin's hall Valhalla. A boar was boiled in it every day for the warriors, and it came back to life.
artifact.story:
Grímnismál in the Poetic Edda sings of the kitchen of Odin's hall Valhalla. The cook Andhrímnir boils the boar Sæhrímnir in the cauldron Eldhrímnir, and few know that it is the best of meats.

Snorri Sturluson's Prose Edda adds an explanation. Valhalla holds countless warriors who died in battle, yet one boar feeds them all, for though it is boiled and eaten every day, each evening it is whole again.

By day the warriors fight one another, and in the evening they eat and drink together as they await Ragnarök. Odin, it is said, gives the meat before him to his wolves Geri and Freki and drinks only wine.
artifact.imageAlt: An Etruscan bronze cauldron of about 550 BCE. The round, deep body is covered with green patina, and an arched iron handle hangs from rings on either side.

annotations.title: Iron handle
annotations.body: An arched iron handle hung from rings so that it swings. This Etruscan bronze cauldron dates from about 550 BCE.

annotations.title: Bronze body
annotations.body: A round cauldron of hammered bronze, covered with green patina over the centuries.

annotations.title: Handle ring
annotations.body: A ring for the handle is fixed to the rim. In Valhalla's cauldron Eldhrímnir a boar was boiled every day, and every evening it was whole again.

artifact.title: Horn of Brân Galed
artifact.power: Whatever drink one wished for was found in it.
artifact.firstRecord: The Thirteen Treasures of the Island of Britain
artifact.summary: One of the Thirteen Treasures of the Island of Britain. Whatever drink one wished for filled it.
artifact.story:
The Thirteen Treasures of the Island of Britain, preserved in fifteenth-century Welsh manuscripts, lists thirteen marvelous objects once owned by the heroes of old Britain. One of them is the horn of Brân Galed from the North: whatever drink one wished for was found in it.

'Galed' in Welsh means 'hard,' that is, stingy. The charm of the tale lies in a miser's horn that pours out drink without end.

Most of the Thirteen Treasures are said to have belonged to kings and heroes of northern Britain around the sixth century, the land the Welsh called the Old North. Later tradition says the wizard Merlin gathered all the treasures and took them to the House of Glass on Bardsey Island.
artifact.imageAlt: A glass drinking horn of about 575–625, probably Lombard. Reddish-brown feather patterns are worked into the clear glass and fine white threads are wound around it in a spiral; part of the wide rim is broken.

source.creditLine: Edward C. Moore Collection, Bequest of Edward C. Moore, 1891

annotations.title: Wide mouth
annotations.body: The flaring mouth, partly broken at the rim. This glass drinking horn of about 575–625 is probably Lombard.

annotations.title: Reddish-brown feathering
annotations.body: Reddish-brown trails of glass are combed into feather-like patterns within the clear glass.

annotations.title: Wound white threads
annotations.body: Fine white glass threads are wound in a spiral. A horn could not be set down, so it had to be drained at once. The horn of Brân Galed held whatever drink one wished.

artifact.title: Halter of Clydno Eiddyn
artifact.power: Fastened to a staple at the foot of his bed, it held whatever horse he wished for.
artifact.firstRecord: The Thirteen Treasures of the Island of Britain
artifact.summary: One of the Thirteen Treasures of the Island of Britain. Whatever horse one wished for would be found in this halter.
artifact.story:
The halter of Clydno Eiddyn, one of the Thirteen Treasures of the Island of Britain, was fastened to a staple at the foot of his bed. Whatever horse he wished for, that horse would be found in the halter.

Eiddyn refers to the region of present-day Edinburgh in Scotland. Clydno was a king of old Britain who ruled that land, and his name survives in the genealogies of the men of the Old North.

Horses were the most precious property of the old British warriors. The Welsh poem Y Gododdin, which mourns the warriors of Eiddyn who rode to the battle of Catraeth and nearly all fell, praises again and again the courage of horses and riders.
artifact.imageAlt: A horse bit made in Italy about 1580–1600. Curved iron bars, chains and rings for the reins form the bit, and gilt bronze bosses are set on each side.

source.creditLine: Gift of Mr. and Mrs. John L. Severance

annotations.title: Gilt bronze bosses
annotations.body: Gilt bronze bosses are fixed on either side of the bit. This Italian bit dates from about 1580–1600.

annotations.title: Curb chain
annotations.body: The iron chain that passes under the horse's jaw. When the reins are pulled, it presses the jaw and halts even a powerful warhorse.

annotations.title: Rein ring
annotations.body: The reins are tied to the ring at the bottom. The halter of Clydno Eiddyn held whatever horse one wished.

artifact.title: Hamper of Gwyddno Garanhir
artifact.power: Put in food for one person, and food for a hundred came out.
artifact.firstRecord: The Thirteen Treasures of the Island of Britain
artifact.summary: One of the Thirteen Treasures of the Island of Britain. Put in food for one, and food for a hundred came out.
artifact.story:
The hamper of Gwyddno Garanhir, one of the Thirteen Treasures of the Island of Britain, was a basket into which one put food for one person and from which, when opened, came food for a hundred.

'Garanhir' is a nickname meaning 'long-shank.' In Welsh legend Gwyddno ruled Cantre'r Gwaelod, a land now under the sea. The tale goes that its keeper of the dikes, drunk, failed to close the sluices, and the sea rushed in and drowned the kingdom.

His son Elffin drew a baby in a leather bag out of Gwyddno's salmon weir, and that baby grew up to be the poet Taliesin.
artifact.imageAlt: A silver fruit basket made in London, England, in 1729. The oval body is pierced with a lattice like woven wicker, with two twisted silver handles and a leaf-pattern rim.

source.creditLine: Gift of Grace Studebaker Fish in memory of her father, John Mohler Studebaker

annotations.title: Twisted handle
annotations.body: Handles of twisted silver are fixed on both sides.

annotations.title: Pierced like wickerwork
annotations.body: The silver sheet is pierced to look like woven basketry. This silver fruit basket was made in London in 1729.

annotations.title: Rim decoration
annotations.body: A border of leaves runs round the rim. Put food for one into the hamper of Gwyddno Garanhir and you took out food for a hundred.

artifact.title: Whetstone of Tudwal Tudglyd
artifact.power: If a brave man sharpened his sword on it, anyone it drew blood from would die; if a coward did, the sword would not cut at all.
artifact.firstRecord: The Thirteen Treasures of the Island of Britain
artifact.summary: One of the Thirteen Treasures of the Island of Britain. Sharpened by a brave man, a sword became deadly; by a coward, it went dull.
artifact.story:
The whetstone of Tudwal Tudglyd, one of the Thirteen Treasures of the Island of Britain, knew the heart of whoever sharpened a sword on it. If a brave man whetted his sword on it, anyone the sword drew blood from would surely die. If a coward whetted it, the sword would cut nothing.

Many of the Thirteen Treasures test the worth of their owners in this way, such as the cauldron of the giant Dyrnwch, which would not boil meat for a coward, and the coat of Padarn, which fitted only the well-born.

A whetstone never left a warrior's side, together with his sword. In the seventh-century royal burial at Sutton Hoo in England, a great whetstone carved with human faces at both ends was found like a royal scepter, showing that the whetstone could also be a symbol of authority.
artifact.imageAlt: A whetstone handle cast in bronze in Luristan, Iran, about 1100–900 BCE. An ibex stretches its long neck, its horns curving into a loop above its head, and the whetstone fitted into the socket below.

source.creditLine: Gift of the Womens Council of the Cleveland Museum of Art on the occasion of its fiftieth anniversary

annotations.title: Looping horns
annotations.body: The ibex's horns curve round like a ring and meet above its head.

annotations.title: Ibex head
annotations.body: An ibex head with large eyes and a beard. This whetstone handle was cast in bronze in Luristan, Iran, about 1100–900 BCE.

annotations.title: Socket for the stone
annotations.body: The whetstone fitted into the socket below. Whetstones were especially important in Luristan, a center of bronze blades. Tudwal's whetstone made a brave man's sword deadly.

artifact.title: Coat of Padarn Beisrudd
artifact.power: It fitted a man of noble blood perfectly and would not go on anyone else.
artifact.firstRecord: The Thirteen Treasures of the Island of Britain
artifact.summary: One of the Thirteen Treasures of the Island of Britain. It fitted the well-born perfectly and would not fit anyone else.
artifact.story:
The coat of Padarn Beisrudd, one of the Thirteen Treasures of the Island of Britain, judged its wearer. On a man of noble blood it fitted perfectly; on a churl it would not go on. 'Beisrudd' means 'red coat' in Welsh.

Padarn is recorded in the genealogies as a leader of northern Britain in the fourth century, under Roman rule. Some scholars think his red coat may have been a mark of Roman office.

A twelfth-century Life of the Welsh saint Padarn tells a similar story. When Arthur coveted the saint's tunic and tried to seize it, the earth opened and swallowed Arthur up to his chin, and he was released only after he begged forgiveness.
artifact.imageAlt: A mail cape, the so-called bishop's mantle, made in Germany or Switzerland about 1520–30. Riveted steel rings, some of brass, cover the shoulders and chest, with a stiff standing collar around the neck.

source.creditLine: Gift of Mr. and Mrs. John L. Severance

annotations.title: Standing collar
annotations.body: The collar around the neck is woven of denser rings to make it stiff.

annotations.title: Mail over the shoulders
annotations.body: A mail cape covering the shoulders and chest. German mercenary foot soldiers favored these about 1500–1550, and they were called bishop's mantles.

annotations.title: Pointed hem
annotations.body: The front hangs to a point. The coat of Padarn fitted a well-born man perfectly and would not go on anyone else.

artifact.title: Chariot of Morgan Mwynfawr
artifact.power: Whoever sat in it and wished to be anywhere would be there at once.
artifact.firstRecord: The Thirteen Treasures of the Island of Britain
artifact.summary: One of the Thirteen Treasures of the Island of Britain. Whoever rode in it was carried at once wherever they wished.
artifact.story:
The chariot of Morgan Mwynfawr, one of the Thirteen Treasures of the Island of Britain, would carry whoever sat in it to wherever they wished to be, at once.

Morgan is said to have been an old king of southeastern Wales, and his epithet Mwynfawr is read as 'of great wealth.' There is also a story that the old name of southern Wales, Morgannwg (Glamorgan), comes from his name.

The wheeled chariot was the pride of the ancient Celtic warriors. The Roman Julius Caesar described in his Gallic War how British warriors drove their chariots across the battlefield and leaped down to fight.
artifact.imageAlt: A red-figure mixing bowl (calyx-krater) made in Lucania, southern Italy, about 400 BCE. In the center of the front, Medea flies up in a dragon-drawn chariot within a sunburst, with winged goddesses at the upper sides and fallen children on an altar below.

source.objectTitle: Red-Figure Calyx-Krater (Mixing Vessel): Medea in Chariot (A); Telephos with Baby Orestes (B)

annotations.title: Dragon chariot
annotations.body: Within a sunburst the sorceress Medea soars away in a chariot drawn by two dragons. The sunburst recalls her grandfather, the sun god Helios.

annotations.title: Winged goddess
annotations.body: Winged goddesses of vengeance watch from either side. The chariot of Morgan Mwynfawr also took whoever rode it wherever they wished in an instant.

annotations.title: Children on the altar
annotations.body: At lower right the two children Medea killed lie on an altar. This vase was made in Lucania in southern Italy about 400 BCE and illustrates Euripides' tragedy Medea.

artifact.title: Cauldron of Rebirth
artifact.owner: The giant king Bendigeidfran, later the Irish king Matholwch
artifact.maker: Unknown (brought by a giant couple who came out of a lake in Ireland)
artifact.power: Dead warriors put into it rose the next day to fight again, but they could not speak.
artifact.firstRecord: The Four Branches of the Mabinogi, Branwen Daughter of Llŷr
artifact.summary: A cauldron that brought dead warriors back to life. It turned the war between Britain and Ireland into a slaughter.
artifact.story:
In Branwen Daughter of Llŷr, one of the Four Branches of the Mabinogi, the giant king of Britain, Bendigeidfran, gives his sister Branwen in marriage to Matholwch, king of Ireland. When their half-brother Efnysien maims the Irish king's horses at the wedding feast and the two fall out, Bendigeidfran gives him the Cauldron of Rebirth as amends.

Dead warriors put into the cauldron rose the next day to fight again, but could not speak. When Britain learned that Branwen was being mistreated in Ireland and the two countries went to war, the Irish revived their dead with the cauldron.

It was Efnysien, the seed of the quarrel, who ended the fighting. He lay among the Irish dead pretending to be one of them and was thrown into the cauldron, where he stretched himself out and burst it into four pieces. His heart burst too.
artifact.imageAlt: A large bronze cauldron made by Greeks in Campania, southern Italy, in the fifth century BCE. A thick rim crowns the broad-shouldered, round-bottomed body, and green patina mottles the surface.

annotations.title: Thick rim
annotations.body: Grooves are cut around the thick rolled rim.

annotations.title: Round body
annotations.body: A large round body of hammered bronze. This cauldron was made by Greeks in Campania in southern Italy in the fifth century BCE.

annotations.title: Green patina
annotations.body: Green patina has mottled the surface over the centuries. Dead warriors put into the Cauldron of Rebirth rose the next day, but could not speak.

artifact.title: Rhiannon's Bag
artifact.owner: Rhiannon and Pwyll, prince of Dyfed
artifact.power: However much was put in, it was never full.
artifact.firstRecord: The Four Branches of the Mabinogi, Pwyll Prince of Dyfed
artifact.summary: A small bag Rhiannon gave Pwyll. Nothing could fill it, and it became a trap for her rival suitor.
artifact.story:
In Pwyll Prince of Dyfed, the first of the Four Branches of the Mabinogi, Pwyll agrees to marry the mysterious Rhiannon. But at the wedding feast a guest asks him to grant a wish, and when Pwyll carelessly promises anything, the guest asks for Rhiannon. He was Gwawl, to whom Rhiannon had been promised.

Rhiannon had Pwyll promise to hold another feast a year later and gave him a small bag. At that feast Pwyll appeared in rags and asked that the bag be filled with food, and however much was put in, it was never full.

Told that the bag would be full only when a noble landholder stepped into it with both feet and said 'Enough,' Gwawl climbed in, and Pwyll pulled the bag over him and tied it shut. Pwyll's men beat the bag in a game of 'badger in the bag,' and Gwawl gave up Rhiannon.
artifact.imageAlt: A reliquary bag of silk woven with gold thread, made in Spain, probably Almería, in the late 1100s–1300s. The long bag is densely woven with a lozenge pattern, crossed by a horizontal stripe, and its edges are frayed.

source.creditLine: Gift of the John Huntington Art and Polytechnic Trust

annotations.title: Silk and gold
annotations.body: Silk woven with gold thread in a lozenge pattern. The cloth, originally woven with lions, was probably made in Almería in Spain in the 1100s–1300s.

annotations.title: Horizontal stripe
annotations.body: A striped band runs across the middle of the bag.

annotations.title: Frayed edges
annotations.body: The edges have frayed and come unravelled. This bag was once kept inside a portable altar commissioned by Countess Gertrude of Brunswick. The bag Rhiannon gave Pwyll could never be filled.

artifact.title: Mac an Luin
artifact.owner: Fionn mac Cumhaill, leader of the Fianna
artifact.maker: The one-eyed smith Lon mac Liomtha
artifact.power: With this sword Fionn defeated countless enemies and monsters.
artifact.summary: The sword of Fionn mac Cumhaill, leader of the Fianna. Ballads say it was forged by the mysterious smith Lon.
artifact.story:
In the Gaelic tradition of Ireland and Scotland, Fionn mac Cumhaill is the hero who leads the warrior band of the Fianna. Duanaire Finn, compiled at Louvain in 1627, and other Gaelic ballads call his sword Mac an Luin.

One ballad tells how the warriors of the Fianna followed a strange one-eyed smith to his forge, and how that smith, Lon mac Liomtha, forged swords for them. Fionn's sword Mac an Luin is said to have been won then.

Fionn is also famous for the tale of the Salmon of Knowledge: he burned his thumb while cooking it and put the thumb in his mouth, and thereafter, by biting his thumb, he could know what was to come. In the eighteenth century he became known across Europe as Fingal in the 'Poems of Ossian' published by James Macpherson.
artifact.imageAlt: A basket-hilted sword made in Britain about 1720–40. A gilded iron basket lined with red cloth encloses the whole hand, and a straight blade continues below.

annotations.title: Basket hilt
annotations.body: A basket-shaped hilt that encloses the whole hand, of iron decorated with gold. This sword was made in Britain about 1720–40.

annotations.title: Oval plate
annotations.body: The oval plate at the front of the hilt is also decorated. A red cloth lining protects the hand inside.

annotations.title: Straight blade
annotations.body: A straight blade. The basket-hilted sword was famous as the sword of the Gaelic warriors of the Scottish Highlands. Mac an Luin is the sword of Fionn mac Cumhaill, hero of Gaelic tradition.

artifact.title: Lúin of Celtchar
artifact.owner: Celtchar mac Uthechair, warrior of Ulster
artifact.power: When its lust for blood rose it blazed up of itself, and only a cauldron of dark poison could quench it.
artifact.firstRecord: The Destruction of Da Derga's Hostel
artifact.summary: The spear of Celtchar, warrior of Ulster. Before battle it blazed up of itself and had to be plunged into a cauldron of dark poison.
artifact.story:
The Irish tale The Destruction of Da Derga's Hostel, preserved in the Book of the Dun Cow, is told through raiders spying on the warriors inside the hostel where King Conaire lodges and describing them one by one. Among them is a spear carried by Dubthach of Ulster: the Lúin of Celtchar mac Uthechair.

When its lust for blood rose, the spear burst into sparks and raged of itself. So beside the warrior who held it stood a cauldron of dark poison, into which the spear had to be plunged to cool it. Otherwise, it was said, the spear would burn up its owner and the house.

The image of a burning spear kept in a cauldron resembles the spear Lugh obtains in The Fate of the Children of Tuireann, and some stories treat the two as one. Celtchar himself, it is said, later died when a single drop of venomous blood from a monstrous hound ran down his spear and struck him.
artifact.imageAlt: A parade spear probably made in Augsburg, Germany, about 1570–1600. The broad, leaf-shaped steel head is etched with ornament, with brass lugs on either side below it, and a woolen tassel hangs from the leather-strapped wooden shaft.

source.creditLine: Gift of Mr. and Mrs. John L. Severance

annotations.title: Etched spearhead
annotations.body: The broad leaf-shaped head is etched with the imperial Habsburg arms on one face and the Burgundian cross of Saint Andrew on the other.

annotations.title: Brass lugs
annotations.body: The brass lugs projecting below the head keep the spear from going in too deep.

annotations.title: Tassel
annotations.body: A woolen tassel hangs from the shaft. Officers of the imperial army carried parade spears like this about 1570–1600 as a sign of command. Celtchar's spear, the Lúin, blazed up by itself before battle.

artifact.title: Talaria
artifact.owner: Hermes, messenger of the gods, later the hero Perseus
artifact.power: Bound on the feet, they carried their wearer as swift as the wind over the sea and the boundless earth.
artifact.summary: The immortal golden sandals of Hermes. Later painters and sculptors gave them wings.
artifact.story:
In Book 24 of Homer's Iliad, Zeus sends Hermes to guide Priam, the old king of Troy, to the tent of Achilles. At once Hermes binds beautiful sandals beneath his feet: immortal, golden sandals that carried him as swift as the wind over the sea and over the boundless earth.

In the Odyssey too, Hermes puts on the same sandals and crosses the sea to the island of the nymph Calypso to deliver Zeus's command to let Odysseus go. Homer never says the sandals had wings, but later painters and sculptors gave Hermes small wings on his sandals and cap. The Romans called these winged sandals talaria.

The hero Perseus also flew in winged sandals in search of Medusa. The Shield of Heracles, handed down under Hesiod's name, sings of winged sandals on Perseus's feet.
artifact.imageAlt: A Roman bronze statuette of Mercury (Hermes) from the first century CE. A young god with small wings sprouting from his hair stands with a cloak over his left shoulder and sandals on his feet, holding a purse in his right hand.

annotations.title: Small wings on the head
annotations.body: Two small wings sprout from his hair. Wings are the sign of Hermes (Mercury), messenger of the gods.

annotations.title: Purse
annotations.body: The purse in his right hand. The Romans also worshipped Mercury as the god of trade and profit. This is a Roman bronze of the first century CE.

annotations.title: Sandaled feet
annotations.body: Sandals are strapped on both feet. Homer's Hermes wore immortal golden sandals that carried him like the wind over sea and land, and later paintings and sculptures gave those sandals wings.

artifact.title: Nepenthe
artifact.maker: Unknown (given by Polydamna, a woman of Egypt)
artifact.power: Mixed into wine, it banished grief so completely that for that day one shed no tears even at the loss of a parent or brother.
artifact.summary: An Egyptian drug Helen mixed into wine. Whoever drank it forgot every sorrow for that day.
artifact.story:
In Book 4 of the Odyssey, Odysseus's son Telemachus visits King Menelaus of Sparta in search of news of his father. When everyone weeps at the memory of the Trojan War and of Odysseus, Queen Helen secretly slips a drug into the wine they are drinking.

The drug quieted grief and anger and made one forget every pain. Whoever drank it would shed no tears that day, not even if his mother and father died, not even if his brother or son were cut down by the sword before his eyes. Helen had the drug from Polydamna, a woman of Egypt, and the poem sings of Egypt as a land where herbs of every kind grow and every man is skilled in healing.

Nepenthes means 'without sorrow' in Greek. Interpreters have long identified it with opium or some other herb, and later it became the scientific name of the pitcher plants.
artifact.imageAlt: A perfume flask (alabastron) carved from travertine in Ptolemaic Egypt about 305–222 BCE. Above a long, slender body are a narrow neck and small knob handles, and a thin disk lid covers the top.

source.objectCulture: Egypt, Greco-Roman period (332 BCE–395 CE), Ptolemaic dynasty (305–30 BCE)

annotations.title: Disk lid
annotations.body: The thin disk at the top is a lid. It covered the mouth so the perfumed oil would not dry out.

annotations.title: Small handles
annotations.body: Small knob handles are carved on either side below the neck.

annotations.title: Long body
annotations.body: The elongated body carved from travertine. This is an Egyptian perfume flask of about 305–222 BCE. The nepenthe Helen mixed into the wine was also a drug she had from Polydamna, a woman of Egypt.

artifact.title: Moly
artifact.maker: Unknown (Hermes pulled it from the ground and gave it to him)
artifact.power: Whoever carried it could drink the witch Circe's potion without being turned into a beast.
artifact.summary: The herb Hermes gave Odysseus. Its root was black and its flower white as milk, and it protected him from Circe's magic.
artifact.story:
In Book 10 of the Odyssey, Odysseus and his men reach Aeaea, the island where the witch Circe lives. Circe gives the companions who go to scout the island food mixed with a drug, then strikes them with her wand, turns them into pigs and shuts them in sties.

As Odysseus sets out to rescue them, Hermes appears to him in the form of a young man and pulls an herb from the ground for him. Its root is black and its flower white as milk; the gods call it moly. It is hard for mortals to dig up, but the gods can do all things.

Carrying the moly, Odysseus drank Circe's potion and was not changed. As Hermes had told him, he drew his sword and rushed at Circe, and she turned his companions back into men. Odysseus and his crew stayed on that island for a year.
artifact.imageAlt: Circe Giving Drink to the Companions of Ulysses, a chiaroscuro woodcut by Antonio da Trento after Parmigianino, Italy, 1540s. In the round scene Circe holds out a cup at center, the companions take cups and drink at left, and animals appear at right and below.

source.creditLine: Gift of The Print Club of Cleveland
source.objectTitle: Circe Giving Drink to the Companions of Ulysses

annotations.title: Circe
annotations.body: The witch Circe, standing at the center, holds out a cup. The companions of Odysseus who drank her potion were turned into pigs.

annotations.title: Companions taking the cup
annotations.body: At left the companions of Odysseus take cups and drink. Hermes gave Odysseus the herb moly, which protected him from Circe's potion.

annotations.title: Andreani's mark
annotations.body: The two interlaced A's at lower left are the mark of Andrea Andreani, who reprinted this block. This chiaroscuro woodcut was cut in the 1540s by Antonio da Trento after a design by Parmigianino.

artifact.title: Tripods of Hephaestus
artifact.power: With golden wheels beneath their legs, they rolled by themselves to the gathering of the gods and back home again.
artifact.summary: Twenty tripods made by Hephaestus. Fitted with golden wheels, they went to and from the gods' gathering by themselves.
artifact.story:
In Book 18 of the Iliad, Thetis, the mother of Achilles, comes to the house of Hephaestus to ask him to make new armor for her son. She finds the smith god sweating at work on twenty tripods. Under the legs of each he was fitting golden wheels, so that they would roll by themselves to the gathering of the gods and come home again.

The tripods were nearly finished; only the ear-shaped handles were still to be attached. Hephaestus stopped work to welcome Thetis and made new armor for Achilles, the famous shield among it.

In ancient Greece the tripod was among the most precious of gifts and a prize in contests, and tripods were dedicated at the temple of Apollo at Delphi. The self-moving tripods of Hephaestus are often cited as the first automata in Western literature.
artifact.imageAlt: A Greek bronze rod tripod stand of the early sixth century BCE. The round ring at the top is decorated with horse heads and animals, and three legs of crossed thin rods end in animal feet. The surface is covered with green corrosion.

source.creditLine: Gift of Mr. and Mrs. Klaus G. Perls, 1997

annotations.title: Horses and animals
annotations.body: Horse heads and crouching animals ring the top. This is a Greek bronze tripod stand of the early sixth century BCE.

annotations.title: Crossed rod legs
annotations.body: Thin bronze rods are crossed to form the legs. Hephaestus made twenty tripods on golden wheels that rolled by themselves to the gathering of the gods and back.

annotations.title: Animal feet
annotations.body: The legs end in the shape of animal feet.

artifact.title: Golden Maidens of Hephaestus
artifact.power: They thought and spoke like living girls and supported their lame master as he walked.
artifact.summary: Handmaidens Hephaestus made of gold. Like living girls, they had minds, voices and strength.
artifact.story:
In Book 18 of the Iliad, Hephaestus rises to greet Thetis, limping. He is supported by handmaidens made of gold. The poem sings that they looked like living young women, had understanding in their hearts, had voice and strength, and had learned their skills from the gods.

Hephaestus was the son of Zeus and Hera. Some say he was lame from birth, others that he was hurled from heaven and injured his legs. In his forge he made the gods' weapons, palaces and ornaments.

Today the golden maidens are often mentioned, together with Talos, the bronze giant said to have guarded Crete, as the oldest examples of imagining a thinking being made by hand.
artifact.imageAlt: A bronze mirror made in Greece, probably Sicyon, about 470–460 BCE. A clothed woman stands holding a round mirror disk above her head, while winged Erotes fly in from either side. A ring for hanging is attached above the disk.

source.creditLine: Purchase from the J. H. Wade Fund

annotations.title: Woman supporting the mirror
annotations.body: A clothed woman stands bearing the round mirror on her head. This is a Greek bronze mirror, probably from Sicyon, of about 470–460 BCE.

annotations.title: Winged Erotes
annotations.body: Winged Erotes fly in from either side. The woman holding up the mirror may be Aphrodite, goddess of love.

annotations.title: Round mirror disk
annotations.body: The disk of polished bronze that reflected the face. Hephaestus made golden maidens who thought and spoke like living girls to support him at his side.

artifact.title: Net of Hephaestus
artifact.power: Fine as a spider's web, it was invisible even to the gods, and once caught, no one could loosen or break it.
artifact.summary: The net Hephaestus hung around his bed to catch his wife Aphrodite with Ares. Even the gods could not see it.
artifact.story:
In Book 8 of the Odyssey, at a feast of the Phaeacians to which Odysseus is invited, the blind singer Demodocus sings a tale of the gods. Helios the sun, who looks down on all things, told the smith god Hephaestus that his wife Aphrodite was secretly making love with Ares, the god of war.

In his forge Hephaestus hammered out bonds as fine as a spider's web, invisible even to the gods and impossible to break, and hung them around the bed. Then he pretended to leave for the island of Lemnos. When the two lovers lay down in the bed, the net held them so fast they could not move.

When Hephaestus called the gods together, they saw the sight and burst into unquenchable laughter. Only when Poseidon, god of the sea, pledged that Ares would pay was the net loosened.
artifact.imageAlt: Mars and Venus Trapped by Vulcan, an octagonal gilt-bronze relief made in Italy in the late sixteenth century by Guglielmo della Porta. Below center the lovers lie caught in a net on a couch, while the gods gather around and above to watch.

source.objectTitle: Mars and Venus Trapped by Vulcan

annotations.title: The lovers in the net
annotations.body: Below center, Mars and Venus are caught in the net on a couch. The smith god Hephaestus snared them with a net as fine as a spider's web that even the gods could not see.

annotations.title: Watching gods
annotations.body: Above, the gods throng to see the sight. In the Odyssey the gods saw Hephaestus's handiwork and burst into unquenchable laughter.

annotations.title: Vulcan
annotations.body: The man at left appears to be Vulcan, the smith god who set the net. This relief was made in gilt bronze by Guglielmo della Porta in the late sixteenth century.

artifact.title: Pelian Ash Spear
artifact.maker: The centaur Chiron (who cut the ash on Mount Pelion)
artifact.power: So heavy and huge that no one but Achilles could wield it.
artifact.summary: The spear Chiron made from an ash of Mount Pelion and gave to Peleus. Only Achilles could wield it.
artifact.story:
In Book 16 of the Iliad, Patroclus borrows the armor of Achilles and goes into battle, but leaves the spear behind. That spear was heavy, huge and strong, and none of the Achaeans but Achilles could wield it.

The centaur Chiron had cut it from an ash tree on the summit of Mount Pelion and given it to Peleus, Achilles' father, to be the death of heroes. Some say Peleus received it at the time of his marriage to the sea goddess Thetis.

When his friend Patroclus fell at Hector's hands, Achilles put on the new armor Hephaestus had made him, took up this spear and returned to battle. Before the walls of Troy he drove it through Hector's neck.
artifact.imageAlt: Achilles Dragging the Body of Hector, an etching made in Italy in 1648. Achilles in a helmet stands in a chariot with Hector's body dragged behind; a winged goddess appears above, and the walls of Troy rise in the background.

source.creditLine: Gift of The Print Club of Cleveland
source.objectTitle: Achilles Dragging the Body of Hector

annotations.title: Achilles in the chariot
annotations.body: Achilles, helmeted, stands in his chariot. His spear was the ash spear of Mount Pelion that his father Peleus received from the centaur Chiron, and no one but Achilles could wield it.

annotations.title: Hector dragged behind
annotations.body: Hector's body is tied behind the chariot and dragged along. With this spear Achilles killed Hector, who had slain his friend Patroclus.

annotations.title: Walls of Troy
annotations.body: The walls of Troy and onlookers appear in the background. This etching was made in Italy in 1648.

artifact.title: Xanthus and Balius
artifact.maker: Born of Zephyrus, the west wind, and the Harpy Podarge
artifact.power: Horses swift as the wind that never aged or died. Xanthus foretold his master's death in a human voice.
artifact.summary: The two immortal horses that drew Achilles' chariot. Given a voice by Hera, Xanthus foretold his master's death.
artifact.story:
In the Iliad the horses that draw Achilles' chariot are Xanthus and Balius. Born of Zephyrus, the west wind, and the Harpy Podarge, they were swift as the wind. The gods had given them to Peleus as a gift to celebrate his marriage to Thetis.

When Patroclus was killed by Hector, the two immortal horses stood still on the battlefield, heads bowed, shedding tears. Zeus pitied them, regretting that he had given horses that neither age nor die to a mortal man.

When Achilles returned to battle and rebuked his horses, the goddess Hera gave Xanthus a human voice. Xanthus foretold that this time they would bring their master back alive, but that the day of his death was near, and the Erinyes, goddesses of vengeance, soon took his voice away.
artifact.imageAlt: A black-figure neck-amphora made in Athens about 520–510 BCE. On the body a warrior departs for battle with a chariot drawn by four horses; below run bands of meander and bud patterns, and palmettes decorate the neck.

source.creditLine: Purchase from the J. H. Wade Fund
source.objectTitle: Black-Figure Neck-Amphora (Storage Vessel): Departing Warrior with Chariot (A); Battling Warriors (B)

annotations.title: Four horses
annotations.body: Four horses stand side by side to draw the chariot. Achilles' immortal horses Xanthus and Balius were the offspring of Zephyrus, the west wind.

annotations.title: Departing warrior
annotations.body: At right a warrior prepares to leave for battle. This is an Athenian black-figure neck-amphora of about 520–510 BCE; the other side shows warriors fighting.

annotations.title: Pattern bands
annotations.body: Below the scene run bands of winding meander and bud patterns.

artifact.title: Scepter of Agamemnon
artifact.power: The sign of kingship handed down from Zeus; whoever held it ruled many islands and all Argos.
artifact.summary: The scepter Hephaestus made, passed down from Zeus to Agamemnon. It was the sign of his kingship over the Greek army.
artifact.story:
In Book 2 of the Iliad, Agamemnon gathers the Greek army and rises, leaning on his scepter. The poem tells its history: Hephaestus made it and gave it to Zeus; Zeus gave it to his messenger Hermes, and Hermes to Pelops, driver of horses. Pelops gave it to Atreus; Atreus at his death left it to Thyestes, and Thyestes handed it on to Agamemnon, to rule many islands and all Argos.

In the same book Odysseus takes the scepter and with it turns back the soldiers who are about to scatter, and strikes Thersites, who mocks the kings, across the back with it.

The Roman-era traveler Pausanias wrote that the people of Chaeronea in Greece called this scepter 'the Spear,' worshipped it as a god and offered sacrifices to it every day.
artifact.imageAlt: A tin-bronze scepter head made on Cyprus about 1450–1050 BCE. An animal head is attached to the end of a hollow tube, with red and blue inlays in its eyes and forehead. The surface is rough with corrosion.

source.creditLine: The Cesnola Collection, Purchased by subscription, 1874–76

annotations.title: Animal head
annotations.body: An animal head is attached to the end of the scepter, with red and blue inlays in its eyes and forehead.

annotations.title: Socket for the staff
annotations.body: A wooden staff fitted into the hollow tube. This Cypriot tin-bronze scepter head of about 1450–1050 BCE dates from the Late Bronze Age, when the Trojan War is said to have taken place.

annotations.title: A king's scepter
annotations.body: The scepter Agamemnon holds in the Iliad was made by Hephaestus and came to him through Zeus, Hermes, Pelops, Atreus and Thyestes.

artifact.title: Cup of Nestor
artifact.owner: Nestor, the old king of Pylos
artifact.power: When it was full, others could barely lift it, but old Nestor raised it with ease.
artifact.summary: The cup studded with golden nails that Nestor brought from home. On each of its four handles two golden doves were feeding.
artifact.story:
In Book 11 of the Iliad, Nestor, the old king of Pylos, brings the wounded healer Machaon to his tent and offers him a drink. The cup his servant Hecamede sets out is one Nestor brought from home, adorned with golden studs.

The cup had four handles, and on each handle two golden doves were feeding; beneath were two supports. When it was full, any other man could barely lift it from the table, but old Nestor raised it with ease. Hecamede poured wine into the cup and sprinkled it with grated goat's cheese and barley meal.

In 1876, when Heinrich Schliemann found a gold cup with birds perched on its handles in the royal graves at Mycenae, people called it 'Nestor's Cup.' A clay cup of the eighth century BCE from the Italian island of Ischia also bears an inscription that begins 'I am the cup of Nestor.'
artifact.imageAlt: A gold kantharos from Mycenaean Greece, about 1550–1500 BCE. Two tall handles rise on either side of a round-bellied cup hammered from sheet gold, which stands on a small foot.

source.objectTitle: Gold kantharos (drinking cup with two high vertical handles)

annotations.title: Tall handles
annotations.body: Two tall handles rise on either side, cut from long strips of gold sheet, bent and attached.

annotations.title: Gold-sheet body
annotations.body: A cup hammered from sheet gold. This is a gold kantharos from Mycenaean Greece of about 1550–1500 BCE.

annotations.title: Small foot
annotations.body: The body rests on a small foot. In the Iliad, Nestor's cup had four handles with two golden doves feeding on each. When it was full others could barely lift it, but old Nestor raised it with ease.

artifact.title: Aaron's Rod
artifact.power: In a single night it sprouted, blossomed and bore ripe almonds.
artifact.summary: Of the rods of the twelve tribes, only Aaron's sprouted, blossomed and bore almonds overnight. It was kept before the Ark of the Covenant.
artifact.story:
In the Book of Numbers, when some of the Israelites rise against the authority of Moses and Aaron, God has the leader of each of the twelve tribes bring a rod. On the rod of the tribe of Levi is written Aaron's name. Moses lays the rods before God in the tent of the testimony.

The next day, when Moses went into the tent, only Aaron's rod had sprouted, put forth blossoms and borne ripe almonds. It showed whom God had chosen. Aaron's rod was put back before the Ark of the Covenant, to be kept as a sign to the rebels.

The Letter to the Hebrews says that in the Ark were the tablets of the covenant, a golden jar holding manna, and Aaron's rod that budded. Also famous is the story in Exodus in which the rod Aaron cast down before Pharaoh became a serpent and swallowed the serpents of the Egyptian magicians.
artifact.imageAlt: The Priest Aaron, a limestone figure carved in France about 1170. A bearded man in a hood sits holding a round object in both hands on his lap, his robe falling in layered folds.

annotations.title: Hooded head
annotations.body: Aaron the high priest, hooded and long-bearded. The figure was carved in limestone in France about 1170.

annotations.title: Object held in both hands
annotations.body: He holds a round object on his lap in both hands.

annotations.title: Pleated robe
annotations.body: The folds of the robe are carved deeply, falling in layers. In the Book of Numbers, of the rods of the twelve tribes only Aaron's sprouted, blossomed and bore almonds overnight.

artifact.title: Breastplate of the High Priest
artifact.owner: Aaron the high priest and the high priests after him
artifact.power: The high priest wore it on his chest before God, and with the Urim and Thummim placed in it he sought God's will.
artifact.summary: The high priest's breastpiece, set with twelve gems engraved with the names of the twelve tribes. The Urim and Thummim were placed inside it.
artifact.story:
In the Book of Exodus, God gives Moses detailed instructions for the holy garments that Aaron, the high priest, is to wear. One of them is the breastpiece worn on the chest. It was woven of gold, blue, purple and scarlet yarn and fine twisted linen, a span square, and set with four rows of stones.

There were twelve stones, three to a row, and each was engraved like a seal with the name of one of the twelve tribes of Israel. When the high priest entered the sanctuary he wore this breastpiece, bearing the names of the people on his heart before God. Inside it were placed the Urim and Thummim, used to inquire of God's will.

The holy garments, the breastpiece among them, were made by the craftsman Bezalel. The first-century Jewish historian Josephus wrote that the stones of the breastpiece shone when God was present, and he also told how Alexander the Great, arriving at Jerusalem, saw the high priest in his vestments and bowed down before him.
artifact.imageAlt: Alexander the Great and the High Priest of Jerusalem, an engraving made in Italy in the mid-1540s. Alexander in armor kneels, and the high priest in a tall headdress stands before him with a raised hand. A domed temple appears behind.

source.creditLine: Gift of The Print Club of Cleveland
source.objectTitle: Alexander the Great and the High Priest of Jerusalem

annotations.title: Alexander kneeling
annotations.body: Alexander the Great, in armor, kneels before the high priest. Legend says that, moved by the high priest's piety, he approached him on his knees.

annotations.title: The high priest
annotations.body: The high priest of Jerusalem in a tall headdress and long robes. The high priest of Exodus wore on his chest a breastpiece set with twelve gems engraved with the names of the twelve tribes.

annotations.title: Domed temple
annotations.body: The domed building behind depicts the Temple of Jerusalem as Renaissance architecture. This is an Italian engraving of the mid-1540s.

artifact.title: Menorah of the Temple
artifact.owner: The Tabernacle in the wilderness, later the Temple in Jerusalem
artifact.power: A seven-branched lampstand hammered from a talent of pure gold, which lit the sanctuary.
artifact.summary: A seven-branched lampstand hammered from pure gold. It lit the sanctuary of the Tabernacle in the wilderness and of the Temple in Jerusalem.
artifact.story:
In the Book of Exodus, God has Moses make a lampstand of pure gold. Three branches extended from each side of the central shaft, holding seven lamps in all, and each branch bore cups shaped like almond blossoms, with calyxes and flowers. A talent of pure gold went into the lampstand and its utensils.

The lampstand lit the sanctuary of the Tabernacle in the wilderness and later of the Temple in Jerusalem. Hanukkah is the festival commemorating the rededication of the Temple after the Maccabees recovered it from foreign rulers in the second century BCE; for eight nights, lamps modeled on the menorah are lit, one more light each night.

In 70 CE the Roman army destroyed the Temple in Jerusalem and carried the menorah off to Rome. The Arch of Titus in Rome shows soldiers carrying the menorah in procession. Today the menorah appears on the emblem of the State of Israel.
artifact.imageAlt: A silver Hanukkah lamp made in Rome in 1773–75 by the silversmith Gaspare Vanneschi. A branched menorah is embossed at the center of a backplate topped by a shell-shaped arch; a row of oil lamps is attached below, and a hanging cord with tassels is at the top.

source.creditLine: Purchase, Acquisitions Fund, Friends of European Sculpture and Decorative Arts Gifts, Renée E. and Robert A. Belfer, Leon D. and Debra R. Black, Betsy and Ed Cohen/Arete, Mark Fisch and Rachel Davidson, Álvaro Saieh Bendeck, Ruth and Andrew Suzman, Ann Tenenbaum and Thomas H.  Lee, and Merryl H. and James S. Tisch Gifts, 2018

annotations.title: Embossed menorah
annotations.body: A branched menorah is embossed in the center of the backplate. In Exodus God had a seven-branched lampstand made of pure gold.

annotations.title: Oil lamps
annotations.body: A row of oil lamps is attached below. Hanukkah commemorates the rededication of the Temple after the Maccabees recovered it; for eight nights, one more light is kindled each night.

annotations.title: Shell arch
annotations.body: The top is decorated with a shell-shaped arch and scrolls. The lamp was made in Rome in 1773–75 by the silversmith Gaspare Vanneschi for the Baraffael family.

artifact.title: Manna
artifact.owner: The people of Israel in the wilderness
artifact.power: It fell from heaven every morning and fed the Israelites wandering in the wilderness for forty years.
artifact.summary: The food that fell from heaven every morning in the wilderness. It was white like coriander seed and tasted like wafers made with honey.
artifact.story:
In the Book of Exodus, the Israelites who have left Egypt reach the wilderness of Sin and complain to Moses and Aaron that they have nothing to eat. God says he will rain bread from heaven, and the next morning, when the dew has lifted, the ground is covered with something fine and round like frost. The people ask, 'What is it?' and call it manna.

Manna was white like coriander seed and tasted like wafers made with honey. Each person gathered only as much as could be eaten in a day; whatever was kept until the next day bred worms and stank. But on the sixth day they gathered twice as much and ate it on the Sabbath.

The Israelites ate manna for forty years, until they came to the border of the land of Canaan. Moses had an omer of manna put in a jar to be kept for the generations to come.
artifact.imageAlt: Gathering of Manna, a woodcut from the devotional book Der Schatzbehalter (The Treasure Chest), printed in Nuremberg, Germany, in 1491. Round manna pours down from beneath the clouds, and in front of a camp of pointed tents people bend down to gather it into baskets.

annotations.title: Manna falling from heaven
annotations.body: Round manna pours down like rain from beneath the clouds. In Exodus the Israelites gathered and ate the manna that fell every morning in the wilderness.

annotations.title: Tents of the camp
annotations.body: The Israelite camp, lined with pointed tents.

annotations.title: People gathering manna
annotations.body: People bend down to gather the manna into baskets. This is a woodcut from the devotional book Der Schatzbehalter, printed in Nuremberg in 1491.

artifact.title: Joseph's Coat
artifact.power: It showed his father Jacob's special love, and it stirred his brothers' envy.
artifact.summary: The long robe Jacob made for his beloved son Joseph. His brothers dipped it in goat's blood to deceive their father.
artifact.story:
In the Book of Genesis, Jacob loves Joseph, the son of his old age, more than his other sons and makes him a splendid long robe. Old translations call it a 'coat of many colors'; the Hebrew is also read as a robe with long sleeves, or one reaching to the ankles. His brothers envied him, and they hated him all the more when he told them his dream that their sheaves of grain bowed down to his.

When Joseph came to his brothers as they kept sheep in the fields, they stripped him of the robe and threw him into a pit, then sold him to Ishmaelite traders for twenty pieces of silver. They killed a male goat, dipped the robe in its blood and showed it to their father. Jacob believed a wild beast had devoured his son and mourned him for a long time.

Sold into Egypt, Joseph won Pharaoh's trust through his gift for interpreting dreams and rose to govern the land, and there he met again the brothers who came to buy grain in a time of famine.
artifact.imageAlt: Jacob Is Shown Joseph's Coat, a maiolica (tin-glazed earthenware) plate painted by Gironimo Tomasi in Italy about 1560–75. Before old Jacob, seated in a chair at right, his sons hold out the robe, with arched buildings and a landscape behind.

source.creditLine: Gift of Mrs. Francis P. Garvan, 1974
source.objectTitle: Plate with Jacob Is Shown Joseph’s Coat

annotations.title: Jacob seated
annotations.body: Old Jacob, seated in a chair at right, looks at the robe his sons hold out.

annotations.title: Joseph's robe
annotations.body: The brothers hold out Joseph's robe. In Genesis Jacob made a splendid long robe for his beloved son Joseph; his envious brothers sold Joseph, dipped the robe in goat's blood and showed it to their father.

annotations.title: The brothers
annotations.body: The brothers at left. This maiolica plate was painted in Italy about 1560–75 by Gironimo Tomasi.

artifact.title: Elijah's Mantle
artifact.owner: The prophet Elijah, later his disciple Elisha
artifact.power: Rolled up and struck on the water, it parted the Jordan so that one could cross on dry ground.
artifact.summary: The mantle with which Elijah parted the Jordan. It fell as he rose to heaven in a chariot of fire, and he left it to his disciple Elisha.
artifact.story:
In the Books of Kings, the prophet Elijah comes upon Elisha plowing a field and casts his mantle over him, making him his disciple. Later, when God is about to take Elijah up to heaven, Elisha refuses to leave his master and follows him. When the two reach the Jordan, Elijah rolls up his mantle and strikes the water; the water parts, and they cross on dry ground.

Elisha asked for a double share of his master's spirit. Then a chariot of fire drawn by horses of fire appeared and separated the two, and Elijah went up to heaven in a whirlwind. Elisha picked up the mantle that had fallen from his master, went back to the Jordan, struck the water with it and parted the river again.

In Western languages, 'taking up the mantle' of someone still means taking on the work and authority of a teacher or predecessor.
artifact.imageAlt: Elisha and Elijah's Chariot of Fire, an engraving by Jan Saenredam after Abraham Bloemaert, the Netherlands, 1604. Beneath a large tree in a forest Elisha kneels with both arms outstretched, looking up at the sky, where the chariot of fire rises in the distance.

source.creditLine: Seventy-fifth anniversary gift of Louise S. Richards
source.objectTitle: Elisha and Elijah's Chariot of Fire

annotations.title: Chariot of fire
annotations.body: Far off, the chariot of fire rises into the sky. In the Second Book of Kings the prophet Elijah went up to heaven in a whirlwind in a chariot of fire drawn by horses of fire.

annotations.title: Elisha kneeling
annotations.body: His disciple Elisha kneels with both arms outstretched. Picking up the mantle Elijah let fall, Elisha struck the waters of the Jordan with it and parted them.

annotations.title: Great tree
annotations.body: A large twisted tree divides the scene at right. This engraving was made in the Netherlands in 1604.

artifact.title: Gideon's Fleece
artifact.power: Dew fell only on the fleece, and the next day only the fleece stayed dry, revealing God's will.
artifact.summary: The fleece Gideon laid on the threshing floor to confirm God's will. Dew fell only on the fleece, and the next day only the fleece was dry.
artifact.story:
In the Book of Judges, when the Midianites invade every year and seize the harvest, God calls Gideon of the tribe of Manasseh to save Israel. Gideon asks for a sign that God truly means to save Israel by his hand.

He lays a fleece of wool on the threshing floor and asks that dew fall only on the fleece while the ground around it stays dry. The next morning, when he wrings out the fleece, a bowlful of water comes out. Gideon asks once more, this time that only the fleece be dry and dew fall on the ground, and so it was.

Gideon chose only 300 men out of 32,000 and routed the Midianite camp by night, blowing trumpets, smashing jars and raising torches. The Order of the Golden Fleece, founded by the Duke of Burgundy in the fifteenth century, honored Gideon's fleece as well as the Golden Fleece of Jason.
artifact.imageAlt: A page of a Biblia Pauperum blockbook, third edition, printed in the Netherlands about 1465. The Annunciation is at center, Eve and the serpent at left, and Gideon with the fleece at right, with prophets and Latin text above and below, printed in brown ink with traces of hand coloring.

source.objectTitle: The Annunciation, flanked by Eve and the Serpent and Gideon's Fleece, from a "Biblia Pauperum" blockbook, third edition

annotations.title: Gideon and the fleece
annotations.body: Gideon and the fleece are cut in the right panel. In the Book of Judges Gideon laid a fleece on the threshing floor to confirm God's will; dew fell only on the fleece, and the next day only the fleece was dry.

annotations.title: The Annunciation
annotations.body: The center panel shows the angel announcing to Mary that she will conceive Jesus. Medieval readers took the dew that fell only on the fleece as a sign foreshadowing Mary's conception.

annotations.title: Eve and the serpent
annotations.body: The left panel shows Eve and the serpent. This is a page of the blockbook Biblia Pauperum (Bible of the Poor), printed in the Netherlands about 1465.

artifact.title: Throne of Solomon
artifact.power: An ivory throne overlaid with pure gold, with lions on each of its six steps. Nothing like it was made in any kingdom.
artifact.summary: Solomon's ivory throne overlaid with pure gold. Twelve lions stood on either side of its six steps.
artifact.story:
According to the First Book of Kings, King Solomon made a great throne of ivory and overlaid it with the finest gold. The throne had six steps, its back was rounded at the top, there were armrests on either side of the seat, and two lions stood beside them. On each side of the six steps stood a lion as well, twelve in all. The Bible says that nothing like it was ever made in any kingdom.

Solomon is remembered as the wise king who judged the case of two women quarreling over one child. By ordering the child cut in two, he revealed that the woman who gave way to save the child's life was the true mother. The Queen of Sheba too came from afar to test his wisdom.

Later Jewish tradition added marvels to the throne: when the king climbed the steps, the golden lions moved to greet him. In the tenth century the palace of the Byzantine emperor had a mechanical throne with roaring lions, and it was called the Throne of Solomon.
artifact.imageAlt: The Judgment of Solomon, stained glass made in the Southern Netherlands about 1530. Courtiers and two women gather before King Solomon, seated on an ornate golden throne. Silver stain gives a yellow tone to the colored and white glass, and lead lines cross the scene here and there.

annotations.title: Solomon enthroned
annotations.body: King Solomon sits on an ornate throne. In the First Book of Kings Solomon made an ivory throne overlaid with gold, with twelve lions standing on either side of its six steps.

annotations.title: Women before the king
annotations.body: The two women quarreling over a child stand before the king. Solomon found the true mother by ordering the child cut in two.

annotations.title: Colored glass and silver stain
annotations.body: Silver stain gives a yellow tone to the colored and white glass. This is stained glass from the Southern Netherlands of about 1530, thought to have been designed by Dirk Vellert of Antwerp.

artifact.title: Keys of Peter
artifact.owner: The apostle Peter, later the popes of Rome
artifact.power: Whatever is bound on earth is bound in heaven, and whatever is loosed on earth is loosed in heaven.
artifact.summary: The keys of the kingdom of heaven Jesus promised to Peter. They later became the symbol of papal authority.
artifact.story:
In the Gospel of Matthew, Jesus asks his disciples, 'Who do you say that I am?' When Simon answers, 'You are the Christ, the Son of the living God,' Jesus calls him Peter, meaning 'rock,' and says that on this rock he will build his church.

Then he says he will give him the keys of the kingdom of heaven: whatever he binds on earth will be bound in heaven, and whatever he looses on earth will be loosed in heaven. From then on Christian art often showed Peter holding keys, sometimes two of them, one of gold and one of silver.

The pope, as bishop of Rome, is regarded as Peter's successor, and two crossed keys became the arms of the Holy See and of Vatican City State. St. Peter's Basilica in the Vatican was built over the place where Peter is said to be buried.
artifact.imageAlt: A fire-gilt bronze statuette of Saint Peter made in Naples, Italy, in 1635–36. Peter, with a curly beard and a heavy cloak, stands holding a book in his left hand, his right hand lowered. The base set with red stone was made later.

annotations.title: Saint Peter
annotations.body: Peter, with a curly beard, stands wrapped in a heavy cloak. The statuette was made of fire-gilt bronze in Naples, Italy, in 1635–36.

annotations.title: Left hand with a book
annotations.body: He holds a book in his left hand, standing for the teaching he handed on as an apostle.

annotations.title: Lowered right hand
annotations.body: The lowered right hand is shaped as if gripping something. In the Gospel of Matthew Jesus promised Peter the keys of the kingdom of heaven, and afterward Peter was often shown holding keys.

artifact.title: Holy Nails
artifact.owner: Empress Helena and her son Constantine the Great
artifact.power: Nails of the Cross found by Helena; tradition says she had them set in the emperor's crown and his horse's bridle to protect him.
artifact.firstRecord: Ambrose, On the Death of Theodosius
artifact.summary: The nails that fastened Jesus to the Cross. Tradition says Empress Helena found them in Jerusalem and had them set in her son Constantine's crown and his horse's bridle.
artifact.story:
In 395, delivering the funeral oration for the emperor Theodosius, Bishop Ambrose of Milan told the story of Helena, mother of Constantine the Great. In Jerusalem Helena found the True Cross on which Christ was crucified, and she found its nails as well.

According to Ambrose, Helena had one nail made into a crown and another into a bridle and sent them to her son. He read this as the fulfillment of the verse in the Book of Zechariah, 'On that day there shall be written on the bells of the horses, Holy to the Lord.'

Many churches in medieval Europe claimed to hold these nails. The Iron Crown of Monza in Italy is said to be lined with an iron band beaten out of a Holy Nail, and it was used at the coronations of Lombard kings and Holy Roman emperors.
artifact.imageAlt: Gold pendant and necklace parts from the eastern Mediterranean, probably Sirmium or Nicomedia, about 324–26. At the center of an octagonal pendant is a gold coin of Constantine the Great ringed by eight small busts, with two Corinthian-column spacers and a jeweled clasp above.

source.objectTitle: Octagonal Pendant with Corinthian Column Spacers and Clasp Set
source.objectCulture: Byzantium, Late Roman, Eastern Mediterranean, (probably Sirium or Nicomedia), Byzantine period

annotations.title: Constantine's coin
annotations.body: A gold coin of Constantine the Great is set at the center, with the emperor's face on one side and his two sons on the other. Legend says his mother Helena had nails of the Cross found in Jerusalem set into her son's crown and his horse's bridle.

annotations.title: Busts around it
annotations.body: Eight small busts surround the coin. Some of them are figures from mythology.

annotations.title: Column spacers and clasp
annotations.body: The gold spacers shaped like Corinthian columns and the jeweled clasp were part of a large necklace that held this pendant. It seems to have been a gift to a member of the emperor's circle, about 324–26.

artifact.title: Pukku and Mikku
artifact.power: Gilgamesh's favorite plaything, which in the end fell into the netherworld and left Enkidu trapped there.
artifact.firstRecord: Sumerian poem Gilgamesh, Enkidu and the Netherworld
artifact.summary: A plaything Gilgamesh made from the huluppu tree. When it fell into the netherworld, Enkidu went down to fetch it.
artifact.story:
In the Sumerian tale Gilgamesh, Enkidu and the Netherworld, the goddess Inanna replants a huluppu tree from the banks of the Euphrates. But a snake settles in its roots, the lion-headed bird Anzud in its branches and the demoness Lilith in its trunk, so Inanna cannot use the tree. The hero Gilgamesh drives them out and cuts the tree down for her.

Inanna made a chair and a bed from the wood, and from what was left Gilgamesh made the pukku and mikku. Interpreted as a ball and stick, a hoop and driver, or a drum and drumstick, these were what Gilgamesh played with among the young men of Uruk. When the people of the city, worn out by the game, cried out, the pukku and mikku fell down into the netherworld.

His friend Enkidu offered to go down and bring them back. Gilgamesh told him the rules to keep in the netherworld, but Enkidu did not heed them and was held there. The tale was later translated into Akkadian and became the last tablet of the Epic of Gilgamesh.
artifact.imageAlt: A figurine plaque of a bearded man playing a drum, pressed in a mold and fired in Babylonia in the seventh–sixth century BCE. A long-bearded man stands holding a round drum against his chest; the clay is worn and the outlines are blurred.

source.objectTitle: Figurine plaque: bearded man playing a drum

annotations.title: Bearded face
annotations.body: The face of a man with a long beard. This clay plaque was pressed in a mold and fired in Babylonia in the seventh–sixth century BCE.

annotations.title: Drum held to the chest
annotations.body: He holds a round drum against his chest and beats it. The pukku and mikku Gilgamesh made from the huluppu tree are sometimes interpreted as a drum and drumstick.

annotations.title: Worn body
annotations.body: Long wear has blurred the outlines of his clothing and legs. The pukku and mikku fell into the netherworld, and Enkidu, who went down to fetch them, never returned.

artifact.title: Net of Marduk
artifact.power: With the four winds stationed at its four corners, it kept Tiamat, goddess of the sea, from escaping.
artifact.summary: The net Marduk made to capture Tiamat, goddess of the sea. He set the four winds at its corners so nothing could escape.
artifact.story:
In the Babylonian creation epic Enuma Elish, Tiamat, the primeval goddess of the sea, gives birth to monsters to make war on the younger gods. The gods promise the young god Marduk that if he defeats Tiamat they will make him king of the gods.

Along with a bow and arrows and a mace, Marduk made a net. He stationed the south wind and the north wind, the east wind and the west wind at its four corners so that Tiamat could not escape. When Tiamat opened her mouth to swallow him, Marduk cast the net over her, drove the raging winds into her mouth and pierced her with an arrow.

Marduk split Tiamat's body in two to make heaven and earth, took the Tablet of Destinies from her general Kingu and became king of the gods. The epic was recited every year at the New Year festival in Babylon.
artifact.imageAlt: The top fragment of a kudurru (boundary stone) carved in limestone in Babylonia under the Second Dynasty of Isin, about 1156–1025 BCE. A horned dragon, the mushhushshu, sits beside a pointed spade-shaped symbol set on a pedestal, with cuneiform remaining below.

source.objectTitle: Top fragment of a kudurru with a mushhushshu dragon and divine symbols

annotations.title: Mushhushshu dragon
annotations.body: The mushhushshu, a dragon with a horned head and a scaly body. It is the beast that attends Marduk, the god of Babylon.

annotations.title: Spade symbol
annotations.body: The pointed spade (marru) set on the pedestal is the symbol of Marduk. In the Enuma Elish Marduk spread his net and captured Tiamat, goddess of the sea.

annotations.title: Inscription
annotations.body: Cuneiform is carved below. A kudurru recorded a king's grant of land and placed it under the protection of the gods' symbols. This one was made under the Second Dynasty of Isin, about 1156–1025 BCE.

artifact.title: Etana's Eagle
artifact.power: It carried Etana on its back up to the heaven of Anu, god of the sky.
artifact.firstRecord: The Legend of Etana (Old Babylonian version)
artifact.summary: The eagle that flew up to heaven with Etana, king of Kish, on its back. Etana was seeking the 'plant of birth' that would give him a son.
artifact.story:
In the Mesopotamian Legend of Etana, Etana, king of Kish, has no son to succeed him. He prays every day to Shamash, the sun god, for the 'plant of birth' that would let him have a child.

Shamash sends him to an eagle trapped in a pit. The eagle had eaten the young of its friend the serpent, and the serpent, taking revenge, had plucked out its wing feathers and thrown it into the pit. Etana rescued the eagle and cared for it until its wings grew back.

Its strength restored, the eagle carried Etana on its back up to the heaven of Anu, god of the sky. The earth grew smaller and smaller, until at last it looked like a little garden plot. The end of the story is lost where the tablets are broken, but the Sumerian King List records that Etana, the shepherd who ascended to heaven, was succeeded by his son Balih.
artifact.imageAlt: A round ceramic jar from western Iran in the Early Bronze Age, about 2500–1900 BCE. An eagle with outspread wings is painted in black on the shoulder of the pale body, with a broad band of wavy lines below it.

annotations.title: Eagle with outspread wings
annotations.body: An eagle with wings spread wide is painted on the shoulder. Etana rode on an eagle's back to seek the plant of birth from Anu, god of the sky.

annotations.title: Wavy band
annotations.body: A broad band of wavy lines wraps the body beneath the eagle.

annotations.title: Round body
annotations.body: A round jar of fired clay, 31 cm high. It was made in western Iran in the Early Bronze Age, about 2500–1900 BCE.

artifact.title: Adapa's Bread and Water of Life
artifact.maker: Unknown (offered by Anu, god of the sky)
artifact.power: Whoever ate and drank them would live forever.
artifact.summary: The bread and water that Anu, god of the sky, offered the sage Adapa. Adapa refused them, thinking they were the food of death, and lost eternal life.
artifact.story:
In the Mesopotamian Legend of Adapa, Adapa is the sage whom Ea, god of wisdom, placed in the city of Eridu. One day, fishing at sea, he broke the wing of the south wind that had overturned his boat, and for seven days no wind blew. Anu, god of the sky, grew angry and summoned Adapa to heaven.

Ea warned Adapa that in heaven Anu would offer him the bread of death and the water of death, and that he must neither eat nor drink. But after hearing Adapa out, Anu's anger cooled, and what he offered was the bread of life and the water of life. Adapa refused them as Ea had told him, and lost eternal life.

Why Ea gave such advice is still debated. The oldest copy of the story is a fourteenth-century BCE tablet found at Amarna in Egypt, apparently used by Egyptian scribes to learn cuneiform. Later tradition counted Adapa first among the Seven Sages.
artifact.imageAlt: An apkallu (sage) figure modeled in clay in Assyria in the ninth–eighth century BCE. A man wearing a fish skin like a hood from his head down his back stands with both hands held before his chest; the surface is worn and the outlines are blurred.

source.objectTitle: Apkallu figure: male with a fish-skin hood

annotations.title: Fish-skin hood
annotations.body: A fish skin is draped like a hood from the head down the back. This is how the apkallu were shown: sages said to have come up from the sea to teach people wisdom.

annotations.title: Hands before the chest
annotations.body: Both hands are held before the chest. Clay figures like this from ninth–eighth-century BCE Assyria were buried beneath the floors of buildings to ward off evil.

annotations.title: Long robe
annotations.body: A long robe reaching to the feet. The first of the apkallu was the sage Adapa, who refused the bread and water of life offered by Anu, god of the sky, and so lost eternal life.

artifact.title: Chest of Osiris
artifact.power: Made to fit the body of Osiris exactly, it floated down the Nile with him sealed inside.
artifact.summary: The chest Set made to trap his brother Osiris. It drifted across the sea and was enclosed in the trunk of a tree at Byblos.
artifact.story:
According to On Isis and Osiris by the Greek writer Plutarch, Set, brother of Osiris, secretly measured his brother's body and had a beautifully decorated chest made to fit it. Then, at a banquet, he promised the chest to whoever fitted it exactly when lying down in it.

One guest after another lay down in it, but none fitted. At last Osiris climbed in and lay down, and Set and his accomplices slammed the lid, nailed it shut, poured molten lead over it and threw it into the Nile. The chest crossed the sea to Byblos in Phoenicia, where a tree grew up around it and enclosed it in its trunk. The tree was cut down and became a pillar of the royal palace.

Isis, wife of Osiris, traveled all the way to Byblos, took the chest out of the pillar and brought it back to Egypt. But Set found the body, tore it into fourteen pieces and scattered them, and Isis gathered the pieces again. Osiris became king of the underworld, and his son Horus avenged him on Set.
artifact.imageAlt: The coffin of Bakenmut, a priest of the temple of Amun, made of gessoed and painted sycamore fig in Thebes, Egypt, about 1000–900 BCE. The lid at left shows a face, a wig, a broad collar and deities, and the inside of the coffin at right is densely painted with gods and symbols.

source.creditLine: Gift of the John Huntington Art and Polytechnic Trust
source.objectCulture: Egypt, Thebes, Third Intermediate (1069–715 BCE), Dynasties 21–22

annotations.title: Face on the lid
annotations.body: The face and wig of the deceased are painted on the coffin lid. This is the coffin of Bakenmut, a priest of the temple of Amun at Thebes, about 1000–900 BCE.

annotations.title: Collar and wings
annotations.body: A broad collar and deities with outspread wings are painted on the chest.

annotations.title: Paintings inside the coffin
annotations.body: Gods and symbols are densely painted inside the coffin too. According to Plutarch, Set made a chest that fitted his brother Osiris exactly, had him lie in it at a banquet, then shut the lid and set it adrift on the Nile.

artifact.title: Webaoner's Wax Crocodile
artifact.power: Thrown into the water, a wax crocodile seven fingers long became a living crocodile seven cubits long.
artifact.summary: A small crocodile the priest Webaoner modeled in wax. Thrown into the water, it became a great crocodile and dragged his wife's lover under.
artifact.story:
The Westcar Papyrus contains tales in which the sons of King Khufu tell their father stories of the magicians of old. In one of them Webaoner, chief lector priest in the reign of King Nebka, learns that his wife is secretly meeting a commoner.

Webaoner took wax from an ebony chest, modeled a crocodile seven fingers long and recited a spell over it. Then he told his servant to throw the crocodile into the water when the man went to bathe in the garden pool. Thrown in, it became a great crocodile seven cubits long, seized the man and took him down into the water.

Seven days later Webaoner brought the king to the pool and called the crocodile out; when he picked it up in his hand, it turned back into wax. When the king gave the man over to the crocodile, it took him down to the bottom and vanished. The papyrus is a copy from about the seventeenth century BCE and is now in Berlin.
artifact.imageAlt: A small crocodile figure made of Egyptian blue in the late Middle Kingdom of Egypt, about 1850–1700 BCE. The sky-blue crocodile lies flat on its belly with scales incised along its back. A museum number in red writing is visible at right.

annotations.title: Head and snout
annotations.body: The long snout and head. This crocodile was made of Egyptian blue in late Middle Kingdom Egypt, about 1850–1700 BCE.

annotations.title: Scales on the back
annotations.body: Scales are incised along the back.

annotations.title: Short legs
annotations.body: Short legs are set beneath the body. In the Westcar Papyrus the little crocodile the priest Webaoner modeled in wax became a great crocodile when thrown into the water and dragged his wife's lover under.

artifact.title: Babr-e Bayan
artifact.power: It is said that fire could not burn it, water could not soak it and no weapon could pierce it.
artifact.summary: The tiger-skin battle coat Rostam always wore over his armor. It is said to have warded off fire, water and weapons.
artifact.story:
In Ferdowsi's Shahnameh, whenever Rostam, the hero of Iran, goes into battle he wears over his armor the babr-e bayan, a battle coat made of tiger skin. In Persian painting too, Rostam is easy to recognize by his striped hide coat and his leopard-head helmet.

The Shahnameh does not say where the babr-e bayan came from. Later tales say that Rostam made it from the skin of a sea monster or a dragon he had slain, and that fire could not burn it, water could not soak it and no weapon could pierce it.

Wearing this coat, Rostam defended Iran in many battles against Turan. In his fight with Ashkabus, he let his weary horse Rakhsh rest and went out on foot; he first shot down his enemy's horse, then pierced Ashkabus with a single arrow.
