artifact.imageAlt: Rustam Meets the Challenge of Ashkabus, a page from a Shahnameh painted in Shiraz, Iran, about 1590–1600. On a purple field scattered with flowers, Rostam, on foot, shoots an arrow, an enemy champion falls at right, and armies with banners gather above.

source.objectTitle: Rustam meets the challenge of Ashkabus, from a Shah-nama (Book of Kings) of Firdausi (Persian, about 934–1020)

annotations.title: Rostam drawing his bow
annotations.body: Rostam, who has come out to fight on foot, draws his bowstring. Rostam always fought in the babr-e bayan, a battle coat made of tiger skin.

annotations.title: Ashkabus falling
annotations.body: At right Ashkabus, a champion of Turan, falls, struck by the arrow. Rostam first shot down his horse.

annotations.title: Armies with banners
annotations.body: Above, armies with banners gather to watch the fight. The flagpoles reach past the frame of the painting into the paper margin. This is a page from a Shahnameh painted in Shiraz, Iran, about 1590–1600.

artifact.title: Ox-Headed Mace of Fereydun
artifact.maker: Smiths (Fereydun drew its shape for them)
artifact.power: The ox-headed mace that struck down Zahhak, the serpent-shouldered tyrant.
artifact.summary: The ox-headed mace Fereydun had smiths make from a shape he drew. With it he overthrew the tyrant Zahhak.
artifact.story:
In the Shahnameh, Zahhak is a tyrant who ruled Iran for a thousand years, feeding the brains of young men every day to the two serpents that grew from his shoulders. When the blacksmith Kaveh rose up, fixing his leather apron to a spear point as a banner, the people rallied to Fereydun, a prince who had grown up in hiding.

Fereydun summoned smiths, drew the shape of a mace on the ground and had them make an ox-headed mace just like it. Because Zahhak had killed the cow Birmaye that suckled and raised him as a child, some read the ox head as a sign of his vow of revenge.

Fereydun struck Zahhak's helmet with the ox-headed mace and felled him, but did not kill him, for the angel Sorush told him the time had not yet come. Zahhak was chained in a cave on Mount Damavand. The ox-headed mace later became the weapon of Rostam and other Iranian heroes, and Iranian Sufi dervishes also carried it as a symbol.
artifact.imageAlt: A steel and gold mace made in Iran in the nineteenth century. The head is shaped like an ox head with horns and ears, its face inlaid with gold scrolling vines, and the long shaft is ringed with gold bands.

annotations.title: Ox head
annotations.body: The head of the mace is shaped like a horned ox head. In the Shahnameh Fereydun had smiths make an ox-headed mace and with it struck down Zahhak, the serpent-shouldered tyrant.

annotations.title: Gold inlay
annotations.body: Scrolling vines are inlaid in gold on the face and cheeks.

annotations.title: Gold bands on the shaft
annotations.body: The shaft is also ringed with gold bands. This nineteenth-century Iranian mace of steel and gold is modeled on Fereydun's ox-headed mace.

artifact.title: Flying Throne of Kay Kavus
artifact.power: Starving eagles chased the meat hung above them and hauled the throne up into the sky.
artifact.summary: The throne Kay Kavus launched by harnessing four eagles, to conquer the heavens. When the eagles tired, it fell into a forest.
artifact.story:
In the Shahnameh, Kay Kavus, king of Iran, falls prey to a demon's temptation and longs to possess the secrets not only of the earth but of the heavens. He has eaglets captured and raises them on meat into powerful birds.

Then he had a throne made of aloeswood, set up long spears at its four corners and hung lamb from the spear tips. When four starving eagles were tied to the throne, they beat their wings toward the meat and lifted the throne into the sky.

But the eagles tired at last, and the throne fell into a forest. Rostam and the commanders found him and rebuked him for his folly, and Kay Kavus repented in shame. A similar tale of a king who tried to fly and fell appears in the legends of Alexander the Great.
artifact.imageAlt: Kai Kavus Ascends to the Sky, folio 134r of the Shahnameh made for Shah Tahmasp of Safavid Iran, about 1525–30. Between Persian verses above and below, Kay Kavus rises into the sky on a throne drawn by eagles as people look up from below. Gold is flecked in the margins.

source.creditLine: Gift of Arthur A. Houghton Jr., 1970
source.objectTitle: "Kai Kavus Ascends to the Sky", Folio 134r from the Shahnama (Book of Kings) of Shah Tahmasp

annotations.title: The flying throne
annotations.body: At the center, the throne with Kay Kavus seated on it rises into the sky. He set spears at its four corners, hung meat from their tips and tied starving eagles to it so that they flew up toward the meat.

annotations.title: People looking up
annotations.body: Below, people look up at the king rising into the sky. When the eagles tired, the throne fell into a forest, and Rostam and the commanders found him and rebuked him.

annotations.title: Gold-flecked margin
annotations.body: Gold is flecked across the paper margin around the painting. This is folio 134 of the Shahnameh made for Shah Tahmasp of the Safavid dynasty about 1525–30.

artifact.title: Enmerkar's Clay Tablet
artifact.power: By writing on clay a message too long for his envoy to memorize, he sent words in writing for the first time.
artifact.firstRecord: Sumerian epic Enmerkar and the Lord of Aratta
artifact.summary: The clay tablet on which Enmerkar, king of Uruk, is said to have written for the first time. The lord of Aratta could not read the writing he had never seen before.
artifact.story:
In the Sumerian epic Enmerkar and the Lord of Aratta, Enmerkar, king of Uruk, sends an envoy to Aratta, a land far beyond the mountains, demanding gold, silver and precious stones to adorn the temple of the goddess Inanna. The two kings send the envoy back and forth, trading riddling challenges and contests of words.

At last Enmerkar's message grew so long that the envoy could not memorize it all. So Enmerkar smoothed a piece of clay and set the words down on it. The poem says that before this, words had never been put on clay. The lord of Aratta took the tablet and looked it over, but he could not read the writing he had never seen before.

In fact, writing first appeared in Uruk about 3300 BCE as signs for keeping accounts. Through this story, the Sumerians remembered that writing was born in their own city.
artifact.imageAlt: A clay tablet letter written in Babylonia about 1632 BCE. Cuneiform is pressed in dense horizontal lines across a palm-sized rectangular tablet.

annotations.title: Cuneiform
annotations.body: Cuneiform pressed into wet clay with the tip of a reed. This is a private letter written in Babylonia about 1632 BCE.

annotations.title: Clay tablet letter
annotations.body: Writing densely fills a palm-sized tablet. In the Sumerian epic, when his envoy could not memorize a long message, Enmerkar, king of Uruk, is said to have written it on a clay tablet and sent it to the lord of Aratta.

annotations.title: Edge
annotations.body: The writing continues onto the edge. The lord of Aratta, it is said, could not read the writing he had never seen before.

artifact.title: Kaustubha
artifact.owner: Vishnu, the Preserver (and his avatar Krishna)
artifact.maker: Unknown (it rose when the Ocean of Milk was churned)
artifact.power: The most radiant jewel to rise from the Ocean of Milk, which Vishnu always wears on his chest.
artifact.summary: A jewel that rose when the gods and asuras churned the Ocean of Milk. Vishnu always wears it on his chest.
artifact.story:
In the Mahabharata, the gods and the asuras together churn the Ocean of Milk to obtain amrita, the drink of immortality. They make Mount Mandara the churning rod, wind the giant serpent Vasuki around it as the rope and pull from either side. At the bottom of the sea a tortoise held up the mountain; the later Puranas say the tortoise was an avatar of Vishnu.

One by one, treasures rose from the sea: the moon, Lakshmi the goddess of fortune, the goddess of wine and the white horse Uchchaihshravas, and then the shining jewel Kaustubha. The Kaustubha went to the chest of Vishnu.

Ever since, Vishnu and his avatar Krishna have been depicted wearing the Kaustubha on the chest. Last of all, Dhanvantari, the god of medicine, rose from the sea bearing a pot of amrita.
artifact.imageAlt: A granite figure of Vishnu carved in Tamil Nadu, South India, in the early Chola dynasty, about 900–950. The four-armed god in a tall crown stands on a base, holding a discus and a conch in his two rear hands, with layers of ornaments on his chest.

source.objectCulture: South India, Tamil Nadu, probably Pudokkatai, early Chola Dynasty, 10th Century

annotations.title: Tall crown
annotations.body: The tall crown marks Vishnu as king. The figure was carved in granite in early Chola South India, about 900–950.

annotations.title: Discus and conch
annotations.body: He holds a discus and a conch in his two rear hands. The discus is carved as seen from the side.

annotations.title: Ornaments on the chest
annotations.body: Layers of necklaces hang on his chest. Vishnu wears on his chest the Kaustubha, the jewel that rose when the gods churned the Ocean of Milk.

artifact.title: Uchchaihshravas
artifact.maker: Unknown (it rose from the Ocean of Milk)
artifact.power: A dazzling white horse born from the Ocean of Milk, the first of all horses.
artifact.summary: The white horse that rose when the Ocean of Milk was churned. It became the horse of Indra, king of the gods.
artifact.story:
In the Mahabharata, when the gods and the asuras churn the Ocean of Milk, a dazzling white horse rises from the sea. Its name, Uchchaihshravas, means 'with ears held high' or 'neighing loudly.' The horse fell to Indra, king of the gods. In the Bhagavad Gita, Krishna says that among horses he is Uchchaihshravas.

The first book of the Mahabharata also tells of a wager over this horse. Kadru and Vinata, the two wives of the sage Kashyapa, bet on the color of Uchchaihshravas's tail. Vinata said it was white; Kadru said it was black.

Kadru, mother of the serpents, told her serpent sons to hang from the tail so that it would look black, and so she won the bet, and Vinata became Kadru's slave. To free his mother, Vinata's son Garuda flew up to heaven to fetch the gods' amrita.
artifact.imageAlt: A Saddled Horse, painted on paper by an artist of the Pahari kingdoms of northern India about 1750. A bridled horse stands facing left, head lowered and neck arched, with a saddle and saddlecloth on its back. It is drawn in line and lightly colored.

annotations.title: Head and bridle
annotations.body: The horse's head in a bridle. The head is lowered and the neck arched.

annotations.title: Saddle
annotations.body: The saddle and saddlecloth on its back. This painting by an artist of the Pahari kingdoms of northern India dates from about 1750; kings had portraits made of their favorite horses.

annotations.title: Slender legs
annotations.body: Slender, straight legs. Uchchaihshravas, the white horse that rose when the Ocean of Milk was churned, became the horse of Indra, king of the gods.

artifact.title: Sharanga
artifact.owner: Vishnu, the Preserver, and his avatars Krishna and Rama
artifact.power: The bow of Vishnu, which only his avatar could string.
artifact.summary: The bow of Vishnu. His avatar Krishna was called 'the bearer of Sharanga.'
artifact.story:
In Indian myth, Vishnu the Preserver bears the bow Sharanga, along with the discus Sudarshana, the mace Kaumodaki and the conch Panchajanya. The Mahabharata repeatedly calls Krishna, Vishnu's avatar, 'the bearer of Sharanga.'

In the Ramayana, Rama, another avatar of Vishnu, breaks the bow of Shiva and marries Sita, and then meets the angry Parashurama, the sage of the axe. When Parashurama holds out the bow of Vishnu and challenges him to string it, Rama strings it with ease. Parashurama recognizes that Rama is Vishnu and withdraws.

The name Sharanga is sometimes interpreted as 'made of horn.' The composite bow, built of layered horn and wood, was the most powerful bow of the ancient world.
artifact.imageAlt: A page from a Ramayana painted in Malwa, central India, about 1650: Rama, Sita and Lakshmana visit the hermitage of the sage Bharadvaja. Against a red ground, blue-skinned Rama, holding a bow, bows with his companions to the sage; the yellow-doored hermitage is at right, trees above.

source.creditLine: Purchase and partial gift from the Catherine and Ralph Benkaim Collection; Severance and Greta Millikin Purchase Fund
source.objectTitle: Rama, Sita, and Lakshmana visit the hermitage of the sage Bharadvaja at Prayaga, from Chapter 48 of the Ayodhya Kanda (Book of Ayodhya) of a Ramayana (Rama’s Journey)
source.objectCulture: Central India, Malwa Region, Madhya Pradesh

annotations.title: Rama with his bow
annotations.body: Blue-skinned Rama stands holding a bow. Rama, the avatar of Vishnu, took Vishnu's bow from Parashurama and strung it.

annotations.title: Sita and Lakshmana
annotations.body: Beside Rama are his wife Sita and his brother Lakshmana.

annotations.title: The sage Bharadvaja
annotations.body: At right the sage Bharadvaja welcomes them. This is a page from a Ramayana painted in the Malwa region of central India about 1650.

artifact.title: Vasavi Shakti
artifact.owner: Indra, king of the gods, later the hero Karna
artifact.power: It could be hurled only once, and whoever it was thrown at would surely die.
artifact.summary: The spear Indra gave Karna in exchange for his armor and earrings. It could be thrown only once and was sure to kill.
artifact.story:
Karna, a hero of the Mahabharata, is the son of Surya, the sun god, and the armor and earrings that were part of his body from birth kept him from being wounded by anyone. Indra, king of the gods and father of Arjuna, feared that his son would lose to Karna in the war to come.

Indra disguised himself as a Brahmin, went to Karna and asked for his armor and earrings. His father Surya had warned him, but Karna, who had vowed never to send away anyone who asked of him empty-handed, cut the armor and earrings from his body and gave them. Moved, Indra gave him in return the spear Vasavi Shakti, which could be hurled only once.

Karna saved the spear for Arjuna. But when the giant Ghatotkacha routed the Kaurava army in a night battle of the Kurukshetra war, Karna had no choice but to hurl the spear and bring him down. The spear returned to Indra, and Krishna rejoiced that Arjuna would live.
artifact.imageAlt: A male figure, possibly Indra, carved in schist in Gandhara (probably the Swat region of present-day Pakistan) in the 300s–400s CE. The figure, apparently unfinished with only its broad outlines carved, stands in a niche and wears a flat-topped crown.

source.creditLine: Gifts of Barbara Greenough Bradley in honor of Mary Grafton Ballou, Howard C. Wechsler, M.D., and Various Donors

annotations.title: Flat-topped crown
annotations.body: A crown with a flat top is a mark of Indra, king of the gods.

annotations.title: Unfinished body
annotations.body: Only the broad outlines of the body were carved. It seems to have been left unfinished in schist in Gandhara in the 300s–400s CE.

annotations.title: Niche
annotations.body: The figure is carved inside a niche. In the Mahabharata Indra took Karna's armor and earrings and gave him in return Vasavi Shakti, a spear that could be used only once.

artifact.title: Chandrahasa
artifact.owner: Ravana, the demon king of Lanka
artifact.power: The sword Shiva granted Ravana; its name means 'laughter of the moon.'
artifact.summary: The sword Shiva granted to the demon king Ravana. Its name means 'laughter of the moon.'
artifact.story:
According to the last book of the Ramayana, Ravana, the demon king of Lanka, defeated his half-brother Kubera, seized his flying chariot Pushpaka and tried to pass over Mount Kailasa. When the mountain blocked the chariot, Ravana in his rage lifted the whole mountain and shook it.

Shiva, who sat on the mountain, pressed it down with one toe, and Ravana, his arms pinned beneath it, roared aloud. Because that roar shook the world, he got the name Ravana, 'the one who roars.' Ravana sang Shiva's praises for a long time.

Shiva released him and granted him the sword Chandrahasa. The name, 'laughter of the moon,' is taken to refer to a blade curved like a crescent moon. Ravana fought many battles with this sword, but in the end, for abducting Sita, he fell to Rama's arrows.
artifact.imageAlt: Ravana Shaking Mount Kailasa, a sandstone relief carved in Madhya Pradesh, central India, in the eighth century. Above, Shiva and Parvati sit side by side on the mountain; below, many-headed, many-armed Ravana lifts and shakes the mountain, surrounded by densely carved attendants.

source.objectCulture: Central India, Madhya Pradesh, Chandela Dynasty, 8th century

annotations.title: Shiva and Parvati
annotations.body: Shiva and his wife Parvati sit side by side atop Mount Kailasa.

annotations.title: Ravana shaking the mountain
annotations.body: Below, the many-headed, many-armed demon king Ravana lifts and shakes the mountain. When Shiva pressed the mountain down with his toe and trapped Ravana, Ravana sang Shiva's praises for a long time.

annotations.title: Rocks of the mountain
annotations.body: Bands of rock crowded with people and animals represent Mount Kailasa. This is an eighth-century sandstone sculpture from central India. Moved by Ravana's praises, Shiva released him and granted him the sword Chandrahasa.

artifact.title: Sita's Hair Jewel
artifact.power: As the token that Hanuman had found Sita, it told Rama she was still alive.
artifact.summary: The hair jewel the captive Sita gave Hanuman as a token when he found her. Rama wept when he saw it.
artifact.story:
In the Ramayana, the demon king Ravana abducts Sita and holds her captive in the Ashoka grove on the island of Lanka. Hanuman, the monkey commander, leaps across the sea to Lanka, shrinks himself, hides in a tree and finds Sita.

Hanuman shows her the ring he received from Rama, making known that he is Rama's messenger. As a token to carry to Rama, Sita unfastens the jewel she wore in her hair, the chudamani, and gives it to Hanuman.

When Hanuman returned and presented the jewel, Rama pressed it to his heart and wept. The jewel, it is said, had been given to Sita at her wedding. Soon Rama led the monkey army, built a bridge across the sea and crossed to Lanka.
artifact.imageAlt: Hanuman Spies Sita in the Ashoka Grove, a page from the 'Shangri' Ramayana painted in Himachal Pradesh, northern India, about 1700–25. On a night with a crescent moon, Sita sits in a white pavilion surrounded by animal-faced demonesses, while Hanuman looks down from a tree.

source.objectTitle: Hanuman spies Sita in the Ashoka Grove, from the “Shangri” Ramayana
source.objectCulture: Northern India, Pahari kingdoms, Himachal Pradesh

annotations.title: Hanuman in the tree
annotations.body: Hanuman, in the form of a small monkey, hides in the tree and looks down at Sita. He had shrunk himself to slip in.

annotations.title: Sita in captivity
annotations.body: In the pavilion sits Sita, carried off by Ravana. She gave Hanuman, who had come to find her, her hair jewel as a token to show Rama.

annotations.title: Demonesses around Sita
annotations.body: Rakshasa women with animal faces surround and taunt Sita. This is a page from the 'Shangri' Ramayana painted in Himachal Pradesh, northern India, about 1700–25.

artifact.title: Draupadi's Sari
artifact.owner: Draupadi, wife of the five Pandava brothers
artifact.power: However hard it was pulled, the cloth went on without end and saved Draupadi from disgrace.
artifact.summary: The garment of Draupadi, dragged into the gambling hall. However hard it was pulled, it went on without end and protected her.
artifact.story:
In the Mahabharata, Yudhishthira, eldest of the five Pandava brothers, plays at dice with his cousins the Kauravas and loses his kingdom, his wealth, his brothers and himself, and at last stakes and loses their wife Draupadi too.

Duhshasana, second of the Kaurava brothers, drags Draupadi into the gambling hall and tries to strip off her garment before everyone. Draupadi prays to the gods, and the cloth he pulls goes on without end; though the fabric piles up like a mountain, Duhshasana cannot unclothe her. Later versions say that Krishna protected her.

This humiliation became the seed of the great war in which the Pandavas and Kauravas clashed at Kurukshetra. Draupadi is said to have been born from the fire of a sacrifice offered by Drupada, king of Panchala, after her brother Dhrishtadyumna.
artifact.imageAlt: A page from the Razmnama, the Persian Mahabharata, painted in Mughal India in 1598: Yaja and Upayaja perform a sacrifice for Dhrishtadyumna to emerge from the fire. From the flames of a roofed altar an armored youth appears, with Brahmins around and people gathered below.

source.creditLine: Gift in honor of Madeline Neves Clapp; Gift of Mrs. Henry White Cannon by exchange; Bequest of Louise T. Cooper; Leonard C. Hanna Jr. Fund; From the Catherine and Ralph Benkaim Collection
source.objectTitle: Yaja and Upayaja perform a sacrifice for the emergence of Dhrishtadyumna from the fire, from Adi-parva (volume one) of the Razm-nama (Book of Wars) adapted and translated into Persian by Mir Ghiyath al-Din Ali Qazvini, known as Naqib Khan (Persian, d. 1614) from the Sanskrit Mahabharata
source.objectCulture: Mughal India; made for Abd al-Rahim the Khan Khanan

annotations.title: Dhrishtadyumna emerging from the fire
annotations.body: From the flames of the altar appears Dhrishtadyumna, a youth in armor. In the Mahabharata his twin sister Draupadi was born from the same sacrificial fire after him.

annotations.title: Brahmins performing the sacrifice
annotations.body: Around it, the Brahmins Yaja and Upayaja and other priests perform the sacrifice.

annotations.title: People watching
annotations.body: Below, people gather to watch the sacrifice. Draupadi was dragged out when her husbands lost at dice and was nearly stripped, but however hard it was pulled her sari went on without end. This painting was made in Mughal India in 1598.

artifact.title: Sanjeevani
artifact.maker: Unknown (it grew on the mountain of herbs in the Himalayas)
artifact.power: An herb that could revive even the dying.
artifact.summary: The Himalayan herb that saved the fallen Lakshmana. Unable to tell which herb it was, Hanuman carried back the whole mountain.
artifact.story:
In the Ramayana, when Rama's army fights Ravana's army in Lanka, Rama's brother Lakshmana falls, struck by an enemy weapon. Sushena, physician of the monkey army, says that only the herbs growing on the mountain of herbs in the Himalayas can save him.

Hanuman flew through the sky to the Himalayas, but the herbs hid themselves, and he could not tell which was which. So Hanuman tore off the whole peak and flew back with it. Touched by the power of the herbs, Lakshmana was healed of his wounds and rose to his feet.

Hanuman carrying the mountain became one of the most beloved scenes in India and Southeast Asia. The herb's name, sanjeevani, means 'that which revives.'
artifact.imageAlt: A bronze Flying Hanuman in the Koh Ker style of tenth-century Cambodia. The monkey god in a tall crown, mouth wide open and one knee bent, raises both arms high in the pose of taking flight.

source.creditLine: Severance and Greta Millikin Purchase Fund

annotations.title: Hand holding the antidote
annotations.body: In his raised right hand he holds an antidote. In the Ramayana Hanuman flew to the Himalayas for the herb that would save the gravely wounded Lakshmana, and when he could not tell which herb it was, he brought back the whole mountain.

annotations.title: Hand of fearlessness
annotations.body: His left hand is raised in the gesture meaning 'fear not.'

annotations.title: Monkey face
annotations.body: A monkey face with mouth wide open, and a tall crown. This is a bronze in the Koh Ker style of tenth-century Cambodia.

artifact.title: Soma
artifact.owner: Indra, king of the gods, and the Vedic gods
artifact.maker: Unknown (pressed from the juice of the soma plant)
artifact.power: The hymns sing that whoever drinks it is filled with strength and inspiration and becomes immortal.
artifact.summary: The sacred drink of the Rigveda and the god of that drink. Indra drank soma and defeated the dragon Vritra.
artifact.story:
The priests of the Rigveda crushed the stalks of the soma plant, which grew in the mountains, with stones to press out the juice, strained it through wool and offered the gods a drink mixed with water and milk. The ninth book of the Rigveda consists entirely of hymns to this drink and to Soma, its god.

Indra, king of the gods, drank down the soma and, gaining strength, struck Vritra, the dragon that had imprisoned the waters, with his vajra and set the rivers free. One hymn sings, 'We have drunk the soma, we have become immortal, we have come to the light.'

What plant soma was has never been settled; some think it was ephedra, others a mushroom. In later texts Soma was identified with the moon god, and the Iranian Avesta speaks of haoma, a drink with the same roots.
artifact.imageAlt: Nine Celestial Bodies (Navagraha), carved in sandstone in central India in the eighth century. Gods stand in a row on a long stone: at far left the sun god in a tall crown with the goddess of dawn, then the moon and the planetary gods in similar poses, and at right Rahu with a huge head.

source.creditLine: Gift of Doris and Ed Wiener

annotations.title: The sun god
annotations.body: At far left is the sun god in a tall crown, with the small goddess of dawn before him.

annotations.title: The moon god
annotations.body: Second from left is the Moon. In the Rigveda soma was the drink of the gods and the god of that drink, and later he was identified with the moon god.

annotations.title: Rahu's head
annotations.body: The huge head at right is Rahu, said to swallow the sun and moon and cause eclipses. This eighth-century carving of the nine celestial bodies once adorned a temple doorway in central India.

artifact.title: Parijata Tree
artifact.owner: Indra, king of the gods, later Krishna and his wife Satyabhama
artifact.power: A heavenly tree whose flowers never wither and whose fragrance spreads far.
artifact.summary: A heavenly flowering tree in Indra's paradise. Krishna brought it down to earth for his wife Satyabhama.
artifact.story:
According to the Harivamsha, an appendix to the Mahabharata, the parijata is a heavenly flowering tree that grows in the paradise of Indra, king of the gods. Its flowers never withered, and their fragrance spread far. Some tales say the tree rose when the Ocean of Milk was churned.

After defeating the demon king Naraka together with his wife Satyabhama, Krishna went up to heaven to return the earrings of Aditi, Indra's mother, which Naraka had stolen. There Satyabhama longed for this tree. Krishna uprooted it, loaded it on Garuda and set off home, and a battle broke out with Indra, who tried to stop him.

Krishna defeated Indra, brought the tree to Dwaraka and planted it in Satyabhama's garden. In India a fragrant flowering tree whose blossoms open at night and fall in the morning is still called parijata.
artifact.imageAlt: Krishna and Satyabhama Storm the Citadel of Naraka, folio 97 of a Bhagavata Purana painted in Kathmandu, Nepal, about 1775. Seen from above, the citadel is ringed by layers of walls like a mandala, and Krishna and Satyabhama fly in from the right to attack. Text is written below.

source.objectTitle: Krishna and Satyabhama Storm the Citadel of Naraka, folio 97 from a Bhagavata Purana

annotations.title: Krishna and Satyabhama in flight
annotations.body: From the right Krishna and his wife Satyabhama fly in on the bird Garuda to attack the citadel.

annotations.title: Naraka's citadel
annotations.body: The citadel of the demon king Naraka, ringed with layers of walls. Seen from above, it looks like a mandala.

annotations.title: Text below
annotations.body: Below is written text describing the scene. This is folio 97 of a Bhagavata Purana painted in Kathmandu, Nepal, about 1775. After defeating Naraka, Krishna brought the parijata tree from Indra's paradise and planted it in Satyabhama's garden.

artifact.title: Golden Chain Mail
artifact.owner: Sun Wukong, the Great Sage Equal to Heaven
artifact.maker: Unknown (given by the Dragon King of the Western Sea)
artifact.power: Armor woven of golden chain links, which with a phoenix-feather cap and cloud-walking shoes became Sun Wukong's outfit.
artifact.firstRecord: Wu Cheng'en, Journey to the West
artifact.summary: The golden chain mail Sun Wukong pestered the Dragon Kings into giving him. With a phoenix-feather golden cap and cloud-walking shoes, it became his outfit.
artifact.story:
In Chapter 3 of Journey to the West, after getting the As-You-Will Gold-Banded Staff from the Dragon Palace of the Eastern Sea, Sun Wukong pesters the Dragon King of the Eastern Sea to hand over clothes to go with it as well. The Dragon King summons his brothers, the Dragon Kings of the Northern, Western and Southern Seas.

The Dragon King of the Northern Sea brought cloud-walking shoes woven of lotus fiber, the Dragon King of the Western Sea a suit of golden chain mail, and the Dragon King of the Southern Sea a cap of purple gold set with phoenix feathers. Sun Wukong put them all on and went back to the Mountain of Flowers and Fruit, swinging his staff.

The angry Dragon Kings denounced Sun Wukong to the Jade Emperor. This became the beginning of the great havoc in which Sun Wukong turned heaven upside down.
artifact.imageAlt: A ceremonial uniform of the Qing dynasty (1644–1911). Brown silk lined with blue silk is closely studded with metal rivets and embroidered with gold thread, with a tasseled helmet, shoulder guards, a round metal plate on the chest and a skirt embroidered with dragons.

annotations.title: Helmet
annotations.body: A helmet with a tassel at the top. This is a Qing-dynasty ceremonial uniform.

annotations.title: Round plate on the chest
annotations.body: A round metal plate is fixed on the chest. Metal rivets closely set in the silk make it look like scale armor.

annotations.title: Dragon-patterned skirt
annotations.body: Dragons are embroidered in gold thread on the skirt. In Journey to the West Sun Wukong received golden chain mail from the Dragon King of the Western Sea and put it on.

artifact.title: Nine-Ringed Monk's Staff
artifact.power: It was said that whoever leaned on this staff would come to no poisonous harm.
artifact.firstRecord: Wu Cheng'en, Journey to the West
artifact.summary: The monk's staff the bodhisattva Guanyin bestowed, with a cassock of gold brocade, on Tripitaka as he set out west for the scriptures. Whoever leaned on it came to no poisonous harm.
artifact.story:
In Chapter 12 of Journey to the West, the bodhisattva Guanyin comes to Chang'an at the Buddha's command to find someone to bring the scriptures back from India in the west. Disguised as a monk, she goes through the streets offering to sell a cassock of gold brocade and a monk's staff with nine rings.

When Emperor Taizong of Tang bought them and gave them to the monk Tripitaka, the bodhisattva told of their virtues: whoever wore the cassock would not fall into hell, and whoever leaned on the staff would come to no poisonous harm. Wearing this cassock and leaning on this staff, Tripitaka set out on the road west.

A monk's staff is a walking stick carried by Buddhist monks; the rings on its head jingle as it moves, driving off animals and insects on the road and announcing a monk come to beg for alms. The real monk Xuanzang left Chang'an about 629, traveled to India and back, and recorded his journey in the Great Tang Records on the Western Regions.
artifact.imageAlt: A Buddhist monk's staff (shakujō) made in Japan in the early nineteenth century. Several rings hang from the round loop of the bronze head, and below it runs a lacquered wooden shaft carved with patterns.

annotations.title: Ringed head
annotations.body: Several rings hang from the head of the staff and jingle when it is shaken. On the road the sound drove off animals and insects.

annotations.title: Lacquered shaft
annotations.body: The wooden shaft is lacquered and carved with patterns. This monk's staff was made in Japan in the early nineteenth century.

annotations.title: Monk's staff
annotations.body: A staff carried by Buddhist monks. In Journey to the West the bodhisattva Guanyin bestowed on the Tang monk Tripitaka a cassock of gold brocade and a staff with nine rings.

artifact.title: Eight Trigrams Furnace
artifact.owner: Taishang Laojun, the Supreme Old Lord
artifact.power: An elixir furnace whose fire was governed by the directions of the eight trigrams; it was said it could melt anything away.
artifact.firstRecord: Wu Cheng'en, Journey to the West
artifact.summary: The furnace in which Taishang Laojun brewed his elixirs. Sun Wukong endured forty-nine days in it and came out with eyes that could see through anything.
artifact.story:
In Chapter 7 of Journey to the West, Sun Wukong, having thrown heaven into turmoil, cannot be harmed by blades, fire or thunderbolts, for his body has grown hard from gorging on the peaches of immortality and elixir pills. Taishang Laojun says he will put him in his Eight Trigrams Furnace and melt him down like an elixir.

Inside the furnace, Sun Wukong slipped into the position of the trigram Xun, the direction of wind, and escaped the flames. Only the smoke blown by the wind reached him, leaving his eyes red and sore, but thanks to it he gained the 'fiery golden eyes' that could see through anything.

After forty-nine days, when the lid was opened, Sun Wukong leaped out and kicked the furnace over. Chapter 59 of Journey to the West tells that bricks that fell from the furnace then became the Flaming Mountains. Sun Wukong's rampage ended only when the Buddha caught him and pinned him beneath the Mountain of Five Elements.
artifact.imageAlt: A tripod incense burner cast in copper alloy in 1346, in the Yuan dynasty. Animal-face motifs and the eight trigrams are cast in relief on a band around the round-bellied body, with characters inscribed below, and it stands on three short, thick legs.

source.creditLine: Purchase, Friends of Asian Art Gifts, 2016

annotations.title: Animal faces and the eight trigrams
annotations.body: Animal-face motifs and the eight trigrams are cast in relief on the band around the body. The eight trigrams stand for the eight things that make up the world, such as heaven, earth, water and fire.

annotations.title: Inscription
annotations.body: Characters are inscribed on the lower body. This copper-alloy incense burner was made in 1346, in the Yuan dynasty.

annotations.title: Three legs
annotations.body: It stands on three short, thick legs. In Journey to the West Sun Wukong was shut in Taishang Laojun's Eight Trigrams Furnace for forty-nine days, but in the fire he gained the 'fiery golden eyes' that could see through anything.

artifact.title: Fahai's Alms Bowl
artifact.power: When it was clapped over the white snake spirit, she revealed her true form and shrank until she was trapped beneath it.
artifact.firstRecord: Feng Menglong, Stories to Caution the World (Madam White Under Leifeng Pagoda)
artifact.summary: The alms bowl in which the monk Fahai trapped Madam White, the white snake. Trapped beneath it, she was buried under Leifeng Pagoda.
artifact.story:
In 'Madam White Is Kept Forever Under Leifeng Pagoda,' from Stories to Caution the World compiled by Feng Menglong in the late Ming dynasty, the young man Xu Xuan takes shelter from the rain by West Lake in Hangzhou, meets the beautiful Madam White and her maid Qingqing, and marries her. But Madam White is in truth an ancient white snake.

Fahai, a monk of Jinshan Temple, gave Xu Xuan an alms bowl and told him to clap it over Madam White's head. When Xu Xuan did so, Madam White grew smaller and smaller until she was trapped beneath the bowl, and when Fahai came she was revealed in her true form, a white snake.

Fahai buried the snake trapped in the bowl in front of Leifeng Temple by West Lake and had a pagoda built over it. When the real Leifeng Pagoda collapsed in 1924, people remembered the tale of Madam White, and the story has been made again and again into Peking opera and film.
artifact.imageAlt: A wide bronze alms bowl made in Korea in the early 1900s. A round sun, clouds and rocky mountains are incised in fine lines on the golden-toned body.

annotations.title: Sun and clouds
annotations.body: A round sun and clouds are incised in fine lines on the body. Bowls engraved with the sun, moon and Big Dipper like this one are thought to have been used in shamanic rites.

annotations.title: Rocky mountains
annotations.body: Rocky mountains are incised below.

annotations.title: Bronze alms bowl
annotations.body: A wide alms bowl of bronze, made in Korea in the early 1900s. In 'Madam White Under Leifeng Pagoda,' the monk Fahai gave Xu Xuan an alms bowl that, clapped over the white snake, would reveal her true form and trap her.

artifact.title: Shennong's Red Whip
artifact.owner: Shennong, god of agriculture and medicine
artifact.power: Striking every kind of plant with it, he learned whether each was warming or cooling and whether it was poisonous.
artifact.firstRecord: Gan Bao, In Search of the Supernatural
artifact.summary: The red whip with which Shennong is said to have struck every plant to tell medicine from poison.
artifact.story:
In Search of the Supernatural, compiled by Gan Bao of the Eastern Jin, begins with Shennong. Shennong struck every kind of plant with a red whip and learned whether each was mild or poisonous, cold or warm, and he examined their smells and tastes. Because he then had people plant all the grains, the world called him Shennong, the Divine Farmer.

Shennong is one of the Three Sovereigns of Chinese legend, said to have first taught agriculture and medicine. The Huainanzi says he tasted every plant himself, encountering seventy poisons in a single day.

China's first book of materia medica, the Divine Farmer's Classic of Materia Medica, borrowed his name. In Japan and Korea too Shennong was revered as the ancestor of medicine, and pharmacies and physicians sometimes hung his picture.
artifact.imageAlt: Shennong, a hanging scroll painted in ink on paper in Muromachi-period Japan, late 1400s–early 1500s. Shennong, with small horns sprouting from his tousled head, holds a leaf in his mouth and stares wide-eyed, wearing a garment woven of leaves.

source.creditLine: Mr. and Mrs. William H. Marlatt Fund

annotations.title: Face tasting a plant
annotations.body: Shennong tastes a leaf held in his mouth. He is said to have tasted every plant himself to tell medicine from poison.

annotations.title: Garment of leaves
annotations.body: He wears a garment woven of leaves. This hanging scroll was painted in ink in Muromachi-period Japan, late 1400s–early 1500s.

annotations.title: Horned head
annotations.body: Small horns sprout from his head. Gan Bao's In Search of the Supernatural says that Shennong struck every plant with a red whip and learned whether each was warming or cooling and whether it was poisonous.

artifact.title: Twin Swords of Liu Bei
artifact.owner: Liu Bei, emperor of Shu Han
artifact.maker: Unknown (Liu Bei had a smith make them)
artifact.power: A pair of swords sheathed in one scabbard, which Liu Bei wielded one in each hand.
artifact.firstRecord: Luo Guanzhong, Romance of the Three Kingdoms
artifact.summary: The twin swords Liu Bei had made after the Oath of the Peach Garden. Guan Yu's Green Dragon Crescent Blade and Zhang Fei's long spear were made at the same time.
artifact.story:
At the opening of Luo Guanzhong's Romance of the Three Kingdoms, Liu Bei, Guan Yu and Zhang Fei swear brotherhood in a peach garden and resolve to fight the Yellow Turbans. When the horse traders Zhang Shiping and Su Shuang give them fine horses, gold, silver and iron, the three have a skilled smith make each his own weapon.

Liu Bei had made a pair of swords sheathed in one scabbard, Guan Yu the Green Dragon Crescent Blade and Zhang Fei a long spear. Liu Bei wielded the twin swords, one in each hand, and routed the Yellow Turbans.

Chen Shou's Records of the Three Kingdoms, the actual history, describes no such weapon for Liu Bei. The twin swords are a creation of the novel, but in later paintings and plays Liu Bei often appears holding two swords.
artifact.imageAlt: A Chinese double sword with its scabbard, eighteenth–nineteenth century. Two straight, double-edged swords with bronze guards and horn grips lie side by side, and at right is a single scabbard covered with sharkskin and fitted with bronze mounts.

annotations.title: Two swords
annotations.body: Two swords that go together into one scabbard. They are made so that, placed side by side, they slide in as if a single sword.

annotations.title: Guard and grip
annotations.body: A bronze guard and a grip of horn. This is a Chinese double sword of the eighteenth–nineteenth century.

annotations.title: Sharkskin scabbard
annotations.body: A scabbard covered with sharkskin and fitted with bronze mounts. In the Romance of the Three Kingdoms Liu Bei had twin swords made after swearing brotherhood with Guan Yu and Zhang Fei.

artifact.title: Eight Steeds of King Mu
artifact.power: Eight fine horses that ran a thousand li a day and carried King Mu to the far west.
artifact.firstRecord: Mu Tianzi Zhuan (Account of King Mu, Son of Heaven)
artifact.summary: The eight fine horses that drew the chariot of King Mu of Zhou. With them King Mu went to meet the Queen Mother of the West at the far western edge of the world.
artifact.story:
The Mu Tianzi Zhuan tells of King Mu of Zhou setting out on a long journey west in a chariot drawn by eight fine horses. The horses were named Chiji, Daoli, Baiyi, Yulun, Shanzi, Juhuang, Hualiu and Lu'er, and the famous charioteer Zaofu drove them.

At Mount Kunlun at the western edge of the world, King Mu met the Queen Mother of the West, queen of the immortals. The two feasted by the Jade Pool and exchanged songs, and the Queen Mother sang to him to come again.

The Mu Tianzi Zhuan was found on bamboo slips in the tomb of an old king of Wei in the late third century. The tomb was closed in the early third century BCE, so the book was written before then. The eight steeds later became a favorite subject of Chinese painting and decorative arts.
artifact.imageAlt: A blue-and-white porcelain seal-paste box fired at the Jingdezhen kilns in eighteenth-century China. Horses walking, galloping and rolling are painted in blue all around the round lid and body.

source.objectTitle: Seal paste box with eight horses

annotations.title: Walking horse
annotations.body: A horse walking with head lowered is painted in blue on the lid.

annotations.title: Galloping horse
annotations.body: On the upper part of the lid is a galloping horse. Eight horses painted around the lid and body make up a picture of the eight steeds.

annotations.title: Horses on the body
annotations.body: On the body is a horse rolling on the ground. This is an eighteenth-century blue-and-white seal-paste box from the Jingdezhen kilns. In the Mu Tianzi Zhuan, King Mu of Zhou rode in a chariot drawn by eight fine horses to the far west to meet the Queen Mother of the West.

artifact.title: Hua Tuo's Mafeisan
artifact.owner: Hua Tuo, the famous physician of the Later Han
artifact.power: Mixed with wine and drunk, it left one insensible as if drunk, so that the belly could be opened for surgery.
artifact.firstRecord: Chen Shou, Records of the Three Kingdoms, Biography of Hua Tuo
artifact.summary: The anesthetic the famous physician Hua Tuo is said to have given before surgery. Whoever drank it felt nothing, as if drunk.
artifact.story:
According to the Biography of Hua Tuo in Chen Shou's history, the Records of the Three Kingdoms, when an illness had formed inside the body that needles and medicine could not cure, Hua Tuo, a physician of the late Han, had the patient drink mafeisan mixed with wine. The patient soon became as if drunk and felt nothing, as though dead, and Hua Tuo cut open the belly, removed the diseased part, sewed it up and applied an ointment. In four or five days the pain was gone, and in a month the patient was fully healed.

In the Romance of the Three Kingdoms, Hua Tuo cuts open the arm of Guan Yu, struck by a poisoned arrow, and scrapes the poison from the bone. Guan Yu, it is said, calmly played go all the while.

While treating Cao Cao's headaches, Hua Tuo incurred his anger and died in prison. Before his death, it is said, he handed a book of his medical arts to a jailer, but when the jailer was afraid to accept it, he burned it. The formula for mafeisan was lost with it.
artifact.imageAlt: Operating on Guan Yu's Arm, a hanging scroll painted on silk by Katsushika Ōi of Japan in the 1840s. People gather around a table laid with objects as a physician operates on Guan Yu's arm, and at left an attendant holds up a tray filled with blood.

annotations.title: Tray catching the blood
annotations.body: At left an attendant holds up a tray filled with blood. In the Romance of the Three Kingdoms Hua Tuo cut open Guan Yu's arm and scraped the poison from the bone, while Guan Yu calmly played go.

annotations.title: People gathered around
annotations.body: People around the table watch the operation. This hanging scroll was painted on silk in the 1840s by Katsushika Ōi, daughter of Katsushika Hokusai.

annotations.title: The artist's signature
annotations.body: The artist's signature and seal are at lower right. The historical Biography of Hua Tuo in Chen Shou's Records of the Three Kingdoms says that Hua Tuo had patients drink mafeisan, sending them into a drunken sleep, then opened the belly for surgery.

artifact.title: Su Wu's Envoy Staff
artifact.owner: Su Wu, envoy of the Han
artifact.power: The token proving him the emperor's envoy; Su Wu never let it go for nineteen years.
artifact.firstRecord: Ban Gu, Book of Han, Biography of Su Wu
artifact.summary: The envoy's staff that Su Wu, a Han envoy captured by the Xiongnu, never let go of for nineteen years. He held it until all its tassels had fallen off.
artifact.story:
According to the Biography of Su Wu in Ban Gu's Book of Han, Emperor Wu of Han sent Su Wu as envoy to the Xiongnu in 100 BCE. But a plot within the embassy to harm the Xiongnu royal house came to light, and Su Wu was taken captive. The Xiongnu chanyu tried to make him surrender, but he never yielded.

The chanyu sent him to the shore of the Northern Sea (today's Lake Baikal) to herd rams, saying he would let him go home when the rams bore lambs. Su Wu survived by digging up the grass seeds wild rats had stored, and he herded the sheep with the Han envoy's staff as his crook. Waking or sleeping, he held the staff, until all its tassels had fallen off.

Nineteen years later, when the Han and the Xiongnu made peace, a Han envoy claimed that the emperor had shot a wild goose while hunting and found a letter from Su Wu tied to its foot, and asked for his return. At last Su Wu came home to Chang'an. Su Wu herding sheep became a model of unbending loyalty, often depicted in the painting and crafts of China and Korea.
artifact.imageAlt: A rectangular inkstone of Duan stone made in Qing-dynasty China, eighteenth–nineteenth century. The grinding surface is cut low, and within it Su Wu herding sheep is engraved in fine lines.

source.creditLine: Gift of Florence and Herbert Irving, 2015

annotations.title: Engraved picture
annotations.body: Su Wu herding sheep is engraved in fine lines on the grinding surface. Su Wu, an envoy of the Han, was captured by the Xiongnu and herded sheep for nineteen years by the Northern Sea without letting go of the Han envoy's staff.

annotations.title: Duan inkstone
annotations.body: An inkstone made of stone from Duanxi in Guangdong Province, China. It dates from the Qing dynasty, eighteenth–nineteenth century.

annotations.title: Rim
annotations.body: The grinding surface is cut low, with a raised rim left around it. Su Wu held his envoy's staff until all its tassels had fallen off.

artifact.title: Laozi's Five Thousand Characters
artifact.owner: Laozi, and Yin Xi, keeper of the pass
artifact.power: A text of some five thousand characters on the meaning of the Way and its virtue, later called the Daodejing.
artifact.firstRecord: Sima Qian, Records of the Grand Historian, Biographies of Laozi and Han Fei
artifact.summary: The text of some five thousand characters Laozi left at the pass as he departed west. It was later called the Daodejing.
artifact.story:
According to the Biographies of Laozi and Han Fei in Sima Qian's Records of the Grand Historian, Laozi was keeper of the archives of the Zhou royal court. Seeing the decline of Zhou, he left the world and headed west.

When Laozi reached the pass, Yin Xi, keeper of the pass, entreated him: 'Since you are about to withdraw from the world, I beg you, write a book for me.' Laozi wrote a work in two parts, some five thousand characters on the meaning of the Way and its virtue, and departed, and no one knew where he ended his days.

The text later came to be called the Daodejing and became the root of Daoist thought. Later tales say that Laozi rode out through the Hangu Pass on a blue ox, and the scene became a favorite subject of painting and crafts in China, Korea and Japan.
artifact.imageAlt: Laozi Crossing the Han Pass, a pale jade (nephrite) boulder carved like a mountain in eighteenth-century Qing China. On a mountain path among trees and rocks are carved Laozi riding an ox and other figures; it rests on a wooden stand.

annotations.title: Laozi on an ox
annotations.body: At the center Laozi rides along on an ox.

annotations.title: People at the pass
annotations.body: Figures stand at lower right. According to Sima Qian's Records of the Grand Historian, when Yin Xi, keeper of the Hangu Pass, asked the departing Laozi to leave a writing behind, Laozi wrote a book of some five thousand characters on the Way and its virtue and departed.

annotations.title: Jade mountain
annotations.body: A jade boulder carved like a mountain, with trees, rocks and figures. This is an eighteenth-century Qing jade mountain.

artifact.title: Sessho-seki (Killing Stone)
artifact.maker: Unknown (the dead fox turned to stone)
artifact.power: It breathed out poison that killed the birds and beasts that came near.
artifact.summary: The stone the nine-tailed fox became when it died on the plain of Nasu. It breathed out poison and killed every living thing that came near.
artifact.story:
In Japanese legend, Tamamo-no-Mae is a beautiful and learned lady who served a retired emperor at the end of the Heian period. When the retired emperor fell ill with a mysterious sickness, the yin-yang diviner Abe no Yasunari revealed that she was in truth a nine-tailed fox that had brought ruin on the royal houses of India and China.

The fox fled to the plain of Nasu in Shimotsuke, and the warriors Miura-no-suke and Kazusa-no-suke led an army there and struck it down. The dead fox became a great stone that breathed out poison and killed any bird or beast that came near. People called it Sessho-seki, the 'killing stone.'

In the Noh play Sessho-seki, the monk Gennō, passing over the plain of Nasu, meets the spirit of the fox dwelling in the stone and, through the Buddhist law, pacifies it so that it attains buddhahood. A performance of this play is recorded in 1503. Matsuo Bashō visited the place in 1689 and wrote that the stone's poison still lingered, with dead bees and butterflies lying in heaps. In 2022 the stone split in two of its own accord.
artifact.imageAlt: A surimono print by Yashima Gakutei, Japan, late 1820s: the warrior Miura-no-suke confronts the court lady Tamamo-no-Mae as she turns into a nine-tailed fox. Fox tails bloom behind the lady at left; at right a warrior with bow and arrows draws his sword. Verses fill the background.

source.creditLine: H. O. Havemeyer Collection, Bequest of Mrs. H. O. Havemeyer, 1929
source.objectTitle: The Warrior Miura-no-suke Confronting the Court Lady Tamamo-no-mae as She Turns into an Evil Fox with Nine Tails

annotations.title: Tamamo-no-Mae
annotations.body: At left the court lady Tamamo-no-Mae reveals her true nature as a nine-tailed fox. She is the fox spirit said to have bewitched the retired emperor Toba at the end of the Heian period.

annotations.title: The warrior Miura-no-suke
annotations.body: At right the warrior Miura-no-suke confronts the fox. In legend he shot down the fox after it fled to the plain of Nasu.

annotations.title: The artist's signature
annotations.body: The signature of the artist Gakutei is at lower left. The fallen fox became Sessho-seki, the stone that breathes poison, and in the Noh play Sessho-seki the monk Gennō pacified the fox's spirit dwelling in the stone.

artifact.title: Onimaru Kunitsuna
artifact.owner: Hōjō Tokimasa, later several warlords and the Japanese imperial household
artifact.power: When its rust was polished away, it toppled over by itself and cut down the little demon tormenting its master.
artifact.summary: A tachi forged by the Kamakura-period swordsmith Kunitsuna. When its rust was polished away, it fell over by itself and cut down a demon.
artifact.story:
According to the Taiheiki, Hōjō Tokimasa, the first regent of the Kamakura shogunate, fell ill, tormented every night by a little demon that appeared in his dreams. One day an old man appeared to him in a dream and said that he was the sword of Kunitsuna, so rusted that he could not leave his scabbard, and asked to have his body cleaned.

When Tokimasa had the sword polished and stood it up, it fell over by itself and cut off the silver demon ornament on the stand of the brazier beside it. From then on Tokimasa's illness vanished as if washed away. For this the sword was called Onimaru, the 'demon sword.'

Onimaru is a tachi forged in the Kamakura period by Kunitsuna, a swordsmith of Awataguchi in Kyoto. After the fall of the Hōjō it passed through the hands of many warlords. Today it is kept by the Japanese imperial household.
artifact.imageAlt: A mounting for a slung sword (itomaki-tachi koshirae) from Edo-period Japan, seventeenth–nineteenth century. The hilt and the upper scabbard are wrapped in silk braid, and the long scabbard, lacquered gold with round crests, carries hanging cords and crest-engraved fittings.

source.creditLine: Gift of Rosemarie and Leighton R. Longhi, in honor of John Carpenter, 2023
source.objectTitle: Mounting for a Slung Sword (Itomaki-tachi Koshirae) with Storage Box

annotations.title: Braid-wrapped hilt
annotations.body: The hilt is wrapped in silk braid. Because the braid continues onto the upper scabbard, this style is called itomaki-tachi.

annotations.title: Hanging cords
annotations.body: Cords for slinging the sword from the waist, and metal fittings engraved with crests. A tachi was worn slung from the waist with its edge facing down.

annotations.title: Gold scabbard
annotations.body: A scabbard lacquered gold and painted with round crests. This is an Edo-period tachi mounting of the seventeenth–nineteenth century. According to the Taiheiki, when its rust was polished away the sword Onimaru fell over by itself and cut down the small demon ornament that had tormented Hōjō Tokimasa.

artifact.title: Umisachi's Fishhook
artifact.power: Umisachi's fishhook, which caught the fish of the sea; its loss led to the tale of the sea god's palace.
artifact.summary: The fishhook of the elder brother Umisachi, which his younger brother Hoori borrowed and lost in the sea. It was found caught in the throat of a sea bream in the sea god's palace.
artifact.story:
In the Kojiki, the elder brother Hoderi catches fish in the sea and is called Umisachi (luck of the sea), and the younger brother Hoori hunts game in the mountains and is called Yamasachi (luck of the mountains). One day the younger brother begs to exchange their tools, and Hoori goes fishing with his brother's hook, catches not a single fish and even loses the hook in the sea.

The elder brother would not forgive him, demanding only his own hook back. Even when Hoori broke up the sword he wore and made five hundred, then a thousand hooks for him, he refused them. As Hoori wept on the shore, Shiotsuchi, the god of the tides, helped him travel to the palace of Watatsumi, the sea god.

Hoori married Toyotama-hime, the sea god's daughter, and only after living there three years did he speak of the lost hook. When the sea god called all the fish together, the hook was found in the throat of a sea bream that complained something was stuck there and it could not eat. With the tide jewels the sea god gave him, Hoori made his brother submit.
artifact.imageAlt: A bone fishhook from Japan. Bone is carved into a J-shaped hook, with a barb left on the inside of the point.

source.creditLine: The Harry G. C. Packard Collection of Asian Art, Gift of Harry G. C. Packard, and Purchase, Fletcher, Rogers, Harris Brisbane Dick, and Louis V. Bell Funds, Joseph Pulitzer Bequest, and The Annenberg Fund Inc. Gift, 1975

annotations.title: Curved hook
annotations.body: A fishhook carved from bone and bent into a J shape. It comes from Japan.

annotations.title: Barb
annotations.body: A barb is carved like a hook on the inside of the point so the fish cannot slip off.

annotations.title: Head for the line
annotations.body: The fishing line was tied to the upper end. In the Kojiki Hoori borrowed his brother Umisachi's fishhook and lost it in the sea, and only in the sea god's palace did he recover it from the throat of a sea bream.

artifact.title: Izanagi's Comb
artifact.power: Lit, one of its teeth lighted the darkness; thrown, it sprouted bamboo shoots that held back his pursuers.
artifact.summary: The comb Izanagi used as he fled the land of the dead. He lit a tooth of it to see his wife, and when he threw it, bamboo shoots sprang up.
artifact.story:
In the Kojiki, Izanagi goes down to Yomi, the land of the dead, to bring back his wife Izanami, who died giving birth to the god of fire. Izanami tells him not to look at her while she consults the gods of Yomi. Tired of waiting, Izanagi breaks off one of the thick end teeth of the comb in the left side of his hair, lights it and looks inside.

In the light, Izanami's body was rotting and swarming with maggots. As Izanagi fled in terror, the hags of Yomi chased him. When he threw down the vine wreath he wore on his head, wild grapes sprang up, and when he broke off teeth of the comb in the right side of his hair and threw them, bamboo shoots sprouted. While the hags ate them, he got away.

At the border between the world of the living and the land of the dead, Izanagi drove off his pursuers by throwing three peaches, and he blocked the way with a great rock. When Izanami, on the other side of the rock, vowed to kill a thousand people of the living world each day, Izanagi answered that he would cause fifteen hundred to be born each day.
artifact.imageAlt: A half-moon-shaped comb of lacquered wood made in Japan in the mid-nineteenth century, decorated in gold, silver and red maki-e with flower-shaped roundels. Fine teeth are closely cut below the golden spine.

source.creditLine: Edward C. Moore Collection, Bequest of Edward C. Moore, 1891

annotations.title: Flower-shaped roundels
annotations.body: Flower-shaped roundels are painted in gold, silver and red on a gold ground.

annotations.title: Close-set teeth
annotations.body: Fine teeth are closely cut. In the Kojiki Izanagi, fleeing pursuers from the land of the dead, broke off teeth of the comb in his hair and threw them; they sprouted as bamboo shoots and held back those chasing him.

annotations.title: Lacquered wooden comb
annotations.body: A hair comb of lacquered wood decorated with gold powder. It was made in Japan in the mid-nineteenth century.

artifact.title: Ame-no-Habaya
artifact.maker: Unknown (bestowed by the gods of heaven)
artifact.power: A feathered arrow given with the heavenly bow; shot upward, it flew all the way to heaven and came back.
artifact.summary: The feathered arrow the gods of heaven gave Ame-no-Wakahiko. When he shot heaven's messenger with it, the arrow came back and killed him.
artifact.story:
In the Kojiki, the gods of heaven send Ame-no-Wakahiko down to rule the land on earth, giving him the heavenly bow Ame-no-Makakoyumi and the feathered arrows Ame-no-Habaya. But he marries a daughter of Ōkuninushi, the god of the land, and sends no word for eight years.

When the gods of heaven sent the pheasant Nakime to ask why, Ame-no-Wakahiko shot the pheasant dead with this arrow. The arrow pierced the pheasant's breast, flew up to heaven and fell before the god Takamimusuhi.

Takamimusuhi saw blood on the arrow and, declaring that if Ame-no-Wakahiko had evil intent he would be struck by it, hurled the arrow back down. The arrow struck Ame-no-Wakahiko in the chest as he lay asleep in the morning. The word kaeshi-ya, 'the returning arrow,' is said to come from this.
artifact.imageAlt: A Japanese steel arrowhead (yanone) of the fifteenth–sixteenth century. A groove runs down the center of the long, pointed head shaped like a willow leaf, and a slender tang extends below to fit into the shaft.

annotations.title: Pointed head
annotations.body: A long steel arrowhead pointed like a willow leaf. It dates from fifteenth–sixteenth-century Japan.

annotations.title: Central groove
annotations.body: A long groove is cut down the center of the head.

annotations.title: Tang
annotations.body: The slender tang below was driven into the arrow shaft. In the Kojiki the gods of heaven sent Ame-no-Wakahiko down to earth with a heavenly bow and the feathered arrows Ame-no-Habaya. When he shot heaven's messenger with one, it flew up to heaven, came back and killed him.

artifact.title: Yashiori Sake
artifact.power: A strong sake brewed over and over, which made the eight-headed serpent Yamata no Orochi drunk.
artifact.summary: The strong sake Susanoo had brewed again and again. It made the eight-headed serpent drunk so that he could cut it down.
artifact.story:
In the Kojiki, Susanoo, cast out of heaven, comes upon an old couple and their daughter Kushinadahime weeping by the upper reaches of the Hi River in Izumo. Every year Yamata no Orochi, a great serpent with eight heads and eight tails, came and devoured one of their daughters, and now it was the youngest's turn.

Susanoo turned Kushinadahime into a comb and put it in his hair, and had the old couple brew a strong sake, refined over and over. He had them build a fence with eight gates and set a vat at each gate, filled with sake.

When Yamata no Orochi came, it plunged each of its eight heads into a vat, drank and fell into a drunken sleep. Susanoo hacked the serpent to pieces with the Totsuka sword he wore; when he cut the tail, the blade chipped, and looking inside he found a great sword. That sword was Kusanagi-no-Tsurugi.
artifact.imageAlt: A Negoro lacquer sake bottle of the Muromachi period in Japan, late 1300s–late 1500s. A slender spout and a tall foot are attached to a body whose shoulders spread wide like a spinning top, and the red lacquer has worn away in places to show the black undercoat.

source.creditLine: Purchase from the J. H. Wade Fund

annotations.title: Narrow spout

annotations.title: Top-shaped body

annotations.body: With long use the red lacquer has worn away to show the black undercoat. In the Kojiki Susanoo set out a strong sake, brewed eight times, in eight vats, made the eight-headed serpent Yamata no Orochi drunk and then cut it down.

artifact.title: Murasamemaru
artifact.owner: Inuzuka Shino, a warrior of the Hakkenden
artifact.maker: Unknown (a treasured sword handed down in the Ashikaga shogun's house)
artifact.power: When drawn, drops of water beaded on the blade; swung, they scattered like a passing shower and could even put out fire.
artifact.firstRecord: Kyokutei Bakin, The Eight Dog Chronicles (Nansō Satomi Hakkenden)
artifact.summary: The treasured sword of Inuzuka Shino, a warrior of the Hakkenden. When drawn, water beaded on the blade, and when swung it scattered like a passing shower.
artifact.story:
In Nansō Satomi Hakkenden, the long novel Kyokutei Bakin published over twenty-eight years from 1814, Murasamemaru is a treasured sword handed down in the house of the Ashikaga shoguns of the Muromachi shogunate. When it was drawn, drops of water beaded on the blade, and when it was swung hard they scattered like a passing shower and could even put out fire. Its name means 'passing shower.'

The sword remained with the Inuzuka family, who had died in Ashikaga service, and the son, Inuzuka Shino, guarded it. But before Shino set out for Koga to present the sword to the Ashikaga, it was secretly swapped for a fake. Shino presented the fake and was branded a spy.

Shino was driven up onto the roof of the Hōryūkaku, the high tower of Koga Castle, where he grappled with Inukai Genpachi, who had come to seize him. Fighting on the roof, the two fell together into a boat on the river, and by the jewels each carried they learned that they shared the same destiny as two of the Eight Dog Warriors.
artifact.imageAlt: The Hōryūkaku from the Hakkenden, a woodblock triptych by Utagawa Kuniyoshi, Japan, 1840. Soldiers swarm up the steep tiled roof of the tall Hōryūkaku tower, two warriors grapple at the top of the roof, and an explanatory text is at upper right.

source.objectTitle: The Hōryūkaku, from Hakkenden (Tale of eight dogs)

annotations.title: Two warriors atop the roof
annotations.body: At the top of the Hōryūkaku roof, Inuzuka Shino and Inukai Genpachi grapple. Shino had come to present Murasamemaru, but because the sword had been swapped for a fake he became a hunted man.

annotations.title: Soldiers climbing the roof
annotations.body: Below on the roof, soldiers swarm up to catch Shino.

annotations.title: Explanatory text
annotations.body: The story is written in the panel at upper right. This woodblock triptych was made by Utagawa Kuniyoshi in 1840. When Murasamemaru was drawn, water beaded on its blade, and when it was swung the drops scattered like a passing shower.

artifact.title: Eight Jewels of the Hakkenden
artifact.owner: The eight warriors of the Satomi clan (the Eight Dog Warriors)
artifact.maker: Unknown (scattered from Princess Fuse's prayer beads)
artifact.power: Each bore one of eight virtues, such as benevolence, loyalty and filial piety, and they bound the eight scattered warriors together.
artifact.firstRecord: Kyokutei Bakin, The Eight Dog Chronicles (Nansō Satomi Hakkenden)
artifact.summary: Eight jewels scattered from Princess Fuse's prayer beads. A character for a virtue appeared on each, linking the eight warriors who carried them.
artifact.story:
In Nansō Satomi Hakkenden, Satomi Yoshizane, lord of Awa, besieged in his castle, says half in jest that he will give his daughter Princess Fuse to whoever brings him the head of the enemy general. His dog Yatsufusa really does bring back the enemy general's head in its jaws, and Princess Fuse, bound to keep the promise, goes with the dog deep into the mountains.

In the mountains Princess Fuse became pregnant through the dog's spirit, and in shame she took her own life. At that moment the eight large beads of the rosary she carried scattered into the sky. On each bead appeared one of the characters for the eight virtues: benevolence, righteousness, courtesy, wisdom, loyalty, faith, filial piety and brotherly duty.

The beads came to rest, one each, in eight children born in different places. These children, whose names all contained the character for 'dog,' grew up, recognized one another and gathered, becoming the Eight Dog Warriors who fought for the Satomi clan.
artifact.imageAlt: A two-panel kabuki actor print made in Japan in 1834: Arashi Rikan II as Inuzuka Shino and Nakamura Utaemon III as Inukai Genpachi in battle. Two warriors with swords grapple on a tiled roof, with the roles and story written in the panels above.

source.objectTitle: Arashi Rikan II as Inuzuka Shino Moritaka and Nakamura Utaemon III as Inukai Kenpachi Michinobu Battling (from the series The Eight Heroes of the Satomi Clan)

annotations.title: Inuzuka Shino
annotations.body: At left the actor Arashi Rikan II plays Inuzuka Shino. Each of the eight warriors of the Hakkenden carried a jewel bearing one of the eight virtues, and Shino's bore 'filial piety.'

annotations.title: Inukai Genpachi
annotations.body: At right the actor Nakamura Utaemon III plays Inukai Genpachi. On his jewel appeared 'faith.'

annotations.title: The roles described
annotations.body: The roles and story are written in the panels above. This is a kabuki actor print of 1834. The eight jewels scattered from the prayer beads of Princess Fuse of the Satomi clan.

artifact.title: Jewel from the Dragon's Neck
artifact.power: A jewel that hangs from a dragon's neck and shines in five colors.
artifact.firstRecord: The Tale of the Bamboo Cutter
artifact.summary: The dragon's jewel Princess Kaguya told her suitor, the Grand Counselor Ōtomo, to bring her. He met a storm at sea and was terrified out of his wits.
artifact.story:
In The Tale of the Bamboo Cutter, Princess Kaguya told each of five noble suitors to bring her a treasure that was hard to obtain. The task she set the Grand Counselor Ōtomo no Miyuki was a jewel that hangs from a dragon's neck and shines in five colors.

Ōtomo gave his retainers great wealth and sent them to find the jewel, but they divided the wealth among themselves and scattered. Ōtomo set out to sea in a ship himself and met a raging storm and thunder. When the helmsman said it was punishment for trying to catch a dragon, Ōtomo, terrified, begged the dragon's forgiveness.

Washed ashore at last, Ōtomo collapsed like a sick man, with both eyes swollen like plums. He cursed Princess Kaguya as a great thief who had tried to kill him, and never again went near her house.
artifact.imageAlt: A blue-and-white porcelain stem cup fired at the Jingdezhen kilns in China in the fourteenth century, during the Yuan dynasty. A scaly dragon with flying mane circles the wide, flaring cup, which stands on a tall foot.

source.objectTitle: Stem Cup with Dragon Pursuing Flaming Jewel
source.objectCulture: China, Jiangxi Province, Jingdezhen kilns, Yuan dynasty (1271–1368)

annotations.title: Dragon's head
annotations.body: The dragon's head, its mane flying. It was painted in cobalt at the Jingdezhen kilns during the Yuan dynasty.

annotations.title: Scaly body
annotations.body: The dragon's scaly body wraps around the cup. The dragon is chasing a flaming jewel, which is on the far side, not visible in this photograph.

annotations.title: Tall foot
annotations.body: A stem cup with the bowl set on a tall foot, a shape the Mongols brought into China in the fourteenth century. In The Tale of the Bamboo Cutter, Princess Kaguya told her suitor, the Grand Counselor Ōtomo, to bring her the five-colored jewel from a dragon's neck.

artifact.title: Swallow's Cowry Shell
artifact.power: A shell swallows were said to hold when laying eggs, believed to make childbirth easy.
artifact.firstRecord: The Tale of the Bamboo Cutter
artifact.summary: The swallow's shell Princess Kaguya told her suitor, the Middle Counselor Isonokami, to bring her. He fell while searching a nest and lost his life.
artifact.story:
In The Tale of the Bamboo Cutter, Princess Kaguya told the Middle Counselor Isonokami no Marotari to bring her the koyasu-gai, the easy-birth shell that swallows hold. The koyasu-gai was a cowry shell, believed to make childbirth easy.

Hearing that many swallows nested under the roof of the palace kitchen, Marotari followed a plan based on the idea that swallows bring out the shell when they lay their eggs: he was hauled up in a basket and groped in a nest. Just as he thought he had grasped something, the rope broke and he fell onto a great cauldron.

What he held in his hand was dried swallow droppings. Badly injured, Marotari sickened in shame and died, and Princess Kaguya, pitying him, sent him a poem. The tale says that the word kainashi, 'without a shell,' meaning a fruitless effort, came from this.
artifact.imageAlt: Calligraphy with Willow and Swallows, a hanging scroll written in ink on paper by the Zen monk Ikkyū in Muromachi-period Japan, fifteenth century. Behind the verse written in flowing vertical lines, willow branches and swallows painted in pale ink show through.

source.creditLine: Gift from the Collection of George Gund III

annotations.title: Ikkyū's calligraphy

annotations.title: Willow branches

annotations.title: Swallows
