In The Tale of the Bamboo Cutter, Princess Kaguya told her suitor, the Middle Counselor Isonokami, to bring her the swallow's koyasu-gai, a shell said to ensure easy childbirth. He fell while searching a swallow's nest and in the end lost his life.

artifact.title: Talhae's Whetstone and Charcoal
artifact.owner: Seok Talhae, fourth king of Silla
artifact.power: With the whetstone and charcoal he had secretly buried as evidence, he claimed another man's house as the home of his blacksmith ancestors.
artifact.summary: The whetstone and charcoal young Talhae secretly buried to take over Hogong's house. He later became the fourth king of Silla.
artifact.story:
According to the Samguk Yusa, Talhae was born from an egg laid by the queen of Yongseong, a land across the sea. The king thought the egg ill-omened and set it adrift on the sea in a chest, which came ashore at Ajinpo in Silla. When an old woman on the shore opened the chest, a handsome boy came out.

As he grew, Talhae climbed Mount Toham to look over the city and judged that a house on a hill shaped like a crescent moon was a site where one could live long. It was the house of Hogong. Talhae secretly buried a whetstone and charcoal beside the house, and the next day he went to the authorities and insisted that it was the house where his ancestors, who were blacksmiths, had lived.

When the ground was dug up, a whetstone and charcoal did indeed come out, and Talhae took the house. King Namhae recognized Talhae's cleverness and married him to his eldest daughter, and Talhae later became the fourth king of Silla. Some read the story as reflecting the arrival in Silla of people skilled in working iron.
artifact.imageAlt: A granite panel from a royal tomb of Unified Silla, late 700s–early 800s. A clothed, standing figure with a rat's head is carved in low relief on a long stone slab: the rat among the twelve animals of the zodiac.

source.creditLine: Gift of The Honorable Joseph P. Carroll and Roberta Carroll, M.D. in memory of Mr. Gregory Henderson

annotations.title: Rat's head
annotations.body: A head with a rat's face is carved at the top: the rat, first of the twelve zodiac animals.

annotations.title: Clothed body
annotations.body: A human body stands, clothed. This granite slab is from the surrounding wall of a Unified Silla royal tomb, probably one of twelve panels carved with the zodiac animals.

annotations.title: Granite panel
annotations.body: Carved in low relief in hard granite, its outlines worn with time. It probably comes from Gyeongju, the capital of Silla. In the Samguk Yusa Talhae secretly buried a whetstone and charcoal, claimed his ancestors had been blacksmiths and took Hogong's house; he later became the fourth king of Silla.

artifact.title: Geotaji's Flower Branch
artifact.maker: Unknown (the daughter of the god of the Western Sea, transformed)
artifact.power: The daughter of the god of the Western Sea, turned into a flower branch; carried home in his bosom, she became a woman again.
artifact.firstRecord: Iryeon, Samguk Yusa, “Queen Jinseong and Geotaji”
artifact.summary: The tale of Geotaji, who carried home in his bosom the daughter of the Western Sea god, turned into a flower branch. Back in Silla, he lived with her.
artifact.story:
According to the Samguk Yusa, in the reign of Queen Jinseong of Silla, the official Yangpae, on his way to Tang China as an envoy, met a storm at Gokdo island in the Western Sea. A divination said they must hold a rite at the island's sacred pond, and an old man appeared in a dream and said the wind would calm if they left one good archer on the island. Lots were drawn, and Geotaji, a soldier skilled with the bow, was left behind.

An old man came out of the pond and said that he was the god of the Western Sea, and that every day at sunrise a young monk came down from the sky, chanted spells and ate the livers of his family. The next day Geotaji shot the monk with an arrow, and the monk turned into an old fox and died.

In gratitude the old man gave Geotaji his daughter as his wife. He changed her into a flower branch and placed it in Geotaji's bosom, and had two dragons escort the envoy's ship all the way to Tang. When Geotaji returned to Silla and took the flower branch from his bosom, it became a woman again, and the two lived together.
artifact.imageAlt: An inlaid celadon bottle of the Goryeo dynasty, thirteenth–fourteenth century. A small loop is attached to the long, slender neck, and white wild chrysanthemums are inlaid on the pear-shaped body. The broken mouth was repaired with gold lacquer.

annotations.title: White wild chrysanthemums
annotations.body: White wild chrysanthemums are inlaid on the body: three stems branch from one root and bear small white flowers.

annotations.title: Long neck and loop
annotations.body: A small loop is attached to the long neck. This is an inlaid celadon bottle of the Goryeo dynasty, thirteenth–fourteenth century.

annotations.title: Mouth mended with gold
annotations.body: The broken mouth was mended with gold lacquer. In the Samguk Yusa the archer Geotaji shot dead the old fox tormenting the god of the Western Sea and came home with the god's daughter, changed into a flower branch, in his bosom.

artifact.title: Peony Painting Without Fragrance
artifact.owner: King Jinpyeong of Silla and Princess Deokman (later Queen Seondeok)
artifact.power: Seeing no butterflies in the painting, she guessed that the flowers had no scent.
artifact.summary: A painting and seeds of peonies sent to Silla from Tang China. Princess Deokman guessed that, with no butterflies in the painting, the flowers had no fragrance.
artifact.story:
According to Kim Bu-sik's Samguk Sagi, in the reign of King Jinpyeong of Silla, a painting of peonies and peony seeds were sent from Tang China. The Samguk Yusa adds that Emperor Taizong of Tang sent a painting of peonies in three colors, red, purple and white, with three measures of seed.

Seeing the painting, Princess Deokman said that the flowers were beautiful but surely had no fragrance, for there were no bees or butterflies in the picture. When the seeds were planted and the flowers bloomed, they indeed had no scent.

Deokman later became Queen Seondeok, Silla's first reigning queen. The Samguk Yusa counts this as one of three things the queen foresaw, and says she also saw through Taizong's meaning: a jibe at her for having no mate.
artifact.imageAlt: An eight-panel folding screen of peonies painted on silk in Korea in the early 1900s. On every panel, red, pink, yellow and blue peonies bloom in layers on luxuriant branches.

source.creditLine: Gift of The Honorable Joseph P. Carroll, KM, and Roberta Carroll, M.D.
source.objectCulture: Korea, Joseon dynasty (1392−1910) or Japanese colonial period (1910−1945)

annotations.title: Eight-panel screen
annotations.body: A folding screen filled with peonies across eight panels. It is a Korean painting of the early 1900s, probably set up for joyful occasions such as weddings.

annotations.title: Layered peony blossoms
annotations.body: Red, pink, yellow and blue peonies bloom in layers. The peony is the flower of wealth and honor.

annotations.title: Peony painting
annotations.body: In the Samguk Sagi, when Tang China sent Silla a painting and seeds of peonies, Princess Deokman (later Queen Seondeok) guessed that, since there were no butterflies in the painting, the flowers had no fragrance. When the seeds were planted, the flowers indeed had no scent.

artifact.title: Wonhyo's Muae Gourd
artifact.maker: Wonhyo (modeled on an entertainer's large gourd)
artifact.power: Dancing and singing with it, he taught even the poor and small children the name of the Buddha.
artifact.summary: The instrument Wonhyo made in the shape of an entertainer's great gourd. Carrying it, he danced and sang and spread the Buddha's teaching from village to village.
artifact.story:
According to 'Wonhyo Unbound' in the Samguk Yusa, after Wonhyo fathered Seol Chong with Princess Yoseok, he declared that he had broken his vows, put off his monk's robes and called himself Soseong Geosa, the Layman of Little Surname. By chance he came upon a large gourd that entertainers played with, strange in shape.

Wonhyo made an instrument in its shape and named it Muae, 'unhindered,' after a line of the Flower Garland Sutra: 'A person unhindered by anything passes out of birth and death by a single path.' Then he made up a song and spread it through the world.

Carrying the Muae, Wonhyo went singing and dancing through a thousand villages and ten thousand hamlets. Thanks to him, it is said, even the poor and small children all came to know the name of the Buddha and to chant 'Namu Amitabul.' The dance performed with the Muae lived on as the Muaemu dance of the Goryeo court.
artifact.imageAlt: A bronze gourd-shaped bottle made in Goryeo in the twelfth century. A narrow spout rises long above a body that swells in two lobes, upper and lower, and the surface is covered with green corrosion.

annotations.title: Narrow spout
annotations.body: A narrow spout rising long above.

annotations.title: Gourd shape
annotations.body: The body swells in two lobes, upper and lower, like a gourd. This bronze bottle was made in Goryeo in the twelfth century; the Goryeo aristocracy used such vessels as they enjoyed tea and wine.

annotations.title: Green corrosion
annotations.body: Green corrosion has formed on the bronze surface. According to the Samguk Yusa, Wonhyo saw a great gourd that entertainers played with, made an instrument in its shape, named it Muae, and spread the Buddha's teaching from village to village, dancing and singing.

artifact.title: Seonmyo's Floating Rock
artifact.owner: Uisang, monk of Silla, and Seonmyo, a woman of Tang
artifact.power: A great rock that Seonmyo became; it rose into the air and drove off the band that stood in Uisang's way.
artifact.firstRecord: Zanning, Song Biographies of Eminent Monks, “Biography of Uisang”
artifact.summary: The rock into which Seonmyo, a Tang woman who loved Uisang, transformed. Floating in the air, it won Uisang the site for his temple, which came to be called Buseoksa.
artifact.story:
According to the Biography of Uisang in the Song Biographies of Eminent Monks, compiled by the Song monk Zanning, the Silla monk Uisang went to study in Tang China and stayed at the house of a lay believer in Dengzhou. Seonmyo, the daughter of the house, fell in love with Uisang, but seeing his firm resolve she vowed to help him forever.

When Uisang finished his studies and boarded a ship home to Silla, Seonmyo, learning of it too late, threw herself into the sea and became a dragon. The dragon guarded Uisang's ship so that he crossed safely to Silla.

When Uisang sought to build a temple at the foot of Mount Taebaek, another band who held the land blocked his way. Then Seonmyo turned into a huge rock a li square and hung in the air above the temple site as if about to fall, and the band scattered in fright. For this the temple was named Buseoksa, the 'Temple of the Floating Rock,' it is said. Even today a great rock carved with the characters for 'floating rock' stands west of Muryangsujeon hall at Buseoksa.
artifact.imageAlt: Orchids and Rocks, an eight-panel folding screen painted in ink on silk by Yi Ha-eung (the Heungseon Daewongun) in 1897–98. On every panel long, slender orchid leaves sweep vigorously around rocks drawn in ink, and some panels bear inscriptions and seals.

source.objectCulture: Korea, Joseon dynasty (1392–1910), Korean Empire period (1897–1910)

annotations.title: Rocks
annotations.body: Rocks drawn in ink rise among the orchids.

annotations.title: Orchids
annotations.body: Long, slender orchid leaves are drawn with vigorous strokes. Yi Ha-eung, the Heungseon Daewongun, was famous for his orchid paintings.

annotations.title: Eight-panel screen
annotations.body: An eight-panel screen painted in ink on silk by Yi Ha-eung in 1897–98. The Song Biographies of Eminent Monks tells that when Uisang founded Buseoksa, Seonmyo, who had loved him, turned into a great rock, rose into the air to guard the temple site and drove off the band who opposed him.

artifact.title: Seodong's Gold
artifact.owner: Seodong (later King Mu of Baekje) and Princess Seonhwa
artifact.power: Gold piled like clods of earth where he dug yams, carried to the Silla palace in a single night.
artifact.summary: The gold that Seodong, a yam digger, had heaped up like clods of earth. When Princess Seonhwa told him it was treasure, he sent it to the Silla palace.
artifact.story:
According to 'King Mu' in the Samguk Yusa, Seodong of Baekje was a poor young man who lived by digging and selling yams. Hearing that Princess Seonhwa, third daughter of King Jinpyeong of Silla, was beautiful, he went to the Silla capital and had the children sing a song in exchange for yams. When the 'Song of Seodong,' which said that Princess Seonhwa was secretly meeting Seodong, spread, the princess was driven from the palace, and Seodong took her in and went with her to Baekje.

When the princess brought out the gold her mother had given her to set up their household, Seodong laughed aloud and asked what it was. In the place where he dug yams, he said, such things were heaped up like clods of earth. The princess told him that it was the greatest treasure under heaven.

The two gathered the gold and went to the Dharma master Jimyeong of Saja Temple on Mount Yonghwa, who by his supernatural power carried the gold to the Silla palace in a single night. King Jinpyeong marveled at this and sent word asking after Seodong, and through this Seodong won the people's hearts and became King Mu of Baekje. King Mu and his queen later founded Mireuksa temple in Iksan, it is said.

annotations.title: Amethyst and rock crystal
annotations.body: The purple comma-shaped jewels on either side are amethyst, and the faceted beads around them are rock crystal. This is an eighth-century Unified Silla necklace. In the Samguk Yusa, Seodong the yam digger had heaped up gold like clods of earth; when Princess Seonhwa told him it was treasure, he sent it to the Silla palace in a single night with the help of the Dharma master Jimyeong.

artifact.title: Cauldron of King Daemusin
artifact.power: Without any fire, it grew hot by itself and cooked enough rice to fill the whole army.
artifact.summary: The cauldron King Daemusin of Goguryeo found on his way to attack Buyeo. Without any fire it grew hot by itself and fed the whole army.
artifact.story:
According to Kim Bu-sik's Samguk Sagi, in the winter of the fourth year of his reign (21 CE), King Daemusin of Goguryeo led his army out to attack Buyeo. When he reached the banks of the Biryu River, he saw what looked like a woman at the water's edge playing with a cauldron. When he went to look, the woman was gone and only the cauldron remained.

When he had rice cooked in the cauldron, it grew hot by itself without any fire, and it cooked enough to fill the whole army. Then a strong man appeared and said the cauldron belonged to his family and that his sister had lost it, and he asked to follow the king. The king gave him the surname Bujeong, 'cauldron carrier.'

On the march the king also found a gold seal and weapons and gathered warriors such as Goeyu and Maro. The next year the Goguryeo army attacked Buyeo, and in that battle King Daeso of Buyeo died at Goeyu's hand.

artifact.title: Jakjegeon's Willow Staff
artifact.owner: Jakjegeon, grandfather of Wang Geon, founder of Goryeo
artifact.maker: Unknown (brought from the palace of the Dragon King of the Western Sea)
artifact.power: The willow staff and pig the dragon maiden had him ask for instead of seven treasures; they led him to the site where the Goryeo royal house would rise.
artifact.firstRecord: Goryeosa, “Genealogy of the Goryeo Royal House”
artifact.summary: The willow staff and pig Jakjegeon received along with the seven treasures after helping the Dragon King of the Western Sea. He became the ancestor of the Goryeo royal house.
artifact.story:
According to the 'Genealogy of the Goryeo Royal House' in the Goryeosa, Jakjegeon was the son of a Tang nobleman. Sailing to Tang to find his father, he met a raging sea in the Western Sea. A divination said that one man of Goryeo must be put ashore, and Jakjegeon stayed on an island with his bow and arrows.

The Dragon King of the Western Sea appeared and asked for his help: an old fox came in the guise of a Buddha and chanted scripture, giving him headaches he could not bear. When Jakjegeon shot the fox dead, the Dragon King welcomed him into his palace and gave him the seven treasures. The Dragon King's daughter told him to ask for a willow staff and a pig rather than the seven treasures.

Jakjegeon married the dragon maiden and returned with the willow staff and the pig. When the pig went and lay down at the southern foot of Mount Songak, he built a house there, and the spot later became Gaegyeong, the capital of Goryeo, it is said. Jakjegeon's grandson was Wang Geon, King Taejo, who founded Goryeo.

annotations.title: Long spout

artifact.title: The Rabbit's Liver
artifact.owner: The daughter of the Dragon King of the Eastern Sea
artifact.power: The one medicine that could cure the Dragon King's daughter of her illness.
artifact.firstRecord: Kim Bu-sik, Samguk Sagi, “Biography of Kim Yu-sin”
artifact.summary: The rabbit's liver sought as medicine for the Dragon King's daughter. The rabbit tricked the turtle by saying he had left his liver on land, and returned alive.
artifact.story:
According to the 'Biography of Kim Yu-sin' in the Samguk Sagi, in 642 Kim Chunchu of Silla went to Goguryeo to ask for troops and was imprisoned there, and Seon Do-hae, a Goguryeo official, plied him with wine and told him an old tale. The daughter of the Dragon King of the Eastern Sea suffered from a heart ailment, and a physician said she would be cured only if a rabbit's liver were obtained for her medicine.

There were no rabbits in the sea. A turtle went up onto land and lured a rabbit, telling it of an island in the middle of the sea with clear springs and fine grass, and carried it on its back into the sea. When they reached the middle of the sea, the turtle confessed that the Dragon King's daughter in fact needed the rabbit's liver.

The rabbit said that, being descended from spirits, he had taken out his liver, washed it and left it on a rock, and that he would fetch it. When the turtle carried the rabbit back and set him down on the shore, the rabbit leaped into the grass and mocked it: who could live without a liver? Kim Chunchu understood the meaning of the tale, devised a ruse and was released. The story lived on in the pansori Sugungga and the novel The Tale of the Rabbit.

annotations.title: Pair of openwork ornaments
annotations.body: A pair of bronze ornaments with herons and turtles pierced among scrolling vines. They date from twelfth-century Goryeo, and traces of fiber on the back suggest they were sewn onto cloth. In a tale in the Samguk Sagi's 'Biography of Kim Yu-sin,' the rabbit tricked the turtle, saying he had left on land the liver that would cure the Dragon King's daughter, and returned alive.

artifact.title: Stone Chest of Tamna
artifact.owner: The three divine men of Tamna: Yang-eulna, Go-eulna and Bu-eulna
artifact.maker: Unknown (sent from a land across the sea)
artifact.power: A chest that came across the sea; three maidens, foals, calves and the seeds of the five grains came out of it, and Tamna began.
artifact.summary: The chest that drifted across the sea to the three divine men of Tamna. From a stone chest inside came three maidens, foals, calves and the seeds of the five grains.
artifact.story:
According to the tale of Tamna in the 'Treatise on Geography' of the Goryeosa, in the most ancient times there were no people on this island. From an opening in the ground called Moheunghyeol, on the northern slope of Mount Halla, three divine men rose up: the eldest Yang-eulna, the second Go-eulna and the third Bu-eulna. The three lived by hunting, wearing hides and eating meat.

One day a wooden chest sealed with purple clay drifted ashore on the eastern coast. When they opened it, inside was another chest, of stone, and an envoy in a red sash and purple robes had come with it. When they opened the stone chest, out came three maidens in blue robes, with foals, calves and the seeds of the five grains.

The envoy said that the king of his country, hearing that three sons of the gods had descended on a mountain in the western sea and wished to found a country but had no wives, had sent his three daughters. The Goryeosa names this country Japan, while later Jeju records call it Byeongnang. The three divine men married the maidens, divided the land, planted the five grains and raised horses and cattle.
